I really like Perfect Golf. It has the look and feel of the PGA Championship PC game that I used to play, but Perfect Golf has the advantage of a strong and growing on-line capability thanks to STEAM. I have just several minor complaints about the game.
First, I wish that the wind was more of a factor in the game to make players think a little more about how to shape shots. Clever  players could then hit fades and draws on purpose to hold the ball against the wind, or use the wind more to move around dogleg corners depending on the situation.
Second, I don't believe that players are penalized enough when hitting into or out of the trees. I have seen many shots go right through the trees like they were thin air, when in real golf the tree limbs or leaves would have knocked the ball down. Fairway bunker shots also seem a little too easy compared to real golf.
Lastly, I suspect that some of the players out there that are using the Motion Plus method to swing the club are using a track or some other kind of aid to move their mouse perfectly each time. It's too much of a coincidence that they have the same shot shape everytime, especially when consistently hitting it with over 100% power. That creates an unfair advantage over those players who use the tri-click method. I recommend that you allow just the tri-click method for on-line play to guarantee that no player has an advantage over any other.

Irrational Games and Looking Glass Studios were really hitting their stride in the late 1990s when it came to first person games. In the last two years of the 1990s, they redefined the stealth genre and came up with this lovely FPS-RPG hybrid, the sequel to System Shock. Featuring two really creepy antagonists, a wealth of mechanics, and the freedom to play how you want, it was hailed as a game that defied genre classification and considered to be quite ahead of its time. It's not without its flaws, however. It turns blisteringly hard towards the end if you don't develop your character strictly within one class and it doesn't quite send the message that you need to conserve your ammo. This new release by Night Dive Studios allows the game to run on modern computers and it keeps mod functionality as well. If you like first person roleplaying games, there has never been a better time than now to discover or relive this classic. That's how much I ♥♥♥♥ing love this game, now buy it.

My specs:
4ghz i7 4790k
16gb ram
Windows 10 64bit
GTX 970 4gb (well, 3.5gb...)

So i like this game. I'm not great at it.
There is a simple learning curve per god.
Each class doesn't neccecarially feel like a class.
Most gods don't feel all powerful when you play them. However there is something satisfying when you are shooting down a god with a harp looking bow while flying and wearing daiper (Cupid).
This game, despite being Pay for extra parts, gives you everything that you need upfront. Great tutorial, plenty of starting gods to practice with. Free god rotation every week. If you do well you'll gain favor to purchase new gods.
If you log in everyday you'll get more favor and eventually Gems (you can also buy gems for too damn much money).
The currency system to buy new/more stuff works like this.  You can get 1,100 favor a week just by logging in for the first 5 days. After that you get 50 gems for the last two days of the week.  Purchasing a new god using favor will cost 5,500 or 200 gems.  In theory you're playing the game. So you could buy a new god every month.  If you win a match of that map style for the first time that day you get bonus 100 favor. 5 different matches mean you could get lucky and get all of those as wins every day and end up with a new god by the end of the week.
But that's a lot of time to dedicate to it too.  Matches are at least 10 mins before either team can surrender to about an hour for some of the longer matches I've been in.
There are multiple match styles and a different MOTD (match of the day).  There is a 4v4 mode with two lanes. 5v5 with three lanes and a 5v5 with a split jungle/ lane map. A single 5v5 lane map.  you can play by yourself against computers for practice, with humans as a collective team against a team of computers for more advanced practice and ful on humans vs. humans.
----PROS:
- Lots of fun
-FREE unless you wanna pay for all the gods/skins upfront, but I feel that playing for it makes for a better player instead of paying for it.
-plenty of challenge against RANKED and EXPERIENCED players
-----CONS
- I've run into a bit of toxic community, but only seldom.  it's rare, but it happens.  (3 times in about 100 hours?)
- you can get easily discouraged if your team isn't all there, physically or mentally.
-I think that's it. I'm drawing a blank for anything else.
All in all I'd say this is a cotton candy meal out of 10.  It's great to eat it as a meal, it's substantial AND filling.  If you do it for too long you're going to hurt yourself with some cavitites.  (so like an 8.5/10!)

Wow, what a game. I have been playing this since release (for about 4 weeks) and I just completed it. Now, this game has had review scores all over the place. Now my guess is because this is NOT a game for everyone. If you like run-and-gun games like Call of Duty then this game isn't for you. If you however likes games where you have to sneak around and be stealthy then you should definitely consider this game.
The game takes place about 15 years after the events in the first Alien movie and is set on the space station Sevastopol where Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley, comes in search of a flight recorder from the Nostromo. She quickly realizes that something has gone very wrong on this space station. I wont say anything more than that.
One of the main bulletpoints in this game is that there is an non-scripted Alien onboard the station. This means that when you die (and you will die, a lot) the Alien won't do the same thing again. It will show up somewhere else so you have to constantly on your toes. Now I have played and completed this game on Hard so my opinion is based on that experience. In any case, this game demands that you take it slow and methodical while traversing it. You can definitely not run and mostly not even walk if you want to survive. I wouldn't even recommend using the Motion Tracker because in my experience it draws the Alien to you like flies to♥♥♥♥♥♥ You can with great accuracy track the Alien just by sound. The Alien is drawn to every sound you make like opening doors, banging in to stuff and so forth so you have to mind your surroundings.
As I said I have played this game for a better part of 4 weeks. Why so long? Well, being a family man I just have so much time to play which comes down to about 1 - 2 hours per day but even if I had unlimited time to play I still wouldn't be able to muster more than about 90 minutes per session. The reason being that the game is so goddamn intense and I get so exhausted playing it that I wouldn't be able to concentrate longer than that. There are very few games that has drained me so much but in this case I think it is a compliment to the game. It means that it is getting the desired effect out of me. If you play this game in lenghtier sections and quicker than I did then you will probably find the game a bit repetetive. However, the game is pretty varied so it shouldn't be a deterrent.
Now, I am an avid watcher of horror movies. I have seen a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of horror movies and in 95% cases they don't scare me at all. This game however has had me on my seat almost through the whole duration. There have been instances where I feelt like I would♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants almost. This game has also had the effect where whenever I am about to play it I have had a big knot in my stomach and feeling a lot of anxiety, which is also a compliment to this game.
Also, this game is looong. It has a slow start and doesnt start to get going until after 4 - 5 hours so if you find it a bit boring in the beginning, hang in there because it will become much better. It took me about 22 hours to complete it but I tried to explore as much as possible and get every thing that got in my way. To pick up everything in this game you have to backtrack at some point, I didn't do it but I plan on doing it because I want all the logs and ID-tags.
Creative Assembly really put a lot of love and detail to this game. You really feel like you are in the Alien Universe and there a lot of fan service. To sum it up, this game is probably my Game of the Year this year. I really enjoyed it and I am gonna play through all DLCs and what not. If you like Stealth/Horror-games and like the first Alien movie, BUY IT!
Edit: I also hope that Creative Assembly get to do an ALIENS game because that would be awesome!

I wasn't really sure what to expect from Isolation. I was intrigued by pre-release information about the game, but a little nervous about its quality. I have no great love for Alien lore (in fact, I've never seen the original movie), so my purchase of the game had nothing to do with Alien fan service. I do, however, have long-standing love affairs with sci-fi  and atmospheric games, and those interests are what led me to pick up Isolation. I have not been disappointed.
Technically, the game is very, very impressive. It looks phenomenal on Ultra settings, and it runs perfectly on my rig (2x 7870 Crossfire, FX-6300 at 4.2, 8 GB RAM). This is the first game I've seen so far that actually looks "next gen." The sound is also fantastic--a fact that comes in handy as you track that pesky killing machine through the vents and hallways of the space station. Seriously, this game deserves to be played with a good gaming headset. If you don't have one yet, go buy one for Isolation. It's worth it.
But who cares about technical stuff, right? Isolation is about getting so scared that you pee yourself a little, and it doesn't disappoint. This is hands down the most stressful game I've ever had the pleasure (?) of playing. It blows Dead Space out of the water in the horror department (yes, even DS 1 and 2), and the game's atmosphere rivals titans like Bioshock and Deus Ex. The space station easily stands next to Rapture, Columbia, and the USG Ishimura, and in many ways I think it surpasses them. Yes, the atmosphere is that good.
In other news, the alien is suitably horrifying (and horrifyingly unpredictable), the pacing is great, and the old-school, manual-save-only structure really helps build the tension. The game is hard, but not in an unfair way. Your first real encounter with the Alien is brutal, but it adds to the game's theme. It also forcibly trains you to save, save, save your game every time you can, teaches you to hide like a frightened puppy at the slightest sound, and conditions you to watch your motion sensor like a terrified hawk--but not for too long, lest the beeps give away your position. There were some times that the game frustrated me, but in retrospect my poor outcomes were my fault, not the game's. Isolation forces you to play smart or die. It's as simple as that.
I should also mention that I very much enjoyed the Metroid-style gadget game, wherein your increasingly sophisticated tools allow you to access previously inaccessible areas as the game progresses. The crafting feels fun without being cumbersome, and the gadgets and weapons all feel useful only if they are applied smartly in the right context--just how a survival horror game's inventory should be.
In truth, I find it very difficult to find something to complain about in Isolation. There are some glitches that see you hitting nearby objects (and thereby alerting the Alien) while hiding under tables, but this is mostly a small issue. I've also  seen a few complaints about the game being too long, but  I'm still having a blast at 15 hours--and I'm nowhere near the end as far as I can tell. Needless to say, there is plenty of content to justify a purchase. And given how superb Isolation is, I find it hard to believe that I'm ever going to think there's too much of it. I suppose I could also complain that neither your character nor your enemies cast shadows (they are all vampires, apparently), but that is such a tiny nit that it's easily eclipsed by the game's otherwise amazing lighting system.
All told, Isolation is the best sci-fi survival horror game I've ever played. Yes, better than Dead Space. Yes, better than System Shock. It may even be the best survival horror game I've ever played, period. Whether you like Alien lore, sci-fi, atmospheric games, or horror, Isolation is your game. If any of those things sound good to you, buy the game. You'll love it.

The Alien Game we all deserved! There's a time and place for M41A Pulse Rifles and M56 Smartguns - this isn't it. The Alien  is presented the way it was way back in 1979 - terrifying, lethal, unstoppable. That's right, while there are weapons within the game, don't for a second think that you can take out the sole Alien with any of them. If it sees you? You die. If you run? You die. If you make a noise? You die.
Every action in this game is risk vs reward - even saving the game makes you think "am i safe enough? How is my inventory? Where did i last save if i get killed mid-save?". Lockers & Cabinets become close friends. You'll find yourself in a puddle of your own urine, under a hospital gurney, not 3 hours into the epic that unfolds. And you'll love every minute of it.
The Art direction is stunning - environments lifted straight out of Ron Cobb's sketchbooks and they look jaw-droppingly gorgeous. You don't even need a particularly powerful PC to turn everything up high, and maintain 60fps either.
However, the thing that makes this quite possibly the best horror game ever, is the sound. Well, the Sound and the AI.
There's no soundtrack as such, in game, its mostly ambient, with a few cues lifted straight from Alien, and some expanded themes that give the in-game universe it's rich, immersive feeling. The game engine knows when you're in peril and ramps up the strings section accordingly, adding to the tension.
As for the AI - while there are a few scripted sequences, the Alien is entirely random - no playthrough will ever be the same, not even loading the game will yield the same result. It hunts for you. It will stop at nothing to find you. Use a noisemaker one too many times and it'll wise up and ignore it for a while. You have to keep changing tactics, you cannot just blaze through and think that a distraction will work. Toss a flare? Sure, first few times, it'll be interested. Then it becomes interested in who threw that flare. At which point, you'll crap yourself and find your head being pierced like a capri sun.
I cannot recommend this game enough, i really can't. If Creative Assembly don't win a slew of awards for this game, i will be very, very surprised!

Quick analysis:
Story: 2/10
Senia goes into the Tower of Eternity to save her sister Magaleta. That's literally it.
No memorable villains/side characters.
Gameplay: 4/10
Battle is a barebones YS Origins styled combat with some skills.
Said skills are a Front Line teleport hit (up to 8 tiles), 3x2 Front AoE, 9 tile front piercing ranged attack, All Around Point Blank AoE - the only one with a cooldown and massive damage.
Skills use MP (20, 20, 10, 40, not listed in game) and you can use SP (gained from killing enemies ogether with EXP) to improve them.
Leveling system is as basic as it gets. Level Up = More stats.
The crafting system is really simple and does not vary between the whole 4 dungeons.
For each armor piece and your weapon, you can craft 4 tiers of gear per dungeon.
You collect the base materials from the dungeon enemies, which enables the first 2 tiers.
An extra material from the midboss in each dungeon for the tier 3 gear, and the last material from the "King" version of common enemies, for the final piece of gear for the dungeon.
Each tier needs the item from the last one.
Dungeon design is pretty linear with small puzzles and some skill usage here and there. There are only around 12 rooms in the whole game that are optional. At the end of each dungeon, there are some NPCs with rewards for # kill for each enemy type, getting all chests, and crafting all tier 4 gear.
Items are there just for crafting or for a small stat boost, limited per dungeon. There is no currency.
There are multiple endings, but they aren't missable. You can get to all of them from the last save point.
Save points are also pretty abundant, and most dub as warp points too.
It's worth noting that most enemies don't attack at all, or even do great damage on contact, making this game way too easy. Even bosses are hard pressed to be a challenge. Even in hard mode (you can choose whether the boss will be easy, regular or hard before each fight. Difficulty only modifies enemy stats).
I didn't die even once, even fighting all bosses on hard mode, with no external aid/guides etc.
Music / Sound FX: 6/10
Pleasant but short music tracks. Some of them are really misplaced in some scenes though.
They are also very cool and you may find yourself humming them in your head :)
Sound effects are pretty good.
Graphics: 8/10
Great sprites, decent UI even if lacking some info, overall great assets in dungeons.
Overall: 9/10

Rome 2: Total War, with an OVERHAUL MOD (remember this) like Divide et Impera is a very fun game. I'd say it's around the same level as Rome 1, when taken as standalone games.
It suffers from the same general AI issues (siege AI can be frustratingly bad at times and pathfinding tends to be buggy), but it succeeds in trying to refine the Total War formula with new takes on city and army management. The bugs have almost entirely disappeared since launch, and the number of new factions is a welcome addition.
The problem comes in when the game is compared to its predecessor, Rome 1. Rome 2 simply doesn't improve enough to justify a full-price purchase. The game is very pretty and a lot of the campaign map mechanics have been refined and improved, but it does not feel like a distinct improvement on the first game, when taken as a whole.
Would I say Rome 2 is an enjoyable and good game? Certainly.
Would I tell you to get the vastly cheaper ROME 1 any day of the week? Yup.
VERDICT: 8/10, but just get Rome 1. Like, that's how good Rome 1 is.

In a few words, Total War: Rome 2 is, overall, a solid game.
*Purchasing the game during the Winter sale, I did not experience the major issues which plagued the launch of this game.*
Campaign is as a Total War game usually is. Its hugely enjoyable to conquer and ally with adjacent factions. I would therefore recommend it. However, there are some issues. Playing on 'Normal' mode during an entire Sparta playthrough, the campaign ai very rarely besieged any of my cities, if at all. Also, beyond maybe the 50th turn or so, if you have managed your cities to a reasonable standard, you will start to steamroll the other factions. Its far from game ruining to easily destroy factions & armies late game but if perhaps one or two other factions grew like I did, a hugely interesting war might have broken out.
Another grievance that I have is that defeated ai armies -which survive huge defeats with only a few men- return the very next turn with full stack mercenary armies. This often leads to the death of your previously victorious, but wounded, army in the city/lands that you just won. Especially during the early stages of a campaign. Again, not game ruining but these incidents put your faction and progress back considerably, as rebuilding takes time and money.
The game does look stunning though in my opinion. And the variety of units are generally well balanced. Cavalry beats swords, spears beats cavalry etc.
To conclude, Rome 2 is a good buy and a game that will keep you entertained for many hours. I would however reccomend that you purchase the game during a Steam Sale, like I did. This way, you can purchase the base game & all of the (ludicrous) DLC for around £40.
I do have some things that I feel should be addressed. Namely:
* Most ***PAID*** factions could do with having their rosters expanded. I paid good money to use them. Why should I be limited to how I can use their tools?
* Bring in the option to manually enter in a amount of $$ that is offered during negotiations. What if I dont want to offer $2000? Especially when $200 would do the trick.
* Siege path finding can be an issue at times. Notably when units are on walls.

At first glance, Hurtworld appears to be another cheap addition to Steam's already massive collection of Early Access survival games. Initially, I didn't pay it much mind, assuming that it would be quickly abandoned, like many other similar titles. However, after watching a few gameplay videos, Hurtworld caught my interest.
While I'll agree that Hurtworld's lack of originality is somewhat offputting, I believe it is fair to say that it is borrowing from the right places. It plays very similarly to Rust, another great survival game, but with tighter controls and combat mechanics. To put it simply, it feels like a refined first person shooter with major survival elements, whereas games like Rust are focused primarily on survival with the addition of slightly loose gun-based combat.
Aesthetically, Hurtworld is a decent looking game, though I can't say I'm a particularly big fan of the game's graphical style. The simplified art works wonders for optimization, putting it miles ahead of many Early Access survival titles in that regard. There is no music to be found, however, there are plenty of sound effects, most of which are crunchy and satisfying.
If you didn't already see this coming, I legitimately feel that Hurtworld is a diamond in the rough. While the game has not been in development for very long, and has its fair share of bugs and issues, there is plenty of fun to be had. If you are a fan of survival games and do not mind the Early Access program, I would certainly recommend picking up Hurtworld.

Honestly this game is in the very early access stages, and I can't stress that enough. I am saying it’s purely an alpha build of a concept, and the concept is very much unfinished. I will list below what you can do currently in this game...
If you don't like to read you can stop here. However if you want to make an informed purchase, you might just save yourself some money by spending 10 minutes to read an honest, informative review.
Before I go into that though, if you are playing alone I highly doubt you will find this game fun or interesting enough to stick with it for more than a few hours. Half of the fun is meeting people, joining up and working together. It is probably the social interaction that keeps people playing this game long term.
Now for the list of what this game currently offers the player:
1-Farm natural resources; shrubs, trees, wild gain provide the essentials to survive in this game. The primary food to stay alive is limited to Oranges and Steaks found on wild animals. Resources for building don't go far. Most likely intend and this is where you will spend 90% of your time.
2-Mine for resources from various rock formations that randomly spawn on the map
3-Harvest resources mainly wood or related material from fallen branches or trunks. Trees are around but you cannot harvest resources from them.
4-Explore a map that is rather large in size, but it as empty as it is large
5-Contruct buildings using Wood, Rock and Steel. The buildings are crafted piece by piece so you must create the walls, the floors, the ceilings and the doors. Nothing is prefabricated and there are no easy plans to learn to make the process quicker. You will spend about 5-10% of your total time building bases and fortifying them, unfortunately because resources are a major limiting factor unless you father enough you won’t be able to complete large projects all at once.
6- Play with other people or against them. It’s a kill or be killed world. Much like it’s a steal or be stolen from world. Many players will kill and rob you, or break into a base you built and steal your supplies & resources.
7- Construct vehicles and drive around. You don’t craft vehicles in the game; you have to locate the parts to construct it.
8- Craft clothing & weapons. Unless you have someone to help you start this is a major hindrance early in the game. It’s very easy to die from Starvation, Heat Stroke, and Hypothermia. You can also die from being attacked by another player or wild animal. Fall Damage is a real thing as well, fall a few feet and you can break a leg, which slows down your movement and makes you highly vulnerable.
9- Craft Owners Totem; this prevents other players from stealing what belongs to you if you have built a base to store it in. However it’s easy to break into bases that are poorly crafted by building bridges over walls or into windows (Windows in this game are just sections you leave open in a wall) You can also destroy the base using C4, although I should mention C4 is extremely rare to come by so this probably won’t happen that often unless an Admin spawns it for everyone on a private server.
10-Run a private server, with very limited options or controls
That is everything you can do in HurtWorld. It’s extremely basic at its core. Now the frustrating part is the world is filled with interesting/weird glitches and the menus are filled with annoying bugs. Key Bindings are a major issue if you wish to customize them. For those who make little or no changes this probably won't be too much of a problem.
If you are looking for a game that has something to do outside of what I listed above, you should probably look elsewhere or wait until the game gets closer to completion (Assuming that day will come). I am not being negative about this I am merely stating the truth that there are countless games on Steam right now that are Pre-Alpha and 95% of them have been for years and the Developer either has abandoned them or does tiny meaningless updates here and there to make it look like they are still actively developing the game.
Only time will tell, maybe this game will get updates that add meaningful content and resolve the issues that plague it. Yes I understand this is Alpha, but these things need to be mentioned for suspect buyers. Stating the game is Alpha doesn't exempt it from scrutiny or constructive criticism. People need to know what they are paying to have access too, and it is my honest opinion that this game is asking for a hefty entry price for what it offers. It was purchased on sale for $19.99, so the price I believe is considerable higher than it should be. This is a fair accessment considering the game was gifted to me by a friend.
Mileage will obvious vary from person to person. I hope this helps others make an informed decision.
I will give the Developer a kudos point for describing the game with some moral accuracy, and by moral I mean they didn't exxagerate the game like many other developers have done with alpha releases. Cheers

Ah, the predecessor of the BioShock games. I had this game ages ago, but I got too scared to play it. It's quite a scary game, even by today's standards. During the summer sale, there was a big discount so I decided to give it another go. Mind, I've barely touched it so far.
Well, first of all I'd like to mention something that's frustrating to say the least. Supposedly, there's an auto-save feature, but it doesn't seem to work as you might expect. Manually saving the game is not what you usually think of in the heat of the moment. You get resurrected if you locate certain pods, but they cost credits to use. What happens if you have no credits? Game over. Yeah, that's right. If you've played BioShock Infinite, you should know about "1999 mode". The reference seems obvious now.
A thing I notice in this game, is that it has a whole lot in common with the BioShock games, but there's a lot more. There are just so many mechanics in this game that it's easy to get a bit overwhelmed. There's a tutorial and heaps of in-game help, but it's quite staggering. I've yet to figure it all out.
Other than these annoyances, this game has kept up very well. The UI isn't quite up to par, combat feels a bit clunky, and in general the game feels aged, but so does Half-Life. It feels a lot like Half-Life, just with all the RPG elements known from BioShock mixed in.
So, can I recommend it? I have to say yes - if you aren't deterred by old school games.

In truth, Dark Souls II is probably one of the best RPGs out there.  It has pretty much everything you want out of an RPG: an involved (if mostly atmospheric) world, awesome customization, diverse playstyles, and kick♥♥♥♥♥enemies and bosses (even if it's less inspired than the original Dark Souls).  There are so many awesome ways to trudge through Drangleic, whether it be bare-fisted like a street-fighter character (yes, I've seen people with this), with an enormous greatsword sparking with lightning, obliterating everything with tornadoes of darkness and pillars of lightning and flame, Darth-Mauling it up by wielding a fiery twinblade, or dual-wielding poison whips.  Hell, you could probably do most if not all of these together if you had enough levels.  Hooray for the New Game Pluses (e.g. NG+3)!
That said, I will caution that this is no game for the ill-tempered.  You will be frustrated, you will curse at your screen, and you WILL die in this game.  You will feel like the game hates you.  But finding the courage, the patience, and the fortitude to keep going is an excellent theme to such a game where death and defeat is not just prominent, it's your character's very existence.  Thus, all I can say is that the game will reward patience and bravery (even in death), and severely punish you for trying to blunt force your way through.
Thus, in a way, the game is more than just challenging.  It's intelligent and clever, encouraging you to explore all options available to you.  Can't beat that jack♥♥♥♥♥fire demon boss?  If you explore the world enough, you might find fire-resistant gear, or even better, the flash-sweat pyromancy (which is gonna save your♥♥♥♥♥alot in that fight).  Summon some buddies for some jolly cooperation (but be sure they know what they're doing), and suddenly that boss is not so bad.  A pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ but not as bad as before.  By the same coin, many enemies early in the game will teach you how to properly dodge, parry, and the like, but only by no small effort on your part.  The work you put in to your skill in the game is rewarding, especially if you go on to the awesome arena PVP later.  If you're an invader, though, well, good luck.
Even further, though, the variety in playstyles gives alot of replayability.  So many crazy setups in this game are actually alot of good fun.  Dual-wielding daggers, greatswords, or even scimitars feels awesome and lends a completely different feel compared to a sword and shield setup.  Or you can go even crazier by being a dragon-bro with the covenant of champions ring and just go around punching bare-fisted for♥♥♥♥♥♥tons of damage (oh and breathing fire on people).  Most base weapons are enchantable, so feel free to become a battlemage or paladin with them sparkling particle effects.
Some people complain about the graphics, but the art style more than makes up for it. Just go look and see for yourself.  Enough said.
There's so much to discover and overcome in this game, and before long, you will have played hundreds of hours in this game....without really knowing why.

Great game, in my opinion there were some features better than DS1 and some worse..
I personally enjoyed the DS1 setting, and how the whole world was interconnected better--I also prefer the leveling system from DS1, but that's my opinion. However, the NPCs in DS2 are much tougher and more challenging to take in larger numbers; I do like the fact that DS2 provides a lot of space for you to move around to take them on--I often felt in DS1 that a room/area was sometimes too crowded, and it became very difficult and frustrating to take on large numbers of enemies. As for the bosses, I havent gotten too far into the game yet, but sofar I think DS1 was more creative, in terms of variety of bosses--I also think they were harder in DS1 (but I also did a lot more Jolly Co-operation in DS2 haha)...
Moreover, the PVP is difficult to get the hang of, but it is very fun once you do--there is always a variety of character builds, and virtually every player you encounter is unique. That being said, I think the combat system is wonderfully done, with the exception of the weapon ranges--especially thrust weapons--, they are MUCH longer range than they look, and this was difficult and a bit annoying to get used to.
As for the graphics: I never put large emphasis on graphics, I prefer a game for its gameplay and story, but the DS2 graphics is pleasing to the eye--it's definetely not the best graphic out there compared to newer games, but nonetheless, you can tell that From Software put a considerable amount of effort to make the game look nice.
Now the cons: honestly, I'll have to say, there are very few, and quite minor. One of them I already mentioned, and that's the range of weapons in PvP... the other one is the fact that it's quite difficult and frustration to try to meet and "jolly co-operate" with friends, or people you know--it took me some research to understand just how the summoing system works. I personally think the developers should include something (anything--an npc, a message, whatever) to explain briefly how the summoning system works. In my opinion, they could also add a feature such as a friend's list to be able to connect with friends better (other than the name-engraved ring--that barely does anything...).
All in all, Dark Souls II stays true to its name as a Soul's series, and is very challenging indeed. It punishes you hard for every minor mistake, but rewards you for the patience to not rush through an area, and to take the time to learn new enemies' movesets. As a result, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who has some time on their hands and is looking for a difficult but rewarding challenge, and of course, a hard-core fantasy RPG. Although I have yet to finish the game, my rating for the game so far would be 8.5/10

It really has been too long since the big publisher, big money, big marketing side of the game's industry took a chance on a survival horror game, and we're fortunate that it did because Alien: Isolation is one of the most refreshing takes on the genre that I've played in years.
Unlike more "Action-Horror" titles like Dead Space or the modern Resident Evils, Isolation deprives the player of weapons in most situations, encouraging environmental awareness and craftable gadgets to distract, outmaneuver, and hide from enemies for quick escapes. That's not to say that you are forbidden from killing enemies, but that the game's design strongly supports a passive approach to challenges most of the time. This decision by the developer to focus on the most vulnerable aspects of the "Survival" half of the genre will not appeal to every gamer, even fans of Survival Horror, but I found it to be wonderfully engaging.
Immersion is the key word here, as Isolation oozes with attention to detail, most evidently in its art direction and sound design. The environments on Sevastapol Station pay loving homage to the clunky, early-80's vision of the future the original 1979 Alien film introduced, a world in which something resembling DOS is the universal computer operating system, spaceships and alien planets are downright gothic in design, and megacorporations control everything. Gas leaks hiss distressingly, gritty vents open and shut with sandy grinds, and somewhere out of sight the echoing thud of a xenomorph dropping from a ceiling hatch pulls loose the breath you didn't realize you were holding.
The Xenomorph is the star attraction of the game, upon whom so much depends and revolves around. Credit must be given to the developer for its A.I. design here, as it's as charming an illusion of a "thinking program" as it is a horrific enemy. The alien has been realized in wonderful detail, perhaps the greatest treatment it has ever received in a game, and it commands a unique presence throughout the experience. Sometimes unintentional ally against other threats, but almost always a constantly lurking danger, the Xeno behaves about as well as I could have hoped for having as little scripting as it does. It stalks you through halls and vents alike, pauses to listen, investigates noises, and assuming you play on Hard difficulty, rarely seems a fool.
Some critics and players will cry foul at the Alien's powers of perception, but in my experiences with the game I've yet to see it break character or detect me without a clear mistake on my part. Within gameplay, and in the the overall pacing of the main campaign mode, the Xeno often takes its time to appear and doesn't overstay its welcome. That being said, the campaign is quite lengthy and doesn't involve constant encounters with its main antagonist, which will be a sore spot for players who aren't drawn into core gameplay of stealth, crafting, and striking only when necessary or you have plenty of time to escape an area. For myself, though, I haven't found the main campaign to be overly drawn out as some critics have, but rather pleasantly meaty on content.
The developer doesn't shy away from tasking the player with learning their level environments, or spacing out the save points either. I enjoy both of these decisions and the quality of their executions in the game, but I also understand how they will frustrate players who dislike needing to explore and find their own paths while constantly juggling the challenge of evading a persistent and fairly radiant A.I. that's hunting them all the while. This is a fairly difficult game, especially if played on the recommended "Hard" difficulty where the A.I. is unshackled from most of its scripts. Personally, I can't imagine not playing the game at this level as anything less will transform the Xenomorph into a considerably less intimidating dunce that will merrily run past you and hop in and out of a nearby vent as if preoccupied with chasing its own tail, with no time to spare for murdering you.
Different strokes for different folks.
The optional DLCs for the movie tie-in levels (based on the original 1979 film) and the game's "Survivor Mode" are also fun, if much shorter and more focused on the constant tension of close encounters with the Alien and other enemies. These levels can be a refreshing break from the long campaign, where you can jump out of the patient suspense and atmosphere the former continually generates, and drop into the heart of the game's fun factor: Cat and Mouse with the monster.
Alien: Isolation is a great game that takes the unexpected and refreshing route of embedding itself happily in a niche corner of the Survival Horror genre. In some ways this stubborn adherance to a genre I'd long thought the big money, big publisher game industry had dismissed as a money sink makes it a fascinating hybrid between an almost indie game design given a AAA treatment. It's a surprising investment from Sega, and while the game's structure isn't always perfect, or for everybody, I have to admire the purity of its take on Survival Horror.

Alien Isolation is a masterpiece. Being a huge Alien fan, I couldn’t be more pleased with the way this game turned out. The game features many different game modes, with the most popular being Conquest.7 Players are formed into two teams, with three to five players to each team. All players begin at opposite sides of a map at their team's 'fountain'. Before the players enter the map, they are granted an amount of gold (usually 1,500) to buy starting items. These items grant special bonuses or abilities that enhance the player's god. There are one to three continuous 'lanes' running from one side of the map to the other. Each lane is defended by a 'Phoenix' which is accompanied by a pair of extra defensive towers. Phoenixes and towers deal a large amount of damage to any enemies that come too close. The goal of each game is to destroy the opposing team's Phoenixes and the Titan, a giant warrior who must be defeated to win the game. The players are accompanied by 'minions', small soldiers with a weak attack; these minions spawn at the Phoenixes every thirty seconds and run along their lane until they meet opposition and attack immediately. Minions will attack not only players and other minions but also towers, Phoenixes and the Titan; in fact, their presence is required for players to deal full damage to these objectives. Defensive positions will prioritize enemy minions over players, allowing players to attack a tower without receiving damage; however, towers will fire upon players if there are no minions nearby or the player attacks an enemy player under their tower. If a game is going badly for a certain team it can decide to surrender, though this requires a majority of the team (4 players to 1) to agree.
With every game, players have to choose a god, (alternatively referred to as an "immortal"), to play. Currently, players can choose between 71 gods and immortals from seven different pantheons: Chinese, Egyptian, Greek, Hindu, Mayan, Norse and Roman mythology. Two players on the same team cannot choose the same god (with the exception of Match of the Day, which rotates daily), although they are free to choose gods from the same or different pantheons.
The player controls the god in a third person perspective, which is a unique characteristic of this multiplayer online battle arena game, as other games of this genre are typically played from a top-down perspective. Each god has a basic attack and four spells with varying effects, such as area of effect damage, crowd control, buffs and many more. These spells are acquired and upgraded when a player's god levels up by gaining experience from being in range of creeps when they are killed, taking down towers or phoenixes and killing enemy players. The maximum level is 20 and each successive level is harder to reach. Gold, which is used to buy equipment that increase power, defense, and passive effects, potions, wards and abilities, is accumulated through standard periodic income, by slaying enemies (player and NPC alike), or by selling owned items.
The large areas between the lanes make up what is called the 'jungle', where computer-controlled monsters such as packs of cyclopes or furies (the latter alternately referred to as harpies) periodically spawn at specific locations distributed symmetrically across the map. Killing certain monsters in said jungle causes a 'buff' to drop on the ground, where it can be picked up by a player. This buff grants the player one of the following buffs for a limited time, depending on which monster was killed: mana (mana regen & cooldown reduction bonus), damage (basic damage & power bonus), speed (movement speed bonus), or attack speed (in-hand attack speed & power bonus). There are two special neutral monsters who spawn less frequently, the Fire Giant and the Gold Fury. When killed, they grant the entire team who killed it a powerful damage buff for a medium length of time or a set amount of Gold, respectively. There also exist monsters which do not offer a buff, only experience and gold.

No level editor, so 'Bridge Construction Set' (BCS), by the same developer, is better. The "improved" graphics may be more intensive and pretty, but the GUI is as or more ugly than BCS with less hotkeys (or at least never shown what they are). The levels are generally the same as BCS, without the custom levels that were bundled with it, so DONT buy this for more levels
Hydraulics are in it, luckily, but since no level editor, I cant have fun just making ridiculous hydralics contraptions.
No reverse hydraulics (pushing out, rather than pulling in), so less functionality, and multi-plane editing seems to not exist, and ive finished up to halfway through 'complex' difficulty levels, so i doubt it will exist
As a game, outside of its predecessors, its quite puzzley, and the income is the biggest thing holding you back from completing the levels, limiting who many beams you can build. Theres a limit to selected beam types in some levels, but thats usually rare.
Sometimes the physics for cars/trucks is stupid and the vehicle will turn over on a road too steep, when it was fine on the same gradient on a different stage of the level. Its reproducable, so I assume its a slight difference from the hydraulics moving a region back and forth.
In BCS, Ive had issues with the split joints (for hydraulic stages) not rejoining when near each other and stalling the level (a failure), but not in this one so far. Not sure if the distance for rejoining has increased or just different bridges, but it has worked well.
Options: Very few, only resolution (from a fixed selection), antialiasing, fullscreen, v-sync and low-res textures. No music, and the sound is too loud for my liking, but no volume slider or mute button for that. Had to resort to Windows sound levels. Performance was NEVER an issue, with max options, and normally I run with 0x or 2x AA, but its not an intensive game
Conclusion: As a game in the bridge building series by Chronic Logic, its quite disappointing, but as a game in its own right, its a decent puzzle game, with rotary-joint, fixed or suspension beamed, bridge builder simulator game, with few options and no level editor.
Go buy 'Bridge Construction Set' from their website. It may be cheaper, maybe not, but it is a better game in every way, with nothing less, except "fancy" graphics, which dont help the game

An excellent bridge building 'simulator' (not sure how realistic it really is) that is well made and perhaps more simulator-like than other bridge-building titles such as Bridge Constructor. It's pretty much the standard affair, with different materials and pieces to use (including hydraulics, suspension, or normal bridge) as well as both rail, motorcar and boat bridges that makes the game varied and interesting. Levels vary in difficulty at a good pace, and you can save bridges or scenarios which is a very useful feature if you've created an especially awesome bridge and want to keep it. Graphics are crisp and enjoyable, and you can rotate around the bridge or view with a cinematic camera bringing a more interesting feel to the game. A feature I also enjoyed using was a first-person view from the car or train or boat crossing the bridge which adds yet another dimension to the game. If Bridge Constructor is a shallow mobile port of a bridge builder, then rest assured this is the real thing. Highly recommended.

I'm gonna be as summarized and straight forward to all the aspects that one needs answers for in a CoD game. SO HERE WE GO
This year's Call of Duty is created for the first time by the talented team at Sledgehammer Games, who has previously been part of the makin' of MW3. This is their entry to the franchise with a very futuristic sight, and my opinion is strongly positive on this one! Let's start off with what the big changes are, as I'm sure you're already aware of the CoD formula...
First of all, the exo suit. This robotic suit of sorts allows you to boost, double-jump, ground-slam, all sorts of different stuff, and as part of your create-a-class, you can apply exo abilities, such as regenerative health, silent footsteps, hover, cloack, all these runnin' on a battery on your exo(this battery lasts only once, so if you want to use your ability again, you have to wait until you respawn, then you'll get a new one).
The choice of weapons are very intriguing. Some of the more unusual ones are an SMG and heavy weapon that's pre-akimbo(it means that the guns are dual wielded by default, and can not be removed), laser projected heavy weapons, 5-burst SMG, all sorts of stuff that really stands out. Not to mention the new supply drop addition! Every 45-minutes of in-game gameplay, you gain a supply drop, which contains between 1-3 items, rangin' from character customization gear, weapon variants, double XP and in-game care packages, all in three different qualities, Enlisted, Proffessional and Elite. With weapon variants, you can get another version of the same gun, but with different stats! For instance, you can get an AK12 variant that shoots faster but has less ammo, or a pistol that has the akimbo attachment built-in(weapon variants with built-in attachments can not be removed, however the attachment won't take a spot in your class points).
I may hear you ask "But how about servers? Everyone says that the game isn't running on dedicated servers! Shouldn't I be concerned?". This is a very controversial topic, as people believe there are no dedicated servers for this game(hence TotalBiscuits input about the game not havin' it). Alright, so the answer is that this game DOES have dedicated servers, however not primarily. It runs on a hybrid system, which means that if there is a dedicated server available with a good connection, you will be sent to that lobby. However if a server can't be found, you will be put into a listen server, where one player is the host. Now this is extremely good, since dedicated servers makes gameplay fair for everyone when there's no host advantage, not to mention the better connection. Now should you be concerned? Well, I live in Sweden, and every match I have ever connected to has ALWAYS been a dedicated server. One strong sign that you're NOT playing on a dedicated server is if a host migration process starts when the host leaves the lobby, and ever since day one, that has never happened! Host migrations used to happen at least 5 times every hour when playing MW2 or MW3, however I haven't experienced a single host migration at all, and I've put down about 200 hours in the multiplayer(the counter may be broken a bit, sorry).
The game runs pretty much flawlessly on PC. My machine is not that über great, but it does the job, and I'm able to play with great settings on my 1920x1080 monitor in 60 fps(I have all my settings pushed to the max, no vsync, as well as Cache Spot Shadow/Sun Maps disabled(That setting makes all the textures extremely blurry, here's an example to show what the caches setting does
Source=PCGamingWiki)). One thin' to keep in mind if you own a 120 or 144hz monitor is that the game is capped at 91 fps(possibly due to clipping issues if this was set to above 91), so unfortunatly you won't get the entire benefit of havin' a higher Hz monitor(unless they patch it). Fortunatly for those with easily affected motion sickness, this game has an adjustable FOV in the settings, which goes from 65 up to 90 horizontal FOV.
I believe this is everythin' I have to say. Wasn't really as summarizin' as I would've hoped. The campaign is fenominal, the multiplyer is fun as heck, survival will get exo-zombies soon in the comin' DLC's(which I am REALLY looking forward to!). Even if this game brings in the verticality and the new movement system this franchise dearly needs, it still feels like a Call of Duty game! If you are tired from how the previous games have been, then be warry if you purchase this. However, if you're still a dearly beloved CoD fan, you really need this!
And don't mind that "mixed reviews" title in the store section here, it just seems that it's part of the pop-culture to hate this franchise. The only one to really judge the game is yourself!
Thank you for readin', and I hope I cleared some thin's up!
~Melee-Chan

It is a casual game. There are no time limits, difficult challenges, or any "endgame". You're there to enjoy the scenery, the slime antics, and the satisfaction of watching your Ranch grow. The Slime Science update does add another layer to the game, however this is more for decoration/cosmetic purposes.
That said; I always find many small moments of hilarity. My slimes escaping their pen and eating all my chickens, a Boom slime blasting a friend into another pen and causing a "Tar" chain reaction, and being "booped" by an invisible Hunter slime.  I generally prefer more objective based "risk vs reward" games but I have enjoyed my time with Slime Rancher.

* If you are easily bored, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME. The concept is repetative, so please do not expect much of it.
* If you are looking for a challenge, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME. Again, this game is meant to be very fun and happy, not a hard-core game.
* This game does NOT support co-op or multi-player
Now I could go on and on about the flaws of this game, but those are just a few basic problems that most people are upset about on their first play. Remember that the game is currently Early Access, which means that it is not completed and could have several updates in the future (Getting off early access as of August 1st, 2017). Again, the concept of this game is extremely simple, but if you look deeper than the surface of this game than you will truly be happy. It has a lot more to offer than pink jumpy balls of slime that expell 'Plorts' when they eat. Please consider buying this game if you already haven't, it is well worth the $19.99! :)

Great game, in my opinion there were some features better than DS1 and some worse..
I personally enjoyed the DS1 setting, and how the whole world was interconnected better--I also prefer the leveling system from DS1, but that's my opinion. However, the NPCs in DS2 are much tougher and more challenging to take in larger numbers; I do like the fact that DS2 provides a lot of space for you to move around to take them on--I often felt in DS1 that a room/area was sometimes too crowded, and it became very difficult and frustrating to take on large numbers of enemies. As for the bosses, I havent gotten too far into the game yet, but sofar I think DS1 was more creative, in terms of variety of bosses--I also think they were harder in DS1 (but I also did a lot more Jolly Co-operation in DS2 haha)...
Moreover, the PVP is difficult to get the hang of, but it is very fun once you do--there is always a variety of character builds, and virtually every player you encounter is unique. That being said, I think the combat system is wonderfully done, with the exception of the weapon ranges--especially thrust weapons--, they are MUCH longer range than they look, and this was difficult and a bit annoying to get used to.
As for the graphics: I never put large emphasis on graphics, I prefer a game for its gameplay and story, but the DS2 graphics is pleasing to the eye--it's definetely not the best graphic out there compared to newer games, but nonetheless, you can tell that From Software put a considerable amount of effort to make the game look nice.
Now the cons: honestly, I'll have to say, there are very few, and quite minor. One of them I already mentioned, and that's the range of weapons in PvP... the other one is the fact that it's quite difficult and frustration to try to meet and "jolly co-operate" with friends, or people you know--it took me some research to understand just how the summoing system works. I personally think the developers should include something (anything--an npc, a message, whatever) to explain briefly how the summoning system works. In my opinion, they could also add a feature such as a friend's list to be able to connect with friends better (other than the name-engraved ring--that barely does anything...).
All in all, Dark Souls II stays true to its name as a Soul's series, and is very challenging indeed. It punishes you hard for every minor mistake, but rewards you for the patience to not rush through an area, and to take the time to learn new enemies' movesets. As a result, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who has some time on their hands and is looking for a difficult but rewarding challenge, and of course, a hard-core fantasy RPG. Although I have yet to finish the game, my rating for the game so far would be 8.5/10

Dark Souls II, unlike its predecessor, received a fine port to PC, with only a few, simple problems to speak of.  It has a relatively high frame rate and runs well even on my old laptop, but still provided a great improvement over the first Dark Souls' graphics.

The multiplayer has received only moderate improvements; while it

It really has been too long since the big publisher, big money, big marketing side of the game's industry took a chance on a survival horror game, and we're fortunate that it did because Alien: Isolation is one of the most refreshing takes on the genre that I've played in years.
Unlike more "Action-Horror" titles like Dead Space or the modern Resident Evils, Isolation deprives the player of weapons in most situations, encouraging environmental awareness and craftable gadgets to distract, outmaneuver, and hide from enemies for quick escapes. That's not to say that you are forbidden from killing enemies, but that the game's design strongly supports a passive approach to challenges most of the time. This decision by the developer to focus on the most vulnerable aspects of the "Survival" half of the genre will not appeal to every gamer, even fans of Survival Horror, but I found it to be wonderfully engaging.
Immersion is the key word here, as Isolation oozes with attention to detail, most evidently in its art direction and sound design. The environments on Sevastapol Station pay loving homage to the clunky, early-80's vision of the future the original 1979 Alien film introduced, a world in which something resembling DOS is the universal computer operating system, spaceships and alien planets are downright gothic in design, and megacorporations control everything. Gas leaks hiss distressingly, gritty vents open and shut with sandy grinds, and somewhere out of sight the echoing thud of a xenomorph dropping from a ceiling hatch pulls loose the breath you didn't realize you were holding.
The Xenomorph is the star attraction of the game, upon whom so much depends and revolves around. Credit must be given to the developer for its A.I. design here, as it's as charming an illusion of a "thinking program" as it is a horrific enemy. The alien has been realized in wonderful detail, perhaps the greatest treatment it has ever received in a game, and it commands a unique presence throughout the experience. Sometimes unintentional ally against other threats, but almost always a constantly lurking danger, the Xeno behaves about as well as I could have hoped for having as little scripting as it does. It stalks you through halls and vents alike, pauses to listen, investigates noises, and assuming you play on Hard difficulty, rarely seems a fool.
Some critics and players will cry foul at the Alien's powers of perception, but in my experiences with the game I've yet to see it break character or detect me without a clear mistake on my part. Within gameplay, and in the the overall pacing of the main campaign mode, the Xeno often takes its time to appear and doesn't overstay its welcome. That being said, the campaign is quite lengthy and doesn't involve constant encounters with its main antagonist, which will be a sore spot for players who aren't drawn into core gameplay of stealth, crafting, and striking only when necessary or you have plenty of time to escape an area. For myself, though, I haven't found the main campaign to be overly drawn out as some critics have, but rather pleasantly meaty on content.
The developer doesn't shy away from tasking the player with learning their level environments, or spacing out the save points either. I enjoy both of these decisions and the quality of their executions in the game, but I also understand how they will frustrate players who dislike needing to explore and find their own paths while constantly juggling the challenge of evading a persistent and fairly radiant A.I. that's hunting them all the while. This is a fairly difficult game, especially if played on the recommended "Hard" difficulty where the A.I. is unshackled from most of its scripts. Personally, I can't imagine not playing the game at this level as anything less will transform the Xenomorph into a considerably less intimidating dunce that will merrily run past you and hop in and out of a nearby vent as if preoccupied with chasing its own tail, with no time to spare for murdering you.
Different strokes for different folks.
The optional DLCs for the movie tie-in levels (based on the original 1979 film) and the game's "Survivor Mode" are also fun, if much shorter and more focused on the constant tension of close encounters with the Alien and other enemies. These levels can be a refreshing break from the long campaign, where you can jump out of the patient suspense and atmosphere the former continually generates, and drop into the heart of the game's fun factor: Cat and Mouse with the monster.
Alien: Isolation is a great game that takes the unexpected and refreshing route of embedding itself happily in a niche corner of the Survival Horror genre. In some ways this stubborn adherance to a genre I'd long thought the big money, big publisher game industry had dismissed as a money sink makes it a fascinating hybrid between an almost indie game design given a AAA treatment. It's a surprising investment from Sega, and while the game's structure isn't always perfect, or for everybody, I have to admire the purity of its take on Survival Horror.

Do you notice a slight pattern here? Everyone giving this game the thumbs down has spent well more than their money's worth, playing the thing. If the game really is as bad as everyone says it is, then why do they spend hundreds of hours of their lives on it? If the game was as bad as everyone attempts to make out then surely they'd play it for several hours, regret that they purchased it, give it a bad review then leave it to be nothing more than a statistical +1 on # of games they own. They don't however, they spend weeks and months playing the thing every evening/weekend and why do they do this?
The answer is simple, it's not a bad game. Far from it, the game is actually very good. Rome II has had A LOT of criticism from die-hard TW fans and I can understand why. There were many bugs on release, the AI should simply be called A as it's certainly not very intelligent and I sometimes find my saved games corrupt after each update. I dislike the city building (as cool as the sharing of structures within a region is) and think they should have kept it moreso like Shogun's. I hate how the game tends to be split entirely with the Tribes (Northern Eu) and the Greeks/Romans (South Eu) as if they are only 2 different playable factions within the game. What I mean is that all of the tribes feel the same, as do all of the Greek nations. So I wish there was more diversity between nations' units and structures. Also, would it be so hard as to create just a few more character models? Seeing an army of 10,000 tribesmen all with the same face and 1 of 2 haircuts is annoying as hell.
All of these things frustrate me and this game could have been a lot better but, it's certainly not a bad game that we should all be trying to discourage others from buying, such as Infestation:Survivor stories. The original TW Rome was for many TW fans, the best in the franchise so Rome II had some pretty big boots to fill and unfortunately, many people feel that because it didn't give them that nostalgia they were seeking, "the game sucked 0/10". I don't think that is at all fair.
Now, is Rome 2 my favourite TW? No, it isn't. I'm not going to lie but, it's certainly worth getting if you are a TW fan, or generally someone who enjoys RTS games. The graphics are definitely the best of all the TW games to date (I don't understand why so many people seem to think Shogun 2 had better graphics, maybe their computers are too sh*te to play Rome II on a high graphical setting) and the DLC is pretty much the same old generic content that you'd expect to find (extra factions and units etc), priced at the amount you'd expect it to be.
Rome II is certainly a lot easier to mod than Shogun 2 was, so if you enjoy modding then you also have that going for you, which is nice. You're actually able to hide units now as hills and trees obscure line of sight. You no longer have to be in the forest to be hidden, simply the other side of them is enough. Many units now have multiple abilities, some even passively activate themselves, such as front line melee infantry letting loose a volley of javelins before charging in to battle without your intervention. Even though the AI isn't so intelligent, I still find it much less predictable than it was in Shogun 2 and diplomacy is key to surviving on higher difficulties so, choose your allies wisely or you can find the game to be quite brutal.
I've personally enjoyed all those hours that I've clocked on Rome II and will enjoy many more in the future to come. If you're unsure about it, wait until a steam sale but you should certainly get it either way, so that you too can waste hundreds of hours of your own life building an empire to span the entirety of Europe! Killing and conquering all, like a boss.

What a little gem! This one has been sitting in my unplayed library for months, until a few days ago. Like many, I got it off of one of those cheap sim bundles. There are so many crap simulators flooding the market these days and I figured this one would easily fall into that category. I was wrong. It's actually quite good and alot of fun to play. A short 3 bridge tutorial gets you started on the basics. After that you're on your own.
The object is simple. Build various length bridges to support cars, trucks, trains and drawbridges that can allow boats to pass underneath, all within limited budget and material constraints. There are several different bridge types and material types with different costs and construction methods. The game claims advanced physics simulation. I wouldn't know because I'm not a mechanical or civil engineer so alot of trial and error are needed on my part.
When you're ready, you press the simulate button and watch how your bridge performs as people drive over it. If you did you're job right, you can move to the next level. Make a mistake and watch the disaster unfold in rather comical fashion. Stress analysis tools and a simulation speed slider help to pinpoint where the failures are occuring so you can beef up construction or use more expensive materials to try and stay together.
A neat cinematic camera view and even driver camera makes things interesting, especially if you want to see what it's like tumbling into a ravine because your bridge is poorly built.
Definitely recommend for sim fans and engineers.

Too good, too addictive and too many hours played.
As many of the negativer reviewers state however is incredibly easy compared to the first one. Just to point out how easy.
The mace, one of the starting weapons is incredibly overpowered. Go buy another one, level your strength to 18 I believe, powerstance and have fun staggering alot of the earlier bosses, making the start of the game too easy. Burn a bonfire ascetic, rinse and repeat, level up lots of times, there you go too powerful.
Don't forget to note that Distorti0n2, a speedrunner completed the game in 17 minutes. The game mechanics are broken. Just google "binoboosting" and "pairywalk" and see for yourself.
However the reason that I recommened this game is because it is still very enjoyable. PvP is still enjoyable, meeting a wide range of players that offer new ideas for your next build. The lore behind the game, while not as strong as in Dark Souls, is still there and enjoyable to learn, with every item you discover offering more background to your environment.
I played the game through as fast as possible first time, wanting to see all the new bosses and areas, and admittably died alot. However second playthrough I rarely died, most often to controller dying during a fight, my error. But that second time I went through and did read all of the lore and found out how much the developers had put into the game.
If you've never played the Souls series, this is a good idea to start on, as it introduces the mechanics behind the games, albeit it's easier than the previous two.
The addition of teleporting to a bonfire straight away at the start of the game is a very useful. You still have to clear an area to get to that bonfire, and it speeds up the pace of the game. Remember in Dark Souls, you went to the bottom of Blightown, hit the bonfire, killed Queelag and then realised that you've got to make that run all again to reach the surface? What's the point? You've killed everything once why do you need to just walk out backstabbing everyone?
You can tell that this game has been made for the masses by making it alot easier, however is still a worthy addition to your collection, just to get the new lore and playthrough it yourself.
No reason to hate on this game. But you will die. No way around it.

CO-OP
A friend and I purchased this game in hopes to do co-op. However, we both had a brain aneurysm before we could even try co-op. To do "co-op" you must first go through a mission to obtain a stupid summon stone of which you will die over and over and over trying to obtain. Every time you die, you turn 'hollow' (in game and reality)  which is a semi-undead state and your flesh starts to rot along with your health. Unfortunately, if you and your friend are both in this 'hollow' state, you cannot do co-op with eachother. The only way to gain back your humanity is to use a human efigy (which are rare), or to lay down a summon sign so someone can invite you to their mission and if you are successful, you gain back your humanity upon returning to your world.
I believe co-op should be easy to connect to without complications, but this game loves complications. You have to jump through many hoops before you can join a friend, and even if you do, if either of you die just once... you can kiss your friend's♥♥♥♥♥goodbye because you will be thrown back into your world in a 'hollowed' state. This to me is just a huge troll to co-op gameplay. So FOR ME, I'll rate co-op 3/10
OVERALL GAMEPLAY
When you first start out, there isn't anything to help you as a noob. You're thrown into a world and you have to use the old 'trial and error' which will get you killed. This will ultimately test your determination and durability. Many will rage-quit after realising the devs have clearly trolled them out of their money. I hope the devs get killed by three little pigs...
HEALTH WARNING: I firmly believe this game should come with some sort of health warning to those that suffer due to stress. DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME IF YOU CANNOT PHYSICALLY OR MENTALLY HANDLE STRESS. This game is the ultimate stress test and you are NOT entitled to compensation if you break your keyboard as a result. Damn their terms and conditions...
I don't even know if there is a storyline to follow as the NPC's just drone on about a load of cr*p which you will eventually get bored of hearing and spam the enter button. For the gameplay, I'll have to say 4/10
COMBAT:
I actually love the combat system, it requires skill and you have to move all the time which keeps you on the edge of your seat if by that point you haven't already thrown it out of the window. 10/10 for this one.
KEYBOARD & MOUSE CONTROLLS:
Unless you connect an XBOX controller, you're screwed. You can play with K&M but it's very difficult to get used to it, and you may find yourself browsing the key-bindings to see what button does what, and if that doesn't fully elaborate, you find yourself seeking help from Google search. 1/10
Overall, I love/hate this game.  That's what this game does to you...
5/10 overall.
Do I recommend this game? Yes and no.

1) I'm a big TW fan since Shogun I and have invested more time in the series along the years than in probably any other form of digital and non-digital entertainment.
2) I was reluctant to buy Rome II because of the disappointmant it seemed to have caused among many TW fans.
3) I ended up buying the game during the Steam Summer Sale.
4) It is an amazing game and an amazing TW game. Launch issues asside people who insist on it being disappointing at the level of polish it is at present are just being stubborn.
Here's why (imho):
The game is very well optimised. It runs great on ultra on my state-of-the-art-at-best rig.
When there are graphical lags, the game is made in such a way that they effect gameplay as little as possible.
There are very few glitches of any kind and this is a big thing when taking into account that:
The game is epicly huge and diverse. There are so many types of units and factions and environments that it boggles the mind.
The UI, while confusing at first (even for TW veterans such as myself), is actually quite well-crafted and once you get used to it, it becomes very practical.
Look, I understand it was upsetting for many that the game was in the shape as it may have been when it launched and I agree that something close to the current version of the game should have been what people who laied their money down first had gotten. I, however, truely believe that in its current state Rome II TW is not only worth its full price but is a bargain for any TW fan, history geek or strategy enthusiast who is looking to invest in long term quality entertainment. The sheer scale and diversity offers a lot of replay value, something which the excellent Shogun 2 lacked (mostly diversity).
There are so many cool features in Rome II I, personally, have been waiting for for so long in the TW series, the unique cities, the combined naval/land battles, port cities, picking any location on the map for a custom battle, these are all truly steps forward for the series that must have tacken huge amount of work to integrate.
Many changes to certain game mechanics are also very welcome. Armies, navies and garrisons function differently than in all previous games in ways that make sense and keep palyers inganged in how they invest assets. Public order managment also makes sense and gives you the feeling of managing the human cost of building a great cities and empires.
Combine all this with the widely different factions with different tech/units/tactics/culture, the great graphics that contain panstaking detail (that also help build amazing atmosphere) and good optimisation and you have yourself another amazing game by the Creative Assembly that makes any future sure-to-be TW games, once again, too good to be true.
If you don't have the game yet because you were discouraged by word of mouth, trust me, just buy it and I'm sure that even if you don't fully agree with my opinion, you definitely won't be disapointed by this great game in this great state!
Thank you again Creative Assembly!

First, the premise of the game is that you are a god- you can choose one from the many provided pantheons. There are several fan-favorites such as Loki and Thor. There are even some that are currently being worshiped. The goal of the game is that these gods are trying to fight for worshipers. They do this by battling other gods to prove their dominance. This plays like a typical moba, except there are many more gamemodes than the standard 5v5 Conquest mode. This mode is slower than all the rest and provides a extremely challenging game for people who queue alone. The rest of the modes are roughly 20 minutes long, but they can drag.
Secondly, the matchmaking of this game is pretty awful. Thinking back to my game yesterday, I was playing Chronos, a nice god in the Arena gamemode and I had 3 teammates who fed their brains out. They went 0/12, 1/7, and 0/17. The first number represents the kills that the player has received and the second is their deaths. You can imagine my anger at this game. This game does not match you up with competent teammates. I can recall several times when my teammates seem to be absolutely mindless. Now, don't get me wrong- I do not care if you like to do things a little differently, as long as you do well. These people do not do well. And I know there is no shortage of good players because the enemy team always has players that perform extremely well. Why is this the case? I don't know.
Thirdly, the servers. I would say about 92% of the time, the servers are fairly stable. But when that 8% rolls around, this game is practically unplayable. They cut the win rewards because of their own problem. There are other very minor and anger-inducing bugs that are too plentiful to name. I used to like this game, I really did. However, the fact that Mr. Hirez is dedicated to other projects like Hand of the Gods and Paladins is taking a serious toll on this game. It's fun until you realize the number of bugs in this game. This is an example of a wonderful idea that is being poorly executed.
