Billed appropriately as a relaxing and pleasurable experience with simple and easily grasped gameplay,
is a short and yet original and emotive ARPG built by one Taiwanese developer using
software.  Its originality comes in the touching and yet somewhat tragic dynamic between the titular deuteragonist - and main playable character -
and her older non-playable 'sister',
.  Whilst the cadence of the written English in the game is a little stilted and awkward due to translational grammatical errors, the potency of the dynamic between the two 'sisters' comes through very lucidly.  If I were to recommend this game, it would primarily be for that reason.
The combat system is a slight revamp of styles similar to
or
.  Enemy sprites are ran into and auto-attacked will, for the most part, counter-attack.  Four skills are learned throughout the game, and all of them have at least one area of optimal use (though the first two of these four skills in general have more global utility).  The bosses, whilst somewhat samey in the mechanics used (e.g. regular use of shield gems, shaded area spells, mob spawning, horizontal or vertical beams), do get harder as the fight progresses, and the last fight on Hard Mode is legitimately quite difficult.  There perhaps aren't as many special/unique enemies like the ghosts or the nuns as there could have been, and a flaw to the giant regular enemies is that they never try to initiate attacks so can always be beaten with patience alone.
There are three main zones to travel through and it's an elegant touch that some comic/trivial NPCs offer perks for fully completing these areas.  This primarily involves quota-killing NPCs for books that permanently boost the Evasion stat, finding all the treasure chests in an area, and crafting the best armour for that area.  Whilst the crafting will require some grinding, it never gets too tedious.  The Demon Frontier is the most interesting from an overall design perspective - the Wisdom area in the castle was probably my favourite individual section of the game - but the Sanctum is the most visually interesting area and has a couple of nice touches related to the game's plot.
My main critique of the level design would be that all levels are very, very linear, and with the Waypoint mechanic enabling teleportation between specific save points, it didn't really necessarily need to be so.  Often, a large appeal to ARPGs is that certain areas are unravelled and fully bloom over time, and only in the first area of the Sanctum and for completion is backtracking at all necessary.  The difficulty isn't quite tuned right, even though it is billed as an easy game, since if one keeps up on gear the second area and third area (up until the last boss) are actually both easier to clear through than the first.  Having said that, the option to take on bosses in hard mode was appreciated, and approach rather than level grinding always wins out on the bosses, which is good.
The music is fine and fitting to its surroundings, and whilst the visuals in general are a bit generic, it's understandable given the use of RPG Maker, although the few pieces of Senia/Magaleta artwork are nice.  The more minor characters are mostly a little cheesy, and whilst I'd prefer they had a little more texture, the Senia/Magaleta dynamic makes up for it.
Oh, and it's free.
tl;dr - If you want a throwback to the SNES-style ARPGs with a poignant and touching story and simple, straightforward gameplay, this game is for you!

When I first heard about Isolation, I thought that it would be a massive let down like Coniol Marines. But when I played the game, it was nothing like it. The thrill of the terror hits you when the Alien is first introduced in the game, but through this period you find it hard to decide whether it is excitement or scared. For me it was both. When the Alien was first presented a shiver ran down my spine as it fell down the vent (but unlucky for me because my computer lagged the whole cinematic) and the sight of this monstrosity made me want to play more! In my opinion the most terrifying moment with the Alien is in the medical facility, or when Ripley contacts the Torrens. But by far the most terrifying enemy in the game wasn't the Working Joes, it wasn't the humans, it wasn't even the facehuggers. No, the most terrifying enemy in the game (in my opinon) was the Alien. This was probably due to the fact that the creature was unpredictable and how ever hard you tried you could never out run it.
The game's visuals were amazing it really showed the fans of the original ASlien how the future would look like through the technology of the 70s. E.g. shaky cameras, flashing lights. But the asect of how the game was played was amazing. By SEGA creating the game in first person gave the player the sense that they could be in that situation. But in my opinion the best mission was the ending mission (I will not spoil it for those of you who have not bought the game) the adrenaline rush inside you makes the experiance just that more realistic.
The game itself took me four weeks to complete, the campaign was huge, not stopping the excitement from start to finish. I will admit though that this game is by far the scariest game I have ever played, so the reason why it took me so long was because my dramatic pauses for a breath. But all in all in my opinion, Alien Isolation is by far the best game of the year in my opinion. Who knows maybe it may even win game of the year. But it is deffinately up there in my top five favourite games of all time.
For those of you who are thinking of buying this game, fare warning you will encounter horrors that will make you more eager to carry on. So yes I would reccomend this game for so many reasons, oh and just remember...enjoy!

Having played through on medium difficulty, I can say that, while it is not a perfect game, it is a very, very good one. There have been reviews that either love or hate ALIEN: Isolation with little between. That in and of itself tells me there is something very different about it.
After the dissapointment of ALIEN Colonial Marines, which should have been and extintion level event for the franchise, this game is a blessing.  Owing to the fact this is a story driven game, some of the mechanics are akward, but intentional to drive you forward in the game. As an example, I rendered a human character with a pistol unconscious. I was able to pick up the ammo for the weapon, but not the weapon itself. (I gained a weapon moments later)
Then there is the Creature itself (deserving of a capital "C"). I was impressed with the AI as it hunted me across the game.  I usd a flare to draw its attention to sneak pasted it a couple of times, but when it came time for a third try at this tactic... it was on to me. When I finally got the flame thrower and drove off an attack, I also knew it where I was and very♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about it.
It took me 28.7 hours to complete the game and towards the end, it felt long, but very much worth it. I gave it a few days and tried some of the DLC content; "Crew Expendable" was a bit rough and had the feel of being a proof of concept project. It was also more frightening than that entire main game. I would have love to fight it out on the Nostromo alone...
Recommending this game is the hard part. Understand this is not Call of Duty. You can't just apply more firepower and get though the mission.  You can't blast away and run through. If the Creature see's you.... game over. Stealth and thinking ahead is mandatory. I spent the better part of the game, hiding under a desk, examininng the map to plot out my next move towards the objective...and have it go balls up anyways.
I'm going to sum it up; Sometimes frustrating but compelling. So I'm hitting Recommend.

This game is more or less Pikmin meets Minecraft farming. You explore the world, collecting slimes and "breeding" them to make new ones, earning money to upgrade and unlock more locations, etc, etc.
The game itself is very fun, I lost several hours at a time to it without even noticing. It's a simple concept that allows for a lot of wiggle room on your playstyle. However, the game is solely based around slimes, so doing other things is to do them just for the slimes, like growing fruit or chickens. Everything goes towards your slimes.
The endgame is quite a ways away and gives you lots of time to explore things. Even when you have explored everything and unlocked every slime there are plenty of things to do and create.
I'd say the strongest part of this game is achievements. I'm achievement based on Steam, or at least enjoy games I can collect achievements on, and they were all fun. They encouraged me to explore, or play in a different way. They're not difficult to get, but require some work and others require a lot of progression.
The game's weaknesses are repetition and frustration. The game only has 4 item slots, meaning exploring a new location takes a long time but only takes that long because you have to go back and forth to drop off whatever items or new slimes you found. It's frustrating when you find a pile of things and can only take back a couple, but from what I've seen stuff doesnt really despawn quickly so you can always go back and get things you know the slimes won't eat.
The game runs suprisingly well on lower-end PCs. I was scared to start it just because I have had struggles with first person games in the past, but it works well on lower graphic settings. I have a GT 610, if that makes a difference, but other than that it's just a cheap pc.
I would recommend you check this out if you like farming games, casual games, cute games, adventure games, or exploration games.

Although in early access only, Black Mesa is an excellent pastime for those who like reminiscing about the past and find it almost exquisite to play one of their favourite, classic FPS games in a greatly enhanced form. Yes, this is Half Life 1 but this time envisioned thanks to the amazing Source engine that made it possible for us to play the sequel along with the Left 4 Dead franchise.
Below are my pros and cons about this conversion:
+++ The game looks stunning! The creators did not just make a conversion but changed some of the environments. Added several items here and there to make severals rooms / hallways more realistic. Laboratories are now full of equipment; towards the end game we can really feel like being part of an ongoing war between the military and the invaders! Also, the faces of the characters look pretty cool - I assume this is a later iteration of the Source engine hence the better facial animations.
+++ Extra dialogue options: Especially true to the first level; just keep pressing E until you hear everything the scientists or guards have to say. And oh boy there's plenty they want to share with you!
+++ Achievements: Good ones, I have to admit! Remember the scientist in the toilet? Pass him the toilet paper!  Also, make sure you ruin the casserole in the microwave oven in the kitchen just like you did it in 1998. As the game is unfinished there are no story-related achievements at this point.
--- Sometimes enemies get stuck in one place. They just get frozen and do not react until you shoot them. It can be pretty annoying sometimes as tough battles can be completed too easily after several reloads.
--- This game is sure quite difficult! Even on normal difficulty level the soldiers can hit you from afar - this is pretty unfair and your kevlar (=HEV suit) gets depleted pretty fast almost all the time. Interestingly, the vortigaunts and the big soldier aliens are quite easy to get rid of (especially the big guys were annoying in the vanilla game). The battle on the dam with the helicopter is particularly challenging as the creators did not put enough cover there.
--- And the biggest issue of all: the game is unfinished. Once you jump into the portal to make your way to Xen the game ends. I initially played Black Mesa 2 or 3 years ago (downloaded from the creators' website - Steam release came only this year) and while many adjustments have been made since the 4 remaining chapters (chapter 15-18) are still missing.
Overall, this is a nicely done conversion. It ups the difficulty level so those getting used to today's casual games may find it quite challenging. While 10 euros are not much for the game (this is the lowered price - it gets discounted regularly) perhaps it's best to wait until Black Mesa is fully completed. However, if you are an avid fan of Gordon Freeman's journey just like myself grab it right away!

"And down it goes"
Bridge building games doesn't look like something that would be that fun at first though. Stick up some pieces without breaking your budget, make sure it doesn't fall apart while a car crosses, and then continue to the next level. Despite this, there are games in the genre that are truly fun, this being one of them. Let me describe why this should be on your wishlist.
Story
Some crazed maniac has managed to destroy a number of bridges over the region, and now that they need new ones, they grabbed the first person off the street to create them. Despite your lack of experience and skill, you are forced to ensure that companies can still get their goods transported where ever they need to be without letting the drivers lose their lives.
Or maybe this has no story at all. Its a bridge building game, we don't need a story. But if you do, just pretend it is the one written above.
Presentation
The visuals are pretty basic, but you know exactly what you are looking at, and it has several camera options, including viewing from the vehicles themselves as they plunge over a cliff. Materials will be recognized, and will change colour to show how stressed they are with a toggle option. Sound is also suitable, with metal groaning as it threatens to ruin your hard work, and noises from the vehicles. Not any music in this game though. Not really a problem though.
Controls
Nice and simple, pretty much everything can be done with just the mouse. Left click will take you through the menu and place pieces of the bridge. Right click is used to remove pieces. Holding the shift key will allow you to select multiple pieces of your bridge so you can copy and paste larger chucks if you want the other side to mirror your current idea. Arrow keys and the mouse wheel can be used to adjust the camera. nothing here to cause any confusion or difficulty.
Gameplay
Working within the limitations set by your budget and available materials, you will be attempting to build a bridge to cross over various rivers and canyons. These will start simple, with only small areas to build across and only basic materials to make it easy to guess the best choices. As you get further in the game, the bridge will need to be much longer and you will need to mix it up with stronger pieces, cables and even hydraulics so your bridge can lift out of the way of passing boats. Later levels are incredibly difficult as it will seem that you just don't have what you need to prevent the latest travelers from taking a swim, but each of the bridges in the game can be finished. With all the available choices for building your bridge, I much prefer this game over similar titles I've played, none of them matching this for variety.
Lifespan
The game should last a while. With a tutorial with 3 levels, Easy difficulty with 6 levels, and then Medium, Hard, Complex and Extra each having 8 levels, you have a total of 41 gaps to cross. While there is no sandbox mode as such, there are a couple of cheats available to increase your budget and unlock all materials for that level. As well as all of the included levels, the game includes a menu option to load other levels within the game, though I'm not sure where you may be able to find these additional locations.
If you have any interest in trying a bridge construction simulator, this is the game to go for. The most options for building your bridges as well as the ability to load custom levels makes this title the best choice.

Don't let the word "simulation" fool you, this is a very clean, pretty, easy to master, yet very challenging puzzle game.
I bought it on a whim and regret nothing.
While the game may not be visually stunning or incredibly detailed in simulation, this streamlined design ends up working incredibly well for setting the stage for creative problem solving. There is no right or wrong way to complete a level. In fact, every level is open-ended, although it never feels like I'm at a loss for what to do due to a very good difficulty curve, yet at the same time increasingly challenging requirements. Levels are bite-sized, so the game could easily be enjoyed during a short break, and toward higher difficulties requirements and resources tend to vary more and more ensuring that there is no collapse to a single working design.
This is not the most graphically gorgeous game, nor does it provide the most extensive simulation, but neither is really needed to properly exercise the brain in the regions other than the overstimulated run/aim/shoot reflexes. And should your destructive needs be overwhelming, there is nothing like collapsing an enormous steel and iron structure, watching the passenger train on top of it plummet to its doom.
Well worth the sale price, runs on pretty much any computer, and is a great amount of fun.

Item shop has "Recomended" pre-set for you too buy, but you always can go wild by opening "All-Items" folder. You can buy 6 items like in Dota or LoL, but you also have 4 additional slots for your active items and consumables (2 for each).
So far the biggest struggle for me are voice commands, but It's nice that they are there, along with Pings on mini-map, this can save your time if you know the right key-combo to say something to your teammates.

I see how devs wanted to go for CoD-like(I'm very funny) experience, but they simply look aesthetically ugly.
There are also rewards for playing game every day and for reffering friend who told you about this game.

Alien: Isolation was released a year and eight months following the disastrous Aliens: Colonial Marines. In that time hype had certainly built up around the title that promised to deliver a tense, authentic experience similar to the classic 1979 film that kicked off the franchise as a whole, but then Colonial Marines had promised much the same relative to 1986’s Aliens, and we all saw how that ended up.
And whilst hopes remained eternally high, as they always do, trust was relatively low. It helped that we were dealing with Creative Assembly here, who despite the Rome 2 fiasco hadn’t quite garnered the consumer hostility Gearbox seem committed to invigorating (particularly because, unlike Gearbox, CA endeavoured to fix the problems with their game). They found themselves in interesting circumstances following up such a catastrophe with another expectant release within the same IP, and the pressure was on to produce a quality product that would do justice to the film series from whence it came.
But would they deliver? Would Alien: Isolation to go turn the tide of player sympathies, or would it go down as just another disappointment following one of the key moments in the collapse of consumer confidence in the AAA gaming industry?
You are Amanda Ripley – daughter of Ellen, and an engineer sent out as part of a team travelling to Sevastopol station after the flight recorder of her mother’s ship, the Nostromo, is recovered.  Arriving at Sevastopol, you find the station damaged and the dwindling population less than receptive to meeting new people, but armed humans prove to be the least of your worries, for something stalks the corridors of the station, something alien…
What sounds like a simple premise is extended (some may say ‘dragged’) out into a rather lengthy experience - just when you think you’re safe, something goes wrong, and you’re thrown back into the fray again to find another way out. The game kicks you in the balls like this three or four times before the final conclusion, and although some reviewers found this to be frustrating, I never had any huge issues with it - while Alien: Isolation isn’t the most groundbreaking in coming up with ways to keep you in the haunted house for longer than you’d like, the experience of being there is enjoyable enough that I never found it to be tedious.
I believe the complaint about the false endings comes from the fact that the gameplay is predominately the same throughout, and when making a stealth-horror game and relying on tension to keep the player captivated and motivated, fear can wear thin when you’re confronted with the similar mechanics and enemies again and again. Fortunately, there's enough creativity and unpredictability at work to keep the player on their toes most of the time, and the game itself is rarely a breeze to get through.
The greatest triumph of Alien: Isolation is the xenomorph itself. It’s likely that you’ve heard all about the AI and how they did what they did within the game, but hype aside the Alien is utterly groundbreaking. There’s an issue I sometimes have with games that try to establish innovative mechanics in that they often feel like a tech demo for said mechanic, and have a rather simplistic or shallow execution of said tech. You could criticise the original Assassin’s Creed for this, I personally criticised Shadow of Mordor for the same reason, and I suppose one could level the same accusation at A:I if you didn’t find the gameplay to be your cup of tea. But the sheer aggressive intelligence of the alien makes it a continually menacing foe and keeps the game feeling fresh and exciting even hours in. It’ll track you by sound, disappear into the vents and reappear unpredictably, and move around behind the walls (apparently all within the actual game world – no ambient sound effects tricking you here). Sometimes you’ll hear it in the ceiling and it won’t appear, sometimes it will, and sometimes all the warning you’ll get is a stream of saliva dripping from a vent before you stumble underneath and it drags you up to your death. It can be distracted by crafted devices, but will be less fooled by these the more you use them, and scared off by flames, but this too produces diminishing returns with use. There can be some frustration accompanying the moments in which the Alien relentlessly patrols that one corridor you need to get by to continue, but if you find it becoming tedious, there are mods out there that improve the unpredictability of the creature, and I personally found these to give the game a new life after my first playthrough.
Other enemies include the aforementioned humans, and the androids that populate the station - the 'Working Joe's; a legion of no-frills synthetics who all bear the same featureless plastic face, and terrifying glowing eyes. They are controlled by the station's central AI, and are not always hostile to the player, but you'll rarely know their particular inclinations until you get too close. Hostile or otherwise though, they are intimidating and creepy, and are another unforgettably oppressive foe that you'll find yourself desperately avoiding.
All this takes place in a gorgeously environment; Sevastopol station is stunningly realised, and you’d be forgiven for thinking that screenshots of the game are photographs as the visuals are photorealistic at times. There's a certain lifelessness to the human characters that tugs at the immersion, but you won't spend a lot of time face-to-face with many humans. The only other quibble I could make about the visuals would be the anti-aliasing (in that even at max settings it is not ideal) and as the camera sways you may notice pixel creeping at the edges of items and scenery, a small flaw that acts as a frayed thread at the seam of the beautiful tapestry that is A:I’s presentation, but generally speaking the game runs exceptionally well for the quality of its presentation.
There was a lot of expectation preceding Alien: Isolation’s release, and I think a collective sigh of relief for many people upon playing the game for the first time. The harshest critics may see it as a one-trick pony, although I personally found it to be a consistently gripping experience, and once you’ve gone a few rounds with the xenomorph, you’re unlikely to forget your first time. As stealth games go, A:I manages to lie a few strides ahead of the pack, and CA’s devotion to the 1979 classic film is one clear and present reason for this. It may not be the type of game you’re used to playing from the studio, but perhaps it’s all the better for that.

Alien: Isolation is a First Person Stealth Action Survival Horror Adventure game developed by Creative Assembly who previously only made Strategy games. Of course everyone was going to doubt that the game could be successful especially with SEGA as publisher, but OH BOY I NEVER HAD SUCH A IMMERSION TENSION JOYRIDE OF UNBELIEVABLE STEALTH SURVIVAL FUN. To put it simply: The best Alien game ever made to date. We are going in depth about the weaknessess and strengths of this game.
Quite simple: You play as Amanda Ripley, a Weyland Yutani Engineer/Technician who got contacted by Samuels, a Weyland Yutani Android, for helping him retrieving a black box from the Nostromo, the ship of Amandas Mum, the infamous Ellen Ripley. Amanda of course desperately searching for her since years, agrees and both head together with a crew and ship called Torrens, towards the destination: Sevastopol Station. Where not everything seems to be as it seems... Alien of course. The story develops further on and everything else would be a small spoiler, so we stay with just the summary.
Of course as a heavily stealth focused survival horror game the AI of the alien, androids and humans (three main enemy types you will encounter) is important. Let´s begin with the humans and androids. Humans and androids have good hearing senses and can spot you quite fast from far if not hiding behind some object. Be careful. Their field of view is limited to a small front angle but within that angle they spot moving targets very quickly. Humans mostly carry weapons and use them with quite an accuracy, so be careful if starting a shootout. It´s more wise to distract them with flares or other gadgets. Androids are tricked or killed or stealthed the same way. They simply respond slower and react different. You craft gadgets by your own like noisemaker, flashbangs, etc. You find scrap and components on your way through the station which you use for crafting. Easy way to take care of androids: Later on you get even on medium difficulty enough shotgun ammo to just go face to face with an android and shoot the ♥♥♥♥ out of it, one hit kill in the face, as long as no alien is in the proximity it´s the best method. Androids don´t use weapons.
It has a lack of eyes. Thing is, the alien has no real eyes, it uses sensoral techniques to sense its environment, meaning you could actually stand in front of one if it were dumb enough to not sense that you are not a human. But your heart rythm, warmth and other things indicate you are its target. Makes it harder to sense you when behind cover but it´s still possible if its sensors sense you strong enough and it notices you. The sensor has to detect something directly while other senses scan the environment with less sensitive efficiency. It´s not the perfect organism, but its an extremely dangerous animal that uses certain abilities of its host trademarks. Humans: walking up straight, full adult; dogs & cats, four legged and dumber, etc. More on lore on wiki. The behavior of the alien AI is adopting meaning it learns. You drag your attention across the whole room twice, it´s definitely going to be waiting for you the third time if it knows you use that route often. Its routing behavior compared to androids or humans is very aggressive and never set, so be thankful if it doesn´t see you quickly hiding somewhere even if you were uncovered for a sec. The alien crawls in the vents most of the time, if it comes down it never looks your way and if it does, due to it´s temporarily blindness that moment, lets you often but not always give enough time to hide. It works like this: You enter a new area, you can explore a bit, make sure you memorize hiding spots, it comes down, you hide. You wait till it goes back into the vents and you can continue, but be careful it´s unpredictable, it can come down anytime, depending on its mood it can come down immediately after climbing up too. You can hide in lockers, small shifting units, under tables, everything really works, even simply cowering behind crates.
There are no autosaves. You can only save at save stations which take some time so the alien can still attack you while saving, it actually never happened for me, you really have to be a loud dork in order to make it attack you during saving. There are always enough save points so don´t worry about dark souls like progress loss. Save points are often designed to be reused during backtracking for new objectives.
The reason I didn´t found the backtracking annoying was because you are always send to new areas and objectives, you only backtrack through once played areas because they are on the way for the elevator or ladder which you need to use in order to get to the new area. Stealth works on it and the game simply works. Level Design was done in a excellent job. Always alternative ways or hiding spots and tables and just a very good amount of levels designed simply to work for stealth or action. Balancing simply works too, you always find enough stuff for crafting, you always find the stuff you want in order to craft something special. You always find enough ammo in areas where you are able to shoot or fight and you always have enough hiding spots for 100% stealthing also called ghosting if you should run out of ammo against androids or humans once. Still be careful with ammo and especially gadgets and mines/bombs/molotovs. They are simply too useful in order to waste em on humans or the alien. Androids can really be ♥♥♥♥♥es in this game.
Like mentioned earlier you always go into new areas, later on in the game you will go to the reactor and other really incredible awesome places, walks outside the station and a nostalgia dripping derelict mission. I really loved how every new level felt unqiue and satisfying and they really pulled it off to drag the player into a 100% immersion tube. Just sucking away at the atmosphere and incredible lighting. The graphics overall are beautiful and fantastic! Only a few low res textures here and there but you don´t notice them anyway. It´s a really great port! I checked it and my R9 280X always was 60fps+ sometimes rampaging at 180fps! It had a usage of 99% all the time, my Xeon E3 1230 v3´s cores were all from 25 to 50% and the RAM was about 3,7GB high. Incredible low usage of VRAM! Only about 700MB at the beginning to max 1GB at huge scenes. This game is playable with cards like a 9800gtx or maybe even older, of course a 9800gtx only has 512MB VRAM so it depends on your settings. The game looks fantastic even on lowest settings! Only shadows should stay at medium if possible and lighting should be turned on, or else you might experience a major atmopshere loss. There´s a typical lack of anti aliasing options, so you will always have to fight with edges, it´s endurable with FXAA or any forced edge detected filter but, I wished they would have implemented good old MSAA. Downsampling, yup... seems like many have problems with it, but who knows... I personally don´t try that out. The game is about 20 to 24 Hrs long easily. Maybe 18. Last of Us length to Thief 2014 length. You really get a lot for your money. Occulus Rift supported by rewriting a file.
Except for the AI misbehaviors here and there, the backtracking and the often use of pull this or that lever, everything works, everything is fun and it gave me a really great time onboard the Sevastopol. Easily 9/10 if played by core gamers with brains. Some stealth like bakas and wonder why they die.

I have had a blast in this game on my first play-through!  I played as Emily and as non-lethal as I could all the way up until the very end.  I domino killed 99% of Delilah's witches and then in the final part, I decided to return to the non-lethal approach.  It was simply a matter of knowing how much ammunition I had available and acting in the best way to manage it all until the end part.

I really like how my decisions actually effect the game.  For example, I chose to put someone to sleep in a mission and when I completed the mission, I came out and Meagan Foster's right arm was restored and that was a very pleasant surprise!  That is just one example of how effectual my decisions were in the game.  I am not going to give spoilers, so you'll just have to play it and see for yourself - which I certainly do recommend.

I love games that I can play multiple times in multiple ways.  I have also played Dishonored (1) as lethal and then as non-lethal and it definitely effected that game's gameplay as well.  So, I recommend that everyone also experience Dishonored (1) as well.

This game is one I was sceptical about buying at first, simply because people had noted the lack of content and the lack of expansion once the core mehanics had been thoroughly explored - but while this is true, I don't believe that these are reasons to write the game off. I think it's important to remember that this game is in early access: if you want a full, complete experience, then don't buy this game. But if you want a very saturated, enjoyable experience that you *will* sometimes be burnt out on because of the essence of the game's mechanics - but equally one that will be expanded upon before and after release - then I whole heartedly recommend this game. I bought this game in its current state, continue to play it, and will commend it for one reason: I think the devs deserve the support and credit, because this does truly feel like an already saturated and very fun game.
That said, you do need to have a particular fondness for the core mechanics: ultimately a farming management sim, with adventure quests part of day-to-day activity, but also quite a lot of collecting 'plorts' (essentially poop from feeding the slime, which are fed into the ever-changing market for newbucks), ensuring there is enough food for your slimes, and harvesting the fruit/veg; ontop of this, there are multiple areas to unlock which expand your ranch, to accommodate more and different types of slime. I personally enjoy this mehanic a lot; I don't mind the routine tasks of maintaining the ranch, simply because it contributes to the wider picture and makes this sim everything it is. The slimes are adorable, you already know this, but you need to keep them alive and happy (as well as ensure they're contributing to your plort income, of course) - and this in itself is a reason to enjoy the day-to-day maintenance of the ranch: I love feeding them, because I love them. Because they're so darn cute - and honestly... tabby cat slimes... who doesn't think that's adorable? I've seen a few reviews mention that the novelty quickly slows down because of the apparent lack of depth, however, I do feel like I've so much yet to discover (at 7 or so hours in, I feel like I've only touched the surface), and I think this vouches for the integrity and depth this game already has. While yes, it can feel like there is a gap that needs to be filled, it does a lot to distract you from that; and I'm sure that the devs will provide us with something to fill that gap continuously in the future.
Another notable thing is that there is no real, obvious objective. The objective is a continuous, day-to-day routine of maintaining the farm. There is no one objective, but multiple that work together to form a sense of success. You strategically combine the right kinds of slimes, and you feed them their favorite food, then you get rewarded for this with even more of the valuable kinds of plorts - so, more newbucks. This could probably feel empty for a person who wants to be told what to do, wants quest objectives, wants an endpoint; but people who like the simple task of maintaining and expanding a ranch, and exploring for new slimes and beautiful scenery, will enjoy this. And who knows, maybe the devs will add more of a quest line in the future; that's even more of a reason to not give up on this game, and check back periodically.
TL;DR, this game stays true to the core mechanics of a farming simulator, it will feel a bit of a grind and you may get burnt out on it, along with there not being a great deal of content - however, this game is in early access so it will likely be expended upon; so, support the devs and buy the game if you don't mind not buying the complete product, although it already feels very polished without it being complete. Besides, the content that already is there does feel enough to justfiy buying and supporting the game.

I'll start off by saying that I have played enough of it to make a somewhat good "review", maybe not convincing but please keep in mind what I say, this is my experience of the game.
Call of Duty - Advanced Warfare Multiplayer is a completely OK FPS game. However I must warn you, that if you liked Titanfall and was looking for something similar THIS IS NOT THE GAME YOU'RE LOOKING FOR. Even though there is booster jetpacks, they are not the same. In this game, they're a pain up the ****. You can boost forward, backwards to the sides, "double-jump", etc. The enemies are going to jump around like crazy. If you want to hit them you'll need to practise quite a bit. This is NOTHING like the previous CoD games, you will get frustrated when the enemies easily enough with their booster flee from you. It promotes running around a lot more (to a level of using SMGs and hip-fire all the time is all you need), what is good with this though, is that it counters camping. It is much harder to camp in this game which must be one of the greatest things ever in CoD history. But overall, I enjoy it, even if I get frustrated about the OP boosters, it's still a fun game. The supply cases that you can get at the end of matches are very interesting and a very nice asset to the game. They can give your Operator (your soldier) new helmets, new body armour, new boots, gloves, exo-skeleton... Yes the game has soldier customization! The supply cases can also give you weapons with already attached attachments (not detachable) and will have different stats from the base version of the gun and they also have skins, random skins, it's actually quite fun to see what you get in your supply cases and try out the new weapons you get to see if they're good or bad for your own style.
That was the multiplayer. Now for the singleplayer a.k.a campaign.
The campaign was fun to be honest. It's the first CoD game since MW2 that I actually enjoyed the campaign of. I grew tired of CoD games because the story in the campaign was always bad (only including games AFTER MW2). And I told myself "I will give CoD a last chance (after not purchasing Ghosts). If AW is a good or at least average enjoyable game, I will keep purchasing CoD games. Because if AW is good, you never know if the next game is gonna be good, if it's bad I'll give up on the series.". I haven't given up. Multiplayer is good, it's easily enjoyable and the campaign was interesting and FUN. Good story, good gameplay.
I recommend the game, because I enjoyed it. You might not like it the same.

Half-Life and it's sequel are my favorite first person shooters. The franchise offers a unique experience to the genre that has yet to be surpassed. I have replayed them hundreds of times!
Black Mesa offers an incredible re-imagining of Half-Life. Both in terms of it's gorgeous visuals and spectacular audio. The people who were responsible for it's detailed  environments, sound design and character development are a top notch level of talent! The Crowbar Collective has offered a stellar tribute to one of the greatest games of all  time. I wouldn't change anything about what the game offers in terms of its presentation.
What I would change is the most important part of any fps, the combat. The developers have decided against an exact replication of the original game. There certainly is nothing wrong with that choice. In fact I am overjoyed they decided to optimize some of Half-Life's more tedious and unnecessarily long chapters. While this has worked to improve the games pacing, it has hurt a crucial area of it's mechanics.
Black Mesa's redesign of the weapons makes fighting enemies far more aggravating. This is partially due to the larger number of enemies that have been included into the new ambush sections. Dealing with these new threats is particularly difficult because the reduced amounts of ammo that can be carried. Also, the damage in certain weapons (Specifically anything using explosives) has been reduced substantially compaired with the arsenal in Half-Life. Let me use the submachine-gun as a perfect example.
The SMG from Half-Life One:
Ammo: 50 round clip - 250 reserve - 10 grenades. Fairly accurate with a fair amount of recoil that was automatically compensated by Freeman.
As anyone knows the amount of ammo and number of guns was reduced significantly from half life one to its sequel. However whatever Valve took away they added something to replace it.
The SMG from Half-Life Two:
Ammo: 45 round clip - 225 reserve - 3 grenades. Very accurate and faster firing speed with a small amount of recoil that was automatically compensated by Freeman.
While we lost a small amount of bullets and large number of grenades, we gained a far
more accurate SMG with a higher rate of fire.
This is what the SMG looks like in Black Mesa:
Ammo: 30 round clip - 150 reserve - 3 grenades. Accurate in small bursts with a fair amount of recoil that is NOT compensated by Freeman. Grenades damage and area of effect was also reduced.
By these numbers the new SMG should be pin point accurate, no recoil at all and should fire even faster. The alternative being that the grenades should be at least 2 times more powerful than either of the Half-Life's.
While I could certainly go over the issues I have for each of the weapons, I won't.
Instead I will offer a quick list of changes that, in my opinion, would make for a better tribute.
1: Pistol - Half-Life 2 - Semi-Auto is love, Semi-Auto is life.
2: Magnum - Half-Life 2 - Suit Zoom + Accuracy = Head shot.
3: SMG - See Above... :-)
4: Shotgun - Half- Life 1 - Needs interruptible reload animation.
5: Crossbow - Remove the arch, faster reload, 25 ammo.
6: RPG - Please fix the laser guidance. Rockets bounce off enemies.
7: Explosives - Half-Life 1 level of devastation!
8: Exotic Energy Weapons - No issues.
9: Xen Weapons - All good.
10: Sprinting - Half-Life 1 - Let me sprint in ALL directions.
This is one of the times I wish the recommendation system had a mixed option.

Total War: Rome II is pure enjoyment. Don't be fooled by the negative reviews, it might have some imperfections but all games do. It has everything that makes PC gaming so great and is a must buy if you're a fan of the series or a fan of strategy games.

UPDATE: The review below was from long ago, and it just doesn't do this game and it's community of players justice to not come back and update it. I eventually acquired all the DLC's on sale, and I have to say they all the different campaigns complement each other beautifully. The grand campaign for me takes a bit of tweaking and modding to find the perfect mix but can lead to one hell of an adventure once you find it (thanks to all the brilliant modders for really keeping the enthusiam alive for this game after an underwhelming launch, which pushed CA to continue polishing on thier end). Also, I have become a huge fan of Historical video series that have been created using this game, it is a testament to how much this game can offer. I tried at one point and maybe will come back to it at some day. Once I build my new PC I plan on getting into multiplayer battles, which I never experienced, and put my tactical expertise to the test (or get wrecked). CA can never get enough credit for allowing someone like me who had watched Gladiator 10 times before I was even a teenager to experience these massive, hellacious battles from the ancient world in stunning detail. To another 20 years of Total War. END OF UPDATE
The previous Rome and Mediaval 2 have set the bar extremely high and I was very excited to see the latest installment to the series. I understand there have been other entries in Total War series since those two gems, but the smaller map of Shogun and the newer technology available in Empire put them in seperate categories in my opinion. The presentation is top notch as usual and really brings you into the time period. Rome 2 tries a number of different things and while some are great ideas that are definite improvements over the previous titles, others are a little dissapointing.
A list of the good changes/improvements from Rome and Medieval:
*Settlements now have garrisons, and different buildings will generate specific troops that will defend the city.
*Agents have more available actions and can enhace armies and settlements in different ways, and also hinder the enemy.
*All characters (agents, generals, admirals) can be upgraded in whatever areas you choose.
*Armies and navies carry traditions, and while the troops may be destroyed the traditions can be reinstated. (This is defenitly one of my favorite features of the game.)
*Allies can be given war targets to conduct a joint attack.
*Armies and Navies operate together and you can launch awesome naval invasions and deliver your troops right to the enemie's gate.
And now some of the new features that are not quite improvements but still have potential:
*While it is more realistic that only generals can lead armies outside of settlements, it also prohibits you from combining forces and the limit on the amount of generals you can have slows the game down. (Admirals and navies work the same way.)
*Holding slaves is a good idea but they don't seem to benefit you in any way and instead simply revolt against you again and again until you realize to stop enslaving your defeated foes.
*The abilities that units have on the battlefield do provide an advantage but it also leads to micro-managing as your constantly activating them and then waiting for the cooldown. Once again good concept but not good execution.
*Only capitals have wall defenses, the other villages cannot be fortified which doesn't make much sense.
*The politics system seems useless and not nearly as engaging as it strives to be. Alot of work can be done in this area.
*At some point Rome will become divided and a civil war will break out, but there should be more factors that lead up to it and affect it's outcome.
I admire CA for trying new things but the diplomacy and politics seems a bit stripped down from Rome 1 and Medieval, and it becomes a bit repetitive. Constantly fighting slave revolts and losing settlements because they can't be fortified becomes frustrating. The battles are thrilling, but the enemy A.I., espicially when you are under siege, is so predictable that you'll be able to win no matter the odds. Most of these issues are just minor annoyances, but its the performance issues that have turned away many Total War fans. Thankfully those of us who have been patient have seen a much improved game, either from updates or fan-made fixes. The fact is that for $60 you would expect more from the developers of such a great series, and I am still shocked at how CA expects us to pay even more just to play as factions that should have been in the game to begin with, like Sparta and Athens. I refuse to pay for the DLC campaigns unless they offer some major improvements to the base game.
All in all, this is a great game and even at full price I can recommend it to strategy and history enthusiasts, and as usual the large amount of mods can offer significant improvements to features you dislike, so try them out until you find the perfect match for you.

This review was written after finishing the game on Hard difficulty:
There's a part at the very early stages of the game, just after my first "encounter" with the Alien (through a cinematic) where I was waiting for a transit to take me to another section of the station. I was sitting next to the transit gate, all crouched up, just like the pre-release videos and inteviews taught me to do, waiting in a big dark room for my transit to arrive.
I knew that there's no way the Alien will suddenly drop down and attack me there. "It's too soon", I told myeself, but then the music kicks in, the transit takes its sweet time and Ripley starts whispering "Come on", so I started feeling doubt; Maybe the Alien will come anyway? Maybe I'm not as safe as I thought? The transit did eventually come, the Alien didn't appear and I moved on to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ my pants in a whole new section of the game.
This is where Alien Isolation truly shines: it makes you feel like you're being hunted even when you aren't.
This game was all that was promised - and more. It is the most fun (in quite the terrifying sense) I had with an Alien related game since Rebellion's AvP from back in 1999, and the best survival horror experience since System Shock 2 (we'll get back to that game later). This game is so good in so many ways it made me forgive it for not having any type of multiplayer.
So what makes this game earn this much praise out of me right off the bat?
Let's start with the visuals: The game is gorgeous. I'm not a big graphics guy and usually the aesthetic aspect of games takes a back seat for me, but the effort that was put into the environments is part of what makes this game amazing. It plays very well with light and darkness and makes great use of the low tech Sci-Fi feel of the original Alien from 1979.
Add to that the amazing sound effects of the game, and you get a sense of total immersion: The station looks very believable with trash, magazinges and games laying around the place, completely selling the notion that people lived here not too long ago. The random pipes that can be frequently found around the station resemble the Alien's dome head in dark areas, while the ventilation shaft and air leak sounds resembe its hisses, adding even more to the scare factor.
The design of the Working Joes is also good and fits into a horror game perfectly. Them being an inferior synthetic design by a failing corporation sells their looks quite well.
As for the gameplay itself: It seems as though the developers of Creative Assemby took everything that was great in System Shock 2 and implemented it in the Alien universe. You arrive  on a station where something has gone horribly wrong and are now trying to figure out what is going on. You learn about the characters and the events that took place on the Sevastopol through notes and Audio Logs, which add a lot of depth to the storyline. Creative Assemby invested a lot of effort in creating the Seegson corporation and making it fit as a part of the Alien universe alongside Weyland-Yutani, and it shows. To the point where by the end of the game you can't even remember what the Alien universe was like without Seegson.
The progression of the game is quite linear, but the game does give you many options for exploration (not an easy thing to do with a homicidal Alien on your tail). It even features backtracking elements that were prominent in in System Shock 2, making you feel like you're truly running around on a space station and not just moving from one scene to the next.
You have three main enemies to watch out for during the game: Humans, Working Joes and the Alien itself. There's a fourth enemy as well that reveals itself to you in the late game, which I will not discuss due to spoilers. Humans and Working Joes are quite dumb and are usually easy to deal with. Some of them will attack you, while others will leave you be. It will be up to you to discover their intentions, which adds to the sense of fear during the game.
The Alien, being the main star of the game, is quite fearsome. Once it finally reveals itself to you, it does not disappoint. It is big, fast, clever and can spot you from a good distance if you cross its line of sight. If the Alien sees (and sometimes hears) you - you're dead. No way to outrun it. While being extra big and extra loud in this game compared to its past incarnations, do not understimate the Alien's ability to sneak up on you. It has killed me from behind, dragged me into vents and even flat out dropped down right on my face more times than I could count. This makes the Alien a menace even when you finally get a Flamethrower.
The hacking ability - another element that seems as if it was taken right out of System Shock 2 - is a rather simple test of mental and reactionary challenges. The trick is that you're never safe while performing them. You'll be surprised how hard (and dangerous) it becomes to complete something as simple as a shape matching challenge while hearing the Alien's footsteps thumping in the background.
The save system of the game is quite nice as well. You can only save the game in special checkpoints that look like payphones. Those checkpoints take time to save and also warn you when hostiles are nearby. The game will have you praying to reach an area with one of those payphones around and to be able to save safely. Yes, you can die while saving. Yes, the Alien managed to get me this way as well.
Every other action you take - opening doors; cutting through barriers; accessing terminals; activating generators - are all designed to slow you down and make you feel vulnerable. Instead of just interacting with a door by pressing E, for example, you'll be required to hit a series of key combinations. Different doors and levers require different key combinations.
In short, the gameplay goes through a lot of trouble to convey that every action you take, even as trivial as opening a door, comes with a cost.
As good as this game is, it does have a few issues that, while minor, can't be ignored:
The first is the Human/Working Joe AI. While their AI is not horrible, the huge difference between their AI and the Alien's impressive AI breaks immersion at times.
The second is the Working Joes during the late game. Missions 11-13 in particular. The Working Joes are scary and interesting in the early game, when you're low on weapons and supplies, but in the late game they become nothing more than a hassle. During missions 11-13 the Alien threat is temporarily removed and the game lets you know it, so the missions turn into Joe hunting missions where you can just go to town on them with the strongest guns in your arsenal.
The third is the lip sync in this game. While the voice acting is, at the most part, impressive, it doesn't seem to sync very well with the lip movements of the characters.
The fourth is the controls option in the menu. For some reason, it shows gamepad keys to me while I use keyboard/mouse.
Overall though, this game is a must in any Alien fan's game library. If you're looking for a game that brings back honor (and horror) to the Alien franchise; if you're looking for a survival horror experience that's based more on atmosphere, immersion and a sense of helplessnes than on jump-scares and scripted events; if the idea of playing a game of cat and mouse with an unkillable foe equipped with an impressive AI speaks to you - you will love Alien: Isolation.

This is the greatest video game ever made.
I realize that's a hard sell.
It's also the truth, at least, in my own personal opinion. Rebind the keys, check out PC Gaming Wiki's modding guide to improve the archaic graphics, put on some headphones, stick it up on a good-sized monitor (something that takes up a lot of your field of view, ideally), get past the initial opening hump, and experience the game that inspired so many greats, from Bioshock to Portal, Dead Space to Fallout 3.
System Shock 2 is the game that inspired a friend of mine to say "hey, you're right, Doc, it is better than Bioshock!" One of the highest-rated games of all time, but System Shock 2 outdoes it. It's a better horror game, a better adventure game, a better RPG, and an all-around better game than Bioshock. Its widespread influence on gaming is undeniable, and at least, if not more influential, than Half-Life.
Yeah, it's old, so it looks ugly and doesn't have the kind of animation quality you might find in a newer game. Yeah, the weapons degrade, and some people don't like that. Yeah, the key bindings are weird and awful. But it's great. This game has some of the best atmosphere and storytelling you'll ever encounter, and the experience will sear itself into your brain, the way staring at the sun sears itself onto your eyeballs.
You may play games you think are better, but you'll be hard-pressed to admit that this isn't one of the best games of all time.
There is no better horror game than this. There are fewer, if any, better gaming narratives than this. Nothing possesses the same emotional highs and lows, even when almost directly copying the game, as Bioshock and Dead Space did.
Remember Citadel. Remember 45100. Have a blast. You won't regret trying.

Pros:
The graphics on Ultra High settings, look great. Of course, I only expect them to get better as development continues, and as the community gets ahold of the CourseForge to create custom courses.
As would be expected, the Early Access version of this game has some issues with the swing meters. However, I still feel that this game has a good foundation to build on with the current meters. Looking forward to the later builds to see what each swing meter feels like.
Also, the simple, in-game match making and chat is decent for an Early Access title.
Cons:
There still seems to be a lot room for growth in this title. Most of the things I would say need to be fixed have already been touched on by other reviewers. However, I would have to differ in my opinion of the severity of the negative comments. I think that the main areas that will help improve the quality of this release are more player customization options, refined motion swing meter / character interaction, and more courses(...CourseForge).
Overall, I am happy with the quality for such an early version of what has the potential to be an amazing golf game. Like I said, I am truly excited about the release of CourseForge, as I believe it will add a great deal of value to this release. I think that some people expect more from Early Access titles, and may be a little harsh on the developers. I hope that they will be able to take the feedback they are receiving, and turn this game into the next big thing in golf simulation software.

Have been following this game for a while now.   The game, at this point, will not dazzle you with its graphics (I'm playing all graphics options maxed out, btw), but what it lacks in glitz, it makes up for with the truest golf mechanics and 'feel' that I've yet come across in a golf video game.
I originally started out with the 3-click meter, because that's what I would normally default to after toying around with other games' motion swings (be it the Wiimote, PS controller or mouse).  However, after deciding to give this game's motion swing a try, I'm hooked.    Finally, a game that nails it.  The motion swing is fantastic.   It feels natural and organic, whether on the full swing, chipping or putting.    It's also deep, and difficult (playing with the assists at 'minimal') but with practice, you see improvement as you start to gain feel and muscle memory, just like in real golf.   The game also provides you with numerical feedback (on the driving range practice mode) to illustrate the errors and there is a guide on Steam that explains the numbers.  In short, there are 3 components - tempo, swing path and face contact, all determined by the speed and directions you move your mouse.
The core game is solid.  Once they put some more spit and polish on this and throw in the course forge and other features, it may just be the definitive golf sim that people have been waiting forever for.

Been waiting for this for some time and it was thoroughly worth the wait. Didn't have to spend a year to learn the game as you can be shooting in the seventies by the second round as I was. It is not easy from there. It shall be many months before I could claim a round average in the low seventies even playing on the easier of the two modes of operation and on the easiest of four settings within that mode. You will get value for money with this game as I see myself never mastering it. The quality of the courses I believe are of a very high standard, better than any other golf sim to date. The in flight ball physics are, in my opinion, near perfect.  Some other ball physics, not so good. Irregular bounce and bounce height need to be tweaked, ball travels too freely through heavy long grass, inconsistent spin on and around greens and ball holds on a bunker face. There is no lie indicator and once on the green the putting, in general, I found it to be a little easy.
But it is early access and as it is with early access there is some work to do which the PP team are already at it. I have no doubt that the team behind this game have their hearts in it and in my opinion they are in this for the long haul, because of this I am unable to see this venture falling over. The game has huge potential.

This game was SO GREAT. Steam says I played it for 2.7 hours, but I played it in offline mode a bunch today. Wow. This game was refreshing. I have a dislike for most AAA games and I'm much more into Indie and RPG Maker games. I'm currently developing 2 games in RPG Maker VX Ace (Which I was delighted to see that this used the same engine) and I must say it was loads of fun thinking about how the programmer went about doing this. Holy Priest really cared for this project, to the point that he thought of it as his child. And that's how I feel about my Poke'Harvest Moon so I can definitely relate! I recommend this game. I'm a stingy kinda guy when I'm spending on myself, especially on Steam, so I probably would not have tried this had it not been free and had an anime look. However, if it did cost money, I would say that I would have gotten my money's worth. Ya know, a good 10-15 dollars like most RPG Maker games. Man. This game was just a treat. Preamble: My Steam account shows 89 hours and last played on Aug. 10th. Not so.
I cant say whether it was a patch or the launch of Win10 since they happened within a couple days of each other but many people suddenly had an issue with the launcher being stuck in an endless loop of wanting to repair itself. It took three rounds with customer service (who responded the same day each time) and was able to fix the problem but the .exe icon on my desktop was seperated from Steam. Not a big deal to me personally.
On with the review:
As many have said, this isnt Skyrim, its an MMO. If your looking for a stand-alone experience and the depth of immersion that comes with it, then opt for Skyrim. That being said, as someone who`s mmo history began shortly after the release of EQ1, Im having a great time with this one having only reach the tender age of level 26.
Different people have different ideas of whats fun in an MMO and ESO allows for this (within its reative sphere).
You can run solo or find a group. Im playing solo and the few time Ive run into a situation where I needed help all I had to do was chill for 10 minutes and someone comes along and we both tackle the baddie and go our seperate ways with no more than a wave. ESO is set up where you can get acheivement credit for a boss as long as you do some damage during the fight. No need to group if you`d rather not. *I think I read early on that with the main bosses you have to do a certain % of damage to get any loot, but I`d need to revisit the forums to verify that.
You can run the quests or grind to veteran rank asap. Ive been doing all the main and side quests and can say Im thoroughly enjoying the journey. Ive found them well written (some really so), engaging and never so long that the feeling of moving along is broken. The rewards offer xp and loot, and have provided me with all the armor and weapon upgrades the PvE enviroment needs.
Every character can equip any weapon or armor but choices matter..and your personal playstyle matters, and can be pretty well accounted for.
Speaking of choices, the character development system is pretty darn ok imo. You aquire points along the way that are applied to both traits and skills. Its easy enough to quickly grasp and deep enough that you will catch yourself chewing your lip over just where to drop that point into. There`s never enough to go around (thats a good thing) so what you choose WILL effect how your toon grows. That being said, the system is forgiving enough that you discover you messed up you can bring things back around within a couple levels usually and if youve completly dropped the whole basket of eggs you can pay in-game gold to reset it all and reapply the points all over again.
There are loads of character build guides available and lots of people use them. Personally, I looked at them just long enough to understand the principles and havent looked back. I want my own character (with all its strengths and faults), not another clone.
The crafting system is robust enough to hold its own imo. Ive been plugging away at all it offers and am only now getting that "ahh, ok. I get this" understanding about what it takes to make the armor sets.
Blacksmithing, alchemy, enchanting, woodworking, clothing, cooking. There`s enough to keep you going and some of this stuff has actual in-game relevance *gasp*.
The download times for the patches and initial purchase can be a bit brutal, so dont buy this thinking to start playing in a couple hours. The game itself took me a solid 24 hours to DL.
Its an mmo and not a single player, so the graphics are geared for an mmo. They arnt the photo realistic quality some people now demand but ya know, my PC is over 5yrs old now so Im running on low settings and it still looks darn purdy.

This review was written after finishing the game on Hard difficulty:
There's a part at the very early stages of the game, just after my first "encounter" with the Alien (through a cinematic) where I was waiting for a transit to take me to another section of the station. I was sitting next to the transit gate, all crouched up, just like the pre-release videos and inteviews taught me to do, waiting in a big dark room for my transit to arrive.
I knew that there's no way the Alien will suddenly drop down and attack me there. "It's too soon", I told myeself, but then the music kicks in, the transit takes its sweet time and Ripley starts whispering "Come on", so I started feeling doubt; Maybe the Alien will come anyway? Maybe I'm not as safe as I thought? The transit did eventually come, the Alien didn't appear and I moved on to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ my pants in a whole new section of the game.
This is where Alien Isolation truly shines: it makes you feel like you're being hunted even when you aren't.
This game was all that was promised - and more. It is the most fun (in quite the terrifying sense) I had with an Alien related game since Rebellion's AvP from back in 1999, and the best survival horror experience since System Shock 2 (we'll get back to that game later). This game is so good in so many ways it made me forgive it for not having any type of multiplayer.
So what makes this game earn this much praise out of me right off the bat?
Let's start with the visuals: The game is gorgeous. I'm not a big graphics guy and usually the aesthetic aspect of games takes a back seat for me, but the effort that was put into the environments is part of what makes this game amazing. It plays very well with light and darkness and makes great use of the low tech Sci-Fi feel of the original Alien from 1979.
Add to that the amazing sound effects of the game, and you get a sense of total immersion: The station looks very believable with trash, magazinges and games laying around the place, completely selling the notion that people lived here not too long ago. The random pipes that can be frequently found around the station resemble the Alien's dome head in dark areas, while the ventilation shaft and air leak sounds resembe its hisses, adding even more to the scare factor.
The design of the Working Joes is also good and fits into a horror game perfectly. Them being an inferior synthetic design by a failing corporation sells their looks quite well.
As for the gameplay itself: It seems as though the developers of Creative Assemby took everything that was great in System Shock 2 and implemented it in the Alien universe. You arrive  on a station where something has gone horribly wrong and are now trying to figure out what is going on. You learn about the characters and the events that took place on the Sevastopol through notes and Audio Logs, which add a lot of depth to the storyline. Creative Assemby invested a lot of effort in creating the Seegson corporation and making it fit as a part of the Alien universe alongside Weyland-Yutani, and it shows. To the point where by the end of the game you can't even remember what the Alien universe was like without Seegson.
The progression of the game is quite linear, but the game does give you many options for exploration (not an easy thing to do with a homicidal Alien on your tail). It even features backtracking elements that were prominent in in System Shock 2, making you feel like you're truly running around on a space station and not just moving from one scene to the next.
You have three main enemies to watch out for during the game: Humans, Working Joes and the Alien itself. There's a fourth enemy as well that reveals itself to you in the late game, which I will not discuss due to spoilers. Humans and Working Joes are quite dumb and are usually easy to deal with. Some of them will attack you, while others will leave you be. It will be up to you to discover their intentions, which adds to the sense of fear during the game.
The Alien, being the main star of the game, is quite fearsome. Once it finally reveals itself to you, it does not disappoint. It is big, fast, clever and can spot you from a good distance if you cross its line of sight. If the Alien sees (and sometimes hears) you - you're dead. No way to outrun it. While being extra big and extra loud in this game compared to its past incarnations, do not understimate the Alien's ability to sneak up on you. It has killed me from behind, dragged me into vents and even flat out dropped down right on my face more times than I could count. This makes the Alien a menace even when you finally get a Flamethrower.
The hacking ability - another element that seems as if it was taken right out of System Shock 2 - is a rather simple test of mental and reactionary challenges. The trick is that you're never safe while performing them. You'll be surprised how hard (and dangerous) it becomes to complete something as simple as a shape matching challenge while hearing the Alien's footsteps thumping in the background.
The save system of the game is quite nice as well. You can only save the game in special checkpoints that look like payphones. Those checkpoints take time to save and also warn you when hostiles are nearby. The game will have you praying to reach an area with one of those payphones around and to be able to save safely. Yes, you can die while saving. Yes, the Alien managed to get me this way as well.
Every other action you take - opening doors; cutting through barriers; accessing terminals; activating generators - are all designed to slow you down and make you feel vulnerable. Instead of just interacting with a door by pressing E, for example, you'll be required to hit a series of key combinations. Different doors and levers require different key combinations.
In short, the gameplay goes through a lot of trouble to convey that every action you take, even as trivial as opening a door, comes with a cost.
As good as this game is, it does have a few issues that, while minor, can't be ignored:
The first is the Human/Working Joe AI. While their AI is not horrible, the huge difference between their AI and the Alien's impressive AI breaks immersion at times.
The second is the Working Joes during the late game. Missions 11-13 in particular. The Working Joes are scary and interesting in the early game, when you're low on weapons and supplies, but in the late game they become nothing more than a hassle. During missions 11-13 the Alien threat is temporarily removed and the game lets you know it, so the missions turn into Joe hunting missions where you can just go to town on them with the strongest guns in your arsenal.
The third is the lip sync in this game. While the voice acting is, at the most part, impressive, it doesn't seem to sync very well with the lip movements of the characters.
The fourth is the controls option in the menu. For some reason, it shows gamepad keys to me while I use keyboard/mouse.
Overall though, this game is a must in any Alien fan's game library. If you're looking for a game that brings back honor (and horror) to the Alien franchise; if you're looking for a survival horror experience that's based more on atmosphere, immersion and a sense of helplessnes than on jump-scares and scripted events; if the idea of playing a game of cat and mouse with an unkillable foe equipped with an impressive AI speaks to you - you will love Alien: Isolation.

Having bought and played the game earlier this month, I'd like to recommend it to anyone who can appreciate the original 1979 film and anyone who is looking for a comprehensive and intense game that doesn't involve endless shooting.
In its best moments the game nails the atmosphere and setting of the film, with superb audiovisual design true to the original analog and 'used future' aesthetic, from the station itself to the lighting to the sound and the music. The star of the story, our perfect organism, is a formidable foe that is not easily fooled and will keep you on the edge of your senses. There are many tense situations where you walk around warily even when there is no sign of the alien, on your motion detector or otherwise, and there are welcome changes of adversaries and scenery, even though the story mostly takes place on the station. The scope is great and those times you witness the vastness and detail of the station from the outside are thrilling in their own right.
At lesser whiles the game can be quite frustrating, where it seems the alien has a homing signal on you. For some levels it is definitely scripted to stay in your vicinity, as it keeps on your tail even when you are very quiet and the part of the station you are in is rather large. Also, not being able to jump over the puniest of obstacles –not being able to jump at all, for that matter– makes for the kind of gaminess that detracts from the otherwise immersive experience. The same goes for the many 'quests', like having to find keycards and passcodes.
But all in all I found this game well worth my while and it was plain to me the developers poured a lot of love and effort into it. I would certainly be up for a 'sequel' and I wager they are too.

I've always thought horror was difficult, if not impossible, to convey in video games, especially when given the tools to fight back.
I was wrong.
You are alone. Resources are scarce. Everything is out to kill you. And it will.
The atmosphere of this game is oppressing, each second as stressful as the previous one, the ship is a convoluted maze filled with terror.
Although it has a few flaws, the story is wonderful, filled with tension and ambiguosity, as you are stuck between SHODAN and The Many, left wondering which of them is the lesser evil.
SHODAN herself definitely earns a place in the pantheon of video game antagonists, not only using deception but also constantly belittling any effort on your part.
As for the gameplay, it's surprisingly advanced for its time, and might seem overwhelmingly complex on your fist run. If you are expecting a shooter, you will probably find it clunky and frustrating, as this game is most definitely a RPG and has all the mechanics of one.
Also worthy of note, the world is fully backtrackable and the level design is incredible, state-of-the-art late 90s fare, albeit falling a bit short towards the end.
A landmark in the scene and a source of inspiration for many others to come, especially the Deus Ex and BioShock franchises, both created by former Looking Glass employees.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone interested in PC gaming history, make sure to play it on the
difficulty setting, which will give you a real challenge and enhance the thick, lingering atmosphere and sense of dread.
if you don't have the game yet then stop playing cod and play a game you will remember for a long time, trust me it is a very good deal for a low price
