Defect 'Spaceship Destruction Kit' pits you as a captain that is located on a dead end planet. As the game opens you build your very first spacecraft, fly it through a mission and then watch in horror as your crew defects to the enemy. You then start the game from scratch. At its heart Defect places you as ship builder, spaceship captain and mercenary in an indie space action-strategy game.
The first and the standout feature of the game is the construction of your spacecrafts. This can be a lot of fun although it often comes down to simple mathematical equations. You have to be wary of how much power and crew that you have at your disposal. You cannot go into the negative in either stat as you wont be able to fly your ship. As a result this places a reasonable limit on what type of ships you can construct. Of further consideration within this feature is the fact that not only do you need to consider power and crew but also armor, speed, maneuverability and of course your attack systems.
Most noteworthy, however, is the fact that you will have your ship stolen from you by your crew on a regular basis. In fact, the 'boss fight' at the end of each mission is you against your old ship. Therefore you are advised not to make your ship too strong. In my opinion this twist on the game limited my enjoyment of this feature. I was always someone who liked creating LEGO spaceships and vehicles with friends. We would then see whose ship was made of the right stuff as we'd smash them to smithereens. Consequently, knowing that I should never make the strongest and best ship possible stripped much of the fun away.
As a result of this feature, however, you the replayability of the game is extended. You can play each mission multiple times with different set ups.
The weakest component of the gameplay, in my opinion, is without doubt the space combat. I've played a number of space shooters this year and something feels a little lacking. The combat outside of the direct control is not rewarding. This is because when not in the mode your crew fires your weapons for you. Your job is simply to guide the ship into the right direction and watch your crew shoot for you.
In direct control mode I feel that the game lacks the fluidity of other space shooters. I would love to tell you that this is based upon just choosing the wrong components for my ships but having attempted a number of varieties they just feel clunky. However, it does feel and play like a twin stick shooter. Left thumbstick controls the direction of your ship, right thumbstick allows you to aim your shots while the right bumper allows you to shoot. One of the best aspects of direct control, however, is the ability to advise your crew which components of your ship they need to concentrate repair efforts on. This increases the strategy involved in the gameplay substantially.
Arguably the strongest component of the combat is the fact that different components of the ships can be destroyed. These include the engines, the guns, etc. This is a nice feature that also increases strategy. If you have the opportunity to aim at the core then this should be your primary target. However, there are times where the protection of the core may make for sense for you to take out the enemy's weapons.
When you do destroy an opponent's ship they drop scrap. This is the in game currency. You'll want to collect as much of it as possible. Scrap also enables you to repair your ships while in combat. Therefore, it is safe to say that scrap should be treated like gold. You're going to need as much of it as possible and wasting it will limit your ability to win.
The graphics are relatively basic but that is all that they really need to be. They get the job done. Missions are played on an isometric 2D board. There is enough flashiness about the spaceships to give it that true feeling of it being a space game. However, the developers did go a little overboard with the neon and the over-saturation of the graphics. However, sometimes this is nice and not necessarily as bad as you may think. Therefore, I'm not going to be overly critical here. Besides, the GUI is a polished deal and that's something so easy to get wrong.
They are far from memorable yet they are far from bad. They appear to have been an afterthought in the development of the game. Arguably the greatest weakness in the audio department is that there is no voiceover work. Had the developers been able to add quality voiceover work it would have added depth to the atmosphere and allowed for a far more immersive experience. Therefore, the sound of the game is arguably the most forgettable part of the game.
Partially. While, as of writing, there are no trading cards there are Steam achievements. There are a total of 16 in all. The majority of them are unlocked as you play through the game the first time. However, there are some that demand you to achieve certain goals in specific levels that may frustrate the achievement hunters out there.
Defect is a game that was made in my hometown. I tend to be a little more critical of things that are made from my hometown so as to show no favoritism or positive bias. What generally ends up happening is the opposite a small negative bias. However, in this case I feel that my review is fair on most points. I would recommend the game to space combat/adventure enthusiasts. Although the game has its fair share of flaws it is a solid game and will provide gamers with a solid experience.

Defect is one of those games that is incredibly frustrating because there's so much here to love, but it's held back by interface design decisions and a massive difficulty curve that leave me simply unable to really recommend it right now.
This isn't because the game is bad, persay - but because after 3 hours of cushy gameplay and having fun with the ship building mechanic, I hit a difficulty spike. 3 hours more, and I've been unable to beat any one of the missions available to make any more progress in the game.
You are going to die a lot in Defect - which is fine. But what isn't fine is how frustrating it is when you die. Not because of how the game chooses to deal with death, but because of how the interface and design decisions of the game make you deal with death.
Build your ship, choose a mission on the map screen, watch the unskippable opening dialogue, play, die, get spat back out to the map screen, watch the unskippable opening dialogue, play, die, etc. If the game didn't waste so much of your time when you died, and allowed you to get straight back into another attempt to finish the level, it may not be so bad.
Later levels feel a little less polished and design-tested than the earlier ones. Early levels feel fairly finely crafted and well-considered, but after a few hours missions rapidly deteriorate into massive waves of enemy ships or torpedos that can instantly destroy you and send you through the cycle of restarting the level all over again.
There's so much here to love. The ship building mechanic is a whole lot of fun, and it makes me wish that they'd gone with a survival mechanic instead of the mission mechanic - survive, destroy enemy ships, gather salvage, upgrade your ship. Instead, the missions get repetetive - complete the objective, destroy your old ship, have your new ship stolen, repeat in the next mission.
The combat is okay, and it feels like tweaking the parts on your ship is hugely important. There is strategy in being a small, fast-moving ship - or a large, hulking one covered in armaments. But the game doesn't seem to fully consider this fact. It may encourage you to build a small, fast-moving ship - only to end a mission by spawning a mass of enemy ships right on top of you.
These are all problems that can be fixed, and I'm willing to give the developers the benefit of the doubt that they will do so. But until then, the game is simply too frustrating to recommend.

First of all, any PC gamer worth his salt already knows this is a masterpiece of sci-fi horror FPSRPG, it's a beast of a game and a cult classic. If you didn't know, that should be enough to convince you, but let me re-iterate it's historical importance and worthiness.
This is the game that not only inspired Bioshock, but everything else like it since (that includes anything from Fallout 3/NV to TES: Morrowind/Oblivion/Skyrim to Borderlands). Here's the basic formula: they took an FPS, added actual RPG elements, a real story, plus a horror atmosphere mixed with a sci-fi theme, and basically created a new genre. That's pretty significant, so if you've played Bioshock and haven't played this, you really should be ashamed of yourself... Fortunately for you, all hope is not lost as SS2 is now available on Steam and fixed to run on modern rigs so you may yet redeem yourself by playing it. Yay!
A word of advice, though SS2 looks and sounds as old as it is, there are excellent texture/model/sound replacement mods available and they work fine with the Steam version. Despite all that, it still feels and plays better than most games of the genre today and remains a very special and highly memorable gaming experience nonetheless.
Let me assure you that if I could have but one single wish answered by the Gods of Gaming it would be for a proper, actual sequel. But for some stupid reason, the license rights are of course tied up in limbo thanks to the absolutely rificulous bureaucratic state of the world, and so us poor gamers are left to suffer without it.

After having sunk 10 hours into this game, I do have a few things to say about it.
Firstly, i'm more of a fast-paced type of gamer (i.e. TF2, Overwatch), but after years of playing the exact same games, I just needed a break. And that's where this game comes in.
When I bought this, I thought this game was just gonna be collecting slimes for about an hour and that was it. But oh boy was it so much more than that. Not only is the style cartoony and lovable, but the world is immersive. You have several different slimes to collect and discover.  You have different paths to choose from, and from these paths an entire, unexplored world may appear. Plus, if you dig a little deeper, there's an entire story for you to read, which isn't what I expected from this type of game.
And to top it all off, the slimes are adorable af. Especially the Hunter slimes. Oh god the Hunter Slimes.
If you're a gamer that likes fun, casual games that you can play at your own pace, or a gamer like me that is looking for a break from competitive games, then you should absolutely get this game. I recommend it all the way.

If you're not especially prone to motion sickness, though, or if you're just more used to play first person games than I am and know your limits better, I ABSOLUTELY recommend this game. It's cute as hell and very easygoing to play. A surprising amount of interesting lore, too! More people should buy it so I can have more videos of it to watch.

It is a great survival horror game for sure. The atmosphere is pretty much the same as Alien and Aliens, albeit there is only one that you are up against. The graphics are real nice and together with the top notch sound effects and music, it creates that eerie atmosphere that keeps you on edge. The first part of the game pretty much puts you up against scripted alien encounters but a few hours later, it turns into a constant chase of cat and mouse. The alien is invincible and the only way for you to "beat" it is to hide and to run. There will be times you will simply hide inside a closet, listening the sound of your tracker. If you keep on using the same paths over and over again, the AI adapts to your moves and your hiding ground becomes the alien's hunting one.
All in all, it is a great game. The only, ONLY downside so far is that you cannot save anywhere you want, but you have to use certain emergency stations (like it was in the old Resident Evil games). It really keeps you on edge but after dying a few times on hard, it may frusturate some gamers.
I saw some complaints about not being able to move as freely as a FPS sandbox game (like seeing a rail and not being able to walk on it rather than using the loooong corridor around). This is not a FPS game, it is a game played from a first person perspective. It doesn't fit the game's dynamics; a girl running around constantly, jumping over gaps and wrecking havoc in her steps. This game is more about hiding, keeping quiet and feeling overwhelmed against an unbeatable predator.
So far, it kept me on edge and I am really having fun. The hospital level was particularly fun!

Cons: The stealth / alien mechanics were clunky at times and you can often find yourself stuck in a locker or under a table while the alien rubber bands around your position, preventing you from making any progress. On hard difficulty it is a serious challenge to creep past the alien and some small sections took 30-45 minutes and many deaths to conquer. It's not so much that the game is difficult and that the alien AI is sophisticated as it ALWAYS seems to patrol around your postion for no definitive reason. Sometimes you find yourself in a zone with other humans and for some reason the alien picks you to follow. It's not really explained if there is any reason why Amanda is such an alien magnet, and the constant proximity of the alien (in the "alien zones") became more frustrating than frightening.
In addition, I found that items and in-world tools (security systems, propane tanks, radios, etc.) that are supposed to help you evade and distract the alien don't really do much. More often than not, trying an elaborate distraction ploy got me killed. I was pretty much constrained to using the flamethrower, hiding in lockers / under tables and waiting until the alien went into the vents to make any progress. After the first few encounters the stealth system felt mundane and repetitive and seemed to rely on dogged patience and occasional foolhardy risktaking rather than cunning or ingenuity.
Pros: The environment is realised exceptionally well, the details are immaculate and convey the essence of the original Ridley Scott film.
The alien never ceases to be terrifying, even when you have weaponary to drive it back. Right up to the last scene in the game I was still jumping and shouting everytime it emerged.
The voice acting by Andrea Deck (Amanda Ripley, the protagonist) is superb and brought me back into the storyline even when the missions were starting to become stale and tedious.
Overall: It's a great game for horror genre enthusiasts and especially fans of the Alien series. It's also the first Alien game that has been done right since the original AvP. That said, it's only probably 20-25 hours of gameplay with limited replayability so I'd recommend waiting till it goes on sale if you are keen to get your money's worth.
I'd also recommend tackling it on a lower difficulty setting than hard if you are aiming for a more "immersive" experience as the alien's infallible perceptual senses on the highest difficulty can make the game something of a grind.

Defect: SDK is one of the most fun games I've played in a while. Honestly, it's simple, fun, yet complex when you actually get into it.
So, let's get to the meat of the game, shall we?
The game focuses on you building ships to complete various missions, however, you may be tempted to make the best ship, and that's where Defect is unique: you fight your own ships.
You see, you're a terrible captain, and the crew (also terrible) throws you out of your ship and claims it as their own in the end of each mission.
The missions at this current state are pretty fun, and seem to be tweaked constantly. The game is really dynamic because of how you build the ship, is how you will play. It's also really satisfying, when you finish that mission that took you so long, or that ship you built that was a great challenge to face.
The weapon diversity is there, you have turrets, beams, beam turrets, just pew pew laser weapons, torpedoes, missiles... A NUKE! (not yet avaliable to build though), shields to protect you from pew pew lasers and specialized shields that block missiles and torpedoes.
The game offers great variety in terms of building, because each component has an unique feel about it and can be rotated to look absolutely different.
So far so good, I'll continue playing this game and update this review as I go.
9.5/10

As someone who counts 'Star Control II' as one of their favorite games of all time, this game is a dream come true.
It's the simple controls and combat of the classic 'Asteroids' added with a easy-to-use ship builder that had me hooked instantly.
Initially you might think that all you need to do in every mission is to build the beefiest combat ship you can afford, but most missions are designed to challenge you to build a ship with very special capabilities to beat it - and just *barely* beat it too, since your current ship will be the final boss of the next mission. This creates an interesting dilemma when you design your ship.
The only annoyance so far to me are the cut-scenes that momentarily remove your controls and/or pan the camera around to show you where ships are warping in or anything important that's going on. While this is perfectly okay and even necessary the first time you play a mission, it quickly becomes an unskippable nuisance when you have to attempt a mission again and again and again. (Thanks again for stopping my ship dead in my tracks for showing me that i really really quickly have to catch up to that one ship over there!)

After having sunk 10 hours into this game, I do have a few things to say about it.
Firstly, i'm more of a fast-paced type of gamer (i.e. TF2, Overwatch), but after years of playing the exact same games, I just needed a break. And that's where this game comes in.
When I bought this, I thought this game was just gonna be collecting slimes for about an hour and that was it. But oh boy was it so much more than that. Not only is the style cartoony and lovable, but the world is immersive. You have several different slimes to collect and discover.  You have different paths to choose from, and from these paths an entire, unexplored world may appear. Plus, if you dig a little deeper, there's an entire story for you to read, which isn't what I expected from this type of game.
And to top it all off, the slimes are adorable af. Especially the Hunter slimes. Oh god the Hunter Slimes.
If you're a gamer that likes fun, casual games that you can play at your own pace, or a gamer like me that is looking for a break from competitive games, then you should absolutely get this game. I recommend it all the way.

I'm only saying I don't recommend it if you're especially prone to motion sickness, like I am. I had fun while I did play it, but once I stopped I noticed myself feeling nauseous. I looked up some tips as to how to ease the symptoms. The devs have been great about trying to accommodate for everyone. But tweaking the FOV could only do so much for me, and I knew I could only fidget so much before going over the 2 hour mark.
If you're not especially prone to motion sickness, though, or if you're just more used to play first person games than I am and know your limits better, I ABSOLUTELY recommend this game. It's cute as hell and very easygoing to play. A surprising amount of interesting lore, too! More people should buy it so I can have more videos of it to watch.

But over time, this cycle begins to feel like a chore; the time for grinding to move on grows larger and larger. An example of this, are the treasure pods scattered everywhere in the game, the player finds them but can't open them, eventually, the player finds out that they need to grind a lot of money to get access to open them, which causes the cycle to occur, discouraging the player to continue playing. Overall though, Slime Rancher is a good game but get it when it's on sale for $13 or less.

Dishonored 2 is more Dishonored and I think that is a good thing.
After the performance issues of the first week the game runs fine on my PC and I am enjoying it a lot.
There are two ways to play the game: As Corvo, the master assassin you took control of in the first game, or his daughter and now Empress of Dunwall Emily. During my first playthrough I am playing as Emily and have to say that the powers she has are a lot of fun. Shadow walk for example lets you crawl around a level more stealthily, and Domino lets you link two enemies in order to have their fatal fate shared. Of course the powers that were available in the first Dishonored do have a comeback here and there are all sorts of Bonecharms that give you extra perks, which can be very helpful to support your playstyle.
The other main character, like in the fist installment of this franchise, is the game world itself. The developers at Arcane Studios have put in a lot of effort to create a living and breathing world with interesting characters and locations that are filled with a ton of lovely details for you to find and fill your pockets with. On top of that the lore you find in books, letters and the environmental storytelling are once more fascinating to me, so I really enjoy to delve into the world of Dishonored 2 every time.
I recommend this game to anyone who liked the first Dishonored and those people who appreciate modern stealth games that draw an interesting world around its mechanics.

I haven't played this on easy or normal, at all. Neither should you. It's a great game with a lot of love put into it and if you like the first movie at all, you might enjoy this. Stealth makes perfect sense for this game and yes, you do have to be patient in it. It's slow, refreshingly so. It doesn't mind taking its time to get things going and for a big budget game, that's pretty rare. This would be a problem if the environments weren't nice to look at or fun to tentatively explore, fortunately they're both.
A:I doesn't rely on fake "I don't want to look at the creepy jumpscare ghost" fear. It's similar to survival horror games in that it's about stress. You don't want to lose that progress/use that item and leave yourself empty-handed later. It's very effective in that respect. Early on, I got frustrated dying over and over again but I realised that this game runs on some strange rules and once I understood them, I was enjoying myself the rest of the way through. You have to be more aggressive than in a typical stealth game, as time is your enemy. The longer you stay somewhere, the more difficult it gets to leave. Also, lockers should be used VERY sparingly. I know this is a little long. I just really like this game.
Creative Assembly said way, way back that they wanted to make A:I like Dead Space 2 and I was pretty worried. I like Dead Space 2, I think of it as a better version of an Uncharted-type game because there's more going on. However, it's an action game with a very chaotic, ADD-ridden pace that would ruin the charm of a proper Alien game. Thankfully it seems all they've taken is some very general ideas and themes. Strangely, it's also kind of similar to The Last of Us with its crafting system and situations where you can fight or stealth your way through.
I love the UI/HUD too, the chunky Atari-inspired block menus and noises and the CRT monitors and the motion tracker (which makes first person stealth work way better). The frequent rewire consoles that a lot of the time don't even do anything useful, just to add a bit of malleability to the world. Everything. I like that even though there are objective markers, there are frequent areas in which the objective zone is 2-3 rooms wide, so when the objective is to find something you do actually have to use your eyes instead of following the on-screen marker like a good monkey.
I like the way the backtracking is done, it makes it feel like a big space station instead of a corridor. I like that you have to plan out some things you want to do with the map screen. I like that the hacking minigames and passcode doors are purely there to make you vulnerable and make more stress. Your character has a body. That shouldn't be a positive point of a game but it's 2014 and a lot of developers are still making the player a floating gun. There are a ton of things I like about A:I and a few I really love about it. No, I wasn't paid to say that.
There are some things I didn't like/could see other people disliking though:
- A lot of cutscenes are video files. For about 5 or less of them, it's justified. There's too much to render without chugging the game. That's fine. Most of them are just people talking or small things happening though. It bloats the file size as a video takes up more space than audio and animation data.
- Bad lip syncing (even in video file cutscenes).
- All character faces are somewhat unsettling. Maybe this is intentional, who knows.
- Occasional glitches/bugs. Not enough to ruin the game but still worth mentioning.  (2 minutes after starting the game I walked into a room to get a mission briefing and nothing happened. I had to restart to get the briefing to actually start when I walked into the room.)
- Not enough time to read a lot of the lore notes on computers. Granted, you can just select them and move on (they get saved in a log) and most of them are pretty generic.

The worst thing about the game (second worst if you do not count the many bugs) is its lack of emotion towards the actual material. We saw when Rome came out, howthis was perfectly implanted, a sense of actually feeling like an empire achieving fame through conquest. This is quite lacking in the game later on and playing through more than a couple campaigns get's tiresome, much more quickly than in the original.
Given that the later games all have tried new things, but never really caught me as much, I wasn't surprised that it didn't gave me the exact same feeling of immersion as the original did. Don't get me wrong Medieval TW and Shogun was fun, but to be honest the lack of choice when it came to the roosters made shogun a fairly short run game for me, while this certainly isn't true for Rome II, the factions just doesn't really add up for this quite enough. They could have made the mechanic and how to deploy units completely different, but I understand why this isn't done. Way to difficult and to much work, but since they hasn't made the faction feel enough of a unique experience, they aren't really justified to charge all them extra money for new DLC's with other factions. The free DLC was great to get, however, in my opinion, the factions could very easily have been a core of the main game and not some extra purchase along the line. This in general comes down to that the game properly was a bit rushed, the bugs, and the enormous waiting time between each round is a clear indicate of this. They should have given themselves a better time.
All this might seem in contrast to my acceptance of the game in general, and perhaps the lack of real great RTS out there have soften me up a little, but with the new patches and all this game does give you more variety then shogun did, and implies some interesting mechanics when building you city. Battles are fun, but it might be difficult to invoke a tactic from a different game in the series, since no unit seem to work exactly how they ordinarily has been.
Mods for the original can still be much more fun, but has soon as they catch up, i think this game might actually be worthwhile. So, purchase when it's cheap and yeah, you'll have a good time. I enjoyed it more than Shogun, and have played it for towards the 200 hours now.

Absolutely love this MMORPG. I've made some solid friends, the community isn't the toxic environment you're used to finding in most massively multiplayer games. While a lot of people would have preferred a combat and stealth system closer to it's single player counterpart, Skyrim, I don't feel it's lacking in charm or fun.
While I may not be a fan of microtransactions within games, I do feel the "Crown" currency is fair in what you are able to get in return--should you be concerned with aesthetics. That being said, you can fully enjoy every bit of this game without having to spend more than what you pay for the game itself, and that's definitely saying something.
Each update and patch to this game, while time consuming to apply, has been worth it. The new content they've added has made the continued play and replayablility remarkable.
I could very easily continue rambling on about the depth this game takes with the lore, the gorgeous soundtrack, or the fantastic balance of PVE/PVP, etc, but this is already becoming a lengthy review. A++

I agree, before the massive update (which changed everything) ESO was a below mediocre mmorpg. HOWEVER after the update in 2015, the game changed completely, it is an amazing game! it really is! The combat is incredible, voice acting is top knotch, the main quest story is fantastic and most of all... the lore! jeesuuschrist i love elderscrolls lore, and ESO brings it in by the dozen. You are constantly learning more about Tamriel and the religions and beliefs around it. The PVP is amazing aswell and completely simulates an actual war and battels, nothing can beat that feeling when you and your group of about 20 are sneaking in a tight group to an unexpecting castle! its really somthing. Obviously however, this isnt all brill, I know u want to know the bad sides too, so here you go: ESO takes a little bit of time to get into, when you start out ur kinda on ur own and you dont really know what ur doing and the quests can get abit tedious, however note that once you hit lvl 15 you kinda know where u are and what to do. You cant really play PVP until your around lvl25 because anything less you will just die immediatly and it will get really fustrating so you can only really start proper PVP at around lvl25 but even then I suggest playing support. But if im honest, I feel this game got a really bad stigma in its early days and know people just think of ESO as a bad game. but what i think the company has done to fix this is make it so good now that it may be underpriced! think about it, yes its a £50 but thats a one off payment and once you start playing it is absolutly not pay to win. yes there are things you can get with realy money but thats in everygame and its not shuvved in your face like it is with other games. so ye, in conclusion i think that this is a fantastic game thats just misunderstood due to its early days, but it is a definite yes.

I played No More Room in Hell for a couple of hours and while it lacks some of the graphical advancements that I would expect from games released in 2014 it did play fairly well. From what I could tell, you don't get the luxury of unlimited respawns and the game is very challenging. You have to take your time and clear the zombies out of the environment slowly and methodically. There is no jumping into a room and hoping your will take everything down (the zombies are strong and will destroy you quickly). There is a minimal hub and though the weapons are plentiful the ammo isn't so you need to make every shot count. I also found this game to have a good amount f atmosphere which added to the enjoyment of playing. The only problem I ran into was trying to get all of my friends into a game on the same server.
If you would like a comparison of games I would say this is sort of like Left 4 Dead but has a slower pace that builds fear through atmosphere rather than the threat of a charging hoard. If you want a "George Romero"-style experience then give this game a try.

System Shock 1 and 2 were very strong pillars of FPS/RPG hybrids alongside the iconic Deus Ex, and are definitely worth playing by any gamer who isn't afraid to play something that isn't a DLC-riddled snoozefest (I'm looking at you, Call of Duty casuals).

Am I allowed to say I'm not wearing nostalgia goggles if I first played Shock 2 in 2012? The FPS RPG survival horror, precursor to Bioshock, Fallout 3, and other "revolutionary titles", still holds strong today as a stellar experience. This is one of those games I wish I could forget, just to get that exhilaration of playing it for the first time again.
This is perhaps my all-time favourite video game. Why, you ask? It's because of that stompin' soundtrack.

System Shock 2 is, so far, my favorite game of all time.  It was one of the first FPS RPGs and it executed wonderfully even as a risk-taking pioneer in the genre.  SS2 provides the player with valid and interesting playstyle choices, from a straight-up military gunner, a navy-trained technician and hacker, to a spec-ops trained psionic wizard.  The player starts with an inclination toward one and can go any direction they want with it after the game starts.  This invested specialization makes the game ideal for repeated play, and the Co-Op mode it supports.
Apparently Co-Op is a feature that Looking Glass never really wanted, but I treasure it and as somebody who has beaten the game multiple times, it's a great tool to get back into the game with friends who have never played.
The game executes wonderfully in lots of ways beyond just good RPG systems and shooting gameplay, such as a truly haunting survival/horror atmosphere, a tense and memorable story (the true innovator of the much-imitated audio-log storytelling device in videogames), the inventor of the sarcastic and manipulative AI villain (GladOS owes her existence to SHODAN), robust body control (with leaning and mantling mechanics)... the game is so feature rich and it all comes together into a wonderfully immersive game experience.
I can't recommend SS2 highly enough with the only caveat being the very dated 1999 visuals.  Install a high-resolution textures and models mod and I'm sure you'll be able to see past it.

Only been playing for a few hours but it's better than I expected.  Easy to pick up and start playing, tutorials feel like normal missions and are quick enough to keep you from getting bored. Graphics are good and the game runs smooth, I haven’t encountered any slowing or stuttering yet.
Combat is fun, your guns will fire automatically or you can control them yourself. Everything you put on your ship can be damaged or destroyed during missions, engines damaged? Your a sitting duck, decided to attack head on, lose your weapons in the process. However, you can repair your parts during the mission as long as you've collected scrap off destroyed ships.
One thing I was worried about was having to re-design your ship over and over and thought it would be very tedious. To my surprise ship building is quick and very easy, you can save your setup or start from scratch but takes very little time at all. With that being said the amount of time you spend in a certain class of ship is very appropriate, you'll unlock new parts every mission but you don't advance to larger ships without adequate time to use most of what you've unlocked so advancement feels good.
Then there’s the mutiny, after every mission you'll lose your ship and you'll have to face it as the last enemy in the next level. Several missions in I thought to myself "this is the best ship I could have built right now it's great" and what a double edged sword that was. During the next mission within seconds I found myself without weapons or wings within seconds of fighting the best ship I could have designed!  Take caution when designing overpowered ship.
There's not a whole lot I dislike about this game, some things are the parts are displayed on the left hand side, but when you get so many you'll have to scroll down to repair some of your parts, an option to resize them or start a second row so they're always on the screen would be nice. Well worth the $15, this game is fun and fighting your old ship keeps things interested.

FULL DISCLOSURE: I received a press copy of the game from the developers.
If you’d prefer a video review, have a look here:

There are a lot of modern video game consumers out there who love designing things. And not just designing things, but designing things that work. Games like Minecraft, Cities: Skylines, and Prison Architect, all very succesful, put a focus on creating something productive, or at the very least functional. So what if there was a game that rewarded you for designing something great, but even more so, rewarded you for creating fatal flaws? Defects, if you will. What if in Cities: Skylines, one day a rift opens up in your city, and if you can’t destroy or stop the rift from spreading within a few months the entire planet gets sucked in and the game ends. Say, you knew it was going to happen at some point in your playthrough. What would you do about it? Put a nuclear device underneath your wonderful city, and the only way to set it off is if you press the button only you have access to? Would you build a dome that could completely cover your city and prevent the rift from spreading elsewhere? What if a huge focus of the game, is sneaking the cleverest Death Star like weakness into your design that you possibly can?
Then you get defect, a sci-fi game where you can build your own ships. The gimmick is that after every successful mission, your crew turns on you and steals your ship. That stolen ship becomes the boss for the next mission you take on. At the very beginning of the game you can get away with creating better and better ships to take on the previous models. But eventually there might be a mission where you have to create the tankiest ship you can. Much tankier than any ship you’ll be making any time soon. That’s when you need to begin putting failsafes into your designs.
Before I get into the meat of the review, I want to mention that this game is in early access on stream, which means it’s unfinished at the time of this review. If you’re watching this at or after the official release, then you’re watching an out of date video. I plan to make another review of the full game which is scheduled for around May 2016, so have a look around my channel for that. The game on release may be unrecognisable from the game I’m reviewing now so bear that in mind, but I doubt that’s going to be a problem for a game that’s as close to being finished as this one is. I’ve put about 6 hours into the game, and there’s easily, just looking at the number of missions, 20-30 hours of content here and probably much more. I think most of the reason for the early access on this game is for getting feedback on the balance, because in Defect much of the game relies on the player not being able to exploit the stats of their ships.
I’m a fan of the way the game’s presented. The missions are all played on a 2D plane that has the illusion of being 3D. The art direction certainly fits with the sci-fi theme, though the character designs are a little strange, I like them. I really liked the dynamic music in the game; as you’re playing a mission, the music will be relatively soft in the beginning, but as you fight more and more enemies it gets more intense. It even changes based on the way you build your ship. There was one time where I think the music messed up, if that wasn’t a bug, then that was some horrible sounding music.
The gameplay is kind of interesting. By default, you’re using the left and right keys to turn your ship and the forward key to go forward, when you get near an enemy your guns fire automatically, and your job is simply lining up the shot. But as the captain of your ship, you can take direct control of a single part of the ship at any time. You can take control of the engines to speed up the ship, the hull to increase defenses, the guns to increase accuracy and fire rate, the wings to increase maneuverability. Basically you are choosing where to delegate your resources as you fight other ships. And it all depends how you’ve built your ship; maybe you built a super light fast ship that needs extra protection, so you take direct control of the hull most of the time. And the game does a really good job of forcing you to build different kinds of ships. Maybe there’s a mission with a super fast ship you have to chase down, or you need a certain type of weapon on your ship. It’s all done very cleverly, and all the while whenever you build your ship you need to consider the fact that eventually you’re going to have to take it down.
The story is as good as it needs to be. Some of the writing is kind of entertaining, but for all intents and purposes there isn’t really a story. Think X-Com, the story is there but that’s not why anyone is playing this game.
The game is $15 on Steam. I mentioned earlier that someone could easily get 20-30 hours out of this game. It’s fun, it’s an original idea, and it’s challenging. The thing that might put you off are that it’s pretty difficult, but for most people that’s not going to be too much of an issue. It’s also in early access and that’s a dealbreaker for most people, and I don’t blame them for that. For what it’s worth, the game played absolutely fine with me, and there is so much content here that you wouldn’t know it’s an unfinished game. That said, if you’re going to wait for release, try not to forget about it. This is a special game, and one that you should look out for. Defect gets a glowing recommendation from me.

As of this review, the Update 1.2 patch has indeed smoothened out performance hitches by a fair margin, but it's still relatively far from being perfectly playable. In order to operate the game a lot better, I disabled all anti-aliasing via my Nvidia Control Panel (I have a GTX 980), and I still get FPS drops, going between 25-45 at times, otherwise staying at 50 most of the time. Optimization is a serious issue that Arkane Studios seriously needs to iron out in order to appease many of their customers.
As I have been able to play the game a lot better since the update came out and since disabling antialiasing, I can more or less look past the performance issues into the quality of the game, and I must say, they have done a remarkable job at building upon the first Dishonored, and managed to make it just as memorable as its predecessor so far.

If you're a fan of the Alien Vs. Predator Game of years past, this may NOT be the game for you. In AVP, you play as an alien, marine, or predator. In Alien Isolation, you play as Ellen Ripley's daughter from the original Sigourney Weaver movies. This is NOT an action game. You are spending 90% of your time hiding from the Alien on board your space station. If you're looking for an Alien game where you get a ton of guns and bombs and just kill a slew of Aliens, this is NOT the game for you.
When you do encounter the Alien (Yes, it's just *One* Alien), you have to resort to hiding in lockers or cabinets, and hitting the right mouse button to hold your breath so it doesnt hear you. This can make the game difficult since there is no way to kill it, until the end of the game of course. There are NO Predators in this game, it is NOT an AVP game.
So if your are an Alien fan, you enjoy you're heart thumping out of your chest from being scared or anxious, and you want something different then the every day "Shoot Everything" game, this is for you. The graphics are beautiful and run well on not-so-advanced comptuers.

Alien Isolation Review
Let me start off by saying that I like challenging games. The first thing I did when I bought this game was turn up the difficulty. If you learn only one thing from this review, it should be this:
Do not play this game on hard.
Let me caveat this review by listing what it does well. Alien:Isolation has masterful art direction, superb visuals and atmospherics, and well executed music. It also has some of the best voice and character animation I've ever seen in a game set in the Alien universe. In short, as far as immersing itself in an established franchise, it is by far one of the absolute best games ever made. It in many ways perfectly captures the feel and look of the original movie. It leans heavily, and successfully, on cues from the movie. It comes very close to breaching the barrier between video games and art (You know, that thing that Roger Ebert says is impossible).
In terms of being a game however, Isolation overshoots it mark. Hard. Simply put, Alien:Isolation is a long-winded masochistic experience that attempts to buck gaming conventions TOO much. It is perfectly acceptable to have a hide-or-die survival horror game (A la the Amnesia series). It is perfectly fine to have a stealth heavy tool based game (I.E. Canonical, non 2014 Thief). You can even combine those two categories. Alien Isolation attempts to do that, but makes the pitfall of including an Omni-potent nine foot death machine that exists in intentional defiance of your tools, weapons, stealth tactics, or any form of learned experience that you may apply to the game over its 15-20 hours of gameplay (Which I didn't get through. I gave up. Congrats, Creative, you made me give up on a game. Rare achievement, that).
In short, victory in Alien:Isolation is not achievable through skill, creativity, or even sheer persistence learning. It is a function of your willingness to die repeatedly in the service of beautifully meshed franchise, all while hunting for infrequently place wall phones (It never occurred to anyone to vary this by making some desk phones or phone booths. That would've actually been humorous to have Doctor Who style Callboxes. But I digress).
The phones are there, mind you, and function as your manual save points (No checkpoints) but not only is progress so slow that they SEEM far away (And there are some savepoint deserts in the game), they also lock out immediately after you save or load from them. So if you walk into a room and beeline for the phone, but miss the blueprint, keycard, or computer terminal in the room, you will have to mentally remind yourself to repeat those actions whenever you reload.
Which you will do a lot of. Some people are apparently really good at this game. Maybe this game just isn't in my skillbase. But based on my experience, you will die a lot, and not for any definable reason. This is where the masochism comes in. As stated, I like challenging games. But the difference between difficulty and challenge is that challenging games dangle success in front of you, daring you to be more creative, faster, smarter, better, and then reward you with attainable, reasonable rewards that advance your progress if you do well. Like Decisive victories in Panzer Corps. You don't need them to progress, but they let you get more points, special levels, etc.
Alien:Isolation is simply difficult. There is no challenge because there are no rules, patterns, or models for you to master. The Alien is one of the most unscripted opponents I've ever seen in a video game. Its behavior is sometimes realistically random and inscrutable. Other times it is predictable. But there is no almost consistency in behavior. Proponents of the game that I've talked to assert that this is its best feature. I find it annoying. Why? Because not only is it in fact unrealistic, but also because it is not challenging. There's no way to learn or beat the system beyond clinging to well worn stealth tactics from other games and hoping that they won't be as unsuccessful in your 10th run at a particular corridor.
And that is the hardest failing of the game. The developers have danced far, far ahead in their apparently adaptive AI programming. The alien does seem to legitimately learn from what you do. But the game does not. The disconnect that occurs is that while the Alien will adapt to you, the game is not cognizant of the fact that the person playing it is beating their head against the wall, despite the fact that is clearly within the expertise of the developers to make the difficulty more dynamic.
Simply put: The alien is scaling his difficulty up as you learn, but the game does not counter that in any way. This means that the difficulty bottlenecks early, in ways that make the game frustrating, repetitive, and pointlessly difficult. The result is that the game becomes a slog. An unenjoyable slog. While the game's concept design appears to expect the fear factor to smooth those parts out, unfortunately, for me, that expectation fell flat. The fear values disappear, because the fear becomes repeatable.
Overall, I can't recommend this game to people unless they are die hard fans of Aliens, are gluttons for punishment, or have 20 hours to sink into this game without any reasonable expectation of reward. Even when I did make progress, I just didn't feel any sense of accomplishment. I constantly felt that I succeeded only through blind luck or fate. It felt as if though I only made it down that particular corridor of death because an unscrutable subroutine rolled a particular value at a particular time, which made the alien jump in the vent and wander away for 30 seconds. And I just didn't find that rewarding, let alone fun.
So what can we learn from this game? For one, as stated, the atmospheric experience of the game is definitely something I'd like to see repeated, not only in the Aliens franchise, but in others as well. The art direction is excellent, and really does immerse you. Unfortunately, this may have led the developers to become too carried away, to the detriment of the players. Further, the way it attempts to balance fear and gameplay is instructive, in that fails in a way that is at odds with how most games traditionally fail to instill fear.
Specifically, most games that don't handle fear properly do so on the basis of inappropriateness (Cheap fears, shocky fears, or just plainly uninspiring fear). Isolation fails at the fear factor in an opposite way: The fear is very real, but the game fails to ration it appropriately. It throws it at you so much that the player becomes normalized to it. In short, the game never lets you feel safe, and as such, the player comes to exist in that fear in a way that ultimately destroys the value of that fear. It in some ways becomes like that really hyped up haunted house roller coaster that everyone in town talks about, but then you ride it, and it is scary, but 1/4 of the way through it starts to repeat itself so much, so constantly, that you really, really want to get off.
After the fifth time the alien murders that person you just met, you're all "Wow, I just met this really helpful and believably cast person with great voice acting. Lets count the lines of dialogue until they die horribly!" No one ever escapes. This ties back to the normalization. You expect everyone you meet will die, and that aspect of the game prevents you from connecting to the characters. Just once, couldn't a minor character have had a close call and said "SCREW IT! I'm going to get in mah space suit and go play outside, I'll be back in time for supper!" It just seems like a lot of great attention to casting and dialogue is wasted by the pathological lengths the game pursues of murdering almost everyone you meet.
Which is true to the original Alien. But the movie is a one time linear two hour experience. Reloading to see that experience on a rinse cycle becomes very disengaging, very fast.

Cons:

Overall, Just Cause 3 captures the style of Just Cause 2, while improving and expanding on it. Any fan of JC2, action games, or destruction will love JC3.

Rome II could use some depth however when all aspects are taken into consideration this game is still fantastic, this review will be my opinions of the pros and cons that someone who plays regularly can see.
CONS:
Long loading times
Too many DLC's things like Caesar's Campaign's and the Punic Wars should come standard.
Too few nations to pick from for the Grand Campaign's.
The over abundance of one specific unit in a factions armies in the campaign (e.g.  javelinmen or hoplites).
The shear killing power of specific units, such as pikemen and war elephants.
The online lacks any... finesse, the set up seems to be identical to that of NTW or ETW.

There is no Punic War campaign that would only focus on the Romans and the Carthiginians.
The game doesnt really just grab you from the beginning, it takes a little time and effort to get into the campaigns or any part of the game for that matter.
If I could make one large complaint to Creative Assembly it would be the DLC's and their absurd pricing, basic things like the Punic Wars or Caesars rise to power should have been released when the game was realeased, I wouldnt mind if they continued to released free content or DLC's, but without DLC's this game lacks basic things for the $60.00 price tag
PROS:
Unbelievable graphics.
Large quantities of units in all factions (something that most Total Wars lacked).
The shear size of the campaing, I put many hours into my Rome Campaign and only conquered as much as the Greeks.
The AI has improved significantly, they no longer retreat all the time.
Naval Battles are just as good as any other Total War game.
The ability to play land and sea in one battle is very interesting.
Each nations advantages are more pronounced (e.g. Carthages and Egypts naval abilities).
The ability to pick which time period or house to play as in the Roman Campaing's.
Special and interesting units such as dogs or war elephants.
Improvement in sieges.
Map size in battles.
Army sizes in battles.
Almost constant updating which means for at least me few to no crashes
Character developments in spies or generals
More in detail given to keeping the Patricians and Plebians happy.
All factors considered the game really starts out as 2 out of 10 however once you get past the getting to know the game phase, it really starts to draw you in and jumps up to an easy 6 or 7 or maybe even 8 out of 10 in my opinion, however Creative Assembly's 'corporate greed' makes the ridiculous pricing of DLC's almost borderline walmart greed, and the DLC's consist of the things that should have been free or put in the game in the beginning, this can really detract from the quality of the gameplay. However apart from the greed of Creative Assembly the game in my opinion is one of the best Total Wars made to this date. Lastly, I think that Creative Assembly should take a look back at how the Medieval II's campaing was developed, where if you defeated a country you could then play as that country in the future campaign's not where you have to pay absurd prices for the oppurtunity to play as countries that youve already spent $60.00 on.
Hope this helps you all

The awards and ratings don't lie, this is one of those games that you are required to have played to be considered a true gamer. System Shock 2 is a HUGE cult classic, and if I was the kind of person who easily picked favorites, this would have a good chance of being it. If you don't want to read my entire comment here, the summary is at the bottom.
The most important thing about this game can be summed up in one word, and that is: atmosphere. This game has a dark Drum & Bass soundtrack, and like all old game soundtracks, it's perfectly suited for the game. It adds to the game's horror atmosphere, which has it's strength in anticipation rather than jump scares. Those of you who have played Dead Space, it draws quite a bit from System Shock 2. A horror game on a derelict ship invaded by strange creatures, with logs of the dead giving you an idea of what happened. System Shock 2 invented that and more.
As Yahtzee said, this is an Action RPG, not an action game with RPG elements. The character customization has a huge effect on your character, and you have to build him carefully. Screw it up, and you'll find yourself in a pretty bad situation, sometimes unable to progress if you really botched it. The higher the difficulty, the more unforgiving that system is, though later game it isn't as bad(in my experience).
So in short, System Shock 2 is a highly atmospheric, creepy, pioneering, often unforgiving RPG, that is probably one of the best games I've ever played. It's WELL worth over twice it's price, there's no excuse for you to not play it. If you want to be seen as a true gamer and not a stereotypical COD fanboy, or if you just want to experience one of the best games out there, then you may want to add this game to your collection of things you've played. No matter how advanced graphics get today, just like Doom, Quake, Unreal and Deus Ex, System Shock 2 is one of those games that left its mark on gaming, and will never go away.

A terrifying survival-horror with great pacing, mechanics (Distraction, Baiting, Rewire tactics) and A.I; Alien: Isolation is worthy of all sorts of praise.
The alien becomes more predictable and less terrifying as you play with it more and more though, and made the game less horror and more stealth game with a horror theme. Even though this made me feel like I was Amanda losing her fear of the alien, this is sure to make future playthroughs less scary; especially since the first few encounters require that the player be unfamiliar with the alien to be scared of it since its tactical prowess comes in when more vents are introduced.
Another problem is that the first well-designed encounter appears quite farther into the game than most players would expect, which means that the first few that the player will have on a 2nd or more run will be rushed through thanks to the players knowledge of the aliens methods.
Despite these problems, the game is wonderfully made, let me just show you a list of what I like about the game, and what I think could be improved on:
+Alien is intellegent, doesn't bug out or let the player feel safe.
+Crafting is rewarding since the rewards are valuable and near required, including: Noisemaker distractions, Pipe-bombs, EMP-Mines, and more.
+Combat, when needed feels punchy with the humans being high power, but easy to dispatch, and the androids taking loads of shots to the face. Weapons feel powerful and dangerous, a feeling that I haven't gotten from any guns in another game
+Difficulty and lack of hand-holding means that the game feels free and non-restricted, as well as being hard as nails from the first encounter with the Xenomorph to the ending sequence.
-The human A.I feels half-baked and clunky, they aren't intellegent and don't seem to have much purpose other than make noise and attack the player.
-The game can bug out quite a bit, with the alien shifting around and some weird things happening with distractions.
I have also had a locker-death where the alien yanked the door off its hinges, but it then walked away with my camera halfway into the death animation; I was invisible, not able to leave the locker and just frustrated.
9/10

What an absolute gem, Creative Assembly really knocked it out of the park and right into 70's themed deep space. This is a gorgeous looking game with very well considered gameplay, environment, character design, sound design and such. I have to give particular praise to the lighting engine, it's absolutely perfect. I'll admit I wasn't blown away by the voice acting or the facial animations but at this point the rest of the game outshines those petty flaws so incandescently as to render them null. This is an extremely tense game, I often found myself terrified at the androids, never mind the alien. I've not really noticed this "adaptive AI" that people talk about but the Alien is quite tricky. Extremely perceptive and always seems to notice the slightest sight or sound, it makes for one terrifying experience every time you encounter it. The story was also praiseworthy, it really captures what a survival horror is about, never too grandiose. The attention to detail here is beyond staggering. The gameplay elements like saving, crafting, minigames, the scattered computers, even the UI capture the 70's feel CA were going for in respect for the original Alien. It's as faithful as any diehard fan (of which I am not) could ever hope for (I imagine). It's a hell of a ride which will leave you with a considerably elevated heart rate, shakes and satisfaction when you finally evade that pesky Alien. Fan or not of the original movie, this is one game you absolutely must get, since I took the time to get out of my locker, hold my breath and write this review. It is worth every iota of praise it gets and more.
Really captures the cat and mouse thrill of the original movie.  Very stable and polished.

A tense and gripping Survival Horror with outstanding atmosphere.
Play as Amanda Ripley - Ellen Ripley's daughter, in a frantic survival for your life aboard the Nostromo as you sturggle to retrace your mothers footsteps.
This game is inspired by Ridley Scott's original iconic vision: There is only one Xenomorph to stalk you through the corridors. It is attracted to sound, so be mindful of your actions. There are plenty of other obstacles to face, whether it be maintenance failures, destroyed walkways, or frenzied androids, you will not have much down time.
The mechanics are simple and gratifying, with a button to sprint, sneak, hide and equip items/weapons. You are given many different instruments to utilize aboard the ship, including the iconic scanner. You can also craft items and equipment by collecting the needed materials and blueprints.
If you dig the first-person immersion, and prefer stealth oriented survival horrors over shoot-fest survival horrors, this game is for you.

A stunning game, satisfied me as a fan of gaming, a fan of horror in general and a fan of Alien.  I was a little unsure at the start as there seemed to be quite long gaps between saves and I was repeating a lot of stuff but I realised that this was clever design - repeating these sections early on forces you to think differently and re-train your brain to enjoy the game.
The atmosphere throughout is crazy tense, it pumps you so full of adrenaline you actually get a genuine high from playing it.  It's tough but really fair - I never once died and thought I had been cheated, I always knew it was because I'd done something wrong.
It's a really unique experience - each level is almost like a puzzle and a you'll need to scout areas, hack terminals and check possible routes before making your move, the game get's better the bolder you get and balancing the risks is where the enjoyment comes in, every move you make feels like gamble rather than a guarantee.
The story is mostly good and nicely plays with the conventions of the series, there are very few cut scenes which really helps in keeping you immersed - even when you're presented with some cool back story from another character later in the game you play this out rather than just watching it which was a great touch.
A bit of a missed opportunity is multiplayer - it would have been great to have one person as the alien and a dozen or so others as humans/androids each with their own objectives or team objectives but I guess they need to keep something back for a sequel.
This has been my favourite game of 2014 so far - I'm looking forward to going through it again :)

Alien: Isolation is a stealth, survival horror with a giant movie franchise behind it. I'm a huge fan of the Alien, Predator games and own every single title. This is by far my most favorite incarnation from the movies surpassing Rebellion's 2000 game AVP by a slim but enthusiastic margin. The game is hard. You will die a lot but those moments where you do succeed you feel a rush from surviving the deadliest monster in movie history. The game is spent eluding your nemesis, using him to kill for you-its a dangerous cat and mouse game with an A.I. that behaves so realistically that you'll swear its alive; scavenging parts to build simple but effective weapons in a rudimentary crafting menu isn't satisfying but servicable. My only 3 negatives are the average voice acting, poorly synced voiceovers to the characters, and occasional clunky animations for the human models. It breaks immerision at times especially since the alien itself is so well animated. I didn't preorder. I waited for the reviews. IGN, GAMESPOT drop the score for the games difficulty and length. PC gamer does a better job with their review. I do not regret spending 90 dollars in getting the Season Pass and extra content. Please support the developer as you can see their heart and soul in this game.

This is the game that every fan has wanted. You play as the lesser known Ripley, Amanda. She's not as cool as her mother at first, but she's a grower and eventually, you'll love her, just like Ellen!
Alien manages to do things to you that most Survival Horror/Action games don't. It scares you even when there's nothing to be scared of. You know the Alien is there, you know it wants to smash through your skull with it's little tongue Alien, and you know that there's a pretty big chance that it will find you and do exactly that. But that's the fun part, the adrenaline rush when you see the Alien scouting for you and knowing that one wrong move is all it takes before it finds you.
As long as you behave in a manner like you would in real life when confronted by this kind of situation (i.e. not running around and generally banging on things to attract attention) then the Alien isn't offensive. You feel like the Alien has another purpose, and it's not solely out to get you. There are other survivors on the ship and at times, you feel like they are the ones that are being hunted rather than you being the sole focus of attention.
Although you're on the same station pretty much all game, it doesn't feel repetitive, yes, there's a lot of running around to fix/get/do things but because of the nature of the AI and the atmosphere of the game, you never really feel like you've been there and done that, and that is something that should be celebrated.
The game itself is huge, and with the DLC you'll be knocking well over 10 hours out of the initial release, and that's something that is pretty rare these days and definitely makes the game great value for money.
The story is gripping, and the characters are excellently voiced for the most part, you get a genuine sense of hate for some of them and you feel like some are truly trying their best to help you out.
Whether you love the films, or whether you're just a fan of survival horrors, this is a game that I can't recommend enough.
If you're still unsure as to whether to get this game or not, then please check my playthrough of it, and make up your own mind from what you see. I've done my best to keep the atmosphere intact so you get a true sense of how the game feels.

I have finally finished the game and I have to say, it's good and I'd like to see sequel or at lest more with this universe. I know how hard it is to build a new world and how long it could take, but it would be worth it. And I think a full review is neccesary.
Honestly its worth a few bucks to play, the good thing is you don't need to. And that is something you rarely see nowadays. At least as singleplayer contained experiences go. And honestly we need more like this.
The combat is a little simple at the start and does become more difficult, though never anything to worry about. The enemies are interesting and all of them are different as you progress. A big problem are the elite mobs who take a lot to kill, but once you figure out how to defeat them they become pushovers with the right equipment. The best enemies are the boss fights. Though few and far between, and some are somewhat optional, the bosses are all a harkoning back to the old schools bosses. Having to memorize patterns and quick movements just hoping to get in a hit when you can. It made some of the better moments of the game.
The story didn't grab me. But that is my opinion, and others might find it a touching tale filled with hope and longing. Issues of abandonment and jealousy. My only real issue with it, and this is what ended up making the story harder to get into, was the grammer. I know it sounds stupid, but at critical moments in the story the grammer just detracts from understanding and the empathy of the narritive. Otherwise no complaints at all.
You can definetly tell this was made with RPG Maker if you've ever played around with the program before. Saying that, it looks good. A few of the chests and switches can be blocked be the scenery, which is a problem for those completionists, otherwise good uses of the assets available. Personally enjoyed a fair bit of the aesthetic, and scenery.
In  Commendment,
The game is good and worth your time. Though you will be hard pressed to find much replay value, past finding the multiple endings and that you can do rather easily with a save game at the room before the last boss. Would have liked a few more levels, but I understand not wanting to each world is fairly large and complex in some areas. With my blessing enjoy this game in all its wonder.

I have a problem: I am compelled to buy half-complete early access titles in the Survival-Crafting Open World PVP genre. It's like a curse, in which my wallet and my happiness must suffer. So naturally, I wanted to give Hurtworld a try. I was
to.
I logged into a server and immediately encountered a neutral player trying to shoo me from his gathering area. He threw his spear at me, missing, all the while communicating to me with voice chat to go away. Point taken, I high tailed it out of there half-naked and with nothing to my name. A couple nights later I had established some basic tools but died of hypothermia. I have not died since. You learn to prioritize resource gathering and craftables, to keep a campfire at the ready for the harsh cold nights. I encountered friendly players, who offered some spare leather or had a kind word in passing. But I also encountered my first hostile player, who tried to coerce me into dropping all my logs. I refused and he chased me with his bow. I turned on him, spear in hand, and wacked him over the head. He didn't like that. I chased him off with my stick and very suddenly a blinding dust storm kicked up. He complained about not being able to see and I used that opportunity to get away -- even though I was the one chasing him. It felt great, as a new player, to be able to defend myself against others. And even better to see how the environment had protected me and given me cover. Cool.
A few hours of gameplay later and I have claimed a plot of land, clothed myself, crafted a back pack, built a small home, stocked up my storage container, created tier 2 tools, and am ready to explore. I feel I have met small milestones and there is a sense of accomplishment and survival. I have hunted and gathered my way to basic comfort and survived the few hostile players.
What the future holds, I am uncertain. I'd like to believe I cannot progress through the game so quickly. I'd like to believe great dangers lurk where great rewards lie, but I have not explored far enough yet.
Here's what I do know: The game is fun, it is a solid title for Early Access, the community isn't totally filled with jerks (at least not on the server I joined), and I can only hope the developers expand on this game as I want more of it.
+While it is an EA title, it feels like a solid game with a full feature list. Highly playable.
+Runs smoothly, no crashes, high frame rates
+Combat is adequate
+Survival takes some effort and thought during the first couple hours
+Basic resources continue to be useful
+Player community
+I not YET encountered a cheater
+The server I play on is not full when I want to play
+Its fun
+You keep your tools when you die, but drop your resources
+HUD is clutter free
-Hypothermia is a bit harsh
-Overheating mechanic is ridiculous. I'd understand if you overheat from the desert sun. But instead you overheat from being near your campfire or firepit, which is required for cooking food and smelting ores. It is ridiculous that I can't be anywhere inside my house while the firepit is going or I will start to overheat. Overheating can very well kill you. This could turn into an interesting mechanic if water is required to cool down from the hot desert or player must find shade or equip special gear. Tedius, but could be interesting. As it is right now its downright annoying.
-Some resources will appear at a certain distance away, but will not be there when you approach, and may reapper after wandering around a bit. Similarly, the LOD on creatures is questionable. Bors can look a bit like logs at a distance because they are boxy until you get close enough for their details to be clear. And sometimes they won't appear at all until right up next them. Minor bugs.
-Building a home is nice, but needs some work. There are no stairs or ladders. And you do not get any of your resources returned when you destroy something you've built. Certain resource requirements make no sense.
-Crafting menus could be improved on, but not really a con. They work as intended.
Overall, for 20$ I am enjoying the game and look forward to playing more of it.
