I said: Screw "Shinji Mikami!"and bought Alien Isolation instead and what I got was a Dark Souls-esque survival stealth game, full of tension.
The atmosphere of the game is immensely rich as it draws from the already well established Alien franchise and pulls you in on much more immersive level. The clunky 70's 80's sci-fi look is gorgeous and is somewhat realistic considering space technology as of now. Music is fairly well threaded throughout, with orchestrated melodies fused with electronic percussion lending itself to the film's own music score, whilst adding to the overall tense feeling that lingers throughout.
The storyline is decently written with good pacing which consequently makes the game is long. However the length is not a negative as I found it made sense when looking at the storyline and the setting.  The pacing also presented different layers of tension with each threat that arises.  As the game goes on, you do gain a bit of more confidence but still tension seeps in you like acid.
On Hard difficulty the games works very much like Dark Souls: a game which prepares you for well for most things in life ;D
Alien Isolation doesn't hold your hand and it does punish one for being cocky,  noisy and even aggressive at times. Saves points are very much like the typewriters of the old RE titles. However even saving can lead to a risk of dying at is leaves one open for a brief moment as so do many other things. Reloading, crafting, using computers, devices and tools all leave you open which furthers adds to the tension. Combat is simple and enjoyable as this is a stealth game. The Alien has the best unpredictable AI that I've experienced and has a lethal grab radius so keep your distance like it's Street Fighter! ;) However if you're not cautious and don't have your wits about you, you will die alot.
Although in my playthrough there were a few Bethesda like glitches (Like floppy corpses, static humans or the odd jittery Alien), the only things I felt that really detracted from the experience of the game was the vagueness of certain items controls when it game to a certain hacking game of matching inputs and the inventory wheel. I use a Xbox 360 gamepad. The wheel itself felt slow when in the heat of quick thinking and panic so it really forces one to be one step ahead of the game in this aspect. The D-Pad does help with quick weapon switches and the hacking game, but again the game doesn't hold your hand for these things.
Another thing that was not entirely clear is the optional collectables in relation to backtracking. Depending on how far you are in the story, you pick up the Nostromo  Logs and need only to simply reload your save. This saves time and a huge hassle when backtracking. Backtracking itself  was only bothersome with me when it came to the archive logs and bouncing back and forth from one switch to another in an area. However the threats are the reason why the backtracking can be nerve wracking  and many other games are far to linear in comparison which hurts their own atmosphere with a lack of engagement and exploration with the detailed environments developers make these days.

As evident in its thoroughly rich and tense atmosphere and its intelligent and challenging game play, Alien Isolation is a true success of the concept and execution of film to videogame.

Game adds a unique take on the Thriller genre of horror games sprouting. It doesn't just use horror as its only suspense. The item system is unique and doesn't detract from the suspenseof the game. The AI in this is the other unique feature with the NPCs acting different with every play through or restart, gives a unique experience.

Alien: Isolation is the Alien game that fans have been waiting decades for. Not only does it faithfully recreate the atmosphere of the original Ridley Scott film, but it finally makes the Xenomorph something to be afraid of again. The graphics are absolutely phenomenal and some of the best in the gaming industry to date along with incredible sound design and an unexpectedly lengthy story. The gameplay may have a few quirks, and the storyline may be hard to follow when your constantly running from hiding spot to hiding spot, too afraid to peek over the counter to grab that extra flare; but this game is the best Alien experience oyu will ever get.
Let's start by talking about the gameplay. Unlike past Alien games, this one focuses entirely on the original film "Alien" by Ridley Scott. Gone are the large assault rifles and grenades that used to make short work of Xenomorphs in past games. In their place is a 26 hour game of hide-and-seek. Alien: Isolation focuses more so on stealth tactics and the methods of deception in order to accomplish your goals. There's absolutely no way to kill the Alien with any items you find, so the game forces you to move carefully from room to room, using any cover or hiding spots you can find. While it may seem easy to just be patient, the more you wait, the more the Alien learns and the easier it is for it to find you. Sometimes hiding in a locker and holding your breath will allow you to slip by undetected, but if you use this tactic too often, the Alien figures it out and rips the door off and.. well.. you know the rest. Though I did feel the gameplay could use a few improvements. For one, the Androids on the ship didn't really feel necessary as they only felt like a place-filler whenever the Alien wasn't present and they certainly weren't nearly as interesting. Another issue I had was with the movement of the character herself. The crouching speed is incredibly slow compared to usual stealth game standards, which makes sneaking up on enemy humans/androids without them turning around close to impossible. I also feel the hint that the game gives you about sitting back inside lockers and holding your breath is not nearly clear enough. It took me several attempts just to read what the hint was saying before the Alien ripped the door off and chewed on my face. Other than these small issues, the game itself is incredibly immersive and really does make you feel like you are in the classic 1979 horror masterpiece.
On a technical level; the graphics and sound design are beautiful in this game. It is incredibly clear that the developers of Alien: Isolation absolutely love their source material and have meticulously recreated the exact same atmosphere that individuals experienced back in the theatre. Lights slowly flicker as they turn on, old green CRT monitors buzz and shake,  and the Alien can always be heard thumping around in the vents above you, ready to jump down at completely random intervals. The actual visuals are gorgeous with light being reflected and refracted off of steam that slowly flows out of vents in the wall, and the slow burning at the end of your flamethrower shedding only a minuscule comfort of light against the sides of the vents you hope are safe. The only real technical issue I can find with the game is it's lackluster human character animations. They feel very stiff and unrealistic. Thankfully, the star of the show looks phenomenal. The Alien will slowly coil itself as it rolls out of a cieling vent and slunks to the floor, only to quickly raise it's head and begin stomping down the hallway, now and again stopping to stair mysteriously down a hall. You can never tell what the Alien is going to do next and it makes your movement choices even more horrifying. The AI for the Alien is done perfectly and not once in my 26 hours of play time did I notice any AI glitches that killed the immersion. Creative Assembly made entirely sure that both the environment and the creature itself are as genuine as the movie, and it shows perfectly.
Now in terms of story, it's pretty straight forward horror/Alien style storyline. The only issue I had with it is that the characters aren't very memorable and it's incredibly hard to even piece together what the story is when you're constantly logging off of computers as you're in the middle of an email only because you heard the Alien thumping around outside of the room you were in. There's tons of hidden messages, ID tags, and email messages that piece together survivor stories of both the Nosostromo (from the movie) and the Sevastopol (the massive space station setting of the game itself), so those willingly to sit there and read the emails to get more out of the story are certainly welcome to try, but the game certainly doesn't appear to encourage it considering the gameplay doesn't freeze when you're reading computer screens or rewiring panels. So to summarize, the story's good from what I was able to make out from it. There's plenty of fan appeal with all kinds of recreated experiences straight from the movie to keep anyone with even a remote interest in the Alien series happy.
So to wrap this all up, Alien Isolation is a fantastic work of art that successfully recreates the exact tension (and maybe even more so) as the original Ridley Scott film. The graphics are fantastic and the Alien certainly steals the show with unpredictable AI and incredible attention to detail. The game can be quite difficult to most, but as long as you're careful and avoid making stupid movement choices and use your scarce resources wisely, you should be able to make it in one piece. I personally played it on the hardest difficulty and was only killed by the Alien throughout the 26 hours around 20 some times. The game even features plenty of bonus levels and challenges to keep you occupied if you haven't had enough after the lengthy campaign, which is great for replay value. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys stealth, horror, and obviously to ANYONE who has ever enjoyed "Alien."

ETS 2: My Review At Around 50 Hours Playtime:
So Euro Truck Simulator 2 is one of my favourite simulators i have on steam, the graphics are amazing, the fps is even more amazing, and i know that the game doesnt look like much, driving trucks across europe in hopes of earning a couple of quid, but honestly its a lot better than it seems.
Specs:
Honestly the specs arent too bad at all, for example, pc i had a 2.4ghz dual core and a gt 710 and on low settings i got around 30fps which was more than enough for me at the time, and atleast for me the fps never really drops. Even on my new pc, 1050ti, AMD-FX 4300 Quad Core, 16GB RAM (the pc didnt come with the 16gb ram, i fit in an extra 8 gigs) on ultra settings the fps rarely drops below 60, VERY RARELY.
Gameplay:
The gameplay feels very nice and smooth, pretty easy to understand and quite addicting at first, i know im saying all of this with less than 3 days play time but this is just my opinion so far.
You get licensed trucks which is a step up for the realism from the original ets, there's a lot more accesibilty to the countries around the world as well.
Controls:
You can play euro truck with a mouse and keyboard of course, but you can also use controllers, joysticks and steering wheels ofcourse. There is an option to use the mouse as the steering wheel which in my opinion is alot more sensitive and useful for those tight turns. It's a step up from just WSAD'ing you're way to munich.
All in all, i give euro truck simulator an 8.3/10, odd ranking but very respectable.

In Broforce's arcade-style campaign, or its suite of alternate modes, you take on the role of a randomized bro and kill your way across jungles and cities, aiming for an exit point or a boss fight. The way you get there is at your discretion, though. The terrain gets blasted away by your weaponry the same as any enemy; in keeping with the Minecraft/Spelunky zeitgeist, tunneling through 20 feet of concrete with a shotgun is as valid a way to the level's end as any other. Such freedom opens up some interesting strategic possibilities, like shooting the floor out from underneath an otherwise imposing foe. It also makes for some zany, unpredictable runs, especially when you're paired with trigger-happy teammates who don't give much thought to blowing up the platform you're standing on. The campaign can be taken online, and there are a few local multiplayer diversions on offer, like a player-versus-player deathmatch, and another variant that sees characters fleeing an encroaching blast from the left side of the screen.

I absolutely love this game!! its a must get for any Total War fan. The graphics are stellar, the gameplay has been improved, having an impressive fleet actually means something, but you dont have to have one for the sole purpose of carting you land units around because land units can deploy on water all on their own. You can have your fleet aid you in land and siege battles which makes them 1000x better. Diplomacy is also more involved allowing you to coordinate targets with your allies, and political intriges have been added to spice up your faction. They added all of this without taking away from what it is to be a Total War game or from why we loved Rome 1 .
My gripes about this game are so insignificant compared to what Total War added that I almost dont want to bring them up, but for the sake of fairness I will include them. Firstly, your generals' talents and retinue take a major hit in this game. you are limited to 3 talents and 2 retinue slots. For me, I liked having an absuredly large retinue in Rome 1 so I was upset when I saw this. I'm guessing they did this for balancing purposes since your individual armies take on a more personalized role. Every army you raise is named and they can gain ranks and aquire skills just like a general. The individual units within the army also rank up.
My second issue is that you are more limited to what you can build in each individual city. This again seems to be a balancing decision as collectable taxes, food consumption/production, and relative happiness are all mitigated by the cities you control within a province. I find it helps cut back the micro managing of each individual city letting you focus on other aspects of the game. Also each citiy benefits from the buildings in other cities if they are within the same province.
My last gripe is that the actions of your agents cost money. usually within the 400-800 gold range but that becomes neglegable mid to late game. so just focus on something else early game and then get into it with your agents once you're more financially secure.
Ultimaltely if you liked Total War: Rome you will like its successor. the $60 price tag is a bit much so if you're on a tight budget or are still aprehensive about the game just wait until it goes on one of the many Steam Sales and get it for like $20.

This game is amazing. Much superior graphics to the original, although graphics were never a big deal to begin with in this game. New stats means more places to put your points which means more thinking is required to make your build for pvp. If you only pve you can play endlessly till you get 99 in everything if you wanted to. Overall the game is good and definitely worth trying.
There are downsides though. One is that pve is way better than pvp currently (as of 6-5-14). Magic has become very overpowered, quality builds are non-existent in dark souls 2 (no one would go 40 str 40 dex in this version of dark souls). Elemental weapons +10 do more dmg than A/S rank scaling weapons at +10 with 40 into the required main dmg stat (str or dex, or both). Players can buff themselves multiple times over, stacking iron skin, numbness, and many others making you basically have god mode. Likewise I don't see dex as being a viable stat to use at all, even if the stat boosts your ability to inflict status ailments (in pvp this is negligable since players can 1 or 2 hit any one or give up because the enemy stacked many buffs)
Besides PVP another issue is soul memmory. Every single soul you get is recorded, and your ability to be matched up with other players is based on your soul memmory. Your soul memmory could be 1 million and anothers also 1 million. The problem with this is that you could be only soul level 80 while the other player is soul level 120 and you have to pvp some one who from the start is already superior than yourself. On top of this they could also have better gear, at which point you should just give up. This makes PVP unfair as you may not get the chance to ever fight some one on equal grounds as yourself. Without this there is no point in PVP at all. (granted some skill is involved, but a hit from a low level without a +10 weapon is nothing compared to a high level with a +10 weapon. A high level would have to suck really bad to lose to an undergeared player)

I said: Screw "Shinji Mikami!"and bought Alien Isolation instead and what I got was a Dark Souls-esque survival stealth game, full of tension.
The atmosphere of the game is immensely rich as it draws from the already well established Alien franchise and pulls you in on much more immersive level. The clunky 70's 80's sci-fi look is gorgeous and is somewhat realistic considering space technology as of now. Music is fairly well threaded throughout, with orchestrated melodies fused with electronic percussion lending itself to the film's own music score, whilst adding to the overall tense feeling that lingers throughout.
The storyline is decently written with good pacing which consequently makes the game is long. However the length is not a negative as I found it made sense when looking at the storyline and the setting.  The pacing also presented different layers of tension with each threat that arises.  As the game goes on, you do gain a bit of more confidence but still tension seeps in you like acid.
On Hard difficulty the games works very much like Dark Souls: a game which prepares you for well for most things in life ;D
Alien Isolation doesn't hold your hand and it does punish one for being cocky,  noisy and even aggressive at times. Saves points are very much like the typewriters of the old RE titles. However even saving can lead to a risk of dying at is leaves one open for a brief moment as so do many other things. Reloading, crafting, using computers, devices and tools all leave you open which furthers adds to the tension. Combat is simple and enjoyable as this is a stealth game. The Alien has the best unpredictable AI that I've experienced and has a lethal grab radius so keep your distance like it's Street Fighter! ;) However if you're not cautious and don't have your wits about you, you will die alot.
Although in my playthrough there were a few Bethesda like glitches (Like floppy corpses, static humans or the odd jittery Alien), the only things I felt that really detracted from the experience of the game was the vagueness of certain items controls when it game to a certain hacking game of matching inputs and the inventory wheel. I use a Xbox 360 gamepad. The wheel itself felt slow when in the heat of quick thinking and panic so it really forces one to be one step ahead of the game in this aspect. The D-Pad does help with quick weapon switches and the hacking game, but again the game doesn't hold your hand for these things.
Another thing that was not entirely clear is the optional collectables in relation to backtracking. Depending on how far you are in the story, you pick up the Nostromo  Logs and need only to simply reload your save. This saves time and a huge hassle when backtracking. Backtracking itself  was only bothersome with me when it came to the archive logs and bouncing back and forth from one switch to another in an area. However the threats are the reason why the backtracking can be nerve wracking  and many other games are far to linear in comparison which hurts their own atmosphere with a lack of engagement and exploration with the detailed environments developers make these days.

As evident in its thoroughly rich and tense atmosphere and its intelligent and challenging game play, Alien Isolation is a true success of the concept and execution of film to videogame.

Game adds a unique take on the Thriller genre of horror games sprouting. It doesn't just use horror as its only suspense. The item system is unique and doesn't detract from the suspenseof the game. The AI in this is the other unique feature with the NPCs acting different with every play through or restart, gives a unique experience.

Alien: Isolation is the Alien game that fans have been waiting decades for. Not only does it faithfully recreate the atmosphere of the original Ridley Scott film, but it finally makes the Xenomorph something to be afraid of again. The graphics are absolutely phenomenal and some of the best in the gaming industry to date along with incredible sound design and an unexpectedly lengthy story. The gameplay may have a few quirks, and the storyline may be hard to follow when your constantly running from hiding spot to hiding spot, too afraid to peek over the counter to grab that extra flare; but this game is the best Alien experience oyu will ever get.
Let's start by talking about the gameplay. Unlike past Alien games, this one focuses entirely on the original film "Alien" by Ridley Scott. Gone are the large assault rifles and grenades that used to make short work of Xenomorphs in past games. In their place is a 26 hour game of hide-and-seek. Alien: Isolation focuses more so on stealth tactics and the methods of deception in order to accomplish your goals. There's absolutely no way to kill the Alien with any items you find, so the game forces you to move carefully from room to room, using any cover or hiding spots you can find. While it may seem easy to just be patient, the more you wait, the more the Alien learns and the easier it is for it to find you. Sometimes hiding in a locker and holding your breath will allow you to slip by undetected, but if you use this tactic too often, the Alien figures it out and rips the door off and.. well.. you know the rest. Though I did feel the gameplay could use a few improvements. For one, the Androids on the ship didn't really feel necessary as they only felt like a place-filler whenever the Alien wasn't present and they certainly weren't nearly as interesting. Another issue I had was with the movement of the character herself. The crouching speed is incredibly slow compared to usual stealth game standards, which makes sneaking up on enemy humans/androids without them turning around close to impossible. I also feel the hint that the game gives you about sitting back inside lockers and holding your breath is not nearly clear enough. It took me several attempts just to read what the hint was saying before the Alien ripped the door off and chewed on my face. Other than these small issues, the game itself is incredibly immersive and really does make you feel like you are in the classic 1979 horror masterpiece.
On a technical level; the graphics and sound design are beautiful in this game. It is incredibly clear that the developers of Alien: Isolation absolutely love their source material and have meticulously recreated the exact same atmosphere that individuals experienced back in the theatre. Lights slowly flicker as they turn on, old green CRT monitors buzz and shake,  and the Alien can always be heard thumping around in the vents above you, ready to jump down at completely random intervals. The actual visuals are gorgeous with light being reflected and refracted off of steam that slowly flows out of vents in the wall, and the slow burning at the end of your flamethrower shedding only a minuscule comfort of light against the sides of the vents you hope are safe. The only real technical issue I can find with the game is it's lackluster human character animations. They feel very stiff and unrealistic. Thankfully, the star of the show looks phenomenal. The Alien will slowly coil itself as it rolls out of a cieling vent and slunks to the floor, only to quickly raise it's head and begin stomping down the hallway, now and again stopping to stair mysteriously down a hall. You can never tell what the Alien is going to do next and it makes your movement choices even more horrifying. The AI for the Alien is done perfectly and not once in my 26 hours of play time did I notice any AI glitches that killed the immersion. Creative Assembly made entirely sure that both the environment and the creature itself are as genuine as the movie, and it shows perfectly.
Now in terms of story, it's pretty straight forward horror/Alien style storyline. The only issue I had with it is that the characters aren't very memorable and it's incredibly hard to even piece together what the story is when you're constantly logging off of computers as you're in the middle of an email only because you heard the Alien thumping around outside of the room you were in. There's tons of hidden messages, ID tags, and email messages that piece together survivor stories of both the Nosostromo (from the movie) and the Sevastopol (the massive space station setting of the game itself), so those willingly to sit there and read the emails to get more out of the story are certainly welcome to try, but the game certainly doesn't appear to encourage it considering the gameplay doesn't freeze when you're reading computer screens or rewiring panels. So to summarize, the story's good from what I was able to make out from it. There's plenty of fan appeal with all kinds of recreated experiences straight from the movie to keep anyone with even a remote interest in the Alien series happy.
So to wrap this all up, Alien Isolation is a fantastic work of art that successfully recreates the exact tension (and maybe even more so) as the original Ridley Scott film. The graphics are fantastic and the Alien certainly steals the show with unpredictable AI and incredible attention to detail. The game can be quite difficult to most, but as long as you're careful and avoid making stupid movement choices and use your scarce resources wisely, you should be able to make it in one piece. I personally played it on the hardest difficulty and was only killed by the Alien throughout the 26 hours around 20 some times. The game even features plenty of bonus levels and challenges to keep you occupied if you haven't had enough after the lengthy campaign, which is great for replay value. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys stealth, horror, and obviously to ANYONE who has ever enjoyed "Alien."

The Elder scrolls Online... Where to start. This is by no means an Elder scrolls game, Though that does not make it a bad game. Previous fans of the Elder Scrolls may not enjoy is nearly as much as The masterpieces that were Skyrim and Oblivion. The story seems like it wants to be and elder scrolls story, and cashes in on some of those big actors Bethesda can get ahold of, but its not the same. If you start this game expecting somthing similar to Skyrim, or even World of Warcraft you will be sorely dissapointed. This game is not the best MMORPG, and by no means a good Elder Scrolls game. But at this point you are probably wondering why I reccomended it, if all I have done is pound it into the ground for the past paragraph.
When I said its not an Elder scrolls game, I ment it, but that does not mean its not a good game. I would rather play Skyrim any day, but for very different reason than this game. ESO focuses more on skills and leveling than weapon strength, which fits a MMORPG well. This way, some newb cant buy a super op weapon, and completly own people in the Vet league. I also think the crafting system is much more in depth and fun than in the rest of the Elder scrolls franchise. Adventuring with friends is a joy in this game, and its really the only way to play it, which mean the game will be pretty boring if you dont have any friends. Guild trading is dont perfectly for the game type, and creates an immersive econony(Though finding a good trading guild is hard). Overall, there are certain things this game does better, and certain thing it could inprove on. But please dont let the negative review put you off, as most of them were written before the Tamriel Unlimited update. I dont regret buying this game, and I hope to enjoy many more hours with it.

A great game, but slower to advance if you're used to Elminage Original. The story is short but is pretty intriguing, if you can progress through the game at a steady rate and remember what's going on, but is otherwise barebones and nonexistant if you go after everything else.
The game is great fun if you've played the classics like Wizardry or Pool of Radiance on the nes/snes/pc and the throwback to the style of play will surely keep you hooked with its dungeon crawling, resource management and cool looking monster art. You'll have a blast so long as musical aesthetics don't bug you, as this game has limited tracks. They annoyed me at first, but have grown on me and suit the atmosphere of the dungeons well enough. Just don't linger on the town menu for too long or you'll really notice that 15 second loop.
That said, the game is pretty unfair, though with multiple saves and reloading being really quick, the unfairness is mostly a hassle that's quickly overcome and you'll continue to advance at a steady pace, maybe losing a minute or two every so often as you reload your save. Unless you're me and you draft for your back row, an alchemist, bishop and summoner in which case progress is slow and painful.
It doesn't look so bad until you realize you need 4th level magic to progress in a sidequest, and you don't get that until level 13 as a bishop, when all the other basic jobs like mage or cleric get 7th level magic by then. It's also not so bad unless you're stubborn like me and have to have all your exp numbers equal and you refuse to replace none of your party members or all of them.
Not to mention you also don't get level 5 magic for healing as a bishop until level 18 and that one carries the revive spell and not having that by the time you reach 3 skull dungeons, ooh boy, you're in a for a long haul and a lot of resetting. Again, these are self inflicted woes and would not befall someone who takes a conventional party, it would be a quick fix to draft a normal cleric and mage and progress through the story at a steady pace and, but I brick walled myself with poor composition and a hard headed ego.
*mild spoiler* Also, speaking of 4th level magic, if you grab the key item from the dungeon and can't cast any spells or haven't cast levitate beforehand, you will lock your party on the bottom floor unless you send a rescue squad or die and have bones slippers in your inventory. (The rescue team took me 6 hours to train up to send down there to fetch them.) Consider that fair warning, the game does not pull its punches and will punish you for not considering all options. I enjoy this aspect though as a lot of games would rather hold your hand instead and prevent scenarios like that.
*end minor spoiler*

A faithful wizardry clone, but not actually a good game.
I really badly wanted to like this game, it does a lot of things well, and it's really hard to find modern updates to the Wizardry formula. But it's just not good.
The first big problem is that this is an intensely, intensely mechanics-driven game that is awful at explaining those mechanics. The entire game is translated from Japanese, and done so poorly. The in-game explanations for mechanics are usually vague or misleading, in a tiny scrolling 1-line box. The manual explains some things, but not nearly enough. At the same time, the game itself is wildly unbalanced. This is normally fine for this type of game, discovering abusive combinations and tricks is half the fun, but you basically can only figure things out through trial and error or going online for guides. A 'blind' playthrough, even for someone with huge amounts of RPG experience, would be practically unplayable. You can't just 'go with sounds good' because the game is intensely punishing for mistakes.
That translation, combined with the natural vagueness of a wizardry clone, also makes questing an enormous pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The interactions with the story and NPC's are incredibly vague: characters stand alone in dungeons and bark a short paragraph of vague, badly translated info at you, and then you're supposed to put 2 and 2 together and figure out what they need. If you forget what they said, you're kind of screwed. Again, this sort of stuff would be tolerable if the game was well made, well translated, with a good UI, but it's just not.
Finally, this just isn't a well designed game. The dungeons are tedious, samey loops designed to be as drawn out as possible. The map system is really ill-considered, I'm actually fine with limiting map access, but this is like a weird worst of both worlds that just winds up being annoying. Character building is FILLED with lots of obscure mechanics that are impossible to know ahead of time without a guide and that can have a big impact. The game is incredibly random, literally in the sense of using random numbers, and forces the player to cope with that without giving them the knowledge to actually plan ahead and do so. The game relies immensely on grinding and repitition, but then has an absolutely awful UI to make that experience as lame as possible.
It's just not a good game. I got this for $3 on a sale. For that price, it's fun and worth it if you like the genre. For the 10 dollar list price though, even at that cheap price, it's just not worth it. The only way you will like this game is if you really love intensely mechanics driven RPG's, know how to play Wizardries, and are willing to put up with a lot of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Even then, it's just not a good example of the genre.

Rating: 10/10
Why?
Simple. This is probably one of the best zombie games i have ever played. Why?, because of the realism, the maps, the guns, and best of all, when they come together to create the most fun ever in a zombie game.
The Realism
No More Room In Hell(NMRIH) is incredbly realistic. The ammo shortages, the gun names and types, all of it! Whereas other games decide to throw loads of guns and zombies in one cramped map and tell the to fight each other to the death, which in some cases is fun, NMRIH gives varied maps, some large, some small, gives you some objectives, and asks you to complete them in order to escape.
The Maps
NMRIH has a large variety of maps, from NM_Favela, a large, Brazillian slum full to the brim with small huts, rooftop walkways and paths, then theres NM_Broadway, an average american street with a cinema to break into, an underground sewer to run through, and a tramline to escape.
The Guns
As with all zombie games, theres gotta be guns. Now, NMRIH is actually alot more melee based, but guns do play a large part. Theres never enough ammo, adding to the games sky rocketing realism, and the names, models, ammo types, and mechanics follow the suite too, with each gun requiring a specific ammo type, having an incredbly vivid viewmodel, and great animations to make you feel like your really there.
The Melee Weapons
How could we forget, NMRIH has a large selection of melee weapons to acompany the guns. They are probably the games least and most realistic feature at the same time. They don't break, and the damage is pretty bad for some, but they all have good attack radiuses and there are alot of them with great animations and models too.

It’s been almost 10 years since I last played System Shock 2. The nostalgia I have for this great survival horror rpg is incredible. Everything that established my love for games can be found in this game. Great atmosphere, great gameplay, a mysterious and enticing story, great environment design, the whole package. Considering it’s a re-release from 1999 with updated compatibility for modern systems, it’s well worth the current price. Night Dive studios have done a great job at fixing up the game and making it available for the modern audience.
Now if you’ve played
of the Bioshock games you will most likely fall in love with System Shock 2. Irrational Games (most notably Ken Levine) built the System Shock games before moving onto the Bioshock games and they share many similarities in terms of pacing and story. I’m going to refer to similarities between both these game series so that more modern gamers can more easily understand System Shock 2.
System Shock 2 really does stand on its own as a unique adventure that throws you into the bowels of a distressed spaceship. Unlike Bioshock though, there are many more RPG elements. Your character uses cyber modules earned by completing objectives to unlock upgrades and skills. You have an inventory that can hold various different in game items. Weapons degrade over time, different armours can be equipped, and parts of enemies can be researched to find weaknesses. Also similar to Bioshock, there’s a lot of scrounging. You have to constantly look for supplies and ways to stay alive. Finding that one clip for your pistol or hiding from enemies as they search for you. Irrational games KNOW how to make tense situations and I love it.
In terms of survival horror, it doesn’t get much better than this. I remember being terrified of certain parts back when I was younger, and to an extent, these parts still scare me! That feeling of dread around every corner is very common. The sound design is made so well that it enhances the atmosphere in ways I can’t easily describe. This is something that was done well in the Bioshock games too.
The graphics are great too! All resolutions are supported up to 1920x1080 and many mods can be applied that further enhance textures, models, etc. You can refer to the user created Steam mod guide for ways to further enhance the experience! There’s also a co-op mode through the main story. It’s not supported officially, but can still be used by creating your own network using Hamachi or similar programs. I’ve yet to try this out for myself.
At the end of the day, System Shock 2 is better than ever and I’m so pleased that one of my favourite games has finally made it to Steam. If you like sci-fi RPGs, give it a go. If you like Bioshock, you should already have played this :P

I don't even know where to begin commenting about Dark Souls 2. There are so many good things about it that it's so hard for me to materialize them into actual words because I was busy immersing myself so much into the game this whole time.
But I guess the things that stand out the most to me was first the concept of ruthless difficulty that for sure will require you to die 3-4 times before you finally understand the patterns, in other words, Trials & Errors. Death in Dark Souls 2 is even more punishing than it was in Dark Souls, that's for sure. But if you compare the severity of the death punishment with the educational benefits derived from each one of them, then it's really not so bad at all. Each death in Dark Souls makes sense, you can't blame anything but yourself. And because of such nature, you're bound to learn more and much faster. And because you tried and died hard, that when you finally overcome the challenge, there will be a strong feeling of gratification.
Unlike the designs in many other games where everything caters to your every single need like a paranoid and clingy boyfriend/girlfriend, Dark Souls 2 absolutely gives you zero♥♥♥♥♥ The functionality, the visuals, the atmosphere, the enemies, etc. They all make sense in terms of what they are, and what kind of impact they should have on you. There is a feeling of coldness, loneliness, paranoia and fear throughout your entire journey in Drangleic. If you die, nobody will be there to help you (unless you put an effort into summoning help, but even then, 90% of the time you will be all by yourself). There is always the paranoia that behind that corner there might just lie something that would jump out and devour you the moment you stepped near. The enemies, of course, never give off the sense that they'll ever hesitate and spare your life. If you manage to kill them, then you earned it. If not, then too bad, sucks to be you.
Personally I love this kind of concept. It's not even brutal. It feels brutal to you because you're so used to games holding your hands throughout the entire experience. Dark Souls is about teaching you the value of learning through your own mistakes, and the feeling of utmost satisfaction when you overcome challenges by the experience you gathered through pain and suffering. In Dark Souls, stats don't mean a whole lot. It's you. You are the sole determinant of success in this game.
Please, by all means, play this game, even if you don't like the RPG genre, because I believe Dark Souls will teach you something very universally valuable.

Крайне противоречивая игра. Скажу сразу: если в первые полчаса не понравилось, можно выбрасывать, потому что дальше только хуже. В этой игре всё сделано максимально неудобным игроку способом. После пары часов игры я стал подозревать, что это сделано специально, после пары десятков - решил было, что создатели просто затачивались на игру высокоуровневыми персонажами, не обращая внимания на трудности низкоуровневых  и игнорируя грубость интерфейса, но последний донжон (съевший у меня не одну сотню часов) всё расставил на свои места: это таки сделано специально.
В остальном перед нами игра, сделанная по канонам первой трилогии Wizardry - ну, только что цветная и более разнообразная. Более того, один из бонусных донжонов прямо является трибьютом оригиналу - он чёрно-белый и без текстур. Игра - Dungeon Crawler в чистом виде: ходишь по лабиринтам толпой из 6 человек в два ряда, от первого лица, походово, уничтожаешь монстров, собираешь лут, повторить до бесконечности. Да, монстры и ловушки невидимы, пока на них не наступишь. Да, они возрождаются после любого Save/Load. И да, разумеется, случайные монстры тоже есть! (Я уже говорил, что игра к игроку недружелюбна?)
Классы здесь украдены из Wizardry же, но ролевая система далеко не такая щедрая: здесь точно так же есть "базовые" классы (боец, вор, маг, клирик, алхимик), которые заточены под одну задачу и быстро прокачиваются, есть и "продвинутые" классы, сочетающие свойства пары базовых, и есть "премиум", которые обладают особыми свойствами и сочетают несколько классов сразу. Но, в отличие от оригинала, смена класса вызвает полное забвение всех навыков, уровней и параметров. Сохраняются только очки жизни и по три заклинания каждого уровня.
Система оборудования крайне идиотская: складывается только Armor Class и бонусы для оружия. Все параметры, относящиеся к магии, не суммируются - берётся наибольший бонус, что означает, что 90% вещей в игре не нужны совершенно ни для чего. Кроме того, все вещи с заклинаниями имеют примерно 30-50% шанс сломаться после использования заклинания. А восстановить их можно только в городе или специальным заклинанием. И да, довольно скоро начинают встречаться монстры, которые ломают и ту экипировку, которая не ломается сама.
Монстры здесь крайне злобные. Очень скоро начинают попадаться враги со спецатаками, среди которых есть и обезглавливание, убивающее любого, независимо от параметров - и нет, 100% защиты от обезглавливания в игре у игрока нет (у монстров - есть). И такие монстры есть уже с четвёртого донжона.
Впрочем, жить с этим можно, если подобрать экипировку... пока проходишь сюжетную кампанию. Бонусные донжоны - особенно последняя башня - имеют монстров, которые безоговорочно убивают часть партии или вообще всех, как ты их не экипируй.
Ах, да, убитых персонажей можно воскресить. Примерно с 80%-ным шансом на успех. В остальных 20% персонаж умирает совсем, и воскресить его можно только в городе. Я упоминал, что игра нас не любит?
Ну, и донжоны. Они хороши и разнообразны. Полный джентльменский набор: есть многоуровневые лабиринты, подводные, есть ямы, ловушки, телепорты, односторонние стены, скрытые двери... здесь есть всё. Включая совершенно пустые сегменты лабиринта, где есть только монстры. Потратьте час-другой, чтобы это выяснить. У высокоуровневых магов, правда, есть заклинание телепортации, которое позволяет попасть в любую точку карты, где вы уже были. Но есть и антимагические зоны, которые блокируют всю магию, отключают все зачарования, и телепортироваться из них нельзя. И блокированные зоны есть, куда телепортироваться не выйдет - в стратегических местах, поближе к боссам. А последняя бонусная башня имеет 25 уровней и при этом блокирует телепортацию совсем. Я уже... ах, да, говорил.
В общем, вот так оно всё и идёт. Если вам нравится бродить по лабиринтам и зарисовывать их руками (автокарта, правда, есть. И это предмет. И он ломается, естественно), если вам нравится убивать бесчисленные толпы монстров, всё усиливая персонажей, если вы согласны ради этого терпеть почти полное отсутствие сюжета и уродский интерфейс а-ля 80-е - игра рекомендуется. Если же всё это вызывает у вас скорее недоумение - лучше не надо.
P.S. После прохождения последней башни убийство Главного Босса дало мне три артефакта (аналогичные тем, что я получал в конце сюжета)... и всё. Ни ролика, ни завершения сюжета, ни-че-го. Достойный конец игры. Можно играть дальше - только зачем?..

I absolutely love this game!! its a must get for any Total War fan. The graphics are stellar, the gameplay has been improved, having an impressive fleet actually means something, but you dont have to have one for the sole purpose of carting you land units around because land units can deploy on water all on their own. You can have your fleet aid you in land and siege battles which makes them 1000x better. Diplomacy is also more involved allowing you to coordinate targets with your allies, and political intriges have been added to spice up your faction. They added all of this without taking away from what it is to be a Total War game or from why we loved Rome 1 .
My gripes about this game are so insignificant compared to what Total War added that I almost dont want to bring them up, but for the sake of fairness I will include them. Firstly, your generals' talents and retinue take a major hit in this game. you are limited to 3 talents and 2 retinue slots. For me, I liked having an absuredly large retinue in Rome 1 so I was upset when I saw this. I'm guessing they did this for balancing purposes since your individual armies take on a more personalized role. Every army you raise is named and they can gain ranks and aquire skills just like a general. The individual units within the army also rank up.
My second issue is that you are more limited to what you can build in each individual city. This again seems to be a balancing decision as collectable taxes, food consumption/production, and relative happiness are all mitigated by the cities you control within a province. I find it helps cut back the micro managing of each individual city letting you focus on other aspects of the game. Also each citiy benefits from the buildings in other cities if they are within the same province.
My last gripe is that the actions of your agents cost money. usually within the 400-800 gold range but that becomes neglegable mid to late game. so just focus on something else early game and then get into it with your agents once you're more financially secure.
Ultimaltely if you liked Total War: Rome you will like its successor. the $60 price tag is a bit much so if you're on a tight budget or are still aprehensive about the game just wait until it goes on one of the many Steam Sales and get it for like $20.

For clarification: buy the base game.  The expansions don't add much, and the bug-fixes that came with them are automatically downloaded.  The game itself is very good, now that they have patched it to the point of playability, however, the multiplayer can still be a bit buggy.
Nevertheless, it does add some very interesting elements, and will probably end up in the same vein as Empire: Total War: terrible at launch, but eventually redeemed to the point of being good, not great.
To be fair, a lot of the features do come off as half-finished ideas, just like in Empire, however, both of these games were ambitious, and Empire led to Napoleon, which was heralded, and eventually to the pinnacle of the series, Shogun 2.
A lot of the negative reviews that you will read are also from people who have been playing Shogun 2 for a while, and yes, compared to that, arguably the best in the series, this does come off as a half-finished mess, however, when asked to stand on its own, it is at least a fun game.

I really wanted to love this game.  I wanted it to be as good as the first one.
But there is something really missing from this game that made the first one so great.
Flow.
It has none.
You reach dead ends constantly that you have to remember to come back to at some point when you get something later in the game so you're forced basically on a march through content in a fairly specific course of events.  To me that made it lose the thing I loved so much about the first game... exploring.
You can't go certain places because you need a key,  you can't go other places because you haven't spawned and come through it from the other direction from a specific campfire so you could kick a barrel into a wall and opened the porcullis.  You can't jump down there, you don't have something that costs 15,000 souls or something you get from a character 4/5 of the way through the game.  It's stuff like that along with the really clunky backstab (which was my most favorite move in the first game) that makes this a game I really wanted to love, but really can't.
They want from hard to sadistic in some of the areas.  Scripted one-hit kills are abundant (giants, king fight, etc).  It's one thing to punish someone for making a mistake.  It's another to simply kill them because it's their first time fighting a boss.
The other thing I didn't like much about the game was the lack of any humanity.  As you die you lose health.. all the way to almost half of it.  ANd you can't farm enemies and respawn them over and over.  Eventually they stop spawning.  So you can literally only get just so many levels each time you play through making the difficulty brutal instead of steep.  Especially if you had the issues I had with falling off a ledge and not being able to recover the lost souls because there was no recovery bloodspot in an area I could access.
The last thing I'll say about this game is:  If you don't like cheaters, don't play it online.  Luckily you can play it with Steam in "offline mode" which turns off the invasion aspect.  But about 95% of the people I went up against had hacks ranging from health to unlimited spells to walking in midair.
Definitely have to say "nonrecommend" on this one.  And believe me, that's about as masochistic of a review as I've ever had to do :(

Just Cause 3 is really fun. Really. But there are few things I'm not a fan of.
-After liberating a base enemies from the general area disappear instantly.
-After liberating ALL bases, which I have done before on a different platform, means essentially
-The rebel drop system and fast travel system is kind of annoying, with a finite number of flares and beacons. I recommend getting mods for infinite beacons and flares.
-The biggest island on the map is incredibly boring and bland. To the south, there's all the cool towns, the one city in the game (a pretty pitiful one though) and then the rest is a few train tracks, some military bases and far too many isolated military outposts which are almost impossible to find.
-The story, which I thought was great at first, although entertaining, is only interesting the first time around. I had the same issue with Just Cause 2, but I should still mention.
-20-30 story missions is impressive over Just Cause 2's pitiful 7 story missions, but at least JC2 had side missions. Some of the side missions in JC2 were amazing and were all pretty diverse in what they did, while I only remember a few of the JC3 missions distinctively.
-It's harder to get the police/military on you, where it was really easy in 2. The chases in Just Cause are ridiculous, so I was a bit annoyed about that, especially if you just want to jump in and have some quick, explosive fun.
-The map as a whole is just not as interesting as 2 in my opinion. Remember some of the great locations in 2? Panau City, the tall hotels, all the military bases with jets to steal and what not? 3 has one major city and a few cool military bases but all the bases are pretty boring when your people are populating them.
-The enemy is pretty stupid too, kind of taking suspense out of the action setpieces.
I got this game for PC mainly because the multiplayer mod is coming out pretty soon. I also want to just regularlly mod this game, but there don't seem to be any real amazing mods out at the moment. If you want to get it to play with friends soon, I'm sure that'll be a blast.
Would I recommend this game to you? Yes. On a few conditions.
1. If you were a fan of Just Cause 2, you will most likely froth at the mouth with the wingsuit and smoother traversal system, although there were a lot of rather questionable decisions made to remove aspects of the HUD such as removing the mini-map and health bar.
2. If you are ready to play through the game story once and only once.
3. The game is just nowhere near as much fun once you capture a whole reigon, where there's no military and wingsuiting or driving is only exciting for so long.
4. If you have a few friends, and you like action adventure games, then buy this game for the multiplayer mod and mods.
Overall, Just Cause 3 is a fun game, but really only once. I just feel like Just Cause 3 could have been a lot better overall. Just Cause 2 had so many great and memorable moments, and Just Cause 3 is lacking the sort of complete over-the-topness that Just Cause 2 had.
For the first time playing through: about an 8/10
Second time playing through: about 7/10 so far

As a huge fan of Just Cause 2, I was very eager to get into JC3 but when I first loaded the game, the hype dropped to the centre of the earth. This game had so much potential and I'm very disappointed at how it turned out.
First off, why on earth is the preformance so poor? Any AAA game that can't run 60 FPS on my gaming PC is not fit for release, I barely get 30-35 FPS on this game, I could get a stable 1k to 2k FPS on JC2, why the sudden FPS drop?
Second, The map is supposedly so "Huge" but only the south side of the map even has content, I was super excited to explore the map after around 3 hours of exploring. I finally headed north where I was stopped dead, the whole north side of the map is practically empty, with hardly ANY citys at all and only a few small army camps... I was quite upset.
Thrid, the cities are all the same, take a police station, tear down a statue, break some speakers and take down some signs. ALL CITIES ARE ALMOST THE EXACT SAME IN DESIGN AND LAYOUT!!!!
Forth, the map feels very "copy-pasted" all the cities and villages look the exact same, even some of the road layouts are the same throughout the map, there is no different types of cities other then "Bigger" and "Smaller" versions of the same thing. In JC2 I could drive for 10 minutes and find a completely new type of city (The Desert villages and Snow Camps looked completely different from the tropical villages) but in this game everywhere in the map looks and feels the same.
Fifth, there are many small but annoying things missing from the game. EXAMPLES (no police sirens or lights, the ocean is very bumpy in all places making it hard to drive properly and many other small things like that)
In all, this game has a lot of added features that I really like but they are blocked out by the MASS of errors and issues in the game, all I can say is "The game is fun to play, but it feels like an early access game that is not finished." Hopefully these issues will be resloved but I'm not too sure the devs are even working on half of this stuff....

I'm not usually one to buy hardcore horror titles, however due for my love for the Alien Franchise I had no choice but to pick this up and return into the dark depths of another deep space adventure.
That said I've played quite a few horror titles and none, NONE, have instilled as much terror into me as Alien: Isolation. I'm still not very far into the game but I'm very much impressed. I didn't need to take more than a few steps to notice the attention to detail in the environments they have done an incredible job in re-creating the original 1979 vibe. You've got original sounding sounds, original voice actors (in the Nostromo scenes) and other little quirks such as the classic delayed hallway lighting...Even with the stuff they just feel... right, new tools look and behave like they belong in the world having obviously been brilliantly thought out and designed.
I could go on all day about the environments, they're beautiful, the lighting in particular. You'll really get the feeling you're in the movie, which is cool...But terrifying at the same time. If you don't have surround sound and really want to experience the game in full I'd suggest getting a surround headset like myself, I'm not sure how scary the game would be when you can't hear the alien clawing at the flooring as it runs after you in the hallways...Or it clambering around in the walls, circumnavigating you through the dark air vents...
The AI is smart...Adding the terror, escaping the alien really is bloody difficult. (I play in hard difficulty, "The way its intended to be played" according to the desc.) The story has got me wrapped up in it right now, its engaging and fresh. I'm even getting vibes from later movies like Alien 3 with the paranoia and survivor groups, which you will encounter.
Either way, to sum it up. Its an awesome game, the Alien game us fans have deserved for a long, long time. Finally they got it right! Dim the lights, turn up the sound, grit your teeth and sing "You are my lucky star..." in vain...
- One last note most of this will really only be appreciated by a hardcore franchise fan, this is based off the original Alien movie, remember what the xenomorph is and is capable of. You're able to defend yourself to an extent but don't expect Colonial Marines, its defiently not that. And thank god...Expect to find yourself hiding, trying to outsmart the "perfect organism".

Weak points include the archaic interface, lack of information regarding some mechanics and questionable design decisions, such as maps being consumable items and inventory management being a pain. Though I have to say that those things are very faithful to the old Wizardry games and are clearly by design. I also strongly recommend playing this with a controller.
Everything else is stellar. The art is of high quality. The soundtrack is surprisingly good and fitting of the theme and mood of the game. Gameplay is decently balanced and all classes feel very useful, with strong and weak points. Combat is interesting, with multiple ways to approach battles. Dungeon design ramps up pretty quickly and can get crazy later on. And there's a ton of content, with 70+ (!) dungeon floors to explore.
Considering the price, it's a steal. Fans of DRPGs should definitely check this game out.

Fans of Ridley Scott's "Alien," or true survival horror games, rejoice! Though it isn't a perfect game it's a dozen steps in the right direction for both the Alien franchise and horror games in general.
Graphics: Simple yet elegant. Some scenes are near photo realistic to my eyes. The graphic buffs with their ever searching eyes may find some muddy textures here and there but let's face it, graphics don't make a game. Not saying this one isn't pleasing to behold because it definitely is.
Sound: The music strikes panic in your heart and the sound design will freeze your veins. Some of the best sound in the business.
Gameplay: Very simple. The majority of the time you will be sneaking around various enemies such as other humans, androids, and yep, you guessed it, an Alien. There are a handful of times when a flamethrower or shotgun will come in handy but for the most part the player will want to steer clear of these situations because it could attract unwanted attention or gain a quick death from the Alien. The game tends to punish you, especially early on, for not taking your time and playing it smart but as you progress and learn the "rhythm" of the game and acquire more gear it will become more natural and manageable.
The Alien's AI is fantastic and reacts in a "dynamic" fashion and not in a "static" fashion that average game AI has. Some will find this hyper realistic survival experience to be too challenging which in turn will cause them to think the AI is cheating. I assure you it is not. Like one of the game's trailer titles says, you need to "improvise."
Scare factor: I personally only jumped a handful of times but the sense of dread and the blood pressure raising atmosphere keeps you on the edge of your seat nearly the entire game. The ease of death for the player is what creates the most tension and dread. Death feels real and replicates what it would most likely feel like if the situation was real. This keeps you on your toes. But be prepared, you will most likely die ALOT in this game.
Replayability: This game is LONG for a single player experience. Some will find the slow pace of the game combined with the length to be too much but when did gamers start complaining about games not being short enough? Towards the end the game throws a few epic would be finales that make it seem like a "The End" sign should drop right after, only to keep you crawling through the dark dodging the xenomorph and other would be harm doers. Even I started rolling my eyes after the game kept going on after what seemed to be a great ending point. Hopefully a sequel can fix the pacing issue this one seems to suffer from toward the end.
PLAY IF: You are a fan of Ridley Scott's original "Alien" movie, love realistic survival horror, enjoy lengthy single player campaigns, love good atmosphere, don't have heart complications, want to experience something that could be viewed as revolutionary (the AI) in the industry, like a challenge.
DON'T PLAY IF: You are a bigger fan of John Carpenter's sequel "Aliens," are expecting Isolation to be more like the sequel and come complete with a pulse rifle, have ADD and prefer your games to only take 6-12 hourse to complete, are a wussy, your afraid of the dark, like predictable enemy AI, don't like challenging games.

From time to time I’ll have a disagreement between my evaluation of the game and what the Steam store’s evaluation of a game is. Games that I feel are deserving of a positive review score will have mixed or even a negative vote while there are some games where I feel the opposite. As I write this reflection a year and a half following the release of Elminage Gothic I see that the review count stands at mixed. However, it is close to a positive (62/34). So while I cannot be too disappointed I must admit that I thought that there was no doubt that the game would have a positive review score.
The biggest problem with the game from my perspective is the overall presentation. The basic things from the appearance of the UI and the menu system appear to be ripped from a game developed a decade prior to that. Given the level of modern luxuries that we gamers enjoy I can appreciate that many modern players wouldn’t find the game appealing from this perspective. This certainly appears to be the case when reading through the well written negative critiques of the game. In fact many of the positive reviews state the same thing. It’s a fair call. But it doesn’t break the game as far as I’m concerned. While you may feel that it negatively impacts your overall experience I find that it’s not one of the most important things for me. I suppose I just have different priorities.  Another issue that players have had is that they have claimed that the game has been ported directly from the PSP version of the game. I never did get around to play that version of the game but if it is it would explain pretty much everything about the presentation quality. Then there is the fact that the game, sadly, hasn’t been Steamified aside from trading cards.That means no achievements and of course no multiplayer (not that the game needs it).
So now that we’ve identified what is bad about the game we need to delve into what its strong points are. Chief among these is that it possesses varying levels of the dungeon and the different atmospheric settings of each such as semi underwater levels, It makes for a genuine dungeon crawling fanatics dream. The depth of the game systems, in loot, in actions and in spells, in specialist skills and abilities (alchemists are important in this game) and the amount of things that you can do could quite easily lead you to spending a couple of hundred hours exploring the game if you wanted to experience absolutely everything.
This is a game where you need to dig deep below the surface. Those who haven’t tend to be the ones who don’t enjoy the game.

First off: If you want to read about the good of this game, read another review. I am aware its not only negative. I'm just glad I finished it and can deinstall it at this point. Here's what I did not like:
Most of the game consists of you hiding, sneaking around and WAITING... avoiding the overpowered Alien or Androids. Depending on difficulty they will find you much easier and literally hunt you all over the place. You will spend alot of time in lockers and other hiding spots, only to STILL be discovered, after the Alien returns for the third time in a row to the room, before you had a chance to leave.
I didn't find the Alien(s) scary, or having to hide from it all the time. It frustrated me and I resorted regularly to cuss words when it got me. This combined with no anytime save system will have you play many parts over and over and over. I found this to be extremely boring and at a point switched from hard to easy, so I could kill off the Androids and chase off the Alien with the flamethrower more often. And often the alien will STILL hit you for half your life (on easy), before running off. There goes another medkit..
You will return to the same places over and over. After gadget upgrades you can open previously locked doors, and you WILL HAVE to go through those doors. Less new, more of the same corridors. And its basically all just corridors of a space station, looking very similar to one another.
The Alien can't just be killed off. It can just be chased off with the flamethrower (and maybe other weapons). But it will return soon and it doesn't look like its actually taking any damage. It's basically invincible until you reach a certain story point.
There are many, many buttons to press, levers to pull, machines to operate, computer logs to read and more minigames. In between that, you sit around and WAIT until the alien (the androids, the "civilians") leaves for a few seconds, so you can operate that thingy and get further in the story. This will repeat itself to exhaustion.
Towards the end the game tries to kill you off in about a hundred different ways, as everything escalates in some sort of cheap action movie finish. Up to scenes where you open a door, make a step and then die, squashed to bits. Next time wait a few seconds before making that step. And on that goes.
All in all I cannot recommend this game to anyone but the most diehard stealth game fans, who don't mind a challenge and who enjoy repeating the same few corridors over and over, until they don't get caught. I personally have other games to play and I'm glad this one is over.

I absolutely recommend this game. At my current hour count (10) I've barely scratched the surface and only haven't continued lately because life has kept me busy:
Highlights:
Hardcore dungeon crawling with 92 or so different dungeon levels. These are not the superficial, "skin" like differences you see in pretenders, but are things like levels that are partially underwater and your party will drown if you don't move quickly, or levels full of wind tunnels that impede navigation.
Difficult, tactics oriented combat in which you cannot solve every combat the same way. While the game starts off simple, it slowly escalates the level of threat it throws at you until you need counter several different game changing abilities so that you stand a chance at all.
Complex character building system in which creative multiclassing will get you far, while at the same time un class changed characters (innocents) get powerful equipment only they can use.
A large base of loot, of which many items have a unique niche instead of being exactly like x, but better or worse.
A complex crafting system in which the bonuses provided by your items can be enhanced or customized.
One of the classes (Summoner) can bind and contract monsters and then use them as seventh party members. This system alone has far more depth than many entire games.
There are people with hundreds of hours on this game still learning new things about it. I only regret that I haven't had the uninterrupted time for a proper runthrough myself.
With all that having been said, if you are a casual gamer or a hardcore pretender you should absolutely stay away. This is not one of those fake hardcore games where you just grind through trivial content, Elminage will not validate you. If you're looking for a grand story... you'll find a alright one, but not for free. This is not one of those visual novel, on rail experiences falsely described as an "RPG". This is classic, old school dungeon crawling fun. About the only legitimate problem I'd say is the interface, it's really poorly designed and could definitely do with better placement of options and keybindings but I recommend it in spite of that relatively minor problem.

Okay, so this is going to be a long review.  So for those who want the short version:
This game is awesome, but I am ABSOLUTELY disappointed of the progress that has been made in development.
--------------------
The long version:
This game came out on Steam around May 7th, 2015 and was put in Early Access.  I bought the game May 17th, 2015,  for the $20 price.  Now,  I had played the Legacy version of game before it was put on GreenLight and then it got on to Steam.  It was amazing and was looking forward to it being finished.
I figured when it would get released onto Steam, it would be the finished product, or at least more progress would be done on it.
But at that time, I didn't realize how f***ing wrong I would be.
When I played through the game and finished, I realized that nothing was greatly changed at all.  It felt like the Legacy version still.  Perhaps Xen needed more time I figured.
Over the following months and years, we would get cosmetic changes, more visuals on previous maps, bug fixes, some changes in the difficulty, and even one section of the game was slightly expanded upon.
We have gotten some screenshots of Xen, but nothing further than that.
--------------------
I hope this review and rant was informative and I will keep on updating this to reflect what I see and believe to be the state of the game. The game is definitely a very good remake of Half-Life. I am just disappointed about its development progress and just cannot fully recommend buying this, UNLESS it is on sale.

Quick review
When you're finished your 9-5 job or just got home from school, you sit at your computer, boot up Steam and do more work! From the guy in front brake-checking you for no reason, to the car in front going 50 in a 60 on highway systems that make no sense.
Summary of this game
This game offers customization and a wide open world that would make newer need for speed games jealous. You start off as a new aspiring trucker who does jobs with other people's truck. Your first drive will be in the truck you picked as your favourite when you create your profile. You can gain levels, and place points to specialize in a certain category of trucking. Levels will also unlock more parts for your truck.
Eventually, you build up enough money to buy your first truck. You will receive a mail from the company your favourite truck belongs to. Buying your first truck will gift you a place to store it. If you did not buy Volvo (best power) you will constantly find yourself shouting "MORE POWER!!!". Running yet more jobs, you can then hire drivers after upgrading your headquarters to store additional trucks.
And then, after all the grinding you hit max level, maxed out your garage, have a monopoly on drivers, have a small fortune of currency and own one of every truck in the game, what do you do? Well, you can go for all of the achievements, try driving with other human drivers at your own peril, mod in your favourite trucks and pull insane trailers (And potentially break something), play around with graphics settings and become a photographer, explore everything, wait for the next DLC, explore everything again.
Done all of that? Good, there's another game called American Truck Simulator which is more or less the same game, set in the United States of America. Do it all again!
For what SCS ask for this game, it's a bargain! Never once does this game nag you buy a DLC, or charge you microtransactions to unlock a truck (Extra points because all of the trucks SCS release as patches are free). All of the DLCs relating to trucks are cosmetic only (skins usually) and do not provide any tangible bonuses.
Who do I recommend this to?
For those who want a calm, relaxing experience offered by few games these days, I highly recomend this game. It's an out of body experience. Maybe you'll even make it something you want to do in real life.
If you're after a game with exciting, high adrenaline content, maybe this isn't the game for you. Still, you might find it better than you were expecting! After all, that's how I got drawn to this game.
A note regarding input devices
This game is fully playable and even fun with a controller or mouse/keyboard. But it is far better experienced with a steering wheel and pedals, added bonus with an h-pattern gear shifter, because then you can play with all of the configurations which mirror real transmission types that SCS implemented for additional challenge as they are supposed to be.
If you already have a G25/27/29/920, fanatec clubsport shifter or a TH8a or TH8 rs shifter, you can buy a device from a 3rd party (CSIO's SKRS shift knob) to add dedicated buttons for manual boxes but this is expensive and typically takes a while to ship. I hear it's really good though.
You're still reading this?
If you've read this far, congrats, you are probably at least interested and should give the game a try. There's a demo you can download to help you make your mind up.
