I've had this review sitting up here mostly as a joke, but with the advent of us finally getting a true System Shock 1 Remake (that I've backed, hehe) I figured I'd rewrite my review to fully reflect my thoughts on one of my all time favorite games and a game I consider a masterpiece of western game development.
The game's story is familiar enough, you're a soldier with amnesia who wakes up aboard a space ship where everything is royally screwed and you're contacted by a particularly angry woman who nags you to complete various tasks in order to undo the chaos that an apparent alien infestation has wrought. It may all seem very blasé at first but once you get about 1/3rd of the way into the game, you'll discover a really shocking (ayyy) plot twist that you won't see coming unless you've played Bioshock before this. But in addition to the game's main plot, you'll also discover audio logs off the beaten path that you can listen to that provide insights, backstory and tension from various deceased crew members that range from a greedy CEO who gradually turns from his precious money to fully embracing the horrors onboard the ship, to a couple who were more or less told to get a room and ended up getting an escape pod outta Dodge. It all really comes together to make the Von Braun feel like it was once a real place and it establishes a sense of humanity the place and makes the scenario all the more depressing and scary.
Now while this is all fine and good, a game like this wouldn't be great without some kickass gameplay, and this game certainly delivers on all fronts. This is a really, really unique game that manages to combine Survival Horror, Old 90's esque FPS Gameplay and Deus ex styled RPG mechanichs into one delicious, although admittedly convoluted slurry that is incredibly satisfying to play through. Before you start the real game you're given a choice of a starting classes, the 'rooty tooty point and shooty' Marine, the xxxMLGPR0xxx techie, and the turbonerd Psionic who serves more or less as the game's mage and you get to pick what your starting skills are, starting with basic RPG stuff (movement speed, HP, inventory space, mana, ect) such as being able to hack various electronics on board the ship to provide you with more resources or modifying your guns to be more effective. No matter what you pick here though, you're free to build your character however you want throughout the game, so if you wanted to be a squishy wizard who wants to carry around the game's equivalent of a BFG 9000, you can. To further expand this, there's also perk stations that can sparsely be found on the ship to further specialize your build, giving this game massive ammounts of replayability that I've unfortunately been unable to find in many other games.
On the topic of guns (admit it, we all play fps games to shoot the♥♥♥♥♥♥outta stuff), there's 4 weapons trees available, Standard, Energy, Heavy and Exotic. Standard is the one most people will start with and probably roll through many playthrus, as it has a Pistol, a shotgun and an assault rifle to you while also increasing the effectiveness of your starting wrench. Energy consists of weapons like the Energy pistol, the Laser Rapier, and the EMP rifle, which are typically more effective against robotic targets but have essentially unlimited ammo thru recharge stations to compensate. Heavy is an odd class as the Grenade launcher you get is the most powerful raw damage weapon in the game, while the BFG9000 you get at the very tailend of your progression is comparable to standard's Shotgun in terms of usefulness with the middle weapon being a useless Freeze ray. Exotic is almost the opposite of Energy, with it's weapons being more effective versus flesh targets and use the alien worm puddles as ammo but is made different by having the best melee in the game. It's really fun to experiment with all the weapons in the game, especially since the game discourages you from using one or two types of weapons at a time.
With all the technical stuff aside, the actual gameplay is really tense. When you move throughout the ship it becomes more and more apparent that you're one of, if not the only survivor, with mangled corpses littered around that really add to the terrifying atmosphere of the game. This is complemented by some legitimately disturbing enemy design, as the main 'grunt' type enemies are ex-crewmembers who have been corrupted by the hivemind known as "The Many" and the results are completely visual. Their great sound design adds to the tension as you'll be hearing these guys calling you to reveal yourself before you see them, and it just gets all the more terrible when you start fighting them only for their humanity to break through and beg you to end their suffering. Add in the fact that ammo is so scarce at times that it will force you into beating stuff over the head with the melee of your choice or just leaving these things alive and roaming and you've got the perfect recipe for a butt-clenchingly tense game that makes you think about every action that you perform.
Graphically, the game needs to be adressed. For 1999's standards it looks ok but it really does look like hot garbo now, so unless you're a weirdo like me and like these retro graphics, you'll want to seek out the fantastic community mods like SHTUP or Rebirth that make the game look all the nicer, and alot creepier too. Even then, the game can look really dated, but if you're the type to put gameplay over graphics this shouldn't matter.
I really want to stress that this game has **SO** much replay value. This is a game that I do at least a yearly 'binge gaming' session, ususally consisting of at least 2 play throughs of the base game and then messing around on one of the game's unforunately few fan maps, but each playthrough can be entirely different based on how you choose your progression. I got into Shock 2 in around late 2009-ish and I'm still enjoying the game like I did when I was 13. This game is just THAT good.
I'm really happy that System Shock is being remade, because System shock is a series that deserves your attention, though Specifically System Shock 2. This is a game that despite some of it's more oldschool mechanics feels incredibly fresh and polished even today. If you liked Bioshock at all and haven't played this yet, I suggest you do yourself a favor and pick this game up. I'm of the opinion that this game is a masterpiece that belongs in the ranks of LoZ OoT and MGS4 as being one of the greatest games of all time.

Wow! What a game we have here. If you are a fan of challenging, punishing, brutal games like Dark Souls, and enjoy dungeon-crawling through beautiful dungeons with lots of interesting encounters, gorgeous artwork and enemies to encounter, and much, much more, then you simply have to check this game out.
You create a party of 6 adventurers from a variety of classes, races and stats, and head out into the world to explore why monsters have returned from a nearby cave. Well, things start to spiral down from there, and you're dragged into an epic adventure, however, the main draw here is the immersive, first-person dungeon-crawling. The dungeon tiles themselves are decent, but repetitive in their visual appearance. However, the monsters are anything but that. The monster and enemy artwork in this game is ridiculously cool, twisted and surreal. You'll face some really outrageous, creepy and even cringe-inducing enemies, all in high definition on your screen. If there were more variation in the dungeon tiles themselves it would just add to the game, but the monster artwork is more than sufficient.
The character development is cool. There are hundreds of unique items to equip and wear, from maces to helmets, as well as other unique loot to find. There are a bunch of classes each with strong advantages and disadvantages that allow you to craft a party of your choosing and discover synergies yourself. You can class switch later on when you meet the stat requirements, and that also has some interesting quirks to it, as you can mix a few traits from different classes that you've already learned. In short, it will keep you playing and developing your party for many hours of old-school CRPG goodness.
You will be crawling through all sorts of crazy locations, from maze-like labyrinths, to dungeons with hidden traps around every corner. To find some of the secret locations in the game, you really have to search, and the game does NOT hold your hand for one minute. The game is indeed brutal. The game is modeled after the original Wizardry trilogy, and they do not pull any punches. You'll die, you'll drag your half-dead party back to town only to have the priest turn your characters to ash. Of course, you can re-load your save to fix that, and unfortunately Elminage Gothic does not include a Hardcore or Mania mode that would make saving more of a risk/reward endeavor. Still, the game is tough.
If you love challenging games and want to endure the gauntlet in this party-based RPG, just buy the game now. For $9.99 it's an absolute steal since it features over 80+ hours of dungeon-crawling gameplay, with some saying they have played for hundreds of hours due to post-game dungeon content where you will really be tested. And it never gets old because you are never quite sure what's around the next corner, and when you will get brutally murdered next!
Try this game now if you're into first-person, dungeon-crawling, old-school RPGs. You will not regret it.

After more than 40 hours of constant thrills and dozens of (admittedly, at some point pretty annoying) in-game deaths (had to adjust the difficulty from hard to medium halfway through), I've finally seen the credits on my screen.
First of all: Alien: Isolation is a really hot contender for the GOTY!  It is my personal game of the year, at least.

I'm not usually one to buy hardcore horror titles, however due for my love for the Alien Franchise I had no choice but to pick this up and return into the dark depths of another deep space adventure.
That said I've played quite a few horror titles and none, NONE, have instilled as much terror into me as Alien: Isolation. I'm still not very far into the game but I'm very much impressed. I didn't need to take more than a few steps to notice the attention to detail in the environments they have done an incredible job in re-creating the original 1979 vibe. You've got original sounding sounds, original voice actors (in the Nostromo scenes) and other little quirks such as the classic delayed hallway lighting...Even with the stuff they just feel... right, new tools look and behave like they belong in the world having obviously been brilliantly thought out and designed.
I could go on all day about the environments, they're beautiful, the lighting in particular. You'll really get the feeling you're in the movie, which is cool...But terrifying at the same time. If you don't have surround sound and really want to experience the game in full I'd suggest getting a surround headset like myself, I'm not sure how scary the game would be when you can't hear the alien clawing at the flooring as it runs after you in the hallways...Or it clambering around in the walls, circumnavigating you through the dark air vents...
The AI is smart...Adding the terror, escaping the alien really is bloody difficult. (I play in hard difficulty, "The way its intended to be played" according to the desc.) The story has got me wrapped up in it right now, its engaging and fresh. I'm even getting vibes from later movies like Alien 3 with the paranoia and survivor groups, which you will encounter.
Either way, to sum it up. Its an awesome game, the Alien game us fans have deserved for a long, long time. Finally they got it right! Dim the lights, turn up the sound, grit your teeth and sing "You are my lucky star..." in vain...
- One last note most of this will really only be appreciated by a hardcore franchise fan, this is based off the original Alien movie, remember what the xenomorph is and is capable of. You're able to defend yourself to an extent but don't expect Colonial Marines, its defiently not that. And thank god...Expect to find yourself hiding, trying to outsmart the "perfect organism".

I absolutely adore this game. I'd had my eye on it for a while, and if I'd realized how much I would love picking out favorite foods to shoot directly into my hungry and grateful slimes' faces, I would've bought it long ago. This game is a needed and appreciated break from grad school stress for me.
I'm avoiding major spoilers here but referencing some game mechanics that you don't discover for a couple hours in.
The appealing parts:
1. You get to be up close and personal with your slimes. It's not like (the older) Zoo Tycoon where you just manage cages. I'm actually reminded of the console Harvest Moon games that I loved in terms of being able to directly interact with the animals and delivering a daily care routine.
2. I'm still shocked by how well the vac pack tool works, which is how you interact with items and slimes. I frequently have slimes, food, and chickens bustling about side by side, yet 80% of the time I'm able to vacuum only what I want to if I'm in close range. You can also use the suction to add momentum to thins without fully sucking them up. I'd like to publicly apologize to the hen I flung across my entire farm, but at least she didn't become wild slime food.
3. I've reached a point where I can't possibly house every type of hybrid slime. You can only have hybrids between two types - three becomes a monster - but that's still plenty of combos. So my initial worry about not having enough variety flew out the window pretty quick.
4. I like the map a lot, and I especially like how interconnected it is. It's big enough that I almost always get lost in new places, but it gradually grows familiar as I return again and again. It's still really cool every time I walk along the top of a ridge and realize that I recognize the neighboring area. Makes getting home quicker, too.
5. Speaking of movement, I'm glad the game let me upgrade so early on, and I love the jetpack. I love climbing in games, and this game really rewards you for doing so. There are tons of flat-topped ridges or canyon walls or tree tops that allow you to survey an area and get around quicker.
6. Exploring is made easy even though you're a rancher. Your slimes can go a long time without your attention, especially if you toss a ton of food in before leaving. I don't scavenge much, but I could easily see that being part of a routine.
Some slight drawbacks:
1. There were a couple things I had to look up, though I could easily see half of the players guessing the right thing to do based on context.
2. The rate of progression has been really uneven for me. Early on, it was possibly because of the above point; I wasn't sure how to move to big new areas. I'll have periods of mostly following a routine and collecting resources followed by a ton of new area discovery. Last night was the worst offender yet when I unlocked a large area and was lead into another, and I kept hoping to find a teleport home but just kept finding new things. My inventory is woefully inadequate for that rate of discovery, so it was a little stressful. I finally bailed by backtracking on foot which was fairly painful.
3. Inventory space. I would pay a hundred thousand for even one additional slot.
4. In early game my money situation was pretty balanced. Now that I have the ranch set up, there's not much I really want to spend money on. As it accumulates, I'm following the sort of perk upgrade system ingame, but that feature feels purely like a money sink for no reason. Many of the tiers have only cosmetics in them that I don't care about but have to buy before later tiers, yet I don't even know what perks are going to be contained in later tiers to make it worth my while. I'm really raising slimes more for enjoyment than money.
5. The crafting system is going kind of painfully slowly. I'm never sure where to find some of the key resources for the warp tech that I really want. The cosmetic items, which I'm actually really interested in, overlap resources with said tech so I'm just ignoring the cosmetics until I can get to a satisfying point with functional items.

Fans of Ridley Scott's "Alien," or true survival horror games, rejoice! Though it isn't a perfect game it's a dozen steps in the right direction for both the Alien franchise and horror games in general.
Graphics: Simple yet elegant. Some scenes are near photo realistic to my eyes. The graphic buffs with their ever searching eyes may find some muddy textures here and there but let's face it, graphics don't make a game. Not saying this one isn't pleasing to behold because it definitely is.
Sound: The music strikes panic in your heart and the sound design will freeze your veins. Some of the best sound in the business.
Gameplay: Very simple. The majority of the time you will be sneaking around various enemies such as other humans, androids, and yep, you guessed it, an Alien. There are a handful of times when a flamethrower or shotgun will come in handy but for the most part the player will want to steer clear of these situations because it could attract unwanted attention or gain a quick death from the Alien. The game tends to punish you, especially early on, for not taking your time and playing it smart but as you progress and learn the "rhythm" of the game and acquire more gear it will become more natural and manageable.
The Alien's AI is fantastic and reacts in a "dynamic" fashion and not in a "static" fashion that average game AI has. Some will find this hyper realistic survival experience to be too challenging which in turn will cause them to think the AI is cheating. I assure you it is not. Like one of the game's trailer titles says, you need to "improvise."
Scare factor: I personally only jumped a handful of times but the sense of dread and the blood pressure raising atmosphere keeps you on the edge of your seat nearly the entire game. The ease of death for the player is what creates the most tension and dread. Death feels real and replicates what it would most likely feel like if the situation was real. This keeps you on your toes. But be prepared, you will most likely die ALOT in this game.
Replayability: This game is LONG for a single player experience. Some will find the slow pace of the game combined with the length to be too much but when did gamers start complaining about games not being short enough? Towards the end the game throws a few epic would be finales that make it seem like a "The End" sign should drop right after, only to keep you crawling through the dark dodging the xenomorph and other would be harm doers. Even I started rolling my eyes after the game kept going on after what seemed to be a great ending point. Hopefully a sequel can fix the pacing issue this one seems to suffer from toward the end.
PLAY IF: You are a fan of Ridley Scott's original "Alien" movie, love realistic survival horror, enjoy lengthy single player campaigns, love good atmosphere, don't have heart complications, want to experience something that could be viewed as revolutionary (the AI) in the industry, like a challenge.
DON'T PLAY IF: You are a bigger fan of John Carpenter's sequel "Aliens," are expecting Isolation to be more like the sequel and come complete with a pulse rifle, have ADD and prefer your games to only take 6-12 hourse to complete, are a wussy, your afraid of the dark, like predictable enemy AI, don't like challenging games.

Please Note: Lengthy review ahead!
A terrifying experience that is true to the Alien franchise. Let's stick to the points and be detailed about it:
The game feels like your back in the 80's tech sci-fi movie. It's brilliant. The attention to detail is magnificent and Creative Assembly have seriously hammered in as much as possible to make this game feel as authentic as possible. Controls are not clunky, work smoothly and I never had any issues on Mouse/Keyboard or Gamepad. So it feels good. Real good. Both ways, control-wise and nostagia-wise.
The sounds are mortifying and beautiful. Every echo, knock, explosion, distant scream, alien hiss is etched into the area as it reverberates through your ear drums. Playing the game with headphones is highly recommended. The soundtrack is frightening, fast and quick violins play as the Xenomorph draws near, slow drawn out compositions play as you explore derelict regions of Sevastopol Station... do want. Headphones, PLEASE. Wear them! It's terrifying and amazing!
Ah. The visuals. The bane of Modern Gaming. Are they good? Does it matter? Well, for a horror title, visuals do matter. They help in creating the setting, mood, atmosphere, feeling, emotion of the player, and the visuals in this game are astounding. You cannot deny that the atmosphere in the game is oozing with depth and detail. Standing in a corridoor and seeing the lights filter through grated fences and watching their shadows cast against the room; the Xenomorph shadow as it lurches past you; the fire effects once you ignite a Synthetic enemy and he paces quietly towards you as the flames flicker off its body; the Xenomorph pacing slowly above you as you peer through a grated floor tile and see the hissing drool spilling from its mouth. A marvel.
Hide, explore, immerse yourself, hide some more, be scared, hide, explore. The gameplay interchanges between enemies. You are faced off against Humans, Xenomorphs and Synthetics. Each with their own level of intelligence. You can run and gun everything, but shooting the Xenomorph only serves to make it even more aggressive and it hunts you more thoroughly. So avoid it! You swap between tense standoffs, constant hide-or-die scenarios and even areas where there is no danger, yet you check around every corner. Running and gunning is an instant deathwish in this game. Crouch, pace, take it nice and slow, but not too slow or the Xenomorph might catch up. Oh, here's the cool thing: bumping into objects makes noise, so the Xenomorph can hear you. Pretty cool eh?
You are Amanda Ripley. Not a Colonial Marine. Not Isaac Clarke. Not Chris Redfield in Resident Evil 5. You are not on steroids, nor do you have the collective firepower of an entire platoon in your arsenal. You are a normal human being who has been thrown into an unnatural scenario and forced to survive. Terrifying? Yes. You cannot feel afraid when you are a walking death machine. You can be armed with weapons such as the revolver or shotgun, but all it serves is to make noise and annoy the Xenomorph.
Ammunition is limited. Oh my, scary isn't it? You're not armed to the teeth, which makes you feel more human. More *vulnerable*. More horror! You are not supposed to be plowing through them like a Marine. You hide. You avoid. You distract it and pray the Xenomorph doesn't go near you. But remember, if you can hear a sound such as gunfire... so can the Xenomorph.
The game does have a few jump-scare moments but it's *very* rare. I came across around 3 or 4 jump scares in the game. No more. The rest of the game has a constant level of tension. You know there is no one around, yet you never truly feel safe. That is what survival horror should be. Surviving. While being terrified all time. The level of terror and horror you feel is constantly changing, however it is
. It never vanishes. That, to me, is true horror. Paranoia, fear and anticipation of something around every corner, in every room.
I would say yes. Others would say no. If you want a survival experience with a blend of horror, action and exploration, go for it. If you are looking for a title where you run and gun down enemies in a horror environment, buy Dead Space 2 or 3. Or even Resident Evil 5 (if you are afraid of Black People).
Alien: Isolation remains true to the Alien Universe. I'm a fan of the series and I always hoped for a day in which we could play a game where the Alien actually frightens you and hunts you down. I dreamed of a title like Penumbra, Amnesia and Outlast in the Alien Universe, hunted by a Xenomorph as you try to escape a colony or space station and this game delivers to me and has given me more than I could have possibly imagined.
I am *very* satisfied. I love this game and highly recommend it to those of you who are (or are not) fans of the series, who want a true Survival Horror experience and are willing to invest time in finishing the game without chickening out ;)
Recommended. Buy it. 9/10! A true horror fan's dream come true! Thank you Creative Assembly!

History always repeats, and once again the royal family in Dunwall is in chaos.  Empress Emily Kaldwin has been deposed by Delilah, the evil Brigmore Witch, and now it is up to her or her fatherly royal protector Corvo Attano to eliminate the conspirators and reclaim the throne.
The first Dishonored was a wonderful mix of stealth, exploration, and arcane mischief as you made your way through the grimy city of Dunwall to avenge the death of the Empress.  The sequel sees a return of all those elements, then ups its game by improving and refining them even further.  Though you revisit Dunwall briefly at the beginning and the end of the story, most of your missions take place in the city of Karnaca, a sun-worn port city prone to dust storms and blood fly infestations.  It is an amazing setting, with the folks at Arkane crafting a city that feels alive and lived in, with dozens of paths to explore, windows to climb through, and enemies to deal with.  This city and its people is all rendered in gorgeous detail, eschewing photo realism to provide a more stylized view of the world in which ugliness has its own beauty.  The missions set in an every shifting clockwork mansion and time-bending exploration of a desolate estate are classics that will be talked about for years.
In this setting, you are once again given amazing powers to traverse and manipulate the world around you.  Corvo can obtain the same abilities he had in the first game, though they have now been tweaked to offer more permutation and options for the player.  Emily has her own set, including the versatile Far Reach, a sort of supernatural grappling hook that allows you to zap across long distances and also pull targets to you, and the wonderful Domino, which allows you to link up to four characters so that what happens to one happens to all.  All the powers allow for creative play, whether you be going full stealth or rampaging death machine.  Combat also has more options, with many ways to knock the enemy off balance to deliver a stunning blow or a lethal takedown.
Storywise, like the first the narrative is mostly functional rather than mindblowing, with it being a thread to give you direction.  As they are now voiced, Emily is a likeable if slightly naive young woman setting out to a hostile world, while Corvo is world weary and cynical, and the supporting cast does some fine work, but never as compelling as say a Bioware or CD Project Red game.  The lore of the world is deep and fascinating, but also in the periphery, to be discovered by those diligent enough to search for it rather than dolled out in exposition heavy chucks.  This means you can miss some of the games best stuff, but even without it the story works if never being as spectacular as the gameplay.
So in conclusion, Dishonored 2 is more Dishonored; bigger, more refined, with some truly nifty tricks up its sleeve.  Like the first, you will only get what you put in, but if you love exploring the amazing setting and getting playful with the creative power set, there is really no game that comes close to this.  Great stuff, one of the best games of the year.

To start off, I think this is a great game. I am really shocked that the review count is Mixed on Steam. It is an absolute beautiful game, with a big map full of contrasting enviornments. Time to start off a pros and cons list, cause who doesn't like those?
Pros:
-Very beautiful graphics with great water
-A wide map with tons to explore
-I haven't experienced any FPS issues or stuttering of any kind. I know this is a common complaint, but I'm running using a 970m with 8 GB of ram with and i7-4720HQ and suffer no interruptions on nearly maxed out settings.
-The online connect feature I have never had a problem with, even in super crap internet, and I don't know why people are complaining about it. And if you are playing it on the go, then there must be somewhere with WiFi cause I can't imagine playing it in a car.
-Clean controls, easy to learn and master
-Story is good when it's there (I'll explain this more in the cons)
-Wingsuit is a nice, new addition to the game
-Multiple tethers and being able to retract them is another great new feature
-Towns are always different, but similar in a nice way
-The Havoc engine is perfect for a game like this and well used for destruction
-Ability to stunt jump across the entire vehicle is an awesome feature
-Characters are unique and funny and important in their own ways
Cons:
-There is not too much story in the game, and when it is there it is sporadic, sometimes occurring back to back or going long periods without it. When it is there though, it is enjoyable with good characters.
-The loading screen is the only loading issue I have. You can't skip it, which is a little frusturating, and it takes a decent time.
I have to say, this game is very, very good and the couple of issues people are seeming to have still aren't enough for me to maybe think about not recommending it. Very good game, and props to SquareEnix and Blizzard Studios for creating such a good game.

Where to begin with this game? Well, let's start with the simple fact that it's fun, enjoyable, and is surprisingly heartfelt as well.
The battle system is simple and easy to master, and the enemies are tough enough to provide moderate challenge, but rarely does a fight feel too difficult.
The game also has plenty of attention to detail. The sprites and levels are all well designed, and the music is delightful as well.
The story is simple enough. A teenage girl named Senia travels to a dangerous place called the Tower of Eternity to rescue her adoptive sister Magaleta. In spite of it's simple concept though, it manages to keep the player interested, and you do feel invested in the chareacters by the end of it all.
Speaking of the end, the game has three different endings, so even if you beat it once, there's still two more ways to experience the ending.
It is worth noting that the game takes some ideas from other ARPGs, but it never gets too in your face(with the exception of one very obvious Zelda reference about halfway through the game)
If I have one issue with this game, it's the abundance of gramatical errors. This game has a fair amount of dialogue, and rarely does a scentence go by where the wording isn't strange, or the wrong form of a word is used. Even so, it's never so bad that you can't understand what's being said.
So, final thoughts: The game is all around good. It has a good story, good design, a good soundtrack, and a combat system that's easy to pick up. It's only real issue comes from poor grammar, and it's not totally intolerable(just very noticable).

If i have to describe Elminage Gothic(EG) in one word it would be: Tedious.
I have grown up with Wizardry and Might&Magic and i played the heck out of Wiz6-8 and MM3-6. I love these types of dungeon crawlers and while EG resembles those games superficially it lacks a soul. The closest match is probably Wiz6 gameplay wise, but it adds much more tedium to it.
- Massivly limited Inventory while bombarding you with junk
- No resting in dungeons, so if your spellcasters run out of their extremely limited spell pool you have to track back all the way through those  Dungeons with Map layouts that make no sense other than to annoy the player and are too hard to navigate without a map which is a consumable item. And i consider that Underground Map to be a consumable too, because it breaks all the time (see next point)
- Crap breaks all the time and due to limited inventory carrying spares restricts the limited inventory even further.
- Losing attributes randomly and wide range of hp gains during levelup forces save scumming early levels (which based on ingame clock and steam play time so far is several hours and im lev 15 ...)
- No difficulty indicator for Traps/Doors (just gonna avoid Magic Drain like the plague)
I wanted to like this, i was craving for a new turn based dungeon crawler (sorry Grimrock), but this one falls flat so far.

Elminage is in every way a full on Wizardry clone.  EVERYTHING is the same except the maps.  Even the artwork looks like it was taken from the Wizardy: Proving Grounds booklet from the late 80s.
Just because it is a clone game doesn't mean you should pass Elminage by.  If you are into RPGs, you will have a blast with this game.
If you'r not familiar with Wizardry, I'll explain.  Wizardy was one of the first RPGs to revolutionize the videogame industry.  Many of the RPGs that were produced for the NES, were inspired by the Wizardy games.  The game starts by forming a party of 6 characters.  You can browse a few places in town such as the Inn and Shop; but most of the game takes place inside an underground maze.  The maze gets harder as you descend, forcing you to make frequent trips to the surface to heal and level up.  The character creation is very in-depth and mimics D&D rules some-what.  Lots of dungoen mapping and slaying :)

An absolutely and unbelievably deep, detailed, and enjoyable remake of the original Half-Life. Just similar enough to be familar, just different enough to make it interesting (weapon drops in different places, the addition of HL2-style flares, etc.). Most fan remakes or indie games have ATROCIOUS voice acting, but it's EXCELLENTLY done here. This is a remake (more like a reimagining, so much is updated)  unlike most others, that can stand on its own two legs as a fantastic game in its own right. The game does not demand your nostalgia to be fun, intense, and just downright awesome, but the nostalgia sure can help!
Overall, 8/10. I want to give it 9.5/10, heck, even 10/10 - I want to SO BADLY - but I just CAN'T. Why? Because two of the most iconic levels in the game - 'On a Rail' and 'Surface Tension' - are unforgivably pared down to unrecognizably tiny versions of themselves. Why the developers felt the need to cut so much iconic, memorable gameplay from the remake I'll never know, and it's truly unfortunate, because it's the only blemish on an otherwise STELLAR title.

a remake, but a whole lot more than that. It is a fresh, new experience that players new to the Half Life franchise could play as a first-timer (That is of course once the Xen levels are added to the game). Plus, with the added ability to upload and subscribe to new things on the Workshop, your experience is always changing. So, overall, Black Mesa is a remake of the best game of all time, but is superior to Half Life in almost every way, thus making it the greatest game to ever exist. (

First off: If you want to read about the good of this game, read another review. I am aware its not only negative. I'm just glad I finished it and can deinstall it at this point. Here's what I did not like:
Most of the game consists of you hiding, sneaking around and WAITING... avoiding the overpowered Alien or Androids. Depending on difficulty they will find you much easier and literally hunt you all over the place. You will spend alot of time in lockers and other hiding spots, only to STILL be discovered, after the Alien returns for the third time in a row to the room, before you had a chance to leave.
I didn't find the Alien(s) scary, or having to hide from it all the time. It frustrated me and I resorted regularly to cuss words when it got me. This combined with no anytime save system will have you play many parts over and over and over. I found this to be extremely boring and at a point switched from hard to easy, so I could kill off the Androids and chase off the Alien with the flamethrower more often. And often the alien will STILL hit you for half your life (on easy), before running off. There goes another medkit..
You will return to the same places over and over. After gadget upgrades you can open previously locked doors, and you WILL HAVE to go through those doors. Less new, more of the same corridors. And its basically all just corridors of a space station, looking very similar to one another.
The Alien can't just be killed off. It can just be chased off with the flamethrower (and maybe other weapons). But it will return soon and it doesn't look like its actually taking any damage. It's basically invincible until you reach a certain story point.
There are many, many buttons to press, levers to pull, machines to operate, computer logs to read and more minigames. In between that, you sit around and WAIT until the alien (the androids, the "civilians") leaves for a few seconds, so you can operate that thingy and get further in the story. This will repeat itself to exhaustion.
Towards the end the game tries to kill you off in about a hundred different ways, as everything escalates in some sort of cheap action movie finish. Up to scenes where you open a door, make a step and then die, squashed to bits. Next time wait a few seconds before making that step. And on that goes.
All in all I cannot recommend this game to anyone but the most diehard stealth game fans, who don't mind a challenge and who enjoy repeating the same few corridors over and over, until they don't get caught. I personally have other games to play and I'm glad this one is over.

Please Note: Lengthy review ahead!
A terrifying experience that is true to the Alien franchise. Let's stick to the points and be detailed about it:
The game feels like your back in the 80's tech sci-fi movie. It's brilliant. The attention to detail is magnificent and Creative Assembly have seriously hammered in as much as possible to make this game feel as authentic as possible. Controls are not clunky, work smoothly and I never had any issues on Mouse/Keyboard or Gamepad. So it feels good. Real good. Both ways, control-wise and nostagia-wise.
The sounds are mortifying and beautiful. Every echo, knock, explosion, distant scream, alien hiss is etched into the area as it reverberates through your ear drums. Playing the game with headphones is highly recommended. The soundtrack is frightening, fast and quick violins play as the Xenomorph draws near, slow drawn out compositions play as you explore derelict regions of Sevastopol Station... do want. Headphones, PLEASE. Wear them! It's terrifying and amazing!
Ah. The visuals. The bane of Modern Gaming. Are they good? Does it matter? Well, for a horror title, visuals do matter. They help in creating the setting, mood, atmosphere, feeling, emotion of the player, and the visuals in this game are astounding. You cannot deny that the atmosphere in the game is oozing with depth and detail. Standing in a corridoor and seeing the lights filter through grated fences and watching their shadows cast against the room; the Xenomorph shadow as it lurches past you; the fire effects once you ignite a Synthetic enemy and he paces quietly towards you as the flames flicker off its body; the Xenomorph pacing slowly above you as you peer through a grated floor tile and see the hissing drool spilling from its mouth. A marvel.
Hide, explore, immerse yourself, hide some more, be scared, hide, explore. The gameplay interchanges between enemies. You are faced off against Humans, Xenomorphs and Synthetics. Each with their own level of intelligence. You can run and gun everything, but shooting the Xenomorph only serves to make it even more aggressive and it hunts you more thoroughly. So avoid it! You swap between tense standoffs, constant hide-or-die scenarios and even areas where there is no danger, yet you check around every corner. Running and gunning is an instant deathwish in this game. Crouch, pace, take it nice and slow, but not too slow or the Xenomorph might catch up. Oh, here's the cool thing: bumping into objects makes noise, so the Xenomorph can hear you. Pretty cool eh?
You are Amanda Ripley. Not a Colonial Marine. Not Isaac Clarke. Not Chris Redfield in Resident Evil 5. You are not on steroids, nor do you have the collective firepower of an entire platoon in your arsenal. You are a normal human being who has been thrown into an unnatural scenario and forced to survive. Terrifying? Yes. You cannot feel afraid when you are a walking death machine. You can be armed with weapons such as the revolver or shotgun, but all it serves is to make noise and annoy the Xenomorph.
Ammunition is limited. Oh my, scary isn't it? You're not armed to the teeth, which makes you feel more human. More *vulnerable*. More horror! You are not supposed to be plowing through them like a Marine. You hide. You avoid. You distract it and pray the Xenomorph doesn't go near you. But remember, if you can hear a sound such as gunfire... so can the Xenomorph.
The game does have a few jump-scare moments but it's *very* rare. I came across around 3 or 4 jump scares in the game. No more. The rest of the game has a constant level of tension. You know there is no one around, yet you never truly feel safe. That is what survival horror should be. Surviving. While being terrified all time. The level of terror and horror you feel is constantly changing, however it is
. It never vanishes. That, to me, is true horror. Paranoia, fear and anticipation of something around every corner, in every room.
I would say yes. Others would say no. If you want a survival experience with a blend of horror, action and exploration, go for it. If you are looking for a title where you run and gun down enemies in a horror environment, buy Dead Space 2 or 3. Or even Resident Evil 5 (if you are afraid of Black People).
Alien: Isolation remains true to the Alien Universe. I'm a fan of the series and I always hoped for a day in which we could play a game where the Alien actually frightens you and hunts you down. I dreamed of a title like Penumbra, Amnesia and Outlast in the Alien Universe, hunted by a Xenomorph as you try to escape a colony or space station and this game delivers to me and has given me more than I could have possibly imagined.
I am *very* satisfied. I love this game and highly recommend it to those of you who are (or are not) fans of the series, who want a true Survival Horror experience and are willing to invest time in finishing the game without chickening out ;)
Recommended. Buy it. 9/10! A true horror fan's dream come true! Thank you Creative Assembly!

Creative Assembly completely mastered the design and technology from the Alien (1979) film, giving the closest experience yet in a game with being in the Alien universe.
The alien AI is generally fantastic and on the hardest difficully it stalks you the entire time, never making you feel safe, deciding to drop down a vent while your looking at a computer screen when you least expect. The tension of being hunted by the alien and employing tactics and equipment to evade it is the best feature of the game.
The times when the alien isn't present the game suffers a bit, as you''re left to sneak past humans and (tough as nails) androids. Thankfullly the games great level design makes these bits bearable, but you'll be wanting the alien back.
The save points are very interesting. They're dispersed in the game usually at great distances, so you're sneaking about the area, anticipating ( and crying for joy ) when you find one. The game doesn't pause when you save, so even when using them you have to make sure the area is clear. I can see why people found them frustrating, but I found it adds tension to a game that's already making you sweat with the fear of the alien killing you -- which it will, in less you have fire.
It's a long game, too, which is nice for a 'AAA' game; it took my 19hrs to finish the campaign. If you're the person that likes to procede carefully and back-track a bit for some goodies, then it will take even longer.
Bottom line: can be frustrating ( oh ♥♥♥♥ no falmethrower fuel left! ), and even boring in parts when your running from robots, but the atmosphere and the unpredicatble alien AI make this game what it is.
And no . . .  the vents aren't safe.

Total War: Rome II is a game that breaks my gamer heart. The game itself is actually gorgeous and when(if) it works it is so much fun to play. To start off, I think this is a great game. I am really shocked that the review count is Mixed on Steam. It is an absolute beautiful game, with a big map full of contrasting enviornments. Time to start off a pros and cons list, cause who doesn't like those?
Pros:
-Very beautiful graphics with great water
-A wide map with tons to explore
-I haven't experienced any FPS issues or stuttering of any kind. I know this is a common complaint, but I'm running using a 970m with 8 GB of ram with and i7-4720HQ and suffer no interruptions on nearly maxed out settings.
-The online connect feature I have never had a problem with, even in super crap internet, and I don't know why people are complaining about it. And if you are playing it on the go, then there must be somewhere with WiFi cause I can't imagine playing it in a car.
-Clean controls, easy to learn and master
-Story is good when it's there (I'll explain this more in the cons)
-Wingsuit is a nice, new addition to the game
-Multiple tethers and being able to retract them is another great new feature
-Towns are always different, but similar in a nice way
-The Havoc engine is perfect for a game like this and well used for destruction
-Ability to stunt jump across the entire vehicle is an awesome feature
-Characters are unique and funny and important in their own ways
Cons:
-There is not too much story in the game, and when it is there it is sporadic, sometimes occurring back to back or going long periods without it. When it is there though, it is enjoyable with good characters.
-The loading screen is the only loading issue I have. You can't skip it, which is a little frusturating, and it takes a decent time.

Ladies, gentlemen, Hyltols and underaged CoD kids, welcome to the best Call of Duty of the millenium.
Advanced Warfare is CoD's first major step towards something new since Modern Warfare 2. Instead of a borring, unoriginal millitary shooter where you run around as characters that are about as durable as sheets of tissue paper...well, Advanced Warfare is still a millitary shooter, but in a far-on future year. All millitary units around the world are equipped with high tech Exoskelletons that let them to everything from Titanfall-Pilot their way from rooftops to windows to punch through Titanium blast doors like thin sheets of ice, while also adding durability.
While you run around multiplayer maps blasting oppononets with dual miniguns, bass cannons, focus rifles and throwing knives, you'll find you and your opponents equipped with numerous gadgets. Deploy a riot shield from your wrist, cloak out from enemy sight, track enemies around corners.
Also, the series' iconic killstreaks are now "Scorestreaks," meaning that you can build credit for them in more ways than one if you're (somehow) not very good at killing. You can also add up to three bonus augmentations to scorestreaks - rip a turret off it's head and run in all Halo style, give your kamikaze assault drone a machine gun and rocket launcher, or give that superdestructive vulcan satellite laser two extra super-wide bursts. Good thing too, because not only are their score requirements quite high at times, but each augmentation an immense ammount of extra score that can throw the cheap recon drone from the 300s to the thousands. Also, did I mention you're now as durable as furnished paper machet instead of wet toilet paper?
Also, the fairly-large range of customization from Ghosts (EEW) is back, giving 9 customization zones, 2 genders, and 17 character body-types to choose from. Oh, and scorecards.
Probably the most infamous feature is the new "Skin" feature. If you've ever played Counter Strike: Global offensive, you'd know that you can occasionaly find (or buy/trade for) weapon skins that change the color and look of a gun. Basically, whenever you finish a game, you have a chance to get a Supply Drop to open. It contains anything from Reinforcement Orbital Care Packages, new customization items to the mentioned skins, all 3 which come in 3 qualities (aside from the stock grey, you have (from least to highest) Enlisted (green), Professional (blue), and Elite (orange). Each weapon skin does something different. For example, the Elite MP11-Squeaker skin adds +2 fire rate, -2 accuracy, adds a red dot sight, removes the stock, and adds an oxydized gold paint and other various fancy details. You can also choose from a separate selection from camos, if you want to spice up a gun you haven't any skins for or if you like a camo's mods but hate it's look.
However, drooling aside, there are two big downsides. One, just keep in mind that, it's a CoD title. So expect things like CoD kids, idiots making false threats to hack you, hacked game lobbies, and faulty sniping. And second, the ONE reason there's so many bad reviews...the lag. You see, the people who made this game, promised dedicated servers (server units that run only advanced warfare and nothing else) for us. Guess what? We didn't get those, and will never get those. While the lag is 110% playable with, you'll find yourself being shot down by the enemy in front of you in two KF5 shots after you put an entire S-12 drum of pulse-shells into their head, only for the killcam to play the catastrophe back and show that you didn't shoot first and were just lagging. This makes trade-offs infuriatingly luck based, but this doesn't happen 100% of the time.
In summary, this is the only CoD game still played that's worth your time, by afar. Wait for it to go on sale for $44, pick it up while it's hot, and have fun actually enjoying a Call of Duty for once dunking a satellite into a giant glowing ball while rockets and .50 cal rounds are flying past you in every direction ever. Oh, and don't forget to play through the campaign a few times to get the story behind the game and to unlock some exclusive items.

RECOMMENDED for any hardcore RPGer or dungeon crawler enthusiast
I have always loved Wizardry-style dungeon crawlers, and Elminage Gothic succeeds in being my 2nd favorite dungeon crawler of all time (Behind Wizardry 8). It is not without some flaws, though.
First, the great things:
+ It's Wizardry. Grid-based maps, 6 party members, 9 different races, 16 different classes (You can recruit monsters too!). You can change classes, too, with some restrictions.
+ 75+ floors across 16 different dungeons to explore, all with a unique environment and music. Lots of variety. Yes, rotating floors, teleporters, pitch black rooms, shoots, pits, traps, ie what you would expect in a Wizardry game.
+ 400+ GORGEOUS hand-crafted monster models. Detailed in-game bestiary as you find more monsters
+ 500+ different items/weapons/armor
+ 65 quests, fairly non-linear
+ Weapon/armor crafting. Endless customization to fit your needs.
+ Great music, especially the 8 battle themes. Soundtrack included!
+ Random encounters are rare. 90% of battles are from preset monster locations that respawn if you leave the dungeon
Now the bad things:
- Pretty bad menus. You get used to them after awhile though and quickly learn how to navigate them efficiently
- Limited inventory space (Warehouse eventually gets expanded to 99 which is fantastic!)
- Maps are consumable, but early in the game you get a reusable map item, and there are magic spells that let you view the ENTIRE dungeon on all floors.
- Leveling up system is confusing for new players. HP gains are based on your vitality and level so don't worry about how much HP you are gaining per level, because it will balance out. If you want to min/max your stats, you have the freedom to.
If you are looking for a huge game that rewards you with exploration and experimentation, Elminage Gothic fits the bill. Having finally done everything possible in the game, I must say that it was some of the best 300+ hours I've spent.
9/10 as there are some things that could be improved. Can't complain though because games like this are pretty rare.

Don't buy this.  It's bad.  In many ways.  And I want to like it, I just can't.  And don't.
Here are just a few since I don't have all day to sit here and write about everything this one did wrong.
To start with the game has a poor interface with huge, scrolling descriptive text where smaller text would have fit on the screen and still been large enough to read.  Easily.
Buying, selling, moving and equipping is tedious.  Searching chests and disarming is also tedious.  Combat... you guessed it, feels tedious.  Really, any game that has a "repeat last set of orders" button for all SIX of your characters (so push one button and repeat all six actoins) is doing something wrong.  I shouldn't want to do the same thing every single turn.  All of my (fairly few) fights have been pretty much like this: 3 melee attack, 3 support defend.  That only changes if someone gets hurt, then I heal with one of the support characters or occasionally have an attack spell tossed out there.  Otherwise support just sits there doing sweet fudge all because I don't have ranged weapons for them.  Yup, classic front row/back row crap.  That's all well and good if you can pick up rocks to throw, or buy a sling right away so characters aren't just sitting there cowering, but from what I've seen you can't.
It also has my least favourite thing in any game - that Wolfenstein 3d style vomit-inducing movement (literally makes me nauseous within 5 minutes) and overall the game has mediocre graphics.  And I didn't expect much.
So, one semi-good point -  I think the game's mechanics could be good but I can't devote enough time in 2 minute sessions, since anything longer makes me start to feel ill, to get into it enough to find out.
So, while I like the concept I don't like the game.  I wish I had three hands so I could give it three thumbs down.

Elminage Gothic isn't bad game but its far to be good game.
+ Nice looking graphics : artwork is fine even if sprite suffer of lack of good animations

- Random bonus system at character creation never allow easily to choose your class (Ninja, Lord, are very difficult to create at start because class require too much bonus points to create).
- HP/SP recovery sucking system : even if you can camp, i never found resting option button to recover all HP/SP  from team. That mean long travel to dungeons->cities to rest in inn.

- Some Ex Skills are exclusive : Sacrifice exist only for cleric pre-generated character level 4, you can't create more characters with such exclusive skills.

- Classes problem : less classes to play than previous Elminage, some like Lord are weakness in protection now. Changing classes must be done as soon as stats match because only some spells can be passed to next class, all others will vanish (Ex Skills, stats above class requirement, class skills)

Elminage isn't bad game but if you already played previous version you'll be disapointed because new rules/options not better. In all case you need to balance your team to kill hard (i think its better to kill hard & fast (aoe) than to be better in protections only).

While playing Etrian Odyssey has spoiled me quite a bit, comparing the two is like comparing apples to oranges. While I would reccomend the former to anyone, Elminage has a few issues that give me a little hesitation.  Some of the sound choices put me off. The music isn't that bad, fortunately, yet the menu confirmation sound is a bit over-loud.  The art direction is very very top notch and the ability to go into an art gallery mode to appreciate the beasties you fight is a welcome decision.
What is NOT a welcome decision was that this port removed the capability to insert artwork from outside sources for your own characters! Some of us like to draw our own characters and thrust them into the character grinder that is the Wizardry series.  This was a missed feature and Starfish really dropped the ball on this.
Gripes aside, the real meat and bones is the wizardry gameplay and from the get-go the game does not pull its punches. If you decide to generate your own characters ( And you should! ) the starter dungeon goes from a challenge for the pregenerated level 5s to a nightmare for your level ones.  Every level you get, even if it's one HP point,  you will savor and each victory comes that much sweeter, especially since party members can now cover each other!  Having a tank character is actually a huge asset and lets your dual-wielders or two-handers take a breather if they get picked on, since he or she can defend them.  It's a nice little touch of teamwork from the usual fight/fight/fight/parry/parry/parry.
Speaking of, the dreaded fight/fight/fight/parry/parry/parry is something that no longer happens nearly as often.  Furthermore, you can also screw monsters over by putting thieves in the front line.  If monsters can't detect them, they can't target them, nor can they aim at the back line, unless they have a longer range weapon.
Oh that's right, kids. Long range weapons are no longer just for your characters. From the second dungeon on, your back row can be exposed to heat from spear wielders and ninja weapons that can behead on a lucky shot. Still, back line members are nowhere near as likely to get pinged off as your front line is, so there is that going for them. Oh, and on the subject of being hidden? Enemies can hide too and screw over your chances at getting at the mages in the back line. If you happen to encounter a group of mages with fighters in the back row, the fighters will gladly advance on you to keep their casters out of the line of fire.
There are also classes that are nonstandard from the classic wizardry series, and in a decision that made me smile, there are also genders that are nonstandard from normal nomenclature. I got a chuckle when I rolled an effeminate "?" gender mage, only to find out later that they also qualify for a valkyrie class change when they get the stats for it, their indeterminate gender qualifying them for the normally female-only class.
There really is a lot to like here, and the ups far outweigh the downs. I just wish that they would have included the ability for us to import our own drawings so we could play as characters we truly make. Alas, it is a fly in the ointment, but if you've ever played, and liked the Wizardry series, this is Wizardry, 110% so.  Fans of the RPG Genre should find enough here to greatly enjoy and I would gladly reccomend it to them, especially at the $10 price tag.  It's a crime not to enjoy another entry in the wizardry series.

This game is very near the pinnacle of quality gaming. There are a few quirks involving enemy AI and targeting but it just becomes part of the difficulty and randomness of the game. Additionally, you basically need a controller to play effectively.
That being said, this game brings back that feeling of accomplishment we all had as gamer kids. Finally beating that boss you tried probably fifty times and wanted to quit after every try. It's there and it doesn't end once you beat the game.
Combat is visceral. Just fighting basic enemies is exciting, scary and rewarding. The bosses are another story. Each boss has it's weak points and it's up to you to fight them over and over and figure out their weaknesses, or just to look it up on the internet. No (required) boss is impossible to beat with any build. There are people who have finished the game using only a shield. So if you're up for a challenge, there are many ways you can approach that. But when you boil it down, the combat in this game is what makes it stand out. Backstabbing, parrying, dodging, timing and approach all play into how you advance through a zone and/or defeat a boss.
The music is awesome and I hope they release an OST for purchase at a later date. The tunes in this game will haunt you outside of your gaming space.
The graphics are gorgeous (and since it's on PC, we may see some improvements/modded graphics in the future).
Co-op is there if you have the patience and willpower to beat the same bosses two times per run (and use up those precious human effigies).
The length of the game is fair (about 30 hours of game time to finish the last boss on a single character). But there is an insane amount of replayability. You will likely play a sword-and-board character first and once you've seen all this game has to offer, you can plan your next build on New Game+ or make a whole new character. Between my friend and I there are probably 10 characters already that we bounce between.  I'm already sitting at 70+ hours and don't see an end in sight for awhile. Maybe on my 4th or 5th playthrough.
This game. Get it. Immerse yourself in it, because face it, that's what you've been looking for for so long.

I really enjoyed the original Dishonored, so my recommendation of Dishonored 2 is easy because the sequel is very much like the first game but with expanded and enhanced: player choice, customisation, graphics and level design.
I haven’t played enough to make a conclusive appraisal of the storyline yet, however the environments and NPC’s haven’t conveyed much of the political/economical/social reality of the world around them unlike the original game, which I thought excelled at that (along with games like Bioshock Infinite).
Finally, there are performance issues as this game is horribly optimised. Patches are being released to address these however and I find it playable on my old hardware, despite having to accustom myself to sub 60 frames per second gameplay (it will never drop below 30 and avg is probably 50 for me). If you buy this game, I highly recommend that you open the game’s steam properties up and elect for the beta stream of updates (as they haven’t been made public as of writing). If it wasn’t for this asinine and egregious error on Arkane Studio’s part (and Bethesda), I’m sure Dishonored 2 would have performed a lot better both in sales and user reviews.
In summary, I’d buy it if you either enjoyed the first Dishonored or just like FPS stealth and/or killing with epic power and style. If the performance is unacceptable on your rig you can always return within 2 hours of playtime for a full refund on steam. Remember beta patch!
My Specs: Radeon 280x, i7-4970, 16gb Ram.
Who liked Dishonored 1 will like the second one too. Be aware of the required system specs though!

Unlike many others, I have not had a problem running Dishonored 2, so I can't comment on the issues that some have seen. What I can say is that if you were a fan of the original game, Dishonored 2 improves on nearly every aspect of Dishonored. The option for high and low chaos is still there and both can be played either in a more action or stealth mode but added to this is the choice to play as either Corvo or Emily. This is not merely a choice of skins as Emily's powers are different from Corvo's. Corvo's is consistent with the first game but Emily offers new powers like Link (what happens to one linked enemy happens to the other(s)); Doppelganger (creating a duplicate of yourself for distraction or fighting purposes); and Shadow Walk (taking on a stealthy shadow form to move about more discreetly). Also, the game adds the ability to break down normal bone charms to create custom charms with multiple traits. Dark and corrupted bone charms can be sacrificed for material but the traits which they held will be lost.
The best feature of the game though is the level design. Dishonored had some great levels, but Dishonored 2 has levels equal to the first and two levels that are among the best in gaming. If you are someone who does not explore levels but simply follows the waypoints to complete objectives there is a lot that will be missed. I'm sure that type of player will find some enjoyment in the game but where the game shines is in exploring the hidden away spots and seeing all the detail that was included in the level design.
Story-wise the game draws a lot from the two story expansions of Dishonored (The Knife of Dunwall and The Brigmore Witches).  You don't need to have played these to understand what happens in Dishonored 2 but those who have played the expansions will have more background on a couple of major players. The story also expands the world of Dishonored as most of the time is spent in Karnaca instead of Dunwall. As in the first your actions will affect some areas of the game, with high chaos leading to more blood fly (the equivalent of rats from the first game; though rats are present here as well) infested areas.
Three games really shine for me this year: Doom, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, and Dishonored 2. The first two seem like worthy titles in their respective franchises. Doom returned to the feel of the first two games and added some elements that made it a lot of fun to play. Mankind Divided was a great sequel that was the equal of Human Revolution. But Dishonored 2 took the step up to the next level for that franchise for me. For that reason, it's my favorite game of 2016.

Slime Rancher is a cute little indie game. The game is about ranching slimes, and it is the cutest game in recent memory. There's a wide variety of different, interesting slimes to find and play around with. Many will try to kill you, but it's hard to face that they do it on purpose because they all are very adorable. The game has a fantastic art style as well. It looks absolutely lovely at 1080p. One of the best mechanics in the game is the ability to essentially interbreed slimes by feeding one slime the "plorp" of another. The slime will then become a mixture of the two slimes. However, if you try to breed this "largo" slime with another different slime, it will turn into a tar, which will kill your slimes and must be destroyed with water. This mechanic is fantastic, and makes it an overall funner, more challenging game. Overall, very good game, wonderful art style and fantastic music makes this game a perfect casual game.

in jc2, it was not that good. you could take yourself over to another place with it or pull an enemy back a little but that was it. this one is new and improved. for one, it is stronger so if you attatch someone to a building they won't fall back down again after 4 seconds. there are up to six tethers (grapple attatchments) this time so you can attatch multiple things to multiple other things. you can make a conga line of civillians on the back of your car or under your helicopter. you can steal a plane by attatching it under your helicopter and flying off. you can steal people. it's glorious. my favourite grapple feature (of course) is the retract feature. when you have a tether, this tightens the it, forcing it to get smaller, forcing the two things on either end to come together. you can do amazing things with this. human catapults, crucifixions..... wait what? yeah, this does lead to very evil intentions. stretching an npc's limbs until he dies (luckily theres not dismemberment). with the retract feature, you can down structures and make them fall on people. also touching down on the destruction and physics category, you can pull down guard towers and, as said before, they are made up of pieces of metal so it will just completely fall into a pile of rubbish (before exploding). and also, if you grapple an npc or animal, you go flying towards them and drop kick them ("you can drop kick a cow GOTY 2025")
+wingsuit
this is new with jc3 and is a very nice feature indeed. yes, it is hard at first but once you use it for a while, you will get used to it and become some kind of epic global elite ninja (VOLVO PLZ NERF). if mastered, you can go very fast with this thing and makes travelling very nice and easy (EZ PZ). vehicles are so overrated.
+mario
this guy is pure banter
+unlimited c4
you don't have to worry about how many bomb you have (apart from grenades) because c4 is unlimited now! you start off being able to plant up to 3 bombs at a time but can go up to 5 (i think). once exploded, you can just plant another set BOOM........ done (pardon the pun)
+jc3 mp coming soon
that's right, they're back. the beasts who made jc2 multiplayer are working on it now and i reckon it won't be long. imagine being on a bridge when suddenly, it starts to fall down, and you die. i played jc2 mp for about 25 hours and i loved it. you could hundreds of players in one server which was amazing but there were no npc's. imagine there being npc's in jc3 mp and everyone using their tether to make the BIGGEST conga line ever to have existed.
+new liberation
in jc2, it was annoying to take over places but now, theres all new task to take over places like killing the base general, disabling the security or missile system etc. although towns are kinda all the same (more below), the army bases are all unique in design and are fun to destroy.
+challenges
there are various challenges whether it's driving, shooting, wingsuiting or flying a plane. most of them are just time trials where you go through checkpoints but other are where you must destroy as much as possible or whatever. they are quite fun to do. by doing challenges, you get gears. the better you do, the more you get (up to 5 available in a challenge). these gars unlock 'gear mods' which are modifications to things like cars, planes, boats, explosives, guns, wingsuit, grapple hook. modifications are little things like more grapple tethers, upping the max c4 in one plant, having nitro on vehicles, wider blast radius on grenades etc.
-some boring missions
a few of the missions kind of drag on a little bit. just the same old 'ride on a car and take out enemy's following'. you know the drill.
-repetitive takeovers
liberating a base or town gets repetitive because most of the time, it's just the same thing. blow up some statues, destroy a gas tank and whatever. of course, some places will have different things like not every town will have a gas station and now every town will have a statue but its all the same really. it is fun to blow up stuff thought as (as i said earlier), the physics make all explosions unpredictable.
all in all, i recommend this game to anyone who likes destruction, open worlds and unpredictable, random and funny physics. it's a good investment and will keep you entertained for hours on end. do not get if you have a low end pc or potato. i have a mid-range pc (specs on profile) that can run at the lowest settings (stupid websites said high). so of course, do not pre-order games and don't believe sites like can you run it. the hype overcame me and forced me to pre-order so take it from personal experience: don't do it.

I'm rating the 0.6 version without knowing if they potantially change or improve things I criticize. I only know very little about the game outside of playing it on my own for 7 hours.
A good concept plagued by some controversial or downright insane design decisions that make this game more boring and tiresome to play that it should be. Limiting is the name of the game - you are so limited in everything you do that it ceases to be fun after few hours.
People compare this game to Stardew Valley, but I can only see vague similarities to it. Imagine if you were limited to only 4 item slots at all times in Stardew Valley, which requires you to go back and forth all the time, or carefully choose what you want to take with you. This not only prolongs the time spend doing mundane things, but it also makes exploration irritating because you just know that you won't be able to take most of the cool new stuff with you, you have to keep coming back.
Building your ranch is equally laughable. Unlike Stardew Valley, which gives you plenty of land to work with and it's just a question of money and time, here you have few limited positions that you can use for different things - later you can buy more, but imagine having a quite a large place, where you only have around 8 spaces to build, which isn't a lot, given how much stuff you can potentially cultivate. The thing is, juggling with stuff and changing it around is just annoying, once again, imagine if you had 1/10 of the space in Stardew Valley, how much fun you would have, having to constantly change things around.
Progression system works well and makes the game more engaging with meaningful rewards and upgrades, but it can't save the super limited virgin like strictness with which the game handles everything.
Last but not least, exploration. This is made far more infuriating than it should be, because there is no god damn map. These levels get quite confusing and complex, and when you get really far from your home, you can easily get lost, or worse yet, don't know how to get back to a place you wanted to keep exploring. I really don't want to draw my own map - having a reasonable map with at least some collectible counter, which would tell me "yes, you have completely explored this area, you can move on" would make the exploration so much better.
Technically, everything in the game works and it's pleasant experience before all the limitations start bothering you. Raising Slimes is fun, but the necessity to always run back and forth, the terrible limitations of your inventory that force you to do busy work all the time and no map or statistics towards the progression all quickly made me annoyed. This is not the type of game I want to play, because it doesn't respect my time. All is made worse because some of these things are easy to change (at least the inventory space), but the creators deliberately decided to waste your time.

Ok I'll be honest, this is a first for me; this game is fun. I'll explain why.
After seeing TotalBiscuit's review of the game, I was intrigued and I decided to buy this game and test it out for myself. TB's word, to me, is gold. He's honest and if he has any bias, he explains it from the start so him saying that this game is rather fun meant a lot to me.
I've put in nearly 20 hours over the course of a few months (since launch, mostly multiplayer I believe, too.) and I have to say I've had a bunch of fun. The games are fast paced and fun. I've had issues with objective based playlists because it requires a bit of coordination so playing with friends is a plus but not a necessity. Team Death Match is my home, I love it and it's a blast. I'm not a huge fan of the series in that I don't buy every game (this is the first one I've purchased since MW2). But in any case, I'm not sure the differences in the guns and how they balance out. I like the AK47 but the Bal is probably the best gun. I like how you're sorta limited in your loadout too. You have an allowance of 13 points (I guess?) and you can fill out your loadout. Each point allows you to add an item whether that's a gun, a perk, or an attachment, it really makes you think about what you need and want and I think it somewhat limits the chance of an OP build or something along those lines.
Speaking of which, sniping is hard in this game. You have to have twitch reactions and sitting still does you no favors. Kill streaks are also harder to get so you have to be getting stomped to see an enemy chopper. That's nice. It feels kinda like an arena shooter, the fast moving exos and all make the experience a lot of fun.
I don't think this game is perfect though. You die a lot. Well at least I do. I've had some good games but most of them have double digit kills. I feel like I can't live very long. Again, only 20 hours and maybe I'm not very good but if that sounds like you too, you're going to die a lot. Another thing is that the maps are constructed such that, you can die from literally everywhere. Especially with the verticality, it seems like anywhere you look, someone is there to take you out. I don't have much of a comment on spawns but I haven't felt any unfair spawns (yet?).
Having said that, I still go back for more. Moving on, the singleplayer is exactly what you think it is; cliche and pretty standard. From the trailers, you can basically guess what it's about. But you're not looking at this page for the singleplayer, are you? I mean, it's a Call of Duty game, there's no deep, enticing, captivating story. It's standard hollywood sillyness.

System Shock 2 is a tense game.
You’re lost in a derelict spaceship, away from everything and everyone, while trying your best to survive and understand what is going on. Every element of this game is masterfully designed to keep you always at the edge; weapons break all the time, ammo is hard to find and the inventory space is limited, meaning you never feel well-equipped and has to make tough decisions.
The levels are claustrophobic and help to create the heavy atmosphere of loneliness, but also feel real, an actual spaceship, not a pointless maze. Even with danger lurking in every corner, exploration feels great; there are various secret caches, and you will slowly uncover the fate of the crew through mutilated corpses, bloody scenes and the now-famous voice logs.
On top of all that, the class system provides many builds for players to try out, various solutions to the diverse challenges and a solid reason for multiple playthroughts of this gem.

A very good old-school dungeon crawler in the classic Wizardry style.  This game may not be for everyone as it does not hold your hand through different aspects of gameplay.  There is a lot of challenge in discovering how to progress forward which is something that some gamers may not be used to considering how today's games usually are.  If you fondly look back on games from the old days where you used graph paper to map a dungeon and a total party kill was always just a bad encounter away, then this game is for you.

First person dungeon crawler, very much like old school wizardry games. With random stat gain and loss on lv. this game is more gear based to determine difficulty instead of being reliant on natural power from levels. With many classes to try and roll for upon creation of a party memeber and the ability to change classes you can be very flexible. Be warned however this game absolutely does not hold your hand and with a brand new lv 1 party the creatures on even the first dungeon can pound you into dust and it doesn't get easier. There is also perma death, revival can fail and a memeber can be lost forever oh and insta death is a thing later on also memebers can grow old and die. The difficulty of it might seem a turn off but managing your six party memebers well and planning ahead can make a massive difference. Can you overcome the challenge? This is very worth checking out
