Ok so this is a very early access review and opinions I have expressed here may change. Hurtworld is very much like RUST. The graphics are relatively similiar and the game plays out similiar.
However this game is very much better than RUST for a number of reasons.
>The community is at this moment nowhere near as toxic. You can happily have conversations with new spawns or even people who can kill you and take all your stuff without you being able to do a thing about it.
> I haven't played RUST in a while but the crafting system in this game comes across a lot better to me. It tells you the recipe clearly and easy to get the hang of.
> The qwerty graphics are very nice and clean. They make the game have a unique feel depsite being a very similiar sandbox survival to RUST.
> The game took me around 3 minutes to install with the download being next to none but the content relatively large.
As this game is in Alpha and only just released hopefully some DEV's see this and can make improvements. These below are all points for improvement, they may be percieved as negative but considering how early this game is into development It is in its current stage very good.
>Add more content - The game itself requires a real grind but when you have M4's and a car and so many resources there isn't anything to play for. I turned to raiding even though it goes against an earlier comment, I did because I could.
>The map itself is relatively small for a sandbox survival, as soon as you hit the desert or far reaches of the polar biome which is surprisingly small you can go no further. The map in my opinion needs to be bigger and given actual towns and more biomes at least.
>Expanding on a previous point and perhaps my most contraversial (R.I.P English) a bigger map would provide more space for vehicles and a stronger variety. Personally I would like to see Aeroplanes. I may be alone at this point but the idea of making a base with a runway or helipad appeals to me. Also a large map, travelling to other parts of an expansive map seems incredible.
> I would like to see more animals and more threats. Sasquatches are not much of a threat and with an M4 easy to kill. Even a Yeti provides no challenge against 2 players with a gun or even a hunting bow. Perhaps add more animals such as lions etc. A big threat yet providing reward for people who kill them. Animals on any level would be appreciated.
> My one complaint will be deer's... They attack you proving no threat whatsoever but Deer's would never attack a human I don't understand why they are so aggressive. Stupid but valid.
In general I have spent around 25 hours on this game and have already enjoyed some great moments. I did run out of things to do but that can be expected in a game within such early stages. I am very excited to see what the DEV's do with this game and where they take it. I hope some people can agree with my aeroplanes point. Regardless lets just hope the devs stay active and add more variety to an already decent game.

There's no meaningful system preventing people from killing on sight all the time.

Environmental and NPC risk factors are even easier to avoid.
Survival games are never going to be interesting or fun until there are legitimate reasons (
) to cooperate and not immediately kill every single person you see. You might as well just play a decent FPS until then, because all this is is an FPS where you have to grind for hours until you're on equal footing with anyone else.

Honestly, one of the best games I have ever played, and I'm not just saying that because of the number of copies of the first game I own and my total playtime on it, either.
I pre-ordered this and suffered the masses of performance problems the game sufferes from (currently using betapatch for v1.2 to get around most of those) with HIGH settings giving 60 in most places, but dropping like a brick in certain places, looking at glass (I think) or entering combat. However, the gameplay and story was just so good that it didn't stop me from playing at 31FPS every now and then.
I've started my second playthrough as Corvo after doing a Ghost run as Emily; and my god. It's a work of art.
From the start it seemed more than good. They've kept most mechanics the same, tweaked and refined some others and added in a metric ton on top of that. But I've come to discover while playing Corvo that I haven't seen the start of it. Just changing my playstyle a bit from *sneaky sneaky chokey chokey* to *sneaky sneaky stabby stabby* has revealed so many more things for me to do. Let me start off by saying I was drawn in by the overall appeal of this cheap little title. Hacker aesthetics? Japanese rhythm game? Keyboard play? Sounds badass, wow, yeah?
Unfortunately, the magic ends there.
It's hard for me to reccomend this. I only played it for a few minutes but it's not really drawing me in. Rhythm games are supposed to draw you in. At the lower difficulties you get a feel for the pace and progression seems natural. Beyond the tutorial this game doesn't have that. You're supposed to get a feel for the rhythm of things on a basic starting level. This game doesn't have that.
A rhythm game should make you feel and look cool and badass at the higher difficulty levels. This does neither. I feel like a tool while playing this. And after just a few minutes I feel like progressing any further is literally gonna give me carpal tunnel. You're better off playing Stepmania or k-shoot mania (a free PC sim for Sound Voltex. It's like what Stepmania is for Dance Dance Revolution) KSM/SDVX especially has the tunnel effect/guitar hero notechart perspective that American players are more used to. Hell, take a book from Harmonix's Amplitude and Frequency. This? Eh.....
I wish this was better. I want it to be better. I want it to improve, but I don't think that's going to happen without a massive overhaul of the engine and retooling of gameplay and difficulty. Sorry guys.

A great game if you can get past the myriad of technical problems. If you played Just Cause 2 and are really, really itching to take that style of gameplay to the next level,
the terrible frame rate and the extremely annoying stuttering audio, then buy the game right now. You won't regret it. If you haven't played Just Cause 2, I'd recommend doing that then refer to the advice above.
Also, I will mention that the game ran far far worse when it was first released. They have improved it a bit but, be aware that you'll still very likely be running into the problems I described above, and more, frequently.
So, with that caveat out of the way, if you know what you're getting into the game is often unbelievably fun. The story is very thin. The AI is bad. The characters are one dimensional and forgettable (including Ricco himself) But, that's not what we're here for. If you buy this game expecting to play it like an open world CoD or Halo, or if you assume it's going to be like Far Cry, you're going to be quite disappointed. Just Cause is all about creative destruction on a massive scale and setting up insane stunts using all your cool yet completely implausible gadgets.
The game map is huge, and while there is a ton of stuff to do, it feels slightly more empty than JC2. That's not to say JC2 is the superior game. All of the game mechanics have been tweaked to be a bit more fluid. Grappling is better, and the new wingsuit is one of my favorite tools ever in a video game. I kinda miss searching for the upgrade crates in JC2. JC3 has collectibles but, not nearly as many as the last game.
And speaking of the upgrades, that's one of my few complaints about JC3. The stuff you start off with is pretty limited. If you don't start collecting gears (which are earned by completing challenges) right away, you'll probably get bored with the game before too long. You can use gears to buy gear upgrades, some of which really open up the game and change some of the dynamics significantly. But, there are hundreds of gears to collect. So if you are earning gears while doing intermittent story missions. You'll probably be nearly finished with the game before you earn all the upgrades. Once you liberate a territory, enemies will never show up in that section again. So once you liberate an area there's little reason to go back there other than finding a collectible or doing a challenge. Some of the upgrades I got late-game and didn't really have much stuff left to destroy with it because I had liberated all the settlements. So, I'd recommend hitting the challenges hard early on so you can use all the tools throughout most of the game.
I'm recommending this game reluctantly because of the performance issues. If I had known how the game ran before I bought it, I may have passed. But, I had so much fun with the game regardless, that I decided to give it a thumbs up
you know what you're getting into, and are willing to put up with it. As I said before they did release a couple of patches that improved things but, the problems still exist. They may release some more fixes but, they just released a multiplayer DLC so my guess is they'll spend all their resources trying to make more money, rather than fix the broken thing they already sold.

Fortuntely for me, it seems I dodged the bullet and I have been able to run the game at max settings without any issues that some players are experiencing.
Now, onto the game itself. If you have played any previous entries in the Just Cause Series, you will be immediately familiar with the gameplay. Rico makes his usual "subtle" arrival to the country of Medici, which has a Mediterranean theme to it. As usual, there is a dictator to be deposed, and in order to do so Rico (you) must loosen the dictator's grip on the land by causing as much chaos as possible.
For those new to the series, causing chaos is essentially destroying the dictator's assets by any means necessary, so shooting up Fuel Tanks, driving cars into Power Generators, and pretty much just wrecking everything however you see fit. Some new mechanics are in place for those familiar with the series, but a few new additions change things up for the better.
Your grappling hook gets a few snazzy upgrades right off the bat, such as being able to manually "reel in" tethered objects allowing you to winch items, as well as the usual making the dictator's forces just "hand around". Another upgrade is that you can now have more than one "pair" of teathered objects.
Something new to the series is that challenges are now required to upgrade various things, with relevant challenges tied to each upgrade. For example, Explosive Challenges upgrade your explosives, Air Vehicle Challenges have air vehicle upgrades, etc. The upgrades range from new gadgets to cause chaos, to improved ammo storage, and even things like nitrous for vehicles. The grapple also has upgrades, so that the "reel in" is stronger for when you want to topple a statue quietly, or even one where you can have even more teathers for making some interesting combinations.
Another change up to the series is that you can secure areas as you go along by clearing out all of the dictator's assets in a specific region. Doing so unlocks various challenges (to earn those upgrades), as well as a few other perks. Hidden Packages are still present, and if you clear out an area the locations are revealed if you do not want to search every nook and cranny beforehand. Some of those hidden packages range from parts to collect, to backstory tapes, and the like. Liberating a settlement also can unlock new items to call in, as well as open up a garage to bring vehicles that you can then call in later. For example, that sweet motorcycle you found can be turned in to make it available anywhere, and you can turn in aircraft, cars, and even boats!
Overall, the game does not try to take itself seriously, which is never really has. While it has its "serious" moments, the characters are usually over the top, and a one liner is usually not too far behind any major plot points/discussions. While some might find it to be groan worthy (as a Dad, we're talking like dad caliber jokes here at times), there are some clever gems here and there. My only real gripe here is that the voice actors from 2 are somewhat missed here, but the current ones are growing on me, so perhaps that is a good thing.
So, I would recommend this game if you are into a game where over the top action gameplay is your cup of tea. There are plenty of ways to cause chaos, and the world is quite large so you won't be running out of things to do anytime soon. Of course, I understand that some people are having issues with performance, but at this time I was not one of them, so I cannot comment negatively about something I never experienced. Like I said in my opening statement, I am running the game at max settings and I have not had any problems yet with crashes or slowdowns.

Survival horror is probably my favourite genre of video game, and this game has delivered on my expectations. The devs have really gone to town to create an alien experience that is true to the original 1979 movie. You're aboard a ship with a very smart and unpredictable alien that will seize on any mistake you make or crop up without warning at any given moment. It's fast, powerful and deadly, but it's not the only thing aboard the ship that is out to get you. This game makes full use of the vulnerability factor that the first movie had; you can't kill this creature, all you can do is hide or make it back off for 10 seconds. You have various tools, like the motion sensor, to aid you in your quest for survival, but even with these gadgets you're far from safe. It definitely pays to be quiet and stealthy as  being loud is a sure way to get yourself killed.
Graphically the game looks amazing, I was particularly impressed with the lighting and audio, which were amongst the best I have seen/heard in a game. Also, the game appears to be stable as I haven't experienced any framerate issues or freezes, although the latest driver updates have apparently caused people problems. In addition, the music is very good and plays a huge role in the scare building and jump scenes.The alien looks incredible and feels like a predator playing cat and mouse, hellbent on finding you and killing you. It will change its directions at will, look under tables, rip doors off lockers and react to any noises made, but it's the sheer unpredictability that is the most terrifying aspect overall. You can spend 10 minutes hiding thinking it's gone away only for it to reappear seconds later or stab you through the chest without even hearing it creep up on you. Sometimes it will go away and not appear again for ages, it all depends on how much attention you bring to yourself.
The game, however, isn't without flaws, notably the story which feels a little directionless at times and unfortunately it's quite easy to become disconnected from the characters. The human AI are very annoying and look badly modelled when speaking and moving, but I see no need looking for negatives with a game that has done its best to breathe new life into a franchise that has suffered so many poorly made titles over the years. Alien Isolation is a step in the right direction. It's a highly immersive experience made by people that really care about the alien franchise. Great game.

Definitely a must play for fans of either of the first films of the franchise, if you don't mind a foray into the Horror.

Well, what can I say... Dark Souls II is quite honestly in my own opinion one of the greatest games ever made. It's predecessor Dark Souls was equally as great (and I highly recommend playing that as well) and just as Silke has said in their review of this game, the combat is the thing that really does make these games great. But to me it's more than that. After dying so many times, after learning and sometimes having to re-learn enemy attack patterns when you move onto new game + and beyond, you begin to understand the game. You begin to learn to appreciate the mechanics that are involved and the level design. You can start seeing what the developers were thinking when they were designing individual aspects of levels and areas. This sense of understanding gives you a certain depth of immersion, a kind of proud achivement that I've personally never experienced in any other title.
The Souls games have always been successful in telling great stories with little and somtimes no voice acting/dialogue. Now I understand that to some people that's a big con, I mean a story that isn't explained to you? How dumb is that right? But the thing is, it doesn't explain it, because in many cases the Devs want it to be your own decision, they want you to personally theorycraft and understand things about this incredible world yourself. Maybe your right, or maybe your way off the mark, but it doesn't matter, if it makes sense then there's no reason for other people to tell you otherwise. The lore in this game is something phenomenal, and definitely not something to be glossed over. Both games have a terrificly deep story and even side quests, but all are open to the players interpretation. Again, something that no other title has ever given me.
So all in all, Dark Souls II is a game that you quite simply can't miss. Especially with multiplayer now through Steam both co-op and pvp work much better on PC. Yes this game is hard. Yes this game is frustrating. And yes there will no doubt be moments that cause you to rage furiously at this game. But if it were void of this challenge then the feeling of achievment would be greatly watered down. If you get this game and find it to difficult I beg you to stick with it, the anger it takes from you will be doubled with how happy it will make you when you eventually succeed- easily 10/10

We all know what this game is all about, it sets you on a post apocalyptic zombie world. You might say "Uh, that's sooooooooo original", but it's FREE and is worthy of your time, so you should check it out.
The game currently has 2 game modes, Objective based maps (NMO maps) and Survival based maps (You must survive a number of round before the rescue arrives). You'll play with another 7 people at the same time in a coop game (there's not a PVP mode right now, but it might be added in future updates).
In No More Room in Hell (NMRH) you're not inmune, you're not from the army and you will be using melee weapons most part of the time. You can get infected if a zombie attacks you, and you'll start looking for medicines to stop the infection for a little longer, because you can become one of the living creatures and start attacking your friends or infect them as well. You can even commit suicide if you don't want to attack your teammates. So yes, NMRH has interesting mechanics that makes it more realistic. But sometimes, this part of the game may be hated by some people, sometimes newer players might get bitten right at the start of the round and that can be frustrating, and if you are one of them you got to wait (generally a long time) to respawn.
This is a source engine game, so it looks exactly like a source engine game, the animations in 3rd person are not the greatest ones, but the ones in 1st person are really good in my opinion. The sound assets are good most of the time, and variety of guns is quite large. I have to say that it has custom maps too, as the game supports them, you can make one in the valve's hammer editor, if you know how to use it, obviously. No More Room in Hell has the standard server browser witch works perfectly fine.
I totally recommend this game, if you want to survive zombies in a big number of maps with your friends, this game is for you and the best part is that it is FREE!

*Disclaimer: I played TES from Daggerfall to Skyrim, so I may be biased a little.
Like:
- Big area, with enough space and opportunity for everyone
- Realtime collision-based combat, unlike so many other MMO which use auto-attack or random dice mechanics
- Character customization is quite thorough, even body shape is customizable. Want a potbelly? No problem
- Very high freedom of character development, it's likely you won't see 10 people with same builds in the same room
- What you do makes you .. level up.
- Stable economy with not so much emphasis on goldly wealth.
- PvP of epic proportion
- Most importantly, not pay to win; almost all Crown Store stuffs are for aesthetic prettiness only
Dislike:
- Big area sometimes makes you wonder if you are actually playing a single-player game instead of an MMO
- Face and body feature customization could use more choices. My hero's chest is not hairy enough.
- Realtime collision-based combat also means the slower and less agile among us would be disadvantaged
- IMO all Class skill lines should also be open to everyone. Dragonknight+Sorcerer would be awesome
- Lack of chat bubbles or dialog subtitles make towns somewhat ... quiet (Chat bubbles feature is on the way though)
- What? No skill lines for Fist weapons?
- *update* No Asian server. I'm from Asia and I find the lag caused by the high ping to US server a big disadvantage for my in PvP
Summary:
I've played many MMOs before, but TESO is a breath of fresh air to me. Sure, it has bad reviews during the Beta, but exposing the rough edges IS the whole point of beta-testing anyway. Also, remember that this is an MMORPG, not a single player game, so of course it will not be 100% like Skyrim. Or TES6 : Elsweyr, if you believe that rumor.
So, yes, if you want to try something new, I recommend TESO.

I have been following Black Mesa from the time it still had the Source name in the title, over 6 years ago. I did not think it would actually be completed or released, let alone be such a loving, faithful homage to the original.
Let's be honest: Half-Life set the bar for a lot of things in its time but it hasn't aged well. The environments don't make much sense, enemy behaviour is erratic and there are only 4 scientists.
Black Mesa updates Half-Life, bringing in all the necessary 21st century sensibilities that the original lacked. At this point, if a friend of mine told me they wanted to start playing the Half-Life games, I'd tell them to start with Black Mesa and simply ignore the original. It is historically important, sure, but for the modern games BM is much more suitable (and less likely to drive them away from this classic series).
I can offer no higher praise for this game (I can't call it a "mod" in good conscience) than to say it  And has surpassed its predecessor. And I am certain Valve agrees.

Dark Souls 2 is a wonderful game but it has its faults.
As a single player game it is outstanding, the enviornment is engrossing and the characters that you meet along the way are interesting if not a little long winded. There is a sense of accomplishment that this game provides that many do not. You really feel that you have done something when you finally move on to a new area and beat a boss.
The learning curve is steep, mostly having to do with your stats and what you should do with all those souls but I never felt lost like I did my first time through DS 1.
It's not all sunshine (Praise the Sun) and flowers though because I do have some complaints.
Firstly I find PvP to be totally unrewarding and hapazard. There is no way to get paired with someone that is your level and no real way to rank yourself so you know that you at least stand a chance.
Second the game can feel like a boss rush mode at times where you go from one big monster to another. At times there really was no build up to a fight and I would come through a fog door asking myself how this monster is a boss (Rat bosses in my opinion).
My biggest complaint is unfair to the game as it is not the way Fromsoftware designed it. I really wish there were ways to set up a co-op story. I know most will say that there are the signs and that you can organize yourself with your friends to get summoned to take on a boss. I want a true co-op experience it would scale to accomodate two players and we could have voice chat. I don't think it will ever happen, but a boy can dream.

Slime Rancher is a cute, addicting game that has truly captured my heart. I originally heard about this game from a friend who recommended it to me, and I have to say purchasing this game has been one of the best choices I've made. They've added quite a lot of new elements since I've bought the game, and  they've only made the game much more enjoyable. I love the brighter colors of the game along with the calming, friendly music it has to go along with it, it's quite different from a lot of games I've played that have darker undertones. The game is about Beatrix LeBeau, you, a slime rancher who moved out onto the Far, Far Range to start a new life. This game allows you to corral slimes and sell their plorts for money to either invest in your farm, home, upgrades, or to unlock new sections of your farm. They update the game quite a bit, making it a fun game to come back to. Their latest update with the Glass Desert has added a lot more new slimes and places to explore, which has only increased my addiction to this game.
Pros:
- Nice music and characters
- Plenty of things to upgrade
- Has detailed descriptions of everything you've picked up in-game
- Lots of updates
- Cute designs for slimes and other creatures
- Plenty of areas to explore
- Has a bit of story to go along with the game
Cons:
- Can be repetitive from time to time (mostly when it comes to being on your farm if you haven't unlocked or upgraded a lot of things yet)
- No map in-game but I did find a map on the game's wiki, I tend to get lost quite easy at times

I am a fan of this franchise, so I'll be biased off the bat.
I love the fact that the developers took the time to try and present a historically based game, with unit histoires, legacies, province names, etc. That being said, there are some units that are fun to play with, but questionablly powerful (war dogs maybe). The map is huge with numerous factions--however, they aren't unlockable upon defeat like the previous version. Instead you have to wait for CA to release them by patch, and even with those you'll likely have to purchase them (put them on wait list and go nuts during a Steam sale!). I also miss the feature where you could zoom into a city and explore it without having to be seiged. If this is still an option, I haven't found it :(
Multiplayer options are great too! Wish that it was possible to do a campaign larger than 1v1 or 1co-op1. I know the turn times would be annoying, and that connectivity may be an issue, but I'd like to see that in a future release or patch of Rome.
So in short:
- great expansive sand box experience
- good historical basis, although not perfect perhaps
- fun multiplayer, some bugs though (for a while you couldn't get past turn 18 which I think they've fixed)
- lots of factions, but to play as most you have to pay
- happy that I get to play as Scipio Africanus

*This review is based on v0.6 (which is almost the complete game), playing with a controller.*
I don't usually buy early access games, but Slime Rancher was recommended to me enough times that I decided to try it, and I'm glad I did! Here are a few things I enjoyed:
-A daily harvest > feed > collect cycle in your home area, which you optimise as you go along. The later in the game you are, the more options you have, and it's fun to balance what you want to place where, and what you can cycle out, because you no longer need it. It's not as extensive as some farming-style games, but it's also only part of what you do.
-Light creature collecting/breeding mechanics. Most of your incentives for choosing slimes and slime hybrids are based on how lucrative they are, but I still found myself keeping the ones I liked around for longer (because they're just that likeable).
-Exploring at your own pace. In between your home upkeep, you have plenty of areas to explore and new things to find and bring back. There is no overhead map, so it can be a bit confusing when you first enter a new area, but it only takes a few trips to get an idea of the layout (it takes a few more to discover all the secrets!) The controls were also pretty intuitive, and I really enjoy floating around with the jetpack!
If any of those sound appealing, it might be worth trying Slime Rancher!

Dark Souls 2 is a wonderful game but it has its faults.
As a single player game it is outstanding, the enviornment is engrossing and the characters that you meet along the way are interesting if not a little long winded. There is a sense of accomplishment that this game provides that many do not. You really feel that you have done something when you finally move on to a new area and beat a boss.
The learning curve is steep, mostly having to do with your stats and what you should do with all those souls but I never felt lost like I did my first time through DS 1.
It's not all sunshine (Praise the Sun) and flowers though because I do have some complaints.
Firstly I find PvP to be totally unrewarding and hapazard. There is no way to get paired with someone that is your level and no real way to rank yourself so you know that you at least stand a chance.
Second the game can feel like a boss rush mode at times where you go from one big monster to another. At times there really was no build up to a fight and I would come through a fog door asking myself how this monster is a boss (Rat bosses in my opinion).
My biggest complaint is unfair to the game as it is not the way Fromsoftware designed it. I really wish there were ways to set up a co-op story. I know most will say that there are the signs and that you can organize yourself with your friends to get summoned to take on a boss. I want a true co-op experience it would scale to accomodate two players and we could have voice chat. I don't think it will ever happen, but a boy can dream.

This review will not focus on the singleplayer portion of the game. I will offer a fair comment on the multiplayer portion, and give reasons as to why you should and should not buy CODAW.
I haven't played much for this game (approx 50-70 hours, the box above only shows you my Singleplayer hours), but based on my past COD experiences I think my gameplay hours are enough to give an unbiased comment on the game.
First off, the Exo elements are quite refereshing, but not in the sense that they are innovative elements (a lot of games have some of these Exo elements in the past). Having new movement abilities and player attributes in CODAW shifted the gameplay style quite substantially - after the first few games CODAW gives me a slight Quake sense to it. When I say this, I do not imply that CODAW has turned super hardcore and skill-demanding, no I don't mean that at all. I just want to  point out that the combat feels like an arena-styled combat, with a touch of COD apparently.
Second, the weapons. Now, we all know that in almost every COD game, a few weapons dominate the whole arsenal. This is no different in CODAW. The Bal-27 and ASM1 are the "go-to" weapons in this game, they basically have the positions of the UMP and AK in MW2. This isn't a gameplay problem, because you can always use other weapons for fun and variety, right? But then, the laser gun, EM1, is ridiculously overpowered in the PC version. Basically it's the Lightning Gun in Quake - if you've played Quake before, or you're an old time Quake player, you'll wreck everyone in this game with the EM1. I wish the EM1 never existed in the game, because of its annoyance.
With the new weapon loots and supply drops, gameplay is quite addictive - you get a supply drop every 45 minutes on average, with the chance of having rare weapon variants or cosmetics. Variants adjust the weapon stats, usually with some improved stats and some worsened stats. Some variants are very good looking, and some variants can even change your playstyle based on the changed stats. It's a really nice implementation in the COD franchiese in my opinion, and even more so when CODAW doesn't have too many weapons to begin with.
Third, the maps. Maps in CODAW aren't the best among all the maps in other CODs, but they are quite fun if you play them in the adequate game mode. I won't comment much on the map design here, because in my opinion COD isn't a competitive shooter at all (I'm a CSGO player), hence I think map design isn't something my critique has to focus on. One comment before I move on: some of the capture points are very difficult to capture or hold, but that's where the fun is at.
Then I move on to the player pool. It seems quite obvious that the PC player pool is way lower than previous COD titles (I play from the Asia region and the player pool reduction is very noticeable). It isn't uncommon to bump into the same group of players in the lobbies. Game modes other than TDM, Mosh Pit and Dom are practically empty on PC. This is a huge issue, but personally I'm fine with the game as long as I can manage to find a lobby when I play.
This is not a 100% thorough walkthrough, I only typed it on the fly. These are some of the primary aspects of the multiplayer portion which I think any buyer would want to know more about before purchasing CODAW. As to whether you should buy this game or not:
1) You should, because
- this is a refreshing COD, with new elements, playstyle and so on
- the PC port isn't too bad with a 90FPS cap, at least I don't see gamebreaking port issues
- the game is honestly fun and even more fastly paced than previous CODs
2) You shouldn't, because
- the playerbase on PC is small
- SH Games doesn't seem to care much about the PC version of the game, like how most PC versions of COD were pretty much neglected
- it doesn't feel like the old CODs anymore
- the weapons aren't exactly balanced, more like the OP and dominant weapons compete with one another
My personal opinion: It's worth buying, but I don't think the game will last long. If the playerbase were larger, I would have bought the Season Pass.

Instead you have to wait for CA to release them by patch, and even with those you'll likely have to purchase them (put them on wait list and go nuts during a Steam sale!). I also miss the feature where you could zoom into a city and explore it without having to be seiged. If this is still an option, I haven't found it :(
Multiplayer options are great too! Wish that it was possible to do a campaign larger than 1v1 or 1co-op1. I know the turn times would be annoying, and that connectivity may be an issue, but I'd like to see that in a future release or patch of Rome.
So in short:
- great expansive sand box experience
- good historical basis, although not perfect perhaps
- fun multiplayer, some bugs though (for a while you couldn't get past turn 18 which I think they've fixed)
- lots of factions, but to play as most you have to pay
- happy that I get to play as Scipio Africanus

I don't often do reviews, but I feel this game is deserving of my attention. This is the game we've all been waiting for, long expecting a game of intense atmosphere and horror for the Alien franchise. A game where we are no longer on equal fighting ground with the Alien but more-so at its mercy.
The game offers a brilliantly designed and crafted sturctural world of dark corridors, sparking lights, that eerie space station feel of vast emptiness and isolation and of course, one of our favourite creatures of all time: Alien. But alas Alien is not the only problem on the Space Station Sevastopol, other survivors and killer androids are also a thing to keep an eye out for as well as a variety of planning, strategy and careful timing to complete each objective you are faced with.
Graphics: 9/10
They did really well with the graphics and rendering of the space station itself as well as all the models of characters and Ai Controlled. The lighting of the game really helps to envelop you in the tense and dreary world you find yourself in for most of the game. Blood spatter, broken structural mainframe, the classic Sci-Fi feel of the original Alien world and even Alien drool, this was really well done and I loved it all.
Music: 10/10
We all know how music and sounds can affect the outcome of a game by either bringing its full potential to fruition or utterly destroying the feel of the game, the designers nailed this games music and sounds. From the Alien crawling around in the vents, to the sheer terror of a music buildup as an enemy approaches your hiding place, I personally think it affected the overall feel and atmosphere of the game and bought what I was hoping to be, to be even better than what I ahd expected.
Atmosphere: 10/10
The Atmosphere? Terrifying to say the least if you really put yourself in Amada's place and forget the outside world, lights off, surround sound, high graphics. The Atmosphere of the game is only as good as YOU want it to be and for me, it's an experience I won't soon forget. This game has one of the most strongest atmosphere's of horror and survival over any other game I've played
Gameplay: 9/10
Being difficult to see and keeping your flashlight off so you don't attract unwanted attention, the game offers a brilliant variety of stealth and distraction techniques you need to employ in order to progress through and to keep your body intact. The construction of in-game items plays a major role in easing your stealth tactics and giving you access to a variety of traps and distraction tools to use at will. Hiding and bypassing Humans, Androids and the Alien alike were all to my liking as I am a very cautious person in these sorts of games and am not hasty in my decision making.
Overall, if you want my advice for the most optimal experience for this game, turn off your lights, play alone in your room with a headset on, put the graphics as high as your PC can run them and play on the hardest difficulty like I did. This is just my opinion on what you should do though, you can decide what to do for yourself.

For some context: I've played every COD since COD 4: Modern Warfare, with a strong preference for the Modern Warfare games, and Advanced Warfare is my favorite since MW2.
Campaign:
I thoroughly enjoyed the SP campaign in Advanced Warfare. I definitely follows some standard COD formulas, so don't expect the next Bioshock, but it goes through those beats in a fun and engaging way. The story was actually more cohesive that most other COD games. It's fairly ridiculous, but cohesive none the less.
The missions are diverse and the big set piece moments are solidly entertaining. But most importantly, the new gadgets are a blast to play with. The Exo suits are really the shining centerpiece in Advanced Warfare and change the dynamic drastically. Being able to double jump onto platforms and dodge out of range of grenades really changed the gameplay in my opinion and made a COD campaign fresh again. The movement is really fluid once you get some practice, and many of the levels are dynamic enough to make use of it.
Going in expecting a COD campaign, I was actually pleasantly surprised. I've never cared much for the Black Ops games and Ghosts was pretty lackluster, but Advanced Warfare really delivered on what I want out of a COD game: crazy over the top action with solid FPS mechanics. My only real complaints are minor in that the campaign is a bit short (8.5 hours on Hardened) and that it seems to be easier than the Modern Warfare games. I'm on my Veteran playthrough right now and it isn't particularly difficult.
Online MP:
I have hundreds and hundreds of hours of online COD play between all of the games, and had honestly gotten pretty bored with it. I played over 1000 of MW2 before 3 came out, and my hours have dropped off with each release. I jumped into MP just for the sake of trying it out, but I've actually gotten a bit invested in it.
The Exo suits again really change things up. Maps have some verticality to them and the movements+abilities really change the online dynamic. It's actually made the game more fast-paced because people tend to camp less and spend more time double jumping with air dodges. It takes a bit of time to master, but is a welcome improvement to a series that got stale a while ago.
I really enjoy the customizing side of things as well. Loadouts are fully customizable so you can focus on the parts you utilize, which adds some nice options. You start out with decent weapons and get better ones quickly. You can also customize your weapons and character, specifically with the items from regular supply drops. It's nice to new items from a method other than grinding kills with specific gear. And I love that when you prestige you can pick any item to be permanently unlocked and remove the level lock from it. Even when I prestige back to level 1, I still get to rock my crossbow build.
Now, I like gameplay and the design, but MP has had some issues on PC. First, I couldn't connect at all for a couple of weeks, but that seems to be fixed now, so bravo for that. Second, You're pretty limited on available games. The player base is pretty small (partially from the overall dwindling base of the series and partially from the early connection issues), so some game types don't have any active lobbies. You can find games, but you're going to be limited to the more popular types. Third and lastly, I get semi-regular hard crashes when playing. All of my other games, including the AW campaign run fine, but MP will crash to desktop from a fatal error (with no text explaining what happened) every few hours.
I'm also not a big fan of the prestige design. You level up so fast these days, so you can get through 15 (15!) levels of prestige. I personally preferred the older MW leveling with took quick a bit of playtime, but I never really cared much for prestige in the first place, so I'm probably in the minority on this. On the other hand, they balanced the challenges perfectly so the ones you want to reset after a prestige become active again and the ones you don't remain untouched.
I doubt I'll end up playing online MP for 1000 hours, but I'm honestly enjoying it for the time being. It's still COD online MP, but with enough new and interesting additions to make it fun again. There are things I'm not a huge fan of when it comes to COD, but at the end of the day, I'm having fun playing it.
Final thoughts:
At this point, I'm guessing most people know if they like COD games or not. This is still very much a COD game, and I don't expect it to change people's minds if they previously aren't fans. But that being said, it's one of my favorite games in the franchise. It's becoming apparent that players somewhat fatigued by the franchise in general, so I'd love to see them slow down development a bit and take more time with releases like AW rather than pumping out completely skippable games like Ghosts every year. That may be an unrealistic hope, but there it is anyway.

I played this game for a while, so hear me out.
TL:DR version
Hope was lost for the future of this game. The playerbase is slowly dwindiling and as it stands - the game is a husk of what it once was. It's a shame. It came so far, but it kept stinging its long term players and financial supporters to the point it probably won't be too much longer until the eventual nuking of the official game servers.
I'm going to re-install and replay this game to see if it can give me back the love I once had for it. I might change this review if I see anything notable worth changing. I love this game, I just wish I could say it's worth it
_________________________________________________________________________
I like what this game is trying to achieve, or rather, was trying to achieve. A fun cops vs robber's scenario where people make themselves look as amazing as they want and duke it out with overly expensive weapons and vehicles. To that extent, it succeeds. If you have a decent internet connection and live somewhat near the hosted server locations along with having at least a mid-range PC to play with, you will probably enjoy the base game.
But alas, this is not why I can't recommend the game. I put in quite a large financial investment into this games store - before you question this, no the game is not pay 2 win. However if you want to look as flash as possible and level up at a decent rate premium subscription is the way to go. If you just looking for a decently fun shooter with average gun variety then this game will suffice.
But I digress, I also put in a large chunk of time into this game and its mechanics, along with getting to know the community and even having contact with some of the staff from Gamersfirst (the current owners of the game) - and not once do I regret my time being there. It's just the company behind it all that makes the game's practices seem so shady and unreasonable.
Broken promises are all we ever recieved from the game's developers. The ATAC, a widely controversial weapon ingame, was meant to get weapon nerfed (yes I'm aware that it's not 100% OP) and instead we just got more ARMAS junk and skins. That whole truck griefing business is still very easy to achieve due to lack of attention in the game's physics engine. Jump exploits were never really patched except for a few major ones. Old content from the game's release is still being used client side which slows performance and has never been looked at, and the list goes on and on.
But I'm ignoring the elephant in the room, the thing that killed half of the PC community surrounding this project, the thing that then cut that half into half and sent it over to consoles, the thing that dissapointed nearly every long term fan of this game. The engine update.
After that mess, it was essentially over.
Hope was lost for the future of this game. The playerbase is slowly dwindiling and as it stands - the game is a husk of what it once was. It's a shame. It came so far, but it kept stinging its long term players and financial supporters.
But who can blame them? We kept funding their lack of attention to patches and updates, exploits and balance. In the end it doesn't matter who's to blame. Let's just hope that this IP isn't abandoned entirely by the end of the decade.
If you'll excuse me, I'm going to re-install and replay this game to see if it can give me back the love I once had for it. I might change this review if I see anything notable worth changing. I love this game, I just wish I could say it's worth it.

Well, where to start with this...
I saw potential in this game. From the outside, initially, it seems fun and creative with a whole array to offer. But honestly, it's far from that.
The first problem I noticed with this game was the loading issues. They weren't really a problem to get by, save for closing and restarting the game, but then I noticed that this game was horribly unfinished. It's very hard for new players to get a feel for this game because, while I did not have much of a problem with it, the interface seemed too spread out difficult to use. I actually had to Google how to find certain things like my player profile, because it's not immediately obvious how to do that, and the fact I couldn't find the controls menu either didn't make things any easier. Maybe this is my fault, but I have to say that I wasn't really keen on spending longer than a minute button smashing to see where things were, and ultimately Googling the answer seemed easier.
Asides from that, the game had a lot to offer in terms of what could be done with it, but lacked in what had been done. The missions in mission mode were fairly simple however they were repetitive. Not to mention the hordes of hackers that seem to be present within this game, making it a lot harder to get by on your own. I can see this putting off a lot of new players, as it has done with me.
To get to a decent point of standing with this game, you'd have to grind for hours on end, or cough up some real cash. I'm not saying this game is pay to win, because it isn't, but it's so hard to get anywhere that it probably should just be play to win. People say APB Reloaded is "a poor man's GTA V" but I would say that you'll probably end up spending more money within APB to get what you want than you'll ever spend on GTA V.
This game offers a "social mode" which really reminded me of Second Life or Playstation Home. Again, a lot more could be done with this but it really seems like they just threw in a social mode and some quickly-made cosmetics to boost the income of this game because it wasn't doing so well in any other aspects, considering this game is free.
I'm really disappointed, because this game could be so brilliant, but it's so horrendously broken almost beyond repair.
In conclusion, I would not really rather not recommend APB Reloaded, but since it's free, this tips the scale for me, and I do recommend that you at least try it. It's not like this game is completely dead though, there's still a fairly large player base so obviously GamersFirst must be raking in some kind of income from this game, so my question is simple; why don't GamersFirst actually put the gamers first and fix this monstrosity instead of beating a dead horse for more coin?

"This is 3rd Officer Jazz - last survivor of Sevastapol Station.
All the other Alien games are dead:
Alien Trilogy, Alien vs Predator, Alien vs Predator 2 ... and Aliens Colonial Marines
Hopefully the Torrens will pick me up soon.
This is Jazz - signing off ..."
...
And, just like the game itself, that is how my review begins.
My review of easily the best ever Alien game - and, I suspect, the best ever sci-fi horror game.
Alien: Isolation.
Most of the best games today are fun while they last, but ultimately a shallow disposable entertainment, like most well-made popcorn movies.
This one is different - there are many unscripted moments in this game that you will remember for the rest of your life. Unfortunately, they are terrifying! I could well imagine someone getting a heart attack playing this - or even suffering PTSD. It's the stuff of nightmares.
Everything is geared towards scaring the hell out of you - including the cheap scripted jump-scares, atmospheric "ghost-in-the-attic" noises and superb dynamic horror music modelled on the orignal motifs from the 1979 classic. The environment is often dark and smoky and beautifully realised - but there are also brightly lit areas that are just as terrifying when ...
The Alien is surely the most terrifying villain ever to grace a videogame (especially on Hard mode) - if this thing even sees you through a window from 20 yards away, you will see it run towards you at lightning speed. You will be dead.
Even if you have a flame thrower, if the alien sees you at close range, it will kill you before you even press the fire button.
It is very clever - it will try to lure you out of a hiding place by pretending to walk away - so you make your move too soon - and its got you!
Above all, it is completely unpredictable and unscripted once it has entered the level (sometimes at prescribed moments and in prescribed places) - the developers have created a unique, self-aware AI; they may sometimes decide when and where it will appear during the game, but once it is in the level it thinks and moves all by itself. It is not scripted. You can't map its "patterns" - there are none. But you can gain a small advantage by observing its behaviour when you get the chance.
I found that being stalked by this thing led me to my own personal character arc.
Like everyone else, I was terrified of the alien at first, hiding in lockers and being a real wuss most of the time - scared to do anything.
But there comes a point - like Ellen Ripley in the movies - where I "grew a pair" and decided to be much more bold; trusting my instincts to carefully navigate around obstacles while the alien was right beside me looking in the other direction (careful not to tread on its tail though - it doesn't like that. Not AT ALL.)  - playing that way was just like in the movie where she's singing "you are my lucky star - lucky, lucky, lucky ". The sweat dripping down my face, the fear of even breathing in real life in case the alien somehow heard me - that's how involving the game is.
None of the above would make any sense if I could just press F5 to quicksave the game every time I hear the alien - it would remove all the tension completely, and turn this into an "ordinary" good game as I mentioned earlier.
Fortunately, this game is unashamedly old-school.
Want to save your game? - then you'll just have to find a save point to do it - braving the alien and other enemies in the process! [rapturous applause from me - modern games have become far too easy!]
This is such an important mechanic for keeping the horror maxed out.
Saving the game became a fist-pumping release of adrenaline and endorphins "yes!!!" [it takes an agonising 5 seconds too - making you briefly completely defenceless while saving]
Seeing the alien hover around the save point you needed to use led to some very tense close encounters - a perfect situation to use a distraction (such as a flare or noise emitting device).
The high you get from reaching the next save point makes you want to keep playing - you become addicted to that feeling of achieving a save point. Every single one, when up against the alien, was like scoring a goal in football - "yess! Get in!" For a brief moment, you are not scared anymore - but the feeling doesn't last ...
There are other enemies in the game - they are slightly more scripted (at least their starting points appear to be the same every time, if not their movements). The androids are my favourite - easy to outrun, but very durable. Much more durable than a human being. You can kill a human with a single revolver shot (and on Hard, you will die yourself if you are shot even twice by a jumpy human being) - but the androids are made of some kind of durable rubber and take several shots to take down, wasting precious short-supplied ammo.
They are also skilled in basic self-defence. If you try to hit them with a wrench, they will grab your wrist and force it downwards instantly - almost like they took night classes in self-defence in their spare time and applied this basic textbook disarming technique ... then they choke or beat you to death while reminding you that "you're being hysterical" or "violence is not the answer".
They inject some much needed humour into the game as they kill you! I think they are a very memorable villain - scary at close quarters, but often hilarious at the same time.
Even when they're being "nice" - they go around spouting company slogans like "With Seegson, there's always someone behind you every single step of the way .." delivered in their scary monotonic English accent. Meanwhile, you're sweating under a table hoping they don't notice you and turn nasty - but chuckling at the same time.
Storywise - I won't spoil anything. Except that a lot of it is close to the original movie - a bit too close in places. But it also has some terrific twists (and even an impressive "non twist") which affects the gameplay in the latter stages.
The voice acting for the main characters varies between "very good" and "adequate" - Amanda is usually top notch in her delivery. I also liked Captain Verlaine - the actress playing her seems to "get" how to do video games voice overs. She was very convincing in her performance (probably helped by excellent animation as well - which, regretfully, sometimes wasn't present for the other characters in the cutscenes).
On a technical level, the game is superb.
My ageing ATI Radeon HD5700 1GB graphics card  - once I updated the drivers - ran the whole game on ultra settings beautifully at 1900 x 1600 resolution. Considering the beautiful dynamic shadows, lighting and multiple particle effects, that's just astonishing. I was prepared to spend £150 on a new graphics card to play this game -  I didn't need to.
As I spent £30 on the game, I made a profit of £120! (haha - maybe not - but it feels great anyway)
I also got the game on first day of release - I experienced only one crash in 20 hours of play and no bugs or glitches (although they do exist from some of the footage I've seen). I think that's excellent going considering the buggy mess that most games these days are on day 1 of their release.
This is clearly a game that has had 4 years of time spent on it before being presented to the public.
FInally, the game sports a "survivor mode" - where you tool up and take on the alien in a timed challenge across a single level. Succeed, and your score and time will be posted for all to see on the internet on a leaderboard.
This is a nice addition - and there will be new "survivor" maps in at least 5 upcoming DLCs - including a "gauntlet mode" where you must complete 3 levels without dieing. Sounds fun to me!
FINAL VERDICT:
Alien: Isolation gives you a unique, challenging horror experience that you will never forget.
If you want to find a better game this year? Well I can't lie to you about your chances. But you have my sympathies.
Loses some steam at the end, but makes the Alien genuininely terrifying again.

Dark Souls 2 is interesting to say the least. This is a game I consider a masterpiece in the modern wave of clone games being released. The experience of playing Dark Souls and DS2 is completly unuiqe. Not many games send you into the world with the full expectation of you dying over and over again(As the opening NPCs remind you). Dark Souls does not just kill you because it can though. Dark Souls wants to teach you that blindly rushing into a fight swinging your massive sword blindly is not always the best option. If you want to succeed in the world of Dark Souls you have to be willing to think before you act. View your surroundings and learn what your enemies are weak to. Trying to run up to a boss and out damage them before they kill you like in some action games is simply just not an option here. You have to study the bosses and learn their patterns before you can truly begin to fight.
Dark Souls will make you question your self confidence. Even the best of gamers can come into this world and be taken down instantly simply because they would assume the tiny skeleton mob was not going to hit 75% of their maximum health. Two to three hits from most mobs in the game is enough to kill most players on their first or second playthrough. But... With each death comes knowledge. The heavy attack used to kill the small mob in one hit did not work on the katana wielding knight because he could draw his sword before the hit would connect. You return to were the katana wielding knight killed you with this new found knowledge and conquer him. You do not win in Dark Souls because the game throws hints at you every time you turn a corner. You win because you have improved and learned since the last encounter.
That brings me to the topic of immersion. Unlike in almost any other game out when you die in Dark Souls you actually DIE in the story. Most games load you to the checkpoint and storyline wise your character never died. In Dark Souls death is part of the story. Dying weakens your body and removes your humanity. You return to the bonfire as a hollow. You feel as if the world did not just stop and go back because you died(Although enemies do respawn upon death).
When it comes to playstyles this game has many options. From wielding a tiny dagger to dual wielding Ultra Greatswords(Yep. Bigger than big swords). Each moveset is unuiqe and some weapons in each catagory of weapon have unuiqe attacks. Spells, Hexes(Dark magic), Pyromancies and Miracles(Light magic) are available to those who would rather play from a distance. You are not limited to one or the other though. A player with the right stats could wield a massive hammer in one hand and a staff for spells in the other.
Now to compare Dark Souls 2 to its predecessor I can say there are some nice changes as well as frustrating ones. In the previous game you started the game with 5 Estus Flasks(The healing potion given upon resting). This game starts you with one. This forces the player to be MUCH more cautious in the early game while killing because it is very easy to die with only one healing item until you acquire more. Although in return now there are other healing items that can be used when found or bought from merchants.   Players can now teleport from bonfire to bonfire at the very beginning but can only level up at a woman found at the main town's bonfire. The combat in Dark Souls 2 feels more precise than it did in one. The heavier weapons feel like they swing at the speed they should. Instead of spawning an infinite number of times enemies are limitied to ten respawns now. This may sound limiting to the Dark Souls one player but with NG+(Discussed later) it is no problem.
Online interactions in Dark Souls 2 are fun and frustrating. A player can be randomly invaded by another player who is a red spirit at almost any given time. On the same note though there are ways for less confident players to ask for help from those willing to. The Sun covenant(Sunbros) and Blue Sentinels are dedicated to helping the weak. Golden and white spirits can be summoned to help clear areas of the game or at most boss fights. Some covenants only wish to protect their own land and will do anything in their power to do so. Killing anyone who might trespass. As to not spoil anything about the covenants further I will leave it at that.
Dark Souls 2 has AMAZING replay value. The player can go into NG+(New Game Plus) once beating the game allowing them play the game with increased difficulty and more enemies. The player keeps all gear and most of the items in their inventory. NG+ goes all the way up to NG+7 before stopping the increase in difficulty. That means the game can be played 8 times before fully defeating the hardest mode. Alongside this there is a new item called bonfire ascetic that allows a player to increase one specific areas difficulty to the next NG allowing them to fight the enemies again.
On an end note I can say that Dark Souls 2 is an amazing and challenging game that anyone seeking a fun and rewarding time should play. I have never felt more rewarded in a video game than during some of the boss fights and difficult areas in Dark Souls. I give it a rating of 9.8 out of 10. With only minor flaws in things such as game balancing and certain online features. All in all I HIGHLY recommend this game.

Get this game.
---------------
+Simple and appealing story.
+Character development, foreshadowing, consistency is all present.
+Atmospheric! If you have a soul, you'll easily find yourself shivering, gasping, exclaiming, maybe even crying in cutscenes. This game sets the mood and uses it at the right times.
+The graphics aren't that bad. Smaller window size means higher quality, if you can stand it. Boss graphics are wellmade, sprites are good, there are subtle changes that you may notice that can raise an eyebrow or send a shiver down your back.
+Simple to learn, simple to master controls. Only five ways to attack and one way to dodge. All you need to use are QWER, and your arrow keys.
+Action-based combat system, maybe even nostalgic for some of the older generations of gaming.
---------------
+About 3 ~ 5 hours of content.
+Homemade, not incredibly detailed or fancy, but an incredible amount of work, enthusiasm, and pride was put into it.
+Enjoyable. While not the best or most refined, it's definitely fun to play.
+If you're a completionist, each area contains a set of equipment to craft, a number of chests to find, four types of stat-increasing books (permanent!), and three generic quests. Not hard to do, but satisfying to complete. Check out RobDeLaMorte's guide if you want more information:
----------------
-Couple glitches, mainly pertaining to using skills in certain areas. Don't use Phantom Strike in areas where you walk into cutscenes, ETC.
-King Monsters are easily exploitable; Use skills, attack, wait for regen. It's basically a battle of stats and patience.
-Noticable grammar issues. But if you're normal, you can look past them.
TLDR: It's free. Download this game. Set aside about 3-5 hours of time. Play it. Enjoy it.
Props to the developer(s)! Support them, we may get a sequel..?!

This game truly captures the feeling of the first Alien movie. Intense, scary, and fun (once you get over your initial fear of being stalked by the xenomorph). This really is the Alien game fans of the series have been waiting for! Highly recommended and kudos to the developer for giving this Alien franchise fan reason to be scared of the xenomorph all over again!

So glad my memories of that turgid dysfunctional mess Colonial Marines have been overshadowed by Isolation. The tension, soundscape and environmental detail provided a truly foreboding atmosphere.
The story, it actually had a coherent story that fitted perfectly between Alien and Aliens unlike Colonial Marines attempt to bridge events between Aliens and Alien 3 which made the latter a head ♥♥♥♥ to complete for all the wrong reasons. I liked the characters of Cpl. Dwayne Hicks and Rebecca Jordan from Aliens but both he and Newt were far better portrayed in the comic series Outbreak. Than either Alien 3 where they were killed off as you know, a waste but I guess it worked for the movie or Colonial Marines ham fisted attempt to tell us how Hicks managed to still be alive through its DLC.
Back to Isolation, yes the story is a bit thin but it sets the scene by giving the character of Amanda Ripley a reason for being on Sevastopol. If you spend the time reading the log entries from the station inhabitants you'll work out why and most of the time how the station got to be in the state of disrepair it's in aswell as how the Xenomorph got there, you'll get the general idea from the missions and cutscenes but the logs help flesh everything out. Then, well then you skulk from place to place doing what needs to be done in order to escape from what is for all intents and purposes a beautifully detailed hell in space.
In my opinion everything's present to create an enjoyable story as you have the reason to be on Sevastopol, the reason why you want to get the hell out of there and the reasons why most things that aren't working need to be fixed. Okay, you're lead on a bit of a merry chase by some of the NPC's but you'll understand why for the most part. Their tangible desperation gleaned through you're own encounters with the Alien lets you see how they've developed a "by any means necessary" complex so to speak, even the guy that directed me to the medical supplies who I'm pretty sure was only doing it to get some morphine or other substance to self medicate with.
As for the fact that most of the other humans alive on Sevastopol are hostile towards the player character I can again understand why they've gone full blown "Lord of the Flies". They've splintered into groups due to being in an unfamiliar situation, sure they're in a familiar environment but the Alien has torn up the rule book over time and distrust is rife among the dwindling population. Societal bonds have been broken and authority means nothing when you may not see another day. It seems to be a human instinct that kicks in when those in charge can no longer provide the expected protection or quell sedition and fear makes decisions rather than thought. It's a human trait and more often than not it causes more problems in the long run, to paraphrase Robert Downey Jr from Tropic Thunder "Never go full Lord of the Flies".
The Synthetics looking suitably inhuman with their rubber faces are brutal when they get a hold of you and you feel somewhat limited when it comes to using a weapon against them, melee is not an option as they will beat and choke you to death without the aid of a rolled up magazine. They can be easily outmanoeuvred if you take it slow and pay attention to their movement patterns but if they see you, then you have the options of running and hiding if possible or pull out a gun or gadget to dispatch them with which causes noise and can ultimately lead to an ovipositor to the face or tail spiked through the spine and stomach.
When it comes to the Alien itself, the word intimidating comes to mind. This adversary makes you second guess every action you contemplate from "which direction to take when more than one is available" to "should I incapacitate this enemy" to "it's dark so I'll use my flashlight". It's an immensely terrifying hunter and will kill you as soon as it sees you. That's not all, it will investigate every door opening, klaxon sounding, machinery firing up, knocked over item and even the motion tracker noise if close enough aswell as any light source it notices. Not to mention it seems to play with you every so often by pretending to not notice you're there only to turn and kill you whilst sneaking out through a door or jumping into the vents and then appearing behind you.
Yes the game does have some issues with the odd bug or possible oversight but none are infuriating. There's "The Scary Door" from Futurama fame which fractures the immersion a bit, the lip syncing is not good and the Aliens tail looks a bit limp like it's dragging around a dead snake attached to its♥♥♥♥♥♥alot of the time. I haven't really noticed bugs or oversights very much at all, maybe "The Scary Door" was an homage.
This is as terrifying as the Alien has been since the original movie and the best game involving the Alien since Aliens versus Predator in 1999. Kudos to CA and SEGA.

Quick review of Alien Isolation.
Coming from a dedicated and avid Alien enthusiast take my word when I say this, this is a game you if:
*You enjoy sitting uneasily for several hours rarely being safe
*Appreciate a well rounded crafting system much similar to the one in Tomb Raider & The Last of Us
*Enjoyed the first Alien movie or the franchise in its' entirety
*Get a thrill of being completely defenseless against a overwhelming and deadly foe but overcoming it with strategical positioning & planning
*Love using fire, seriously. You feel like a caveman in this game.

This game is simply awesome. The art direction, especially, is right on, making the player really feel like they are on an actual station. I don't want to drone on, so I'll keep it quick:
<Good, Middle & Bad>
+The alien is unpredictable, can attack from anywhere, and it is terrifying. Unlike other aliens games, the xenomorph is tough, is a killer and is sneaky.
+The Motion tracker. It is very, very, very important, and it can give your position away if you're too close to an enemy.
+Again, art direction. Everything feels like they ripped it right out of the set of the original Alien movie.
+Atmosphere is perfect. Later in the game, when♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan, it's possible to defend yourself (albeit not constantly).
+Sound design is flawless.
+Think Outlast in space without roaming enemies. because.....
+....the enemies will hunt you down. Nowhere is safe. The alien can also sniff you out if you're hiding in the vents.
+/-Some people say the game takes too long. It took me 14 hours to beat the game on hard, but that's good! I hate it when I spend $40+ for a game that lasts less than 10.
+/-The story is, well, predictable. The notes found on the station, audio logs, etc really make the game better. Story is ehhh... but hey! It's still scary.
+/-The "Working Joes" are androids and are deadly, even to the enemy humans. However, by the end of the game, it's easy to kill them. Looking back, I should have used MORE ammo against them.
-Lip syncing is terrible. It's okay in some cutscenes, but everything else is BLAH!
-the crafting system is stupid. You only need to make four items to beat the game: Noisemaker (to lure enemies, including the alien, away), the flashbang (doesn't work on the alien or androids, but it'll blind humans), the medkit (you can guess why), and molotov (it can scare off the alien). Other than those three, everything else isn't worth it. The other items are pretty neat, but useless for any practical use.
-There's atmosphere building late in the game which can be easily cut out of the game. Mostly drawn out walking down certain hallways. It'd shave off 30minutes of gametime... Boring gametime.
All in all, Alien Isolation  is the best survival horror in awhile.

Dark Souls II is a worthy successor to the Souls series. If you loved either of the previous games, you will love this one as well. This comes to you from someone who has played each of these games to death, beaten them all numerous times with different character builds, has gotten all of the achievements in all three games, and even beat Dark Souls II without dying or resting at a bonfire.
For those unfamiliar with the Souls series, Dark Souls II is an action RPG with an emphasis on skill and fair difficulty. The game will kill you over and over again, expecting you to get better and grow as a player. It makes you own your mistakes, and makes you feel like you earned every victory, no matter how small. It's a game that requires you to spend time mastering it, but once you do, you'll feel very accomplished.
I should start by saying that this game runs beautifully on PC. Unlike Dark Souls, you have a lot of graphical options right in the game, so you don't need mods just to make it look okay. I experienced very few bugs and crashes in the game, and I didn't run into any noticeable framerate drops. This is running a mid-tier gaming PC that's now three years old. There have been a few complaints on the forums about the keyboard and mouse controls, mainly because the default keybindings are difficult to use, there's a small amount of delaying when doing a standard attack from the mouse, and the on-screen prompts always show Xbox 360 buttons, not keyboard buttons. The first two can be addressed by using Autohot Key and rearranging the keybindings to suit your preference, but the last one is something that you will have to put up with if you play with a keyboard and mouse. This game is designed for a controller, and plays wonderfully with one. There are many players who use a keyboard and mouse, and prefer it, but as far as I'm concerned, this game is meant to be played with a controller and anything else is going to be subpar.
Compared to the previous games, Dark Souls II keeps many of the core tenants that were successful, such as their unique multiplayer, covenants, and maximum health reduction upon death from Demon's Souls. There have been a few mechanical improvements and expansions of previous systems that really enhance the experience. The biggest new addition is the ability to dual-wield, including power stances that add new moves once you've surpassed the Strength and Dexterity requirements for the weapons. This adds a lot to the game, allowing for a player to sacrifice defense for higher damage output when the time is right. Besides that, there are some interesting new effects on items, like shields that can parry spells, items that can negate backstabbing, and armour that creates a poison aura around you. The upgrade system has also been revamped to make it easier to upgrade items and experiment with different upgrade paths without having to farm over and over again. There are lots of new options here, so you'll be spending a lot of time trying new things to really fine-tune your build.
Magic deserves its own section, since it's been greatly expanded. The dark sorceries that were added to Dark Souls in the Artorias of the Abyss DLC have now been spun off into their own school of magix, Hexes, which now brings us to a total of four: Pyromancies, Sorceries, Miracles, and Hexes. In addition to adding a new school of magic, each of these schools has many more spells than Dark Souls had, providing a great deal of depth for all characters, regardless of if you want to be a pure caster, dabble in magic, or just want to counter these spells when you get invaded by another player. Some of the new spells include Lingering Flame, a pyromancy that acts like a proximity mine; Profound Still, a hex that deprives your opponent of the ability to cast magic for a short period of time; Soul Greatsword, a sorcery that swings a massive magic sword directly in front of the caster in a wide arc; and Heavenly Thunder, a miracle that causes lightning bolts to strike around the caster for a short period of time. These are joined by most of the spells from Dark Souls, resulting in a massively expanded repertoire that keeps the magic system feeling very interesting, and keeps opponents guessing what you might pull out next. There's now a casting speed stat, providing players with explicit feedback as to what changes to their character and equipment will do. Lastly, the Attunement attribute has been made more interesting, since in addition to giving you more attunement slots for spells, it now provides you more casts per attuned spell, faster casting speed, and an increased ability to dodge attacks by rolling.
There has also been more care put into the New Game+ system, since From Software knows that most players use it. Each time you beat the game, you can move the game to another instance of New Game+, where the game resets but you keep your items and stats and everything gets harder. To make things more interesting, in Dark Souls II the first instance of New Game+ also adds new enemies and items to some of the areas, and even makes small changes to some of the boss fights besides just increasing health and damage numbers. It forces you to proceed a little slower and be prepared for the unexpected once again, something that's great about your first time through the game. They've also added Bonfire Ascetics, which allow you to move only specific areas to New Game+ and above, allowing for items and bosses to respawn. This is great for further customizing your character by allowing you to get some of the New Game+ items earlier, or to get multiple copies of a spell that's crafted from a boss soul.
With all of these positive notes on the game, I will make a concession about where the game falls a little short. While the lore, music, atmosphere, and level design in Dark Souls II are all fantastic, they do fall a little short when compared to Dark Souls. There aren't any boss fights that have the same build-up and lore backing as Great Wolf Sif in the original game, for example, and you won't find any music as memorable as the Four Kings' theme. The world is also much more sprawled and linear, resembling Demon's Souls much more than Dark Souls, which is a little unfortunate. As I said, it still has great music, lore, and atmosphere, but Dark Souls just did so well in that regard that it shadows its successor.
To bring all of this together again, Dark Souls II is a game that you'll find yourself heavily immersed in. It's difficult to put it down, despite it having a few flaws, because it's just so well put together and so rewarding. This has been my favourite game so far this year.
