Broforce is a wonderfully responsive and fast-paced homage to 80's action movies. It feels like it wwould be as much at home on XBL or an arcade as on Steam with its simple but incredibly fun gameplay. Almost the entire environment is destroyable, making explosives feel great, and often forcing the player to keep moving around the environment.
Every character is a protagonist from an action movie (but with their name including the word 'Bro' eg. Indiana BROnes, RamBRO, Time BRO), with one primary attack and one special which can be replenished, bith of which fit the character. Neo punches,  Blade cuts, McGuyver uses handmade explosives, etc. Along with that, characters can climb up any wall and have a melee attack. In order to unlock new 'Bros' you must break open cages and after a specified number of rescues (shown after each level) one more is available. However, each time one is opened you switch to any one of the 'Bros" already unlocked with an extra life as a pay-off of sorts.
Beyond that the gameplay is simple: kill your way to the end of the level, murder Satan, raise the American flag, and ride away on a helicopter, with occasional boss sequences to change the flow. Alone, it's hilarious, fun, and despite its complexity strangely compelling (those minion death screams are hilarious, and hearing them yell "Broforce!" never gets old), but with friends it's infinitely better. Things get chaotic, but it's always a blast.
As it is now, I'd give it an 8/10. I can hardly wait until it's finished.

FREEDOM!
Take control of your tiny pixelated action
BRO and LIBERATE the world from TERRORISM and maybe CORRUPT EVIL CORPORATE PEOPLE depending on who that red dude with the horns and the business suit is (could it be... SATAN?!). LIBERATE the forests. LIBERATE the jungles. LIBERATE the villages. LIBERATE the cities. LIBERATE the xenomorph hives.
Oh, you basically annihilated the level because your massively overpowered BRO GUNS blew up all the terrain? GREAT. You had to destroy the village in order to save it? AWESOME. Let EXPLOSIONS ring like FREEDOM all across the land.
Buy this game because it is fun on steroids and to strike a blow for LIBERTY and


. If you don't, you're clearly a Commie TERRORIST.
***
In all seriousness, it's a platforming shoot-em-up with destructable everything and chained explosions that can really scratch that arcade itch. It doesn't take itself seriously at all and with levels taking about five minutes if you happen to take your time and try to play smart (rather than just blowing everything up, which can be fun), there's no problem with it being arcade-hard at times since you never lose that much progress. The one absurdly tough boss they had--the infamous massive helicopter--they nerfed, which is kinda sad, because when you beat that thing you felt a real feeling of achievement. The pacing is actually pitch-perfect because while frenetic explosions-a-go-go happen
you can often times hang back and decide whether or not you really do want to rush in where angels fear to tread (of course you do).
This game's only gone from strength to strength in its development. It built some solid platforming fundamentals first--even the Brototype was absurdly fun--and has added new levels, tweaked graphics, actual recognition from the action hero community, different play modes, and a joyously over-the-top announcer type who can scream with you when you inevitably blow yourself up in some insane chain reaction. The developers are engaged with the community--often in ALL CAPS OF AWESOME--and the semi-regular themed level "competitions" are great.
All this being said, it is unapologetically an arcade game. There is no plot to speak of. The game is not intelligent or particularly witty, nor is it trying to be. You will fail, a lot, and then you will succeed gloriously. If that's not your cuppa, then wave off, though I'd recommend watching a friend play since it certainly is colorful and beautiful in its pixel-art way and can be a treat to watch.
In very rare circumstances so much can be going on that the game will actually slow down. This somehow fails to be a problem because then it just feels like slow-mo in an action film, so it can't even be called a bug (plus, you'll either survive and it'll speed up or you'll die and the level will reset, so it's hardly a big deal).

I was a huge fan of Dark Souls. I hadn't played Demon Souls and had no idea what I was getting into when I rented it from Redbox one night. To put it simply, I purchased it the very next day. Dark Souls II picks up right where the first left off with gameplay and builds on it. The already great controls have been tightened. The weapons and magic are more balanced. And there is a stronger feeling of progression in your character. The addition of fast travel, new caster options, and scalable difficulty make the game much more inviting than it's predecessors.
"Inviting" should not be confused with "easier." Dark Souls II is a very challenging game. The point of entry is slightly more forgiving, with a optional psuedo-tutorial section, and anyone familiar with the series should feel at home quickly. FromSoft caught a lot of flak over the idea that it would be possible to alter the difficulty of the game. Much to fan's relief, you are only able to increase the difficulty from the already unforgiving base level.
The sound design is shoddy at best. While I appreciate the minimalist approach to music and some of the voice acting is fantastic, everything else is a train wreck. It can be difficult to tell where sound is coming from, which is particularly frustrating when you are trying to locate an enemy. Further, the levels are mixed at seemingly random volumes. At one point a lightning effect is so loud I had to turn down my speakers to the point that I could hear almost nothing else when it was not striking.
The visuals are improved, particularly on the PC version of the game. As someone who played Dark Souls on the PS3, I was appalled by the port to PC. This game does not suffer from those issues. It looks the best on PC this time. That said, this game will not be pushing your high-end gaming PC to any limits, it looks like a very nice PS3 title at best, and sadly can sometimes look like a release title for the 360. It is not a deal-breaker by any means though, and does an adequate job delivering the gameplay.
The multi-player is still hit and miss. When it works it is fantastic, when it doesn't, it borders on unplayable. FromSoft is pushing the boundaries of single-player and multiplayer, so you can forgive some of the mis-steps with the mechanics. One of which that almost ruins the game for me is the Soul Memory feature. This was an attempt to cull the "twinked" character issues that plague the previous title. It does it's job within the context of a standard player (exploits around this are far too easy and not bannable at this point). The problems lie in how it effects the other parts of the game's multiplayer. It is a complex issue, and I won't go into details, but it's effect on end-game PvP can be frustrating.
Despite my complaints, Dark Souls II rises above due to it's balanced challenge and spot-on controls. The game is highly replayable, whether you are starting a new character or going through a virtually endless cycle of playthroughs (see Diablo). I hope and pray for DLC content and more patches focused on balancing PvP. If you are prepared to die, do yourself a favor and do it in Dark Souls II... over and over.

Hmm, what to make of Worms WMD. When a new Worms game is released I think "why should I buy it? I already have several Worms games". Well, a glowing review from Ben plus the fact it was pretty cheap on special caused me to give it a go. I really wasn't losing out that much buying it, really.
I enjoy it. I pretty much only play single player stuff (campaigns and matches against computer enemies) so my thoughts are obviously regarding that particular aspect of the game. The overall 'feel' of the game is great, the physics and control are spot on, unlike Reloaded, which just felt... off in some indescribable way. The fundamentals the game gets right, and that's a good start.
Having a new Worms game means a wnole new set of single player missions, which as I mentioned above, appeals to me. Giving secondary objectives gives some incentive to replay missions to try to chase full completion of missions, which is something that I'd like to do when I've gotten through them all. There are plenty to get through, so it will certainly keep me busy.
Having access to community maps is a great addition, I've downloaded a heap of maps to play random matches on, and I've enjoyed a lot of them, especially the ones that are recreations of Lemmings maps. They seem to bring out some fun games. For some reason user created speech banks aren't an option, which is very disappointing- it was one thing that was great about Armageddon. I loved my Zapp Brannigan speech bank!
I have at best mixed feelings about crafting. I get where they are coming from, but it injects luck as a factor too much into the game. I wish that the weapons that are available thorugh crafting were available in non-crafting game setups, but sadly that's not the case. It gives me something to do while the other teams are takig their turns (and I think the computer teams were programmed  to faff around on purpose to allow time for crafting) but overall I'm pretty meh about it.
I like the addition of vehicles, them plus the turrets you can use add some variety to the gameplay. Their propensity to explode after not a huge amount of damage is done to them is always a factor, just as planning how barrels and mines will behave needs to be planned for when making your move.
I can't speak for online play, as I haven't tried it.

A game that puts you in a nostalgia trip to the first Alien movie but with you as the main character.
The AI is buggy as far as I have experienced (NPCs walking through walls and instantly notice you from the other side of the area), but if you enjoy Amnesia and the classic Alien movies then this is a game for you.

Captures the first Alien movie quite well with stunning visuals, outstanding use of audio and AI, and (somewhat) unforgiving gameplay. Yes it's a "long" game and quite frankly this is a good thing, as you're given plenty of time to absorb the atmospherics and detail, all of which has a purpose. It feels like it could even give classic titles like System Shock a run for its money.
Personally, I feel it could have been better still by making the AI even harder and taking a little of the linearity out of level design. Just the same, I feel the game was toned down to make it actually beatable -- so an "impossible" or "directors cut" edition would be interesting to see.
Launch DLC not worth full price due to length of gameplay, but would definitely buy at a bargain as it captures the first Alien movie extremely well.

White Noise Online is essentially an iteration of Slender: The Eight Pages, the goal to walk around a scenario collecting tape recorders, the more tapes you collect the more the difficulty and music ramps up. The more you play the game, the more Investigators you unlock, each with their own pros and cons that are good for different situations. Since this game has since been long dead by the making of this review, don't expect to just happen upon a multiplayer game anytime soon, though the singleplayer is promising enough. The only cons I have against this game is that the shadows don't look right when you get up close to them, the scaling in some parts of the scenarios (which is more evident in the scenario Bunker 51) is way off, and that you just move so dang slow, though Investigators like Hannah and Alex can fix that.
Since the concept is very similar to Slender: The Eight Pages, I might as well compare the two. For atmosphere, I say Slender definitely succeeds, as the fact that three other people can be present can demean the atmosphere by a lot. In Slender, the difficulty escelates on its own if you take too long between pages, and while White Noise Online doesn't have this, it can still be very challenging on the Nightmare difficulty once you get far in-game. I'd still go with White Noise Online though, as there are multiple maps, more places where tapes can spawn, and the fact that you can play it with your friends!
So in short, White Noise Online is multiplayer Slender: The Eight Pages, but you should only buy it for the singleplayer.

An ultra-destructible 2D action game that takes heavy influence from Contra, (though without the difficulty), and lets you play as various action heroes. This game is basically the 80’s with more testosterone.
3 hours
8/10
2015-04-02 (Early Access)
Broforce is a game very much influenced by 80’s action movies. As a fan of this kind of movie (though I’ve not seen all the ones this game takes influence from), it’s a pretty fun thing to play.
The gameplay is pretty simple; it’s a 2D shooter that takes a lot of influence from Contra. That said, it’s also a lot easier of a game. You move left to right, shooting your enemies, and destroying the environment. In fact, that’s part of the fun. Everything goes boom, and you can destroy most of the environment. If one path through a level isn’t working out so hot for you, you can blow up some of the terrain and see if you can go around.
The character you play as dies in one hit, so you do need to show some caution while playing, but thankfully not too much, allowing you to still run into danger with a headstrong reckless abandon. You start each level with one life, but you can collect more in the level, you’ll receive one extra life every time you rescue a bro.
And that’s one of the things we need to focus on for this review. The bros. Each bro is based on various characters from different movies, tv shows, and even comics; and each one plays differently. Most of the bros are based on 80’s action movie heroes, but we’re also treated to characters from earlier and later time periods. The core mechanics for the bros give you a main attack, which you can use as much as you want, and a special attack, which you have only a limited number of (1-6, depending on the bro).
The levels have cages scattered throughout them, containing captured bros. Each time you rescue a bro the game will automatically switch your character to a random bro, and give you another life. You unlock new brows to play as by increasing the total number of bros you’re rescued. When you die in a level, you’ll re-spawn from the last checkpoint as another random bro.
All this talk of bros begs the question, who are the bros featured in this game? Well, I won’t list all of them since part of the fun is being surprised, but I will talk about a few of them. When you first start the game, you play as Rambro (yes, all the bros have “bro” in their name, usually as a pun on either their name, or their franchise’s name). This is of course a pretty solid choice to begin the game with. Both as he’s an iconic action hero, and in game he’s armed with a machine gun and grenades, making it easy to dive right into the action and get to shooting.
As for the other bros, I was quite happy to see that Bro Hard (John McClane) included, and they even left him barefoot, which is a pretty nice touch. I was also pretty happy (and surprised) to see Bro Dredd (Judge Dredd) included, who’s gun fires bullets that both have (limited) homing abilities, and bounce off walls, (another nice touch, managing to incorporate two of his bullet types from the comics, heat-seeking and ricochet). Another fun one I was happy to see (though much less surprised) was Robrocop. The Terminator also makes an appearance, with a powerful gatling gun, and he’s a lot of fun to play as. Some of the other bros (with their non-broified names) included are Snake Plissken (Escape From New York), Blade (Marvel Comics), Men In Black, Neo (The Matrix), Indiana Jones, and quite a few others.
So, let’s talk about some of the weapons the different bros have. Machine guns are par for the course, with quite a few bros packing rapid fire heat. Others have more unique firearms, with shotguns, homing shots, spread guns, and more populating the game’s arsenal. Others opt for more literal firearms, and by that I mean a flamethrower. While others take less modern weapons, such as swords, knives, and whips; still others go for the future route, with high tech lasers and futuristic guns. And some simply prefer to do their dirty work with just their fists. As for some of the special weapons available for use, the bros are equipped with things like grenades, cluster bombs, Molotov cocktails, more powerful gun attacks, the ability to call down an air strike, and even a giant exploding turkey. The weapon variety is a lot of fun, and along with the selection of bros, is one of the game’s greatest strengths. Though sadly, some of the bros are less effective than others. Sometimes the difference is small, and sometimes it’s quite large.
The game’s graphics are done in a simple pixel art style, in the vein of old school shooters, though it looks a bit more polished than those of yore. They’re pleasant to look at, and I don’t have any real complaints about them.
The story and the setting for the game are pretty simple, you’re sent into a war zone, and must fight for freedom. It feels a bit too “America, ♥♥♥♥ yeah” for me at times, but it’s easy to overlook once you start shooting and making things go boom again. The final levels in the game pit you against alien invaders from another world, clearly inspired by the Alien franchise. (And they are the best levels in the game).
The game also features support for multiplayer fun, and while I only took a brief excursion into this myself, it was pretty good fun.
I should also note that while you can play the game with a keyboard, this is one of those games that is far better when played with a controller. As such, I’d highly recommend using an X-Box 360 controller for Windows when playing Broforce.
Now, the game itself is very short. The campaign mode will only take about a mere 3 hours to play through, and while it’s a lot of fun, it does leave one wanting for more. Thankfully, the game is still early access, so we should get more levels in the future. Even if we don’t, the game is still a blast, and certainly worth playing, but at its current length it’s probably better to pick it up on sale, instead of paying the full $15 for it. That said, the new levels that were added just before I purchased the game (the Alien Infestation update) were thrilling, and while there weren’t too many of those included, they were easily some of the best in the game. If this is the kind of content that future updates will be, then I very eagerly look forward to more.
If you’re still not quite sure on if you should pick up Broforce or not, you could grab The Exependabros on Steam for free. It’s a game that features characters from The Expendables 3, but set in Broforce style levels. It’s not as good as the actual Broforce game, but it works pretty well as a demo if you need a little convincing before plunking down your cash for this one. (Or if you simply need more Broforce action after completing this game, go grab it for a quick hour long romp).
When all’s said and done, Broforce is a hell of a lot of fun, and being able to fight your way across levels as an assortment of different characters with different weapons is quite enjoyable. Give it a chance, start blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up with your favourite action heroes.

Dark Soul II takes everything that made Dark Souls such a awesome game and builds upon it. More weapons, more armors, more locations, and many more ways to die. Plus it actually runs on PC this time! No need for DSfix or any other mods just to play it. (Though I did encounter a slight mouse delay after rebinding my keys, so I had to download a hotkey scripting program to fix it but other then that it works beautifully). Oh yes and how could I not mention that the game runs on a server now. Thats right no more getting 30 failed summons in a row or waiting 30 minutes in game for you to register better with other players.
This is by far my favorite entery in the Souls series. Is it harder then Dark Souls? No. Is it easier? No. Is getting invaded as a hollow a hell of a lot better cause if you die you don't lose your humanity? Hell Yeah it is.
Course the number one thing to remember if your a new comer to Dark Souls is: This is a game about learning from your mistakes. Understanding the world, figuring out how to defeat bosses or large groups of enemies. It's all in the game, but it's up to you to figure it out. So don't expect any hand holding or arrows pointing you where to go next.
So here's a few things to remember.
1: Talk to everyone multiple times in a row. Alot of npc's give items or information as new area open.
2: Read item discriptions. Lots of items fill in the blanks to the story as well as build on the lore of the game.
3. Don't be afraid to try everything in mulitple ways. For instant, effigies can be both used as a item and burned at bonfires      for different effects.
4: Explore, Explore, Explore. Sometimes good things lay off the beaten path
5: Be prepare to be frustrated. There are moments when you will hate the living daylights out of Dark Souls, whether it's by a large group of enemies.... or a small group of enemies.... or one enemy.... I really hate those mages in the Shrine of Amana.
6: Play the game without any guides or wiki's. Having beaten DS1 with a guide and beating DS2 without one, I can clearly say you get a much better feeling of accomplishment without the use of a guide and the world feels so much more majestic when you don't know what area you'll be coming upon next.
7: PREPARE TO DIE

Dishonored 2 is a great continuation of Dishonored, and manages to keep the previous game's mechanics and even improve upon them.
Dishonored, if you don't know, is a game about a man who is blamed for the assassination on the old Empress, Lady Kaldwin. After recieving help to escape from the prison you're captured in, escaping lethally or non-lethally. You meet up with a loyalist group that wants to bring back the power to young Lady Emily.
Dishonored continues from the ending of Dishonored, although the actions that you had done in the original are not transferable to Dishonored 2. None the less, the game does a great job of keeping it neutal to the events of what happened in the last game, leaving the player of the original to believe whatever they want about the past. The game machanics are well done and are improved and make the game have more difficulty, which can be a good or bad thing if you're as *great* as I am at the game. The new progression tree for the powers add to replayability as you the player will have to make the choice of whether you want to get the Blink upgrade first or if you want to go straight into the Bend Time power, and with the new New Game+ update, replaying will allow you to have the powers you previously didn't and improve over and over as you replay the game.
In short, would I recommend this game? Yes... Yes I would.

Alright, so. Where to begin?
APB had been one of those games that I heard about, thought sounded amazing on paper, but then forgotten about because I had no money, meaning that upon initial release, I couldn't play it. I had already spent a good amount of money on my Steam library, so I assumed that it probably wouldn't be a good idea to invest in it, regardless, and I turned out to be right.
For all of the wrong reasons.
See, the original APB is no longer with us, instead leaving with us APB: Reloaded, a rebooted version of the game with fixes, a few additions, and a few new bugs as well, on top of being free-to-play. That being said, I could finally mess with the character creator, make my own decals, and do what I wanted as a criminal druglord.
Pfft, I ♥♥♥♥ing wish, dude. Turns out, there's a reason Realtime Worlds went out of business during the short lifespan of the original game, and the free-to-play service doesn't do it any favors. Instead of the matchmaking being a bit cheap, it's now absolutely broken. Instead of slogging through bare-bones missions that set you up against players of the same caliber, you're set up against the 50. cal's that all bought their♥♥♥♥♥♥through the ARMAS Marketplace, the premier one-stop shop for everything you'll need to reach gold-level instantly. The game engine runs at a solid 15 FPS throughout, unless it bluescreens your computer,
, and generally just isn't that good of a game to play.
Unless you got a crew, in which case, it's always fun to share the headaches.
Do I recommend it? Yeah, for one reason and one reason only. Developers of any and all multiplayer games, including past, present, and future, heed my words. Play this for two hours, if you can handle it. There is nothing else quite like it, and I mean that in the worst way possible. Learn from it. As for every gamer reading this, at least give it a shot. For what it's worth, I sort-of enjoyed it, but it's not something I go back to religiously. So, I know what you're thinking. Another early access survival game?? Don't we have enough of those already? Why should I buy this when I already have rust.
I was thinking the same thing when I first pondered about purchasing the game and boy, did I make the right choice on giving it a chance.
What makes this game better then rust, is that it makes most players ''think'' before they kill another player. Why is this?? Infamy. Infamy is no good and you really don't want it, especially if you have good gear. Infamy is a timed effect that is applied to you when you kill a player and lasts for 15 minutes. But it can stack if you kill more players during the duration of your infamy. basically, if you don't have infamy you will not drop any of your tools, weapons and clothes when you are killed. If you have infamy, you'l probably drop your prized goodies that you worked so hard for. So this in turn makes players more, interactive. Which is great! I've made quite a few friends so far and only ran into a few sour apples. So sure, some players will still KOS people and not give a ♥♥♥♥ about their infamy. But most will care and that is why I like this game.

Rome 2's battles are stunning. Great attention has been lavished on making troops more responsive. If a unit is under fire they'll lift up their shields, and the incoming projectiles will turn them into wooden porcupines. They'll erupt into rowdy celebration when they rout a unit, and you'll see the exhaustion of the fleeing enemies in their gait. A cinematic battle-cam puts you right into the melee, where you'll hear men yelling to each other and see differences in the way units fight. Praetorians use their huge shields to haul barbarians over and behind them to be stabbed by supporting ranks. Attack dogs, released from their handlers, tear into a fight with terrifying speed and drag down opponents with a flying bite to the arm. If you encounter an exotic unit you like, you might be able to recruit them as mercenaries for a high ongoing cost. Mercenaries are the only troops you can hire in enemy territory, but Romans can construct auxiliary barracks that will let you recruit other factions' units properly. This reflects how the Roman army historically used foreign troops and encouraging a sort of military tourism. I'm still on a quest to unite elephants and Celtic skirmishers in the same army.

Great Alien game, fantastic horror game and a decent stealth game. This is a game that doesn't use loud noises and suprises to startle you and mistakenly call it "horror". The horror comes from uncertainty and tension, therefore it's real horror, not just sudden surprises meant to pointlessly stimulate reflexes. This game gives you an terrifying adversary that stalks you constantly. It's always there, somewhere, and all you can do is to stay alert and try to avoid it.  There are very few scripted confrontations with it, almost all encounters are organic and unpredictable, so you always need to adapt to the situation and use the scarce resources at your disposal to survive.
As an Alien game you can't ask for more. The level of respect for the source material and attention to detail is insane and the art direction is absolutely perfect. It looks exactly like the future that was created in 1979. The sound design is similarly spot-on, with many familiar sounds taken from the movies. Even from a gameplay standpoint the sound works. The noises that the alien makes when moving around give the player extra feedback to help avoid the creature.
Stealth is simple but it works. It might be a bit difficult for players who are not fans of old-school stealth games to get a hang of it because of how realistically little feedback is given to the player, but after the game gives the player tools such as the motion tracker, it becomes easier. The game is basically one large level, and there is quite a bit of backtracking and non-linear exploration. Reminds you more than a little of games like System Shock 2. The pacing is also pretty good, alternating between moments of extreme tension and pauses of relaxation.
A small annoying feature is that many actions such as using terminals, flipping switches and pulling levers have a static animation sequence tied into them, where the player gets locked in place for such interactions. Also many of these actions have completely unnecessary button prompts that don't really make sense in the context of what those controls normally do. The game would have been much more immersive without things like that.
Also I can't really appreciate the publisher locking content behind a pre-order. Day zero DLC. Fortunately I was able to get the full game without having to pay ransom when making an educated purchase decisions after release. But still... it just shows how little confidence you have in your product when you feel the need to scam people into buying blind in order for them to get all the content that was separated from the full product before release. It's a shame considering how good the game actually is. This is the kind of thing that incentivizes piracy, and I'm sure it caused many people to download this game for free.
Regarding the PC port. There is really nothing to complain about. The game runs amazingly well considering how good the graphics are. You can set the desktop display friendly field of view of 90° though the setting in the options has some weird inverse numbers thing going on. Basically the smaller the number, the wider the FOV. If instead you're playing on a couch, farther away from a TV screen, you can set a more narrow FOV. Keyboard controls can be rebound, but there are no secondary keybindings. In the game there is also no mouse acceleration, in other words the game was actually made to support PC controls, and it's therefore justified to call it a PC port. Apparently someone thought it was actually not necessary to deliberately ruin the game's controls. There is however the matter of the annoying decision to not let players have separate keys for leaning to the sides or peeking over obstacles. You need to hold a button that makes your movement keys function as leaning keys, as if the PC keyboard is short on buttons. Some players might also want to toggle things like holding the motion tracker or aiming their weapon instead of having to hold the button.
P.S Graphics are great but graphics are also irrelevant in determining a videogame's quality. The only things that aren't all that great about the visual fidelity are human facial animations. So if you don't like good videogames and just want to see some fancy animations, I'd suggest you play Assassin's Creed instead.
Bottom line is... the line at the bottom. No arbitrary numerical score here. Numbers tell you nothing.

So, i was gonna make a review a few days ago, but then something magical happened: They put out word of a sequel! Finally, this game gets a well deserved successor, and i will be redoing this review and editing in what it fixed and which would be better to get. Anyway, onto the review:
[TL;DR play if you have friends or know a place to schedule a play session, but otherwise not worth it.]
This is your standard slender clone, as far as base gameplay, but with a few twists. One is that there are statues that distract and/or kill you, and two is that there's multiplayer. The multiplayer i'll get to in a bit, as it's big enough to warrant its own section of this review. You walk around picking up tapes with people and avoid the monster as best you can, which becomes increasingly difficult. You have various skills to help, such as being able to walk faster (a must considering how ♥♥♥♥ing slow you go) and a better flashlight, among other things. The game features a mechanic that allows you to come back as a ghost in multiplayer, which allows you to actually see the map. Fairly standard stuff.
What makes it interesting, however, is the multiplayer, which is the core concept of the game. Finding someone to play with is difficult if you dont have friends with this game, but if you do find someone it's pretty ♥♥♥♥in fun. If you have friends to play with, it's even better. Plenty of tension can be dissolved from the comedy that comes from camaraderie, which is its savior. If the comedy of playing with friends wasn't there, a lot of people wouldn't play this game often, or at all. It's pretty freaky to play by yourself, but honestly there's not a lot of substance. Unlocking all characters takes maybe ten hours at most with friends, and upwards of 14+ by yourself, a ♥♥♥♥ton of time considering the lack of substance. Lots of replayablility is included, but wanting to actually replay it is not.
Honestly, i give this game a 7/10. The gameplay is solid, it looks alright, and with friends you can have a heckin good time. The cons of the game, however, are too big to ensure any higher than a seven. Slow walking speed, plenty of bugs (though they did update a while back, perhaps fixes are in the works?), and a lack of interest are the main characteristics that make this game go down in rating. I have to reccomend it if you have some friends to play with, but honestly if you dont know anybody who plays this i'd not bother, especially with a new release right around the corner (the hype is real for wn2 oml)! if bugs get fixed and people start picking up on this game, there's a chance that it will break into 8+ category, but for now it's a solid 7.
(also if the devs see this, pleeeease add workshop content if it's at all possible in the new release, because ffs we all want it)

I bought this game solely for the cute graphics and overwhelmingly positive reviews. A casual, stress free game (until your slimes start to bounce around, escape and wreck havoc around your farm), Slime Rancher has incrediblely adorable characters and a fun exploration element to the game. However,  as with anything in early access, there are some cons to the game
- There is no mini map, or any map at all. As a fairly new player, having a map would be extremely helpful in exploring the different parts of the world. Perhaps the developers wanted exploration to be part of the game? If so, i would recommend a hidden map where parts will show up once you've discovered it. It might be a personal problem but my sense of direction isn't all that great...so wondering around while trying to remember certain landmarks was (and still is) fairly difficult for me
- Be aware of motion sickness, again, this might be a personal issue, but i find if i play the game for more than 45min without looking around, i'll start to feel nauseated. I believe this has to do with the fact that it's a first person vacuuming game that requires a lot of jerking around left, right, up, down. If you're used to this kind of POV, you should be fine. But as someone who mainly plays 2D, 3rd person games, this was a little unsettling for my stomache.

On the surface, the game is alot better than the original: Combat is faster paced, movement is more organic, complex mechanics are actually explained, and overly complex things like crafting and upgrades are streamlined for the better.
While the game trumps the first mechanically (Soul Memory and arguably bad PvP balancing aside), the game lacks one of the biggest and most gripping things the first one had, imagination. This game just isn's as gripping or compelling because of it, and while on the surface the game is "bigger and better", all the enemies are mostly humanoids with big weapons, and most of the bosses are relatively very small in scale compared to the original, hell, some of the early-mid game bosses are an absolute joke in terms of both design and difficulty. The game difficulty ramps up in the second half thankfully, but I could never shake the feeling that the team behind the story and world building phoned it in this time around.
That does not mean the game is bad, it still has some of the best combat mechanics out there, some of the areas are absolutely jaw dropping, the atmosphere is still gripping, story and lore are still shrouded in mystery, and are an absolute joy to learn about, and this game will still punish you for making dumb mistakes. Still a phenomenal game, better than most games out there, and the purchase is still highly recommended, but I can't help but shake the feeling of slight disappointment coming from the original (which is one of my favorite games ever). Still a fun time, and there are hundreds of hours of enjoyment to be had. Embrace the dark, buy this game, prepare to die

Rome 2's battles are stunning. Great attention has been lavished on making troops more responsive. If a unit is under fire they'll lift up their shields, and the incoming projectiles will turn them into wooden porcupines. They'll erupt into rowdy celebration when they rout a unit, and you'll see the exhaustion of the fleeing enemies in their gait. A cinematic battle-cam puts you right into the melee, where you'll hear men yelling to each other and see differences in the way units fight. Praetorians use their huge shields to haul barbarians over and behind them to be stabbed by supporting ranks. Attack dogs, released from their handlers, tear into a fight with terrifying speed and drag down opponents with a flying bite to the arm. If you encounter an exotic unit you like, you might be able to recruit them as mercenaries for a high ongoing cost. Mercenaries are the only troops you can hire in enemy territory, but Romans can construct auxiliary barracks that will let you recruit other factions' units properly. This reflects how the Roman army historically used foreign troops and encouraging a sort of military tourism. I'm still on a quest to unite elephants and Celtic skirmishers in the same army.

Upon launch this game was an unoptimized piece of trash which lacked any kind of entertainment value. The old tried and tested systems were thrown out of the window in favour of wishy washy casual rubbish that really has no place in the strategy games market.
Total War is supposed to be a deep historical strategy game that allows you to command armies as well as taking a Grand Strategy light approach to diplomacy, trade and city building. While recent total war games have been hit and miss, this is truly a smack in the face to the long-term fans of the series. The game has marginally improved with months of patching... I'll emphasize that key word for you - Marginally. It still runs terribly, mods make the game semi-enjoyable - but it lacks that 'just one more turn' allure that Shogun 2 had.
It feels clunky and many of it's mechanics (like family trees and the senate) remain a complete mystery; in fact one can safely assume that they are cosmetic attachments, designed to appease fans before release. This games development was clearly marred with marketing and really poor design choices. It feels like the dev team didn't care what they put out. They promised much and delivered little. It's sad really as from the screenshots flashing above as I type this you kind of wonder what could have been.
The future also looks grim as CA constantly churn out awful and overpriced DLC packs mostly focusing on 'story-driven' 'cinematic' campaigns. These add pitiful amounts of new units and some new factions that honestly feel like re-skins or are actually just unlocked factions already in the base game. Don't buy these, they encourage the disgusting practice of churning out DLC that adds nothing to the game. Instead, download the mods from the Steam workshop - as these are more likely to provide you with new factions with interesting units.

Rome II takes the success from Shogun II and murders it in its sleep. CA made plenty of money off of lovers of the Total War franchise by hyping the game up to be the best in the series, but unfortunately it couldn't be further from the truth. The launch was met with widespread complaints regarding stability and performance, and though much of this has been addressed, their efforts have only served to highlight the real problems: this is a dumbed-down version of a great franchise.
I expected it to move forward, especially in terms of political schemes and family structure, and I was terribly disappointed. I don't hate the game, but it's not as good as Shogun II, or even Napoleon/Empire.
If you're happy enough with the game as presented and find the aesthetics pleasing enough to keep you interested, fair enough. As for me... I've found infinitely more enjoyment out of playing Crusader Kings 2, because plotting the takeover of a nation is more fun to me than fighting 5 minute long battles with a barebones diplomacy system that feels like it's designed for 3-year olds.

Alien Isolation: Nominated for the “Even Better Than I Expected” Award 2017
I have just finished the game after about 21 hours and think Alien Isolation is excellent. Everything looks like it should (Based on the films) and while playing you get the same scare you do from the films. They have nice space views (when you find windows) and most things are clear enough to figure out without too much thought (I did on one occasion go the wrong way). The station is relatively open to explore at times and still has moments when you are trapped trying to make your way through an area (I think it is a nice mix of situations). I have can honestly say I have been satisfied with this game.
As for the things I would done differently if I were making this game I have made a small list as some people might find them 'good to know':
1) I would allow for the Alien to die with any weapon you have (after the correct shot (fire arms) or damage taken (blast or flame weapons)).
2) The Alien should not charge at you when fleeing from the flames of the flame thrower.
3) I found one large door/wall that I could not get right up against and I think that should be corrected as it did break the seamlessness of the experience (I was randomly exploring so I doubt it will be noticed by many people).
I also found a quirk were you can hide for a long as you want under desks from the Alien but the Robots will find you under these. I would not change this in game as I have stated above you can not damage the Alien at all so it's kind of a nice compromise with how the game works.
I also noticed that some people have said the game is 'too long' but I think that the length actually aids in the experience. Simply because it allows for you to adjust to the scenario of an Alien monster you have to evade while completing objectives and makes you more a part of the experience. This also allows for you to improve your responses to the Alien and make it more of skill based progression than a 'run-luck' event between save points (I did save at every opportunity having said that).
I also liked that the game gave you a sense of urgency without actually introduce timers (I did not test to find out if you can run out of time during certain events). I found the game in general did a really good job of allowing natural reactions actually progressing the plot and add to the experience of playing the game. I think this is my favourite Alien game to date.
Hope this is of use to people who are thinking about buying Alien: Isolation.

I've only ever seen the first Alien movie, and that was prior to playing this game. If you want to get the most out of Alien: Isolation, I definitely recommend watching Ridley Scott's 1979 movie 'Alien'.
This is important because Creative Assembley has probably created the most accurate, most visually stunning representation of Ridley Scott's Alien movie in videogame form since the movie itself came out.
Pros:
- The claustraphobic feeling from the original Alien film is captured perfectly in this game and is utilized to its fullest extent
- The xenomorph in its classic form, and most frightening. I have quite a few things to say about the Alien, but i'll keep it short--this is the most terrifying ♥♥♥♥ing thing i've encountered in a horror game to date. CA managed to pull off an amazing AI script for the Alien, making its decisions and movements randomized when on the move, or pin-point accurate in its encounters with you; thus, creating a believably living Alien haunting you throughout the halls of the Sevastapol.
- As I've said, the graphics and attention to detail are superb.
- The game is tense as ♥♥♥♥, but it's more of a stealth suspense game than horror, though the Alien is horrifying nonetheless.
-Not a constant Alien grindfest. You will encounter other enemies throughout the game, which will almost seem strangely refreshing seeing as encounters with the Alien can become very tedious and suspenseful.
Cons:
-Voice acting sounds a bit strange/unnatural in some situations
-Lipsync animations for the voice acting are actually god awful. Sometimes an NPC will be talking and their lips will be mouthing the Bohemian Rhapsody when really they're telling you to go find medical supplies.
- Alien can become somewhat tedious later on in the game.
Overall this is one of the best horror/thriller games I've had the pleasure of playing in a long, long time.  9/10  buy it now

I bought this game solely for the cute graphics and overwhelmingly positive reviews. A casual, stress free game (until your slimes start to bounce around, escape and wreck havoc around your farm), Slime Rancher has incrediblely adorable characters and a fun exploration element to the game. However,  as with anything in early access, there are some cons to the game
- There is no mini map, or any map at all. As a fairly new player, having a map would be extremely helpful in exploring the different parts of the world. Perhaps the developers wanted exploration to be part of the game? If so, i would recommend a hidden map where parts will show up once you've discovered it. It might be a personal problem but my sense of direction isn't all that great...so wondering around while trying to remember certain landmarks was (and still is) fairly difficult for me
- Be aware of motion sickness, again, this might be a personal issue, but i find if i play the game for more than 45min without looking around, i'll start to feel nauseated. I believe this has to do with the fact that it's a first person vacuuming game that requires a lot of jerking around left, right, up, down. If you're used to this kind of POV, you should be fine. But as someone who mainly plays 2D, 3rd person games, this was a little unsettling for my stomache.

This review comes from roughly around 70+ hours of both Demon's Souls and Dark Souls. Needless to say, I am a fan of the franchise.
Dark Souls 2 is by no means "a bad game" on its own. It's also not a good starting point nor does it fully get the player to grasp what the franchise began as. I believe Dark Souls 2 sits in a really awkward "grey area" where, contrary to both previous games, I was never blown away by anything. I didn't end up having a favorite boss I'd start a new game for.
This list will have more cons than pros, sadly. I believe that criticism is more important than back patting.
Pros:
- More stats, making builds slightly less cookie cutter when aiming for a specific goal.
- More freedom for weapons as far as having the choice of multiple weapons for general builds.
- Redesign of "infusions" (elemental damage added to weapons). Weapon upgrade levels and imbuements aren't tied anymore and imbuements (elemental damage) scale off of certain stats. So if one chooses to re-spec from a Faith build to a STR build, one can very much switch their weapon from a +10 Lightning Mace to a +10 Normal Mace by simply visiting a Blacksmith.
- Better spells design. The addition of weapons able to cast spells as well as multiple schools of magic being affected by stats makes casters very versatile and overall more fun to build.
- NG+ specific stuff.
Cons:
- Bosses. They are honestly boring. If they aren't ridiculously cheap with extremely wide, strong and fast attacks, they have a boring 1-shot mechanic or spawn adds. The only real "challenging" bosses of the game are the ones that completely overwhelm you. Gone are the days of recovering from a mistake, entering beast mode and finishing off a boss. You either zerg the ♥♥♥♥♥ or circle strafe em to death. I won't spoil it in the review, but let's just say one of the fights that should have been the most climactic fight of the game, turned out to be the ♥♥♥♥♥iest boss in Souls history.
- The combination of the Small white soapstone + the over abundance of bonfires. On paper, the max HP reduction + the usual death penalties + the fact that the item used to revive is limited made death sound like such a bad thing! Sadly though, they chose to implement the small white soapstone which is exactly like the normal one, except you don't have to kill an area boss, or sometimes even not have to kill anything at all! The way it works is that you join someone's game, and when the game thinks you've helped enough, you win (and revive). Thing is, sometimes you only have to kill 2 enemies to "win", making revival extremely trivial and invalidating all the death penalties which, in turn, encourages suicide runs. Especially since there's a bonfire every 20 feet.
- General enemy attack patterns. For many enemies in the game, including some very boring bosses (Dragonrider(s)), the last hit of their main combo will always SNAP-ONTO the user. If you require visual aids: Remember Havel in Dark Souls 1 and how, if you were behind him at the start of his swing, he would cheatingly turn around and land the hit where you were? Most enemies do this now.
- The ADD nature of the world design. The devs simply don't want you to enjoy places. If you're used to the franchise and can progress fairly quickly, you will go through zones like butter and almost forget you've been there the next time you play. Honestly, most zones are either disappointing, short, or just not memorable at all. The best looking, most epic zones in the game are also the least exploited, shortest and disappointing ones.
- PVP Zones. Now, don't get me wrong! I love PVP and Basin in Dark Souls 1 was awesome. The problem with Dark Souls 2's PVP zones is that they're just filler zones that last no more than a few minutes and you are done with them. They are short. They were clearly the designer's afterthought given that they aren't visually stunning, nor do they offer anything exciting in particular. See them as PVP arenas a lot more than an actual "place in the world".
- Weapon balance and the power that is Strike-type. So many enemies and some bosses are extremely weak to Strike. Yet there are barely any worthy DEX strike weapons. For anything other than DEX builds: There is "A Mace". Even a caster could carry around a Mace for spell use saving and still kick major♥♥♥♥♥
Conclusion:
The designer for the character customization changes is brilliant. I honestly think it's more fun to mess around with builds in Dark Souls 2 than both predecessors. Customization is the clear "Pro" of this game. It is, however, just a "video game feature". Most of the cons are about the actual game itself. The bosses, the world, systems and designs feel sub-par. I really want to make more characters and mess around with builds, but at the same time I don't feel like going through a boring world full of either unchallenging or cheap enemies.
If you're a fan, get it. You just have to. If you're not: PLAY THE OTHER ONES BEFORE! Don't spoil the Souls franchise with this one. Demon's Souls had the challenge and level design. Dark Souls 1 was the "jack of all trades" with all aspects of the game being enjoyable. Dark Souls 2 just has too much "sub-par" overshadowing the "good" to be considered a full on "step up".

FREEDOM!
Take control of your tiny pixelated action
BRO and LIBERATE the world from TERRORISM and maybe CORRUPT EVIL CORPORATE PEOPLE depending on who that red dude with the horns and the business suit is (could it be... SATAN?!). LIBERATE the forests. LIBERATE the jungles. LIBERATE the villages. LIBERATE the cities. LIBERATE the xenomorph hives.
Oh, you basically annihilated the level because your massively overpowered BRO GUNS blew up all the terrain? GREAT. You had to destroy the village in order to save it? AWESOME. Let EXPLOSIONS ring like FREEDOM all across the land.
Buy this game because it is fun on steroids and to strike a blow for LIBERTY and


. If you don't, you're clearly a Commie TERRORIST.
***
In all seriousness, it's a platforming shoot-em-up with destructable everything and chained explosions that can really scratch that arcade itch. It doesn't take itself seriously at all and with levels taking about five minutes if you happen to take your time and try to play smart (rather than just blowing everything up, which can be fun), there's no problem with it being arcade-hard at times since you never lose that much progress. The one absurdly tough boss they had--the infamous massive helicopter--they nerfed, which is kinda sad, because when you beat that thing you felt a real feeling of achievement. The pacing is actually pitch-perfect because while frenetic explosions-a-go-go happen
you can often times hang back and decide whether or not you really do want to rush in where angels fear to tread (of course you do).
This game's only gone from strength to strength in its development. It built some solid platforming fundamentals first--even the Brototype was absurdly fun--and has added new levels, tweaked graphics, actual recognition from the action hero community, different play modes, and a joyously over-the-top announcer type who can scream with you when you inevitably blow yourself up in some insane chain reaction. The developers are engaged with the community--often in ALL CAPS OF AWESOME--and the semi-regular themed level "competitions" are great.
All this being said, it is unapologetically an arcade game. There is no plot to speak of. The game is not intelligent or particularly witty, nor is it trying to be. You will fail, a lot, and then you will succeed gloriously. If that's not your cuppa, then wave off, though I'd recommend watching a friend play since it certainly is colorful and beautiful in its pixel-art way and can be a treat to watch.
In very rare circumstances so much can be going on that the game will actually slow down. This somehow fails to be a problem because then it just feels like slow-mo in an action film, so it can't even be called a bug (plus, you'll either survive and it'll speed up or you'll die and the level will reset, so it's hardly a big deal).

A simply fantastic game! I had never played the original Half-Life myself but this fan project did a wonderful job of getting me into the franchise. I ended up purchasing Half-Life 2 and its episodes after I finished Black Mesa. The voice acting is well done and it's remarkable how much this project's voice actors sound like the original. It's definitely one of the hardest games I've ever played if not THE hardest. I found that Half-Life 2's hard mode feels more like this game's easy mode. Gameplay progressively gets harder the farther you play through with health, battery, and ammunition becoming harder and harder to find. The graphics are amazing as well, however, I can't say I'm the best at telling how good a game's graphics are. The game in my opinion has better graphics then Half-Life 2 but of course it doesnt compare with the 4k games coming out nowadays. I haven't noticed all too many glitches in the game through my normal playthrough but, as with any game, there were some. I only experienced two glitches that I can remember. The first, a scientist's tie spazzing out and streching outside walls and the map. The other would be blood splatters that don't properly mesh with wall colors unless your flashlight is on, sometimes creating a weird pink color on white walls. These bugs however only happened once or twice and it wasn't really a bother. Theres also the fact that the Xen chapters haven't been released yet but, I'd rather have a game that's good and well developed then one thats rushed and underdeveloped. At the end of the day I'd say if you want to play Half-Life for the first time, this is the way to go! This remarkable little fan project is one of my favorite additions to my Steam library and I'd recommend it for those seeking challenge.

You take on the role of Gordon Freeman, the thinking mans Rambo, who is working for the titular R&D company funded by the government. This knight in shining HEV suit will have to travel to the farthest reaches of space/time to defeat the otherworldly enemy, and perhaps enjoy a cold beer owed to him when it's all said and done.

Rome II takes the success from Shogun II and murders it in its sleep. CA made plenty of money off of lovers of the Total War franchise by hyping the game up to be the best in the series, but unfortunately it couldn't be further from the truth. The launch was met with widespread complaints regarding stability and performance, and though much of this has been addressed, their efforts have only served to highlight the real problems: this is a dumbed-down version of a great franchise.
I expected it to move forward, especially in terms of political schemes and family structure, and I was terribly disappointed. I don't hate the game, but it's not as good as Shogun II, or even Napoleon/Empire.
If you're happy enough with the game as presented and find the aesthetics pleasing enough to keep you interested, fair enough. As for me... I've found infinitely more enjoyment out of playing Crusader Kings 2, because plotting the takeover of a nation is more fun to me than fighting 5 minute long battles with a barebones diplomacy system that feels like it's designed for 3-year olds.

Let me start off by saying that yes, I do recommend this game to
. Are you a person who enjoys destruction? Do you also enjoy finding more creative ways to destroy things than just by shooting them? Does the idea of wingsuiting around, hijacking vehicles, and claiming enemy bases sound fun? If yes, then this game is definitely for you, but it is not without its flaws.
The biggest flaw of JC3 is the lack of variation. If you can't find a way to spice up the manner in which you make things go boom, you
get bored. Aside from that, there's:
-Performance issues (even on certain high-end PCs)
-Poor vehicle control (the motorcycles especially suck a lot of♥♥♥♥♥
-Lack of interesting landmarks
-Annoying challenges (excluding the Wingsuit ones and some of the races, which can occasionally be fun)
-What even is story
However, if you can stomach all of those things, I believe you will find a game that is well worth your money with the amount of content that it brings (despite feeling "samey" at times) and the sheer level of joy it can lead to. Maybe wait for it to go on sale before getting it, but if you liked JC2 you'll like JC3.

Alien Isolation: Nominated for the “Even Better Than I Expected” Award 2017
I have just finished the game after about 21 hours and think Alien Isolation is excellent. Everything looks like it should (Based on the films) and while playing you get the same scare you do from the films. They have nice space views (when you find windows) and most things are clear enough to figure out without too much thought (I did on one occasion go the wrong way). The station is relatively open to explore at times and still has moments when you are trapped trying to make your way through an area (I think it is a nice mix of situations). I have can honestly say I have been satisfied with this game.
As for the things I would done differently if I were making this game I have made a small list as some people might find them 'good to know':
1) I would allow for the Alien to die with any weapon you have (after the correct shot (fire arms) or damage taken (blast or flame weapons)).
2) The Alien should not charge at you when fleeing from the flames of the flame thrower.
3) I found one large door/wall that I could not get right up against and I think that should be corrected as it did break the seamlessness of the experience (I was randomly exploring so I doubt it will be noticed by many people).
I also found a quirk were you can hide for a long as you want under desks from the Alien but the Robots will find you under these. I would not change this in game as I have stated above you can not damage the Alien at all so it's kind of a nice compromise with how the game works.
I also noticed that some people have said the game is 'too long' but I think that the length actually aids in the experience. Simply because it allows for you to adjust to the scenario of an Alien monster you have to evade while completing objectives and makes you more a part of the experience. This also allows for you to improve your responses to the Alien and make it more of skill based progression than a 'run-luck' event between save points (I did save at every opportunity having said that).
I also liked that the game gave you a sense of urgency without actually introduce timers (I did not test to find out if you can run out of time during certain events). I found the game in general did a really good job of allowing natural reactions actually progressing the plot and add to the experience of playing the game. I think this is my favourite Alien game to date.
Hope this is of use to people who are thinking about buying Alien: Isolation.

This game attempts to insert a number of features from the elder scrolls into an MMO and fails to do so.
But I'll break as much as possible down in edible chunks of opinion.
Elder scrolls copy paste features: --
Pickpocketing and stealing feel clunky, is repetative and I don't really see why anyone would bother with this.
Crafting: --
The crafting system is nothing special compared to other MMO's. The different 'styles' in which to craft armor will make sure to fill up your inventory 60/60 slots so you are constantly deleting things you don't want or force you to make trips to the bank every 5 minutes.
Skilltree: --
Skilltrees are a mess, mashing up guild skills, personal skills both combat and crafting, weapon skills to pick from.
It's like taking weapon based system from GW2, throw in half a Final Fantasy's crafting tree and finishing up with more classical personal combat skills.
Combat: --
Combat really is a drag here. I'd rather handle the combat on an excel sheet.
There's no real action-reaction, it's static and frustrating, no fun at all, especially for healers where at best you can figure out a optimal healing cycle and at worst you mash buttons like it's 1995 and you're playing streetfighter against your little brother. I started avoiding combat as much as possible from level 10+ due to the annnoying combat so I'm not that sure if there's more variety later.
PVP: ??
Did not even try to PvP because that can only be worse if PvE is already static and frustrating.
Social: -
Social: Guilds and other social options are lackluster. Go play with friends on Playstation 4 if you want this game that bad, because not much is done to promote social interaction and party building on PC.
Storyline and questing: +/-
If you're interested in elder scrolls lore background you can probably enjoy this, but to me it was pretty tame. Sidequests are just the regular grind, the game takes your hand and guides you from area to area. *supressed yawn*
PS. the voice acting is bad too.
World: --
Similar area's over and over, the buildings area even copy-pasted, boring mobs.
That's about all I can come up with.

I've only ever seen the first Alien movie, and that was prior to playing this game. If you want to get the most out of Alien: Isolation, I definitely recommend watching Ridley Scott's 1979 movie 'Alien'.
This is important because Creative Assembley has probably created the most accurate, most visually stunning representation of Ridley Scott's Alien movie in videogame form since the movie itself came out.
Pros:
- The claustraphobic feeling from the original Alien film is captured perfectly in this game and is utilized to its fullest extent
- The xenomorph in its classic form, and most frightening. I have quite a few things to say about the Alien, but i'll keep it short--this is the most terrifying ♥♥♥♥ing thing i've encountered in a horror game to date. CA managed to pull off an amazing AI script for the Alien, making its decisions and movements randomized when on the move, or pin-point accurate in its encounters with you; thus, creating a believably living Alien haunting you throughout the halls of the Sevastapol.
- As I've said, the graphics and attention to detail are superb.
- The game is tense as ♥♥♥♥, but it's more of a stealth suspense game than horror, though the Alien is horrifying nonetheless.
-Not a constant Alien grindfest. You will encounter other enemies throughout the game, which will almost seem strangely refreshing seeing as encounters with the Alien can become very tedious and suspenseful.
Cons:
-Voice acting sounds a bit strange/unnatural in some situations
-Lipsync animations for the voice acting are actually god awful. Sometimes an NPC will be talking and their lips will be mouthing the Bohemian Rhapsody when really they're telling you to go find medical supplies.
- Alien can become somewhat tedious later on in the game.
Overall this is one of the best horror/thriller games I've had the pleasure of playing in a long, long time.  9/10  buy it now

I love this game more than any other team-based zombie apocalypse survival game I own through Steam. Its very gritty and unforgiving towards blunders made by new players, and yet still has time to put relaxation times in its unbeleivably long levels. The game is built for multiplayer, so playing solo can be alot harder than with others.
A few issues:
1. Running zombies are overpowered as all hell. I put 5 55.6 carbine rounds in a normal runner's head and it still slapped the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me. I'll blame that on RNG. Plus their damage rolls are pretty ♥♥♥♥ing high.
2. Zombies do a buttload of damage, regardless of difficulty, although on easy you get the respawn function.
3. Melee combat can be very buggy. Zombies are supposed to stumble when hit with a "power attack" or when beat upside the head. RNG turns it into a 40% chance that it will do so, and if it doesn't, there's a good chance all or most of your health and ammo can be kissed goodbye.
4. The range on the zombies' slaps can be downright ridiculous and enraging. I really don't think a child-turned-flesh eater can stretch its arms over a meter and a half to punch a full grown man half to death.
Other than these issues (which can make me not want to play this anymore, but I keep coming back for the awesome gameplay and music), the game itself is amazing. I love playing while getting lost in the music and atmosphere of the game. I reccomend this for any Left 4 Dead fans or zombie fans in general.

I could write an essay on why this game is great, but I will keep it simple.
For those of you who have played previous Souls games, you know what to expect.
For those of you who have not, Dark Souls II is a great starting point as the story and lore of each game are independent of the others. Dark Souls II is also more beginner friendly than the other games. So, everyone should at least give it a try. Trust me, you will not be disappointed.

Dark Souls II is a game many are crazed about. You have probably heard that the game is hard, which is undoubtly true. There are lots of twists in the environment that makes progression quite a challenge. What you will find is patience and thorough thinking as keys to success.
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys RPG's or who played Dark Souls I. Your game characters are completely customizable to your build making the possibilities endless. While some builds are more suited for certain enviornments, you will find the game mostly balanced.
New players will find the game confusing as the story line is not as clear as many other games try to present it. There are few cut scenes and dialogue is minimal. My suggestion is to immerse yourself in the Dark Souls community to read up on lore and theories of the story.

Dark Souls 2 is a Dark Fantasy RPG, that focuses on its intense yet slow combat system. The game is known for its challenging difficulty, and is surely not as forgiving as you are might accustomed from other games.
While the second part of the Dark Souls Series is certainly one of the best games this year, and I would recommend everyone to play it, I am quite disappointed in Dark Souls 2, since it does feel like the developers did two steps back for every step forward.
You can expect to die a lot, and live a ton of moments of frustration when playing Dark Souls 2. The basic idea of the game is for you to memorize patterns, and try a certain strategy to defeat even some simple monsters. If you die, you probably have learned a little bit more, and will react properly next time. Just like in the first part, you probably will have as much problems when it comes to progressing through the world, as you will have with defeating tough enemies or bosses. Never give up hope, theres always a safe and sometimes even easy way to make your way through Drangleic, the world of Dark Souls 2.
On your journey, you will acquire different kind of weapons, armor, sorceries, hexes, miracles and pyromancies. You are free to spend your stat-points and build a character the way you like it. While you should focus on a certain build, master your weapon and spend your stats accordingly, flexibility in your weaponry and means of combat can always be good.
Despite that, the game still can't compare to the first of the  series, when it comes to detail. The plot and characters aren't as interesting, the level design is really bad sometimes, bosses are repetitive (a lot of big human-like creatures with a huge weapon and nearly the same animations) and "artificial difficult", (just adding a few small extra monsters, instead of making the boss actually interesting and challenging himself) hitboxes are really broken and the music seems very weak. In a way the developers just tried to make the game as difficult, and sometimes frustrating as possible, and didn't mind that the actual game isn't as interesting as its predecessor and doesn't have as many memorable moments either.

For a free game, this was quite the nice experience.
The game itself is rather simple.
You touch enemies to  hit them and as you progress you learn 4 skills. You can also craft some weapons and armors, though the crafting itself is just as simple as the fighting, with a sword recipe and 3 armor recipes for each level, and 3 upgrades for each piece that always require the same, simple steps.
Now, simplicity isn't a negative here. It works to the game benefit, as the short story the game is trying to tell and the characters it tries to enstablish take on a more prominent role. This simplicity in the gameplay keeps the game fairly enjoyable without distracting us from Senia's struggle on her search for her sister but it also keeps it somewhat challenging with boss fights, where you can decide the difficulty.
Doing boss fights on hard can be quite the challenge: I had a very difficult time with the last boss true form because I chose hard, but winning that fight made me really excited.
The game suffers from a shaky translation here and there (some weird word choice, some not elegant phrasing), but it still manages to deliver its message, it still manages to convey the feelings these characters portray, so in the end the shaky translation didn't really negatively affect me. I still wish it had a better translation, because this short, free game feels like a nice, little jewel that could be even better with just that little more polish.
Graphically, it follows the same principle as its gameplay. It's simple yet effective. If the translation is a bit shaky in the delivery, the character portraits do a perfect job conveying the feelings they're expressing, while the sprites show some nice little touches (like Senia's changes after using a certain skill).
Another thing that really help in conveying the feeling and struggles of the characters in the story is the music, which I have to commend. It's good, really good. It always feels on point and well executed.
As I said at the start, this was a very nice experience. More so because I wasn't expecting a game as charming as this, a game that would grab me so much.
Because of this and because of its free nature, if I had to give this a vote, it would be a pretty high one.
Even if this game has a little lack in polish and it's very simple, it made everything up with the way it touched my heart.
My rating for this game would be: Excellent
My vote for this game would be: 9/10

Community can be pretty toxic, but the game itself is great.
I imagine, like other games, there are many butthurt adolescents (and surprisingly adults get in on that immature action as well). It's very likely to encounter many an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but that's just what happens when asinine people hide behind their anonymity.
So, overall, people can be massive jerks, but the game design is better and more innovative than other MOBAs. I've played DOTA and League of Legends before, and I can say I definitely prefer Smite. As in all games, matchmaking can be pretty terrible, so I hope Hi-Rez can develop a solution in the near future. Perhaps a system calculating how each player performs in matches along with factoring in the level would be nice, but most likely rather complicated.
Smite is not just a League of Legends clone. Granted, the whole premise is similar because of the genre being what it is. If you don't like MOBAs, I don't know why you would really want to play Smite, but it's a good one to test out if you're unsure. Those who are more familiar with MMORPGs may appreciate the similar third person perspective and game design choices. I'd say it's very aesthetically appealing as well with pretty textures and all that.  Hi-Rez develops new content fairly quickly and they do a pretty good job with community interaction.
And now a "little" deity rant:
People complain about character designs all of the time, but most of the time the gods are fairly accurate to their actual lore. Many feminists complain about the over-sexualization of the goddesses, which I can see from the standard hourglass bodies featured on most of the godesses (but, I mean, look at the perfectly sculpted muscle on the gods too - when they're not supposed to be chubby), but in the clothing, the majority of the time it is mostly accurate with a hint of sexy. They try too hard to find the "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t sexism." People especially like to complain about Nu Wa -- who was normally depicted practically naked and Aphrodite -- who was depicted actually naked. We're lucky some of the Greek gods are clothed at all, really. Let's not forget the whole Kali fiasco. She had a more accurate character design before, but people complained, so she got a new, less accurate design.
Honestly, as a female myself, I don't see a problem with sexy characters in a video game.
On the subject of sexism, I recently read a post that talked about the number of evil/good/neutral gods by gender and complained that the female gods are mostly good whereas the males are balanced. It was defined as "benevolent sexism." This is frustrating because people acted like Hi-Rez was at fault for the actual lore. Maybe it could be argued that they are only picking good/neutral gods for females, but really, it's ridiculous to be upset by that. It's highly unlikely they are calculating the amount of evilness in the goddesses.
However... I do see fault in the faces of the gods. A large amount of the non-beast/animal gods are completely and utterly whitewashed when they shouldn't be. Typically, gods resemble those who believe in them in their depictions, so we really shouldn't have all white gods. Even the Chinese gods don't look remotely Asian. They don't necessarily have to have the stereotypical "Eastern features" and all that, but they're very obviously white and it's an obvious choice when everyone else in the game has the same features. (Sometimes the deities do appear to be more like their race in their character illustrations). I don't think Hi-Rez is necessarily racist or anything, like so many people insinuate, but their decisions may be due to the desire to not appear racist or the general beauty standard as it is.
And side note -- it's sort of weird that Hi-Rez is willing to use Hindu gods, but not other (currently) popular religions.
tl;dr rant -- Hi-Rez tries so hard to be somewhat accurate in their god design, but the people are never satisfied. There are only some complaints I can see being justified: whitewashing, minor over-sexualization, and some cultural appropriation.
