Possibly a review of Worms as a franchise rather than just WMD specifically.
I've enjoyed Worms for a long time, not just for the MP, but mostly the Single Player. Worms is a strategy game that's both simple, and also has absolutely no RPG elements. There's no grinding a unit or worry about how terrible that level up was for Lyn or farming for equipment and hoarding for later missions. Every mission in Worms, is a carefully crafted area to give you a fair but hard trouble (At least, later in the game. They start off jokingly easy of course). The later missions will outnumber you 4 to 12 worms with twice the health, and it's you'll feel great when you outsmart their dumb-but-superaccurate AI.
Worms MP is probably the most popular though, and many people play it as a joke for stupid fun. It's the type of game where when you make a mistake, it's pretty funny how it stacks up. It also has goofy weapons such as a super sheep and even a Grandma. Despite the stupid fun, I equate this game to Smash Bros in terms of "You play it for stupid fun, but then you'll end up playing it as an esports". This game has the possibility to be a legit competetive game with the proper ruleset, and Team17 is definitely acknowledging this with their ESL support in WMD.
Worms WMD as an entry in the franchise is great. It goes back to cute 2D graphics with 60fps animations, rather than stupid ugly 3D graphics in a 2D game with 30fps animations. The rope is back to being unrealistic (can rope straight up, fast, hard and not wiggly), large variety of weapons, full length campaign and extra challenges, fully-featured multiplayer.
The surprise is what they added, crafting. At first, "oh my god why does everything have crafting", then I realize the genius. This diminishes the RNG of crate drops by being able to craft what you want, but the real improvement? You have something to do on someone elses turn. No more waiting boringly. Speaking of which, this game switches turns fast (I recall an earlier Worms, there's a 10 second wait from when a turn ends and when a turn starts)
Highly recommend this Worms in particular, and the franchise in general.

Alien Isolation... Well, this is quite the challenge.
I enjoy scary/terrifying atmosphere games, but this one got me by far.
The entire ship is alive. I was amazed all along by the immersion level you are in when you play this as it should be (meaning a 7.1 headset full volume, a big screen, a dark room, and there you go).
By challenge I mean the difficulty itself, not the scary part. Being scared is "harder" than any other games as Amnesia or such, since here you have some tools and weapons at hand, so you're not entirely "naked" (besides that you have a tracker, so you can't possibly lose your way or forget hostiles). I beat the game in Hard and I believe, as the game tells us, that it is just the way it has to be played. Of course I had some jump-scares, but I was not "terrified". I had difficult times, some more than others, but not all were scary.
The game makes you think twice about how to react around you. At first I got confused - and killed, with all these buttons, all these doors, all this plastic style (an amazing work from the designers by the way). But then I got my way in, started to think twice before doing something rather reckless and kept an eye on my surroundings.
And that's what Alien is about: a place, unique in its style, and a truly outstanding atmosphere. I'd play it twice just because of it, this is an amazing time in space.
Graphically immersive (lights, design) and an unbelievable sound design (the ship itself has a very soul as the surroundings do), the story never keeps you low and always expects the best from you at all time.
A formidable and unforgettable adventure with the most dangerous creature from space. Really. I mean it.

This game is truly a masterpiece.
At first look, the game looks like a simple horror game:
-Get from point A to B without being spotted
-Hide so your not caught
-Croutch everywhere
-Use item A to distract monster
-Get to point B, complete objective, get BACK to point A without being caught.
It is all of the things above, but what suprises me is how much i'm on edge. There have been a few times where i've RAGED because i couldn't get past one area. Usually, when i beat areas like this in a game, i just feel annoyed because i know i'll be running into the problem again.
However, with this game, i am always terrified. Now about 10 hours into the game, i STILL feel scared when i'm out in the open. The atmosphere is amazing, as well as the AI.
The Alien's AI, however, is unique. It relies on hear and SMELL. Thats right, it can SMELL you. I myself have never played a game in which smell is something you must worry about, but in this game, it is. And you MUST keep on moving, or it WILL find you.
All in all, Alien: Isolation can be rage inducing at some points, but overall, it is an AMAZING game that deserves a high rating.

Good but not without (avoidable) flaws.
The game itself is pretty solid. The Level design is really nice, lots of attention to detail and none of the areas feel too repetitive. Sound and Lightning are top notch and the game just oozes 80's sci-fi flair everywhere. It captures the spirit of the first Alien movie extremely well.
The game is *reasonably* scary, but it's really more a survival game than a horror game. Avoiding the Alien is scary first, but quickly becomes routine and slightly tedious as you just try to always be on the opposite of what ever object is between you and it.
I encountered quite a few bugs in the game sadly. Mostly non-responsive NPCs (they just stand there, doing nothing), some times your sound is bugged when you reload one of your weapons, and some times you are simply left unable to interact with objects or draw your weapon. These bugs really take away from the experience, because standing in the open and getting murdered because you can't open a door or use your inventory is really frustrating, but LUCKILY it is not happening *too* often.
Overall I'd give the game a 8/10.
Summary:
Graphics: 9.5 (GREAT lightning, good textures across the board, SOLID performance even on ultra settings, nice use of volumetric lights and good particles)
Sound: 9/10 (good sound design overall, good voice acting, athmospheric background sounds. Can't really ask for more)
Music: 9/10 (Amazing soundtrack, staying very true to the 1979 Original. The Dynamic music sometimes goes slightly overboard, but overall its really good)
Gameplay: 7.5/10 (solid mechanics, but tends to get repetitive after a short while)
Overall: 8/10 (The game looks and feels polished, hide&seek gameplay is a matter of taste but generally well realized. minus points for potentially gamebreaking bugs and slightly repetitive feel after a while.)
Having said that, I'd still recommend the game. Just do yourself a favor and play it in the dark and with (good) headphones or surround sound. It really adds to the experience.

Imagine being stuck with a butcher, a firefighter, John Goodman, and Christian Bale inside a cabin with plenty of undead outside, walking and begging to eat your flesh.  It sounds like a funny scenario, yes, but when you put on some headphones and play...
It is not so funny anymore.
Jokes aside, the game is suprisingly well done for a title with its roots from a mod.  (Well, I do play TF2, but you know, it has a huge paint job to cover it.)
Story
NMRiH has no major narrative, but for each map you play on, there is a mission with voice-overs directing you to set objectives.  Besides each objective, there are zones in the map that you are required to protect as you do the mission.  For the whole map, there are rounds of zombies spawning, but players can join to even the odds.  Each player has a skin, but beyond that, you can't really say there is too much character depth, as mentioned with actual Patrick Bateman and Walter Sobchak models put in the game to play as.
Gameplay
With a bunch of zombie-themed games and shows nowadays, it is often difficult to find a good zombie simulator.  (You can take DayZ, perhaps, but the "broke" people have to find free games.)  NMRiH takes this challenge and passes with flying colors by having stamina and health bars.  When playing, they do not show up, just like the crosshairs, and add to the sense of realism.  There are plenty of weapons, though mostly melee tools since guns and ammo are scarce.  You spawn with your trusty Zippo lighter that provides a source of light in the mostly dark maps.  Zombies can bite you when you have your guard down, and when bitten, there is no cure-you can only postpone it by painkillers.  You will feel as if you were truly in an undead apocalypse.
Visual Quality
Now, this will pretty much be a beacon for judgement.  Yeah, gameplay over graphics is true, but lacking aesthetic beauty brings down the gameplay.  Being a Source game, you don't really expect eye-popping graphics like, say
However, the darkness helps in this game, providing silhouetted zombies and the textures on them make them even scarier.  The models do repeat often, but this isn't a high budget, Triple-A Blockbuster from some big name company.  My only gripe is the animations.
Grade

Nostalgic to some, impressive to all, easy to none. Black Mesa is challenging. Black Mesa is hard. Black Mesa will eat your soul, but not before making you die a couple hundred times in-game. Black Mesa will send you back a few years, and punch you back to reality just as you start begging for more.
Without any further delay, I present to you my review of Black Mesa.
It’s not possible to talk about Black Mesa and not mention Half-Life, but to be honest, other than the lambda symbol, and all the internet memes, I’ve no knowledge of any of the HL games, so it’s safe to say I’m part of the 0,1% that never played them.
When I started my Black Mesa adventure, I wasn’t expecting top notch graphics, state of the art technology or anything alike, and that was a good thing, as I didn’t find those. What I did find was a great adventure, or, well, a great semi-adventure, as I was stopped by a “To be continued” screen, which left me wanting more, but not better. Why am I not wanting better, you may ask. The reason is quite simple actually. From shooting aliens, to killing headcrabs, to swimming in radioactive waste and even bombing a gigantic alien-octopus, there are very few things that can get better. And just when you think you’ve got it all under control, with all the overpowered weapons, it hits you, literally, and you’re back to square one, in a way.
I like to think a good story can make up for most of the stuff, but there was nothing to make up for with Black Mesa.
If I loved this game without being a previous Half-Life admirer, I’d say it’s pretty safe to say everyone can, and will, find this game extremely entertaining.
Considering it's an Early Access (EA) game, I've decided to add a "Neutral" category, for details I consider important, but not gamebreakers, and could easily improve the gameplay if attended.
Hardly anything in the "Cons" section.
I'd give it a
, which will undoubtedly turn into a 10 by the end of the game’s development. I might even end up joining the Half-Life 3 hype bandwagon...
.

Do not underestimate this game simply because it's free and it's very RPG-Maker. Actually, this is one of the best free games I have ever seen.
You play as Senia, a lovely heroine that lacks bravery but instead has the will to sacrifice anything to save her dear sister. This ARPG plays much like Ys: walk into an enemy to attack, but most of the time you'll get reflected damage and also be bounced back. There are also skills to use that drain MP. The skills are stronger, and never cause reflected damage on you. Both HP and MP recovers over time, and doing a physical attack also recovers MP. These mechanisms make this game extremely easy to control, and thus can be played by everyone.
Despite script writing, the author also spent very considerable effort on making the hit effect satisfactory. When Senia slashes an enemy, a slashing sound, a cutting-through-monster-flesh sound, and two corresponding animations are all played at finely tuned times. These carefully chosen sound and visual effects make slashing an enemy feel very fluent, natural and satisfying, almost comparable to a big-title action game. I'm serious: this important yet often ignored aspect of an action game is done extremely well in this game.
Another thing I love is the boss battles. The variety of battles doesn't seem to be affected by the constraints of RPG-Maker at all. I never expected anyone could craft such intense battles with RPG-Maker. To give examples, there are bosses that do area attacks (with ample beforehand warnings), bosses that summon regular monsters, bosses that create barriers that need slashing, and bosses that cut down the available space you can walk on as battle progresses.
And everything else in this game is just right. There's no shop, so you have to craft all equipment, and to gather all materials required, you have to do a little bit of farming. The game provides dungeons specifically meant for farming, and the amount of farming required is just right so that you can enjoy the fun of farming, and not feel bored at all. There are also collectibles to gather, which are also at just the right amount, so you get the satisfaction of thoroughly exploring the map without any frustration of not being able to find one particular chest.
For such a small team, Eternal Senia is really a masterpiece. The author, Holy Priest, has all the right to be very proud of creating this game and of himself. I can't start to imagine what jaw-dropping works will be created next if he can build another game from ground up, not in the constraints of RPG-Maker.

Man, I love these games. The first one was a trial of patience, but it lead to giving us its sequels which makes me dislike it much less.  They're just about the perfect, chill, vast arcade shooter.  It's already really simple and these developers seem to continue to streamline the interface and gameplay. Not a whole bunch of goofy, gimmicky customizations to deal with at the core.  Filled with action.  Even the title is a clever little innocent double entendre!
I could see how people would dislike it for its simplicity and repetitive arcade nature. However, the action you participate in is some of the greatest and most original due to the main hitch of the game, the grappling hook/parachute.  It's most accurate when played on a keyboard/mouse, but I almost always play 3rd person games with a controller and this series of games does really well with the controller.  I prefer the controller for more fidelity with the vehicles and parachute at the expense of accuracy blasting away those oppressive militants.
They added a wingsuit to the series.  I mean...  I didn't think it needed to be any more bonkers, but they went ahead and gave us heaping piles of bonkers with that.  You get a fresh supply of crazy special weapons again too.
There is a limited ability to take stealthy non-lethal approaches in the game. Basically, only by destroying things while out of sight in villages and cities.  Entering restricted areas and blowing things up is an automatic alert to the militants and there's no sneaking up on people and cutting their throats.  Though the story cutscenes will enforce some strong imagery that may not be suitable for the youngins' out there.
If I had to bring a con to the table, it would be that GTAV took a good first leap into a first person open world interface, and I wouldn't be sad if that was also incorperated into this game along with a JCOnline.  Speaking of multiplayer, I just noticed that it's being modded into this game. Wonderful.
All that said, they've never been too invested in the story, but it's not as painful as it could be.  It's always the same baseline goal of liberating a massive land of communities.  Always about toppling a dictator, and you play a lot of crazy, naturally cinematic missions along the way.  The voice acting isn't terrible, they give themselves a buffer with the silly script to compliment the action/comedy.  I don't think you're necessarily supposed to feel like a hero in this game, just an arrogant badass that does crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥to save people, or turn them into collateral damage.  Early on, I questioned if Rico was on the right side this time. The cutscenes helped clear that up.
If you've got time to burn and hay bales of marijuana, this game is for you.

A game with a lot of potential that went downhill really fast.
As the first MOBA to employ both a third person perspective and an 'only skillshots' rule, SMITE had a lot of possibilities. In its early days, it had a little bit of startup trouble, but gradually grew to discover a nice balance that kept the game on a good pace. High risk was met with high reward, and if you knew what you were doing, you would have a profound impact on the game.
Unfortunately, that didn't last. With a series of balance changes, the discrepancy between offense and defense based characters  in terms of damage output has shrunk to the point where the entire game became a snoozefest. With damage output being nerfed almost incessantly, high risk characters now actually have less reward attached to them than low risk characters.
As a result of every single character in the game growing weaker, the crowd has also grown more frustrated. There's more anger going around, more insults being flung, more bile. And as far as I can tell, the balance only worsens with every patch.
I do not recommend this game. Just like all other MOBAs, save for DotA, the game has just shifted too far in favour of defense.

This game is truly a masterpiece.
At first look, the game looks like a simple horror game:
-Get from point A to B without being spotted
-Hide so your not caught
-Croutch everywhere
-Use item A to distract monster
-Get to point B, complete objective, get BACK to point A without being caught.
It is all of the things above, but what suprises me is how much i'm on edge. There have been a few times where i've RAGED because i couldn't get past one area. Usually, when i beat areas like this in a game, i just feel annoyed because i know i'll be running into the problem again.
However, with this game, i am always terrified. Now about 10 hours into the game, i STILL feel scared when i'm out in the open. The atmosphere is amazing, as well as the AI.
The Alien's AI, however, is unique. It relies on hear and SMELL. Thats right, it can SMELL you. I myself have never played a game in which smell is something you must worry about, but in this game, it is. And you MUST keep on moving, or it WILL find you.
All in all, Alien: Isolation can be rage inducing at some points, but overall, it is an AMAZING game that deserves a high rating.

Good but not without (avoidable) flaws.
The game itself is pretty solid. The Level design is really nice, lots of attention to detail and none of the areas feel too repetitive. Sound and Lightning are top notch and the game just oozes 80's sci-fi flair everywhere. It captures the spirit of the first Alien movie extremely well.
The game is *reasonably* scary, but it's really more a survival game than a horror game. Avoiding the Alien is scary first, but quickly becomes routine and slightly tedious as you just try to always be on the opposite of what ever object is between you and it.
I encountered quite a few bugs in the game sadly. Mostly non-responsive NPCs (they just stand there, doing nothing), some times your sound is bugged when you reload one of your weapons, and some times you are simply left unable to interact with objects or draw your weapon. These bugs really take away from the experience, because standing in the open and getting murdered because you can't open a door or use your inventory is really frustrating, but LUCKILY it is not happening *too* often.
Overall I'd give the game a 8/10.
Summary:
Graphics: 9.5 (GREAT lightning, good textures across the board, SOLID performance even on ultra settings, nice use of volumetric lights and good particles)
Sound: 9/10 (good sound design overall, good voice acting, athmospheric background sounds. Can't really ask for more)
Music: 9/10 (Amazing soundtrack, staying very true to the 1979 Original. The Dynamic music sometimes goes slightly overboard, but overall its really good)
Gameplay: 7.5/10 (solid mechanics, but tends to get repetitive after a short while)
Overall: 8/10 (The game looks and feels polished, hide&seek gameplay is a matter of taste but generally well realized. minus points for potentially gamebreaking bugs and slightly repetitive feel after a while.)
Having said that, I'd still recommend the game. Just do yourself a favor and play it in the dark and with (good) headphones or surround sound. It really adds to the experience.

If being absolutely powerless whilst scurrying around in a crouch, hiding in whatever available spaces you can find appeals to your gameplay instincts, go for it.  The meagre story (much of which you are responsible for ferretting out from old e-mails and tape recordings bizarrely left laying about) can't sustain the game's ambition to scare the hell out of you, and neither can the wonky gameplay mechanics.
The game is brutally, punishingly difficult, but it's not a
kind of challenge; in that game series, you slowly learn to stop sucking, and your reward for playing better is dying less.  In AI, the deck is by design so heavily stacked against you that it often doesn't matter what you do.  With its old-school save-point system, this often means a wasted 30 minutes of playtime, sending you far enough back that rage-quitting seems a more pleasant option.
The Alien's programming is an impressive piece of work, and it often succeeds in making you feel hunted and vulnerable. Unfortunately, Creative Assembly have hoisted themselves on their own petard with the Alien, endowing it with magic powers of teleportation and the ability to see through walls.  Giving the Alien free reign of the Sevastopol to hunt and kill you with impunity mostly works, but after your first few physics-defying deaths, the absurdity of what the Alien can do takes away a lot of the tension.
Case in point: while hiding in a locker from the Alien, I am prompted to press a key to lean back, and press another key to hold my breath.  After a few seconds of breath-holding, the screen pulses red around the edges, as if Ripley is suffocating.  The Alien sniffs around the locker, apparently decides I'm not there, then turns around and
.  I can hear its footsteps getting fainter.  Relieved, I resume breathing...only to have the Alien materialize out of nowhere, rip the locker door off, and tear me to shreds.  It's absurd.  It's frustrating.  It appears to be totally random, and "playing better" won't help me avoid it.
Perhaps some will argue that is part of the appeal: instant, violent death out of nowhere, when you least expect it.  I'm not going to call anyone who feels that way wrong.  I will say it's not for everybody.
Creative Assembly is to be commended for their superb art and sound direction, and obvious respect for the Alien universe.  They took a bold step casting their protagonist as essentially helpless, and AI is, despite its flaws, a unique gameplay experience.  However, wonky mechanics and obtuse AI combined with brutal difficulty and far too thin a story make
a massive missed opportunity.

There’s been hundreds of games inspired by the Alien movies. Going all the way back to Alien Breed on the Amiga, to more recent titles like System Shock and Dead Space. This means a ton of novelty value is lost in Alien Isolation before you even start it. Almost everything in the game will remind you not just of the movies, but the mountain of things it inspired.
Despite all this I was pleasantly surprised by how effective this game is. At times it can feel like any other space horror game you’ve played before. But when the stars align it’s like you’re on the set of the movie. You’re transported to something that feels wholly owned by the game and movie alone. It’s thanks to a herculean effort by Creative Assembly to make sure that everything looks, sounds and feels exactly like it should, down to the smallest details. Like even the lens flares look just like they did in Alien. It had a distinctive style thanks to the lenses they used. All the big things, and the smaller subliminal things are here to make it feel just right. This is better than I ever dared hope an Alien game would ever be. Much of it is thanks to it being released today. It’s built with state of the art tech, on top of everything we’ve learned from horror and stealth games over the past 20 years. It’s of its time, in a good way.
What hit me 10+ hours into the game was that while this has collectibles and achievements like any other AAA production, it doesn’t shove them in your face like I’m used to. The developers obviously took things like “tone” and “atmosphere” seriously. It’s a videogame, but it doesn’t feel the need to shove that in your face. It’s the subtle touches that achieve this feeling. Like how the waypoint arrow is part of the motion tracker, instead of having a dot in the game world. And how the mini-game interfaces look like designs that belong in the world. They’ve sacrificed just a bit of usability across the board for the sake of immersion. As a whole this pays off, even if it opens them up to players nitpicking every detail as being just a bit more of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥than they’re used to. It’s about the big picture!
As a whole the game looks amazing. But there’s little issues here and there that prevent it from being perfect. The character models look good, in stills. The second they start talking they look more like mannequins than people. The animations can also flip out, with the alien making sudden sharp turns that take you out of the moment. Similarly the audio is outstanding, but with glaring issues here and there. At some sections of the map the audio disappears. Like you’ve wandered out of the sound and music propagation zones. It’s a rare problem, but it stands out, especially since it most of the time is one of the best sounding games of all time.
The greatest failing of the game is the story. The characters are all flat, and devoid of anything interesting at all. They’re inoffensive, but bland. You play Amanda Ripley, and while she does a lot of talking, she failed to create a firm image in my head of her character. Her motivation in the entire game fits in a single sentence and don’t deviate from that. She doesn’t have an arc, so you don’t feel like you get to go on a journey with her, where you end up somewhere different on the other side.
The story feels more like a series of objectives instead of an actual story. You don’t feel like it’s going anywhere, which makes it impossible to guess when it’s going to end. I’ve heard complaints that it “goes on forever”, and that’s a failing with the story. The actual process of playing it is fine! The environments and challenges keep things fresh all the way to the end. But because the story is vague about where it’s going and what you’re trying to achieve you can’t intuitively sense where you are in the story. On paper it has threads and subplots like any story should. But they’re all weak, and fail to make an impression. It feels diffuse. The story isn’t complete♥♥♥♥♥♥ just a jumbled mess. Which I guess is a degree of♥♥♥♥♥♥ just not on the absolute bottom end of the scale.
As with anything I can live with bad elements if the good outweighs it. And thankfully there’s a lot to like about Alien Isolation that makes it a no-brainer recommendation. The setting is super strong, it manages to come up with new scares even in later parts of the game, and most importantly it feels right. There were parts in the game where I experienced a level of stress I haven’t felt since the scariest parts of Amnesia. When Alien Isolation fires on all cylinders it’s the most effective “being chased by a murderer” simulator I can imagine ever being made. At those moments all the issues fade into the background and don’t matter so much anymore.

Before I start, if you want this game you are going to need a controller. One of the critical things they didn't improve on, that they should have improved on was PC control optimization. It's still a failure. IMO a controller is required to play this game comfortably. Alot of the visuals in this game, aswell as playability in terms of graphic optimization have been fixed. The game runs steadily at 60 frames for me, and my computer is well dated at this point. In terms of gameplay, its hit and miss. Some people think it's too easy, some think it was dumbed down, some think its incredibly hard. For me, neither this or the first game were hard. It's a matter of using the brain you have. The game holds the players hand like any other, just in a different manner. In it's map design and enemy placement, you just have to think. PVP has lacked in improvement IMO aside from connectivity. Which has been improved massively, playing with other people has become alot easier than before. Not perfect, but a welcomed improvement (this also applies to co-op, it is very simple to play with friends). PVE is completely different. It might not seem so at face, but once you get further in you start to see the fundimental changes they have made to the combat, and the enemy design. It's hard to compare to DS1 because of that. Hacking is still an issue, alot less prevalent but still an issue. Sometimes you will be invaded by someone who has infinite health and you can't do anything other than kill yourself to escape it. In the end I think it's worth the purchase, it still holds the souls charm and the improvements they have made are good enough for me to justify the buy.

The game is super hard, if you have never played a dark souls game before. I was super furstrated at it, but perservered read some game guides realised the mistakes I was making.  The game then changed from super hard to challenging, which made it much more fun.
Give you some idea, I spent the first 3 hours restarting, not understanding why I couldn't blap my way thro' these creeps, falling off ledges, getting owned by the smallest monsters and the big ones.. HA I didn't stand a chance.
Then I read a guide, picked a sorcerer, followed the guide.. Things started to make sense, I started killing stuff, sure I still died loads (and you will die loads, get use to that) but i progressed.  Without a guide (plenty online) you are going to be screwed.
The controls are quirky, but eventually you get use to them. I had to install my Razer mouse drivers and use that software to adjust my DPI down (to about 400) so playing with mouse/keyboard is possible. (in game mouse sensitivity is stupid quick and adjusting it did nothing).
The greatest weakness (and possible strength) of this game as a new player is not knowning. It's quirky, like having to chat to the same NPC several times over to be able to (initally) level up, it's not normal, it's not expect so you miss it. Its the same with other NPC's, talk to them repeatedly until they either give you something, or a menu pops up allowing you to level up or buy something.
You kill stuff, gather souls, if you die you drop them at that point, you can go pick them back up so long as you can get back there without dying again. Souls are currency, thus, dying can have a massive penalty attached. Spending souls (to level up and buy stuff) is the own way to bank them.  Bonfires are rest points use to restore health replenish spells or fast travel between them, but using one means all the creeps you've killed respawn (after a time they don't and some never respawn, not worked out why yet).
Give you some idea of difficulty, there is a statue in town, the plaque tells you the number of deaths in total in dark souls 2. Look at it, look at it again a second later, normally it will have jumped up by 5 to 10 people in that second!. It is doing this ALL THE TIME..
So yes, it's a great game, but you must be some sort of masochistic to enjoy it :P

Nostalgic to some, impressive to all, easy to none. Black Mesa is challenging. Black Mesa is hard. Black Mesa will eat your soul, but not before making you die a couple hundred times in-game. Black Mesa will send you back a few years, and punch you back to reality just as you start begging for more.
Without any further delay, I present to you my review of Black Mesa.
It’s not possible to talk about Black Mesa and not mention Half-Life, but to be honest, other than the lambda symbol, and all the internet memes, I’ve no knowledge of any of the HL games, so it’s safe to say I’m part of the 0,1% that never played them.
When I started my Black Mesa adventure, I wasn’t expecting top notch graphics, state of the art technology or anything alike, and that was a good thing, as I didn’t find those. What I did find was a great adventure, or, well, a great semi-adventure, as I was stopped by a “To be continued” screen, which left me wanting more, but not better. Why am I not wanting better, you may ask. The reason is quite simple actually. From shooting aliens, to killing headcrabs, to swimming in radioactive waste and even bombing a gigantic alien-octopus, there are very few things that can get better. And just when you think you’ve got it all under control, with all the overpowered weapons, it hits you, literally, and you’re back to square one, in a way.
I like to think a good story can make up for most of the stuff, but there was nothing to make up for with Black Mesa.
If I loved this game without being a previous Half-Life admirer, I’d say it’s pretty safe to say everyone can, and will, find this game extremely entertaining.
Considering it's an Early Access (EA) game, I've decided to add a "Neutral" category, for details I consider important, but not gamebreakers, and could easily improve the gameplay if attended.
Hardly anything in the "Cons" section.
I'd give it a
, which will undoubtedly turn into a 10 by the end of the game’s development. I might even end up joining the Half-Life 3 hype bandwagon...

I have come from a series of other MOBA's and for me Smite was the only that got me to stay... Sometimes i don't agree with some changes that Hi-Rez does but i deal with it... Like i said i have played several MOBA's like Heroes of Newerth, Strife, Arena of Fate, LoL, DoTA2... pretty much anything worth a while of my time...
I have been playing this before this came out from beta testing so don't really judge me on my (currently) 62h of gaming... i have easily over 2000h invested here, and i must say i just almost every hour on it.
the gameplay:
if your a fan of RPG or TPS or something like that you will immediatly like it... you seem so small in such a "huge" map, like when i'm farming somewhere on any MMORPG. it just ringed to me instantly putting a smile on my face.
the community:
Like in every MOBA there are good and trash players... i mean trolls are everywhere, i have trolled and raged myself quite some time but normally we find good players who are enjoyable to play with.
the concept:
i've always enjoyed the fact that Smite has a sense of truth in their characters, since all of 'em are from different mythologies (greek, roman, norse, chinese, mayan, egyptian) and being a fan on mythology myself this also made me smile.
graphics and server communication, etc:
the game on max settings is quite beautiful altough i must say that LoL takes the cake when it comes to graphics... the servers normally don't lag but lately there's been something rough going on because players kept getting disconnected and/or lagging a lot, but generally it's very playable (fps over 60 and ping lower than 65)
the differences between Smite and everything else:
besides the concept itself and the camera, Smite offers a unique Daily Reward system that just by logging in they can get rewards... the rewards are week based and from 1st to 5th days players are rewarded a decent ammount of favor (game currency) and the 6th and 7th days players are rewarded gems (the pay to get currency, similar to RP in LoL) which makes the player connect to smite atleast once a day, just to get that... joining with that there's the "first win of the day" on EVERY different mode that you play which rewards a small ammount of favor which after a week allows him to buy a god without too much trouble. Another thing is the events... events happen quite often and they are also quite rewarding... the rewards are normally gems and they come in quite a substantial way. 1 more thing, the best thing in every MOBA i played... the VGS (Voice Guided System) which allows players to communicate fast and efficient without having to stop, press enter, and writing stuff like ss, mia, be careful, etc. there are a lot of commands that simplify the game and keeps the whole team connected without anyone actually having to say a word... and joining with this! there are VP (voice packs) for EACH god and A LOT of skins which changes the whole VGS which allows the player not having to hear the same repetitive sounds over and over and over again.
Overall:
the game is balanced is very enjoyable to play!

Don't listen to the people who tell you this is a good game or "has potential". It doesn't. It's "Survival Game #4378463" without ANY innovation at all. Let me be precise:
* The map is utter crap. No chance in hell that anybody worked more than a day on this. Take a random Unity terrain, spray some rocks onto it (and yes, there are many rocks, and they are all the same), slam some ugly, random 3D assets onto it (and call it "cities"), add some static mob and node spawns and you are done. The world is ugly as hell.
* You have a "handful" of items to craft, really the bare minimum, and you will be "done" within 2 days of stupid grinding.
* Car physics are a joke. There's actually two good car physics assets on the Unity Asset Store. But I guess $50 were too much for this studio, so one of the coder newbies apparently got the task to come up with something himself. The result is ONE buggy and ONE trike. The buggy easily flies a couple of hundred meters, while the trike can't be driven in the desert at all because it keeps rolling over all the time. Yeah. All the time.
* The combat system is cheap and boring. Funniest thing is that when you fire a bullet, you aggro basically all NPCs from one horizon to the other which makes guns in PVP utterly useless. Oh, yes, even with the best equipment a boar kills you in no time. Freaking funny to have an automatic assault rifle and be owned by a random boar while you tried to defend yourself from another player. Slime Rancher is an open world exploration game full of adorable blob creatures that can be collected throughout various areas of the game. Of course there is also a farming aspect to the game as well in which I can almost say is the secondary objective of this game, as exploration is rewarding enough, with enough work and dedication, with the right materials the farm can basically run itself, it's your job to expand it...
I find that the primary objective this game hits right on the nose is exploration. The first day I got this on the Steam Summer Sale (6/22/2017) I played about three hours before becoming truley adept to the strategy therefore becoming addicted to the game like Nicotine, I ended up pulling an all nighter like an idiot totalling to 10 hours the first day! But still there was something I could not grasp...the landscape. There could easily be 20+ hours of exploring the vast acres of wildlife, and by acres I mean literal miles upon miles or unique landscape. I have never gotten physically lost in a videogame before, I know the maps of Skyrim, Cyrodiill, Morrowind, and even Destiny like the back of my hand, even with hours upon hours of wondering the wilderness I can barely grasp the layout of the 2nd area.
Onto the orginisation of the game; the variety of slimes, food and landscape is astonishing. Right when it seems like every type of food and slime has been collected there always seems to be a few more you missed. Don't even get me started on the breeding system, I want to keep this review under a 10 hour read. Basically every Slime can be inbread with eachother casuing specific effects that may prove benifical to significant siduations.
Finally for the most important aspect of this game; personally this game hit hard. And I'm not talking performance wise, no, this game is a smooth 60 fps on highest settings, wonderfully optimised. This game got me in the feels. The tranquility of the sunsets, the quietness of the nights, the welcoming laughter of the playful pink slimes bouncing around in their open habitat. Each time I launched this game my common day-to-day stress withered.
I could go on and on about this game, honestly I left out about 90% of it but I just wanted to make a brief review so...
In conclusion, the design of this game is truly a masterpiece, even in Beta format. I'm excited to see what the devoloper has in store for the next update. Truly imagination is the essence of discovery, so get out there and see what the Ranch has to offer.

This is the first time I have reviewed a game, and that is because I believe in this game's potential so much.  I love survival games, and was pleasantly surprised by some of the aspects of the game.  I do not want to see this game fade into obsurity, which is why I write this in the hopes that someone with more influence than me can make this game more amazing.   First, what I loved.
The environment is nice to look at and does its job of making me feel like I'm stranded in the Siberian wilderness, scavenging long abandoned homes and buildings to survive.  Encounters with other players are- naturally-  cautious and untrustworthy, but how else would you react in a world where most of the population is dead?  NExt, the act of opening each individual drawer, locker, wardrobe and cabinet while scavenging for supplies goes a long way in immersing the player into the world- no menus or search timers.  The firearms are appropriately challenging to find (although sometimes you can find too much, for better or worse) and the realistic acts of loading the bullets you scavenge into magazines and being able to unload both gun and magazine is something I never knew I wanted in a survival game until I had it.  The crumbled buildings and abandoned structures are great for creating that lonely atmosphere that I love in a survival game. Food and drink are also tough to find(it is random, after all), but you won't always find mountains of food after the apocalypse (also, you need a can opener, screwdriver, or scissors to open canned food, which is a nice touch).
These were only a few of the things that sparked my interest in this game, and I strongly encourage you to play it, and see what grabs your attention.  Now, let's move onto what I did not like, and some of the ways I think they could be fixed.  Please note that none of the following examples are NOT deal-breakers and are simply things that, if changed even slightly, can vastly improve the already immersive experience of this game.

First, temperature management; spawning in nothing but your underwear in the cold Russian expanse is lethal, but only having two ways to raise your temperature (a campfire and beer) and RNG making their discovery unpredictable is a great way to end up with stacks of frozen corpses.  I believe this can be fixed by making your core temp. decrease at a slower rate and having any clothing you are wearing protect you from the cold (that should be self-explanatory, right?)
Next, wolves;  Yes, this is Siberia.  Yes, wolves are natural predators that will hunt you down relentlessly.  No, I do not enjoy being ripped apart by them immediately upon beginning my harrowing tale of survival.  You can easily fend them off with firearms and melee weapons, but until you get your hands on one, there's nothing to do except run.  This makes it difficult to scavenge for a weapon once a wolf has your scent, and the best strategy I found for dealing with them unarmed is to exit back to the menu and load back in hoping that they are gone.  Obviously, this is not a great way to play the game.  I recommend being able to attack unarmed and make the wolf retreat would be a great way to keep unequipped players alive long enough to find some basic gear.
Multiplayer only servers.  Okay, this is more of a personal issue of mine and not any fault on the developers.  Unlike most people, I prefer to be the last man on Earth sometimes, I don't enjoy collecting backpacks full of gear and food only to be shot in the back of the head and realize I was basically doing someone else's grocery shopping.  I worked around this issue by always creating a new server when playing and then quitting out and starting another one when the number of players exceeded 4.  I would just like to get by and die on my terms, I hear wolves make great companions.
Finally, and probably most basically, there's no settings or options menu.  Either I'm way more stupid than I think I am, or there is no way to change the settings of the game.  This is simple stuff here.
So there... my first game review.  I love the way this game plays and feels.  The little things play a big part in making the game feel more real, and as I stated above, the problems are NOT deal-breakers, at least for me.  I think anyone on the fence about this game should give it a chance.  And if anyone with the ability to influence this game in any way reads this, then that's even better.
Now if you'll excuse me, I'm going to running around shootingmy M1911 at the wolves in my underwear.

If being absolutely powerless whilst scurrying around in a crouch, hiding in whatever available spaces you can find appeals to your gameplay instincts, go for it.  The meagre story (much of which you are responsible for ferretting out from old e-mails and tape recordings bizarrely left laying about) can't sustain the game's ambition to scare the hell out of you, and neither can the wonky gameplay mechanics.
The game is brutally, punishingly difficult, but it's not a
kind of challenge; in that game series, you slowly learn to stop sucking, and your reward for playing better is dying less.  In AI, the deck is by design so heavily stacked against you that it often doesn't matter what you do.  With its old-school save-point system, this often means a wasted 30 minutes of playtime, sending you far enough back that rage-quitting seems a more pleasant option.
The Alien's programming is an impressive piece of work, and it often succeeds in making you feel hunted and vulnerable. Unfortunately, Creative Assembly have hoisted themselves on their own petard with the Alien, endowing it with magic powers of teleportation and the ability to see through walls.  Giving the Alien free reign of the Sevastopol to hunt and kill you with impunity mostly works, but after your first few physics-defying deaths, the absurdity of what the Alien can do takes away a lot of the tension.
Case in point: while hiding in a locker from the Alien, I am prompted to press a key to lean back, and press another key to hold my breath.  After a few seconds of breath-holding, the screen pulses red around the edges, as if Ripley is suffocating.  The Alien sniffs around the locker, apparently decides I'm not there, then turns around and
.  I can hear its footsteps getting fainter.  Relieved, I resume breathing...only to have the Alien materialize out of nowhere, rip the locker door off, and tear me to shreds.  It's absurd.  It's frustrating.  It appears to be totally random, and "playing better" won't help me avoid it.
Perhaps some will argue that is part of the appeal: instant, violent death out of nowhere, when you least expect it.  I'm not going to call anyone who feels that way wrong.  I will say it's not for everybody.
Creative Assembly is to be commended for their superb art and sound direction, and obvious respect for the Alien universe.  They took a bold step casting their protagonist as essentially helpless, and AI is, despite its flaws, a unique gameplay experience.  However, wonky mechanics and obtuse AI combined with brutal difficulty and far too thin a story make
a massive missed opportunity.

There’s been hundreds of games inspired by the Alien movies. Going all the way back to Alien Breed on the Amiga, to more recent titles like System Shock and Dead Space. This means a ton of novelty value is lost in Alien Isolation before you even start it. Almost everything in the game will remind you not just of the movies, but the mountain of things it inspired.
Despite all this I was pleasantly surprised by how effective this game is. At times it can feel like any other space horror game you’ve played before. But when the stars align it’s like you’re on the set of the movie. You’re transported to something that feels wholly owned by the game and movie alone. It’s thanks to a herculean effort by Creative Assembly to make sure that everything looks, sounds and feels exactly like it should, down to the smallest details. Like even the lens flares look just like they did in Alien. It had a distinctive style thanks to the lenses they used. All the big things, and the smaller subliminal things are here to make it feel just right. This is better than I ever dared hope an Alien game would ever be. Much of it is thanks to it being released today. It’s built with state of the art tech, on top of everything we’ve learned from horror and stealth games over the past 20 years. It’s of its time, in a good way.
What hit me 10+ hours into the game was that while this has collectibles and achievements like any other AAA production, it doesn’t shove them in your face like I’m used to. The developers obviously took things like “tone” and “atmosphere” seriously. It’s a videogame, but it doesn’t feel the need to shove that in your face. It’s the subtle touches that achieve this feeling. Like how the waypoint arrow is part of the motion tracker, instead of having a dot in the game world. And how the mini-game interfaces look like designs that belong in the world. They’ve sacrificed just a bit of usability across the board for the sake of immersion. As a whole this pays off, even if it opens them up to players nitpicking every detail as being just a bit more of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥than they’re used to. It’s about the big picture!
As a whole the game looks amazing. But there’s little issues here and there that prevent it from being perfect. The character models look good, in stills. The second they start talking they look more like mannequins than people. The animations can also flip out, with the alien making sudden sharp turns that take you out of the moment. Similarly the audio is outstanding, but with glaring issues here and there. At some sections of the map the audio disappears. Like you’ve wandered out of the sound and music propagation zones. It’s a rare problem, but it stands out, especially since it most of the time is one of the best sounding games of all time.
The greatest failing of the game is the story. The characters are all flat, and devoid of anything interesting at all. They’re inoffensive, but bland. You play Amanda Ripley, and while she does a lot of talking, she failed to create a firm image in my head of her character. Her motivation in the entire game fits in a single sentence and don’t deviate from that. She doesn’t have an arc, so you don’t feel like you get to go on a journey with her, where you end up somewhere different on the other side.
The story feels more like a series of objectives instead of an actual story. You don’t feel like it’s going anywhere, which makes it impossible to guess when it’s going to end. I’ve heard complaints that it “goes on forever”, and that’s a failing with the story. The actual process of playing it is fine! The environments and challenges keep things fresh all the way to the end. But because the story is vague about where it’s going and what you’re trying to achieve you can’t intuitively sense where you are in the story. On paper it has threads and subplots like any story should. But they’re all weak, and fail to make an impression. It feels diffuse. The story isn’t complete♥♥♥♥♥♥ just a jumbled mess. Which I guess is a degree of♥♥♥♥♥♥ just not on the absolute bottom end of the scale.
As with anything I can live with bad elements if the good outweighs it. And thankfully there’s a lot to like about Alien Isolation that makes it a no-brainer recommendation. The setting is super strong, it manages to come up with new scares even in later parts of the game, and most importantly it feels right. There were parts in the game where I experienced a level of stress I haven’t felt since the scariest parts of Amnesia. When Alien Isolation fires on all cylinders it’s the most effective “being chased by a murderer” simulator I can imagine ever being made. At those moments all the issues fade into the background and don’t matter so much anymore.

Before buying this game you should ask yourself one question. "Did I like the movie Alien?" If you answered yes, this game is something you should pick up. Developed by, The Creative Assembly, Alien: Isolation is a survival horror game. The developers designed the game more like Ridley Scott's Alien, as opposed to James Cameron's more action-oriented Aliens. Unlike most other video game adaptations of the Alien franchise, Alien: Isolation features a single Alien throughout the title's duration that cannot be killed, requiring the player to use stealth tactics in order to survive. Although the game features some weapons, they will be lethal only against the human occupants and android "Working Joes". Instead of following a predetermined path, the artificial intelligence of the Alien has been programmed to actively hunt the player by sight, sound, and smell.
I loved the atmosphere of the game. I am a sucker for games set in space. The audio in this game is amazing; if you have a nice pair of headphones put them on while playing to admire the little things such opening a door, crawling through vents, and spacewalks. The game is also visually impressive! Finally the gameplay was fun but does get repetitive after a while. Another awesome aspect is the crafting system. The Last of Us (PS3/PS4 exclusive) introduced a robust crafting system into the gaming world. Alien: Isolation essentially steals this idea from Naughty Dog and executes the crafting system perfectly.
The only flaw in the game was length. Rarely do I complain about a game being too long, but I will admit there are some missions that really aren't needed for the story progression.
This game is not made to appeal to everyone. It is made for fans of the original Alien movie. With that said I highly recommend this game.

I have come from a series of other MOBA's and for me Smite was the only that got me to stay... Sometimes i don't agree with some changes that Hi-Rez does but i deal with it... Like i said i have played several MOBA's like Heroes of Newerth, Strife, Arena of Fate, LoL, DoTA2... pretty much anything worth a while of my time...
I have been playing this before this came out from beta testing so don't really judge me on my (currently) 62h of gaming... i have easily over 2000h invested here, and i must say i just almost every hour on it.
the gameplay:
if your a fan of RPG or TPS or something like that you will immediatly like it... you seem so small in such a "huge" map, like when i'm farming somewhere on any MMORPG. it just ringed to me instantly putting a smile on my face.
the community:
Like in every MOBA there are good and trash players... i mean trolls are everywhere, i have trolled and raged myself quite some time but normally we find good players who are enjoyable to play with.
the concept:
i've always enjoyed the fact that Smite has a sense of truth in their characters, since all of 'em are from different mythologies (greek, roman, norse, chinese, mayan, egyptian) and being a fan on mythology myself this also made me smile.
graphics and server communication, etc:
the game on max settings is quite beautiful altough i must say that LoL takes the cake when it comes to graphics... the servers normally don't lag but lately there's been something rough going on because players kept getting disconnected and/or lagging a lot, but generally it's very playable (fps over 60 and ping lower than 65)
the differences between Smite and everything else:
besides the concept itself and the camera, Smite offers a unique Daily Reward system that just by logging in they can get rewards... the rewards are week based and from 1st to 5th days players are rewarded a decent ammount of favor (game currency) and the 6th and 7th days players are rewarded gems (the pay to get currency, similar to RP in LoL) which makes the player connect to smite atleast once a day, just to get that... joining with that there's the "first win of the day" on EVERY different mode that you play which rewards a small ammount of favor which after a week allows him to buy a god without too much trouble. Another thing is the events... events happen quite often and they are also quite rewarding... the rewards are normally gems and they come in quite a substantial way. 1 more thing, the best thing in every MOBA i played... the VGS (Voice Guided System) which allows players to communicate fast and efficient without having to stop, press enter, and writing stuff like ss, mia, be careful, etc. there are a lot of commands that simplify the game and keeps the whole team connected without anyone actually having to say a word... and joining with this! there are VP (voice packs) for EACH god and A LOT of skins which changes the whole VGS which allows the player not having to hear the same repetitive sounds over and over and over again.
Overall:
the game is balanced is very enjoyable to play!

:12/17/2015: Alpha Review - *Review copy received from "Fulysic Giveaways"*
My initial thought towards this game was a less graphically appealing rust.
After around 1.5-2 hours of gameplay I feel more like I've been playing the beta to rusts alpha...
Graphics: (The less important part.) (Smooth framerate, +1)
Obviously I didn't get into this game expecting anything amazing from its graphics.
The textures are hit and miss depending on the object, for me the trees are really the only ones that stand out as paticularly bad. The rest are fine or good enough.
Models look between standard and higher quality, the only low quality model I've seen so far is the actual player character (naked, starting gear).
Shadows look standard, obviously was never intended to look like a cryengine game or anything HQ like that. They make up for it in smooth movement, (sun position adjustments) and keeping it in line with the rest of the general look of the game. Perfectly fine looking for what the game is.
UI: (Would you like grey box, or grey box?)
The overall UI feels "good enough". It's definitely not bad but I feel it could be slightly more polished.
I've dealt with way worse in other games that made me just outright stop playing them. Ingame UI looks like it was made in paint, literally just dark or light grey boxes, which is fine, it serves its purpose even if it doesn't *LOOK* appealing.
Gameplay: (Can I stop yet?)
Due to bugs preventing me from getting past the point where I can create a hatchet, if I even get that far, I can't really force myself to play anymore. According to the forum, there's a bug preventing the smaller resource nodes from respawning, (aka, small stones and fallen branches), after their initial harvest, making servers with higher populations extremely hard to progress in until they've been restarted to refresh resource nodes.
AI seem to be slightly past barebones stage, nothing to be proud of and definitely nothing to advertise as good. I've seen worse in other games, but that doesn't mean this version is good just because its "better". (They spawn in looking like giant crates!)
Crafting seems to be about on par with rust. It has a ingame guide showing you all the recipes you can craft and whats needed to craft them, pretty standard anymore. Nothing amazing, but it works. Resource gathering starts out with collecting small pebbles for flint and fallen tree branches for wood, then you'll be able to start making tools and a workbench. Due to bugs, I can't get far enough to try anything past this point.
Combat is pretty typical hack 'n slash, point and click, etc. Nothing that really makes it stand out in a good or bad way, standard. The only thing that stood out was that you can't physically attack anything before building your first tool/weapon, aka, you cannot punch. If you make the AI angry enough to attack you then you better have a weapon/tool to use. (Flight-or-Flight)
The survival aspect is exactly what you'd expect, eat to survive, find shelter, keep warm, etc. Not really anything new you'll see here until we start surviving on alien planets.
My time spent playing overall pretty much just made me want to go play rust again. This really doesn't offer anything exciting or new, just another part of the dayz survival boom.

NMRiH is an excellent example of a well constructed Source mod. It's difficult until you get the hang of it, has no really major flaws, and will simply take time and practice to get the achievements. Even now after I've sunk some time into it, surviving until the end of a map (and indeed, making it to the extraction point on time) is still quite a challenge unless you have a good team.
As with most mods I've played, I changed the key bindings first up to prevent spontaneous screen destruction further down the track, and having played over 600hrs of Day of Defeat I couldn't really imagine playing any other way. And since I've mentioned DoD - for any of you who have played DoD zombies - this is nothing like it. NMRiH is WAY darker, grainier and gritty...er. Where DoD feels like you're in a picturesque WWII game of lazer tag, NMRiH feels like you're in a toilet, surrounded by homicidal junkies, with no lights, and you have a wet toilet roll to defend yourself. Learn to shove, and obey rule #1.
Balance is where NMRiH delivers on pretty much every aspect of gameplay in my opinion. Guns are powerful, but ammo is rare, and the "unload" mechanic of being able to strip ammo from guns you find along the way adds another aspect to teamwork survival that stands out for me when compared to other games of similar ilk. I mean, let's face it, the zombie survival genre is more saturated than the floor of a Primary School toilet floor, so it's always refreshing to see something new or something delivered differently enough that you want to keep playing it. Using weapons like fire extinguishers, blow torches and single-shot flare guns also adds a little bit of badassery to your inventory as well.
I wasn't really expecting much from a free-to-play Source mod, but I've enjoyed NMRiH more than some of the AAA titles I've played this year, and definitely got more gameplay hours out of it.

Total War: Rome II (Or just RTW2) is a game of two halves. One half is filled with potential, graphical accomplishments and a sense of community through the additions in the Workshop.
The other half is a mess of bugs, poor balance and a total lack of attachment to a campaign. Bugs on release and balance issues have been part of Total War since the days of RTW1, but not after 20 patches and certainly not with the level of game-breaking effects present even nearly a year later after I pre-ordered it.
The attachment is where it really hurts for me as a long time fan. Shogun Total War II made you feel attached to every member of your clan, they each gained skills and traits that made them feel genuinely unique. Rome Total War 1 was arguably the epitome of this though, with sprawling family trees and a real sense that you were taking a Roman family (or an enemy of Rome) through one of the greatest eras of history. Now most turns feel like a slog, destroying factions is commonplace thanks to the huge number of seperate areas, and characters all end up with similar traits (If everyone in my faction likes Romans then it's not really a very unique feeling to each person).
Siege bugs are the worst I've seen in an RTS game, missile units sometimes don't fire and melee battles sometimes just look like two blobs fighting eachother. Naval Battles, while initially absolutely awful, have been improved but still feel totally void of character or any real sense of strategy. Mods solve some of these issues, but the game appears to irrepairable without the right combination of mods that match the the patch your at.
In short, I cannot recommend it. It's easily the worst Total War game ever made and has essentially killed any chance of me pre-ordering a Creative Assembly game again

I am not more than 8 hours in, but I dont usually write reviews, just want to give my first impressions from a gamer that typically plays single player games because I hate online gameplay.
I loved Skyrim, i have a tonne of hours in it, I've also unofficially had tonnes of hours playing Oblivion, and some in Morrowind. These games have always been my favourite, and I decided to give TESO a shot since it was no longer subscription.
My first impression of the game was, it's like they've tried to mimic the UI and perspective of Skyrim, but with MMO-style skills and NPC AI/looting. But I get thats kind of how you have to do it in online games and the first-person perspective still makes combat fun. I actually really like the combat system so far, playing as a Templar, which is my favourite class. In Skyrim, I found it difficult to play a Templar because in order to use any spell, you'd need to switch away from a sword + shield to use magic. Whereas in Oblivion and Morrowind you could simply cast the spell when equipped in the 'spell slot', so when I'm playing TESO I've got 8 different abilities at the touch of a button.
As I started to play the game, I didn't mind the players so much, they weren't very disruptive but occasionally they'd clear out all the hostile NPCs before you can, which can be annoying to some people, I suppose you could always try to play at different times so there would be less people too, depending on your timezone. If you were playing with friends or playing in a clan or something, I'm sure the game would be a lot more enjoyable for you. Support spells in singleplayer Elder Scrolls games didn't really work well, but now classes feel more meaningful, even though there's a little less room to play with customizing roles and classes.
I will give a big compliment to the graphics in this game, they are quite gorgeous. High Rock is a place I've always wanted to visit, and the original Daggerfall game wasn't my cup of tea, and now as I explore it I feel like I've found a new spark of love for The Elder Scrolls series, fill me with hope and anticipation for the next Elder Scrolls game!
Highlights.
Pros:
> Graphics
> Fun MP
> Large world
> Classes are great
> Combat still vaguely feels like an Elder Scrolls game
> Skills system makes more sense
Cons:
> Kind of feels like an MMORPG
> Overcrowding
> A little bit laggy
> Not great for people who dislike multiplayer

One very important part of MMO games, or multiplayer games period.... The ability to play with other players.
You cannot truely quest with other players.  You cannot truely help other players (if they're doing a quest you've done already, they turn invisible - so when they fight the bad-guy, you can just listen to your partner die).  You cannot (easily) talk to other players.  I literally spent 10 minutes chasing another player so I could click on his image, drag the option-bar over to "talk", and then try to type before he was out of range...  Not exactly very...  multiplayer.  This is a multiplayer game where a bunch of other players wander around as if they were silent NPCs.  And I doubt it's the player attitude, it's the mechanic.
Also, for those of you who are long-time fans of the Elder Scrolls games.  This game has a class-system.  That means you can't play however you want.  Also, instead of exploring at your leasure, there seems to be a heavy drive (probably because of respawn rate) to hack and slash your way through levels.  No more enjoying the countryside, chit-chatting wtih NPCS and collecting flowers and butterflies.  No more hunting either, from what I can tell.  Like many of the MMOs out there, it's just a level grind.
That being said;
The world is BEAUTIFUL, and IF you play it thinking of it like a single-player game, then this game has some charming qualities.  I do enjoy seeing all the various cultures of Tamriel, meeting NPCs (which are fully voice acted).  The storyline for the quests (that I've seen so far) seem to be pretty good.  If "hack and slash" is how you like to do your RPGs, then this one will fill your needs.
But if you want community.  Look elsewhere.
It is good that there's no fee-per month anymore, but compared to other MMOs (and even compared to it's previous single-player titles), this game seems... lacking... Except for in Environmental beauty and lore depth.

To start off with the most important thing, because you probably won't read until the end:
I'll be a little bit more precise by working out each of these points:
Eternal Senia is a 3d pixel game showing the protagonist "Senia" in the aerial perspective (not rotating). You attack enemies by walking against 'em or using one of your four skills, which you get while progressing through the game. Only some buttons and other triggers can be hit by pressing z, spacebar or return. When there's a gape, you also jump by just walking forward. Picking up items, you can guess already, also works by walking above 'em.
This probably becomes too much of a manual, so the short conclusion:
The genre mix-up:
But this game is a genre mix-up, combining the gameplay above with some visual novel elements to point out the plot and the related emotions, a pixel game can't show in such detail. This "visual novel"-part of the game is clearly structured like a visual novel should always be and none dubbed like most visual novels (also like many visual novels, there's more than one ending).
The difficulty:
The game, like mentioned already, contains four skills, you can improve by spending points, you get from killing enemies. That's pretty easy since you earn a lot of these points and spending 'em for mistake isn't fatal at all.
The crafting system is also pretty clear, grinding items in the normal areas isn't necessary, since you can easily, and unavoidible if you want some good equipment, do that in the repeatable farming dungeon, every theme level has.
But for the best equipment each theme level offers and the "ultimate" equipment, there's a bit more to do, finding all chests the game has and killing some "Elite"-monsters. Still, the "only good" equipment is enough to beat the game (if you don't go for killing the bosses on hard mode).
First, without spoilering: This story is awesome, and the visual novel elements point it out perfectly. It's very emotional and who doesn't like that is totally wrong here.
Now the spoilers:
This soundtrack is truly epic. It fits the story, the events so perfect. Also it fits the game's style pretty much since you have got very emotional songs for example on piano, most of the time fitting the visual novel elements, but also one theme, played often while the "walking"-gameplay, using some techno and also some kinda metal for special bosses.
Since the story is so important, and the score fits so perfect, the mood is pretty good. Though in the combat you don't feel it that much, but that doesn't matter, since:
This part isn't that important, but I want to go for it anyway. I for myself had some questions while playing and found myself again in the community-hub, sadly filed with spoilers I couldn't avoid to spy at. It took me some time thinking about whether I should spoil the game (even if I use spoiler tags) or just say "It's awesome, play it for youself", but that was a bit too superficial to me and also unfounded. I knew one Ending before, still I loved to go for it and didn't felt too spoiled to go on playing.

CON:

NMRiH is an excellent example of a well constructed Source mod. It's difficult until you get the hang of it, has no really major flaws, and will simply take time and practice to get the achievements. Even now after I've sunk some time into it, surviving until the end of a map (and indeed, making it to the extraction point on time) is still quite a challenge unless you have a good team.
As with most mods I've played, I changed the key bindings first up to prevent spontaneous screen destruction further down the track, and having played over 600hrs of Day of Defeat I couldn't really imagine playing any other way. And since I've mentioned DoD - for any of you who have played DoD zombies - this is nothing like it. NMRiH is WAY darker, grainier and gritty...er. Where DoD feels like you're in a picturesque WWII game of lazer tag, NMRiH feels like you're in a toilet, surrounded by homicidal junkies, with no lights, and you have a wet toilet roll to defend yourself. Learn to shove, and obey rule #1.
Balance is where NMRiH delivers on pretty much every aspect of gameplay in my opinion. Guns are powerful, but ammo is rare, and the "unload" mechanic of being able to strip ammo from guns you find along the way adds another aspect to teamwork survival that stands out for me when compared to other games of similar ilk. I mean, let's face it, the zombie survival genre is more saturated than the floor of a Primary School toilet floor, so it's always refreshing to see something new or something delivered differently enough that you want to keep playing it. Using weapons like fire extinguishers, blow torches and single-shot flare guns also adds a little bit of badassery to your inventory as well.
I wasn't really expecting much from a free-to-play Source mod, but I've enjoyed NMRiH more than some of the AAA titles I've played this year, and definitely got more gameplay hours out of it.

Slime Rancher is an open world exploration game full of adorable blob creatures that can be collected throughout various areas of the game. Of course there is also a farming aspect to the game as well in which I can almost say is the secondary objective of this game, as exploration is rewarding enough, with enough work and dedication, with the right materials the farm can basically run itself, it's your job to expand it...
I find that the primary objective this game hits right on the nose is exploration. The first day I got this on the Steam Summer Sale (6/22/2017) I played about three hours before becoming truley adept to the strategy therefore becoming addicted to the game like Nicotine, I ended up pulling an all nighter like an idiot totalling to 10 hours the first day! But still there was something I could not grasp...the landscape. There could easily be 20+ hours of exploring the vast acres of wildlife, and by acres I mean literal miles upon miles or unique landscape. I have never gotten physically lost in a videogame before, I know the maps of Skyrim, Cyrodiill, Morrowind, and even Destiny like the back of my hand, even with hours upon hours of wondering the wilderness I can barely grasp the layout of the 2nd area.
Onto the orginisation of the game; the variety of slimes, food and landscape is astonishing. Right when it seems like every type of food and slime has been collected there always seems to be a few more you missed. Don't even get me started on the breeding system, I want to keep this review under a 10 hour read. Basically every Slime can be inbread with eachother casuing specific effects that may prove benifical to significant siduations.
Finally for the most important aspect of this game; personally this game hit hard. And I'm not talking performance wise, no, this game is a smooth 60 fps on highest settings, wonderfully optimised. This game got me in the feels. The tranquility of the sunsets, the quietness of the nights, the welcoming laughter of the playful pink slimes bouncing around in their open habitat. Each time I launched this game my common day-to-day stress withered.
I could go on and on about this game, honestly I left out about 90% of it but I just wanted to make a brief review so...
In conclusion, the design of this game is truly a masterpiece, even in Beta format. I'm excited to see what the devoloper has in store for the next update. Truly imagination is the essence of discovery, so get out there and see what the Ranch has to offer.

I am not more than 8 hours in, but I dont usually write reviews, just want to give my first impressions from a gamer that typically plays single player games because I hate online gameplay.
I loved Skyrim, i have a tonne of hours in it, I've also unofficially had tonnes of hours playing Oblivion, and some in Morrowind. These games have always been my favourite, and I decided to give TESO a shot since it was no longer subscription.
My first impression of the game was, it's like they've tried to mimic the UI and perspective of Skyrim, but with MMO-style skills and NPC AI/looting. But I get thats kind of how you have to do it in online games and the first-person perspective still makes combat fun. I actually really like the combat system so far, playing as a Templar, which is my favourite class. In Skyrim, I found it difficult to play a Templar because in order to use any spell, you'd need to switch away from a sword + shield to use magic. Whereas in Oblivion and Morrowind you could simply cast the spell when equipped in the 'spell slot', so when I'm playing TESO I've got 8 different abilities at the touch of a button.
As I started to play the game, I didn't mind the players so much, they weren't very disruptive but occasionally they'd clear out all the hostile NPCs before you can, which can be annoying to some people, I suppose you could always try to play at different times so there would be less people too, depending on your timezone. If you were playing with friends or playing in a clan or something, I'm sure the game would be a lot more enjoyable for you. Support spells in singleplayer Elder Scrolls games didn't really work well, but now classes feel more meaningful, even though there's a little less room to play with customizing roles and classes.
I will give a big compliment to the graphics in this game, they are quite gorgeous. High Rock is a place I've always wanted to visit, and the original Daggerfall game wasn't my cup of tea, and now as I explore it I feel like I've found a new spark of love for The Elder Scrolls series, fill me with hope and anticipation for the next Elder Scrolls game!
Highlights.

> Classes are great
> Combat still vaguely feels like an Elder Scrolls game
> Skills system makes more sense
Cons:
