I literally spent 10 minutes chasing another player so I could click on his image, drag the option-bar over to "talk", and then try to type before he was out of range...  Not exactly very...  multiplayer.  This is a multiplayer game where a bunch of other players wander around as if they were silent NPCs.  And I doubt it's the player attitude, it's the mechanic.
Also, for those of you who are long-time fans of the Elder Scrolls games.  This game has a class-system.  That means you can't play however you want.  Also, instead of exploring at your leasure, there seems to be a heavy drive (probably because of respawn rate) to hack and slash your way through levels.  No more enjoying the countryside, chit-chatting wtih NPCS and collecting flowers and butterflies.  No more hunting either, from what I can tell.  Like many of the MMOs out there, it's just a level grind.
That being said;
The world is BEAUTIFUL, and IF you play it thinking of it like a single-player game, then this game has some charming qualities.  I do enjoy seeing all the various cultures of Tamriel, meeting NPCs (which are fully voice acted).  The storyline for the quests (that I've seen so far) seem to be pretty good.  If "hack and slash" is how you like to do your RPGs, then this one will fill your needs.
But if you want community.  Look elsewhere.
It is good that there's no fee-per month anymore, but compared to other MMOs (and even compared to it's previous single-player titles), this game seems... lacking... Except for in Environmental beauty and lore depth.

I found Alien Isolation to be a great addition to the survival horror genre.  It gave me a lot of what I was looking for in terms of gameplay.  (this review has spoilers)
1) Stealth or direct confrontation - you can go in guns blazing, you can set traps, you can distract, or you can attract the alien and have him kill others.  Even just plain hiding and waiting the alien out as he looks around the room made me tense.  Amanda is not a tank so engaging a group of people or synthetics at a time is risky.
2) Cool stuff - I enjoyed the weapons and all of the craftable items.  I've actually managed to use every item in the game (some I used poorly and will practice on a second playthrough) and all the items in my inventory made sense.  The weapons are straight forward but what I expected.  Of course my heart yearns for the weaponry and motion tracker of the colonial marines.  I hope those will appear in a future DLC (season pass hint for the devs).
3) Crafting - crafting was simple and uncomplicated.  Find the components and craft items on the fly.  You do not need a bench or tool area or shop or anything.  I would have liked maybe a little more depth - say advanced items available in a machine or tech shop.
4) Utility items - got a kick out of the cutting torches, upgrades for them and how they allowed access to new areas, and the tension present while it took me a minute to cut through a panel.  Got to play this game with headphones and listen for the alien while you are working.  The security tuner (hacking device) was at times difficult.  Probably because of my fat fingers trying to mash the keys and get the code in quickly.  Maybe allow those to be remapable to save some frustration and grief.
5) Radial menu & quick action keys - I only found the keys for the weapons.  The number keys.  The radial menu was required to access my crafted items.  I'll go through again and see if I can assign keys to crafted items or if there are shortcuts.  I found using the radial menu  a bit of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥  I consistently would select a weapon or item and have it change to something else on the main screen.  That is a definite issue that needs to be addressed for me.  It caused a lot of frustration.  I'm neutral about accessing crafting from the radial menu.  That seems ok.  Could be split off to somewhere else but it's good enough for now.
6) Save game check points - I adapted to it and so I guess I'm ok with it.  In a few locations I became frustrated with the distance I had to travel after reloading 20 times because I kept getting killed.  There are a few maps that could use an extra save terminal.  This is an easy fix for an update and wouldn't tie up a lot of time/effort for the devs.
7)General observations -
a) Shotgun and spike gun should slightly injure and repel the alien.  The revolver should have no effect (as it does).  Pipe bomb should also repel the alien.
b) Time delay on a placed noise maker should be an extra 5-7 seconds longer.
c) Where alien is waiting in a vent overhead to ambush you, you should be able to fire up your flamethrower and drive      it away.
d) more friendly or neutral humans and synthetics.  It would increase the tension and make me check more often.  I knew after a while that I had to fight everyone and everything.
e) Amanda is an engineer or tech by trade.  Not getting through certain doors didn't make sense to me.  Locked or low power?  I'd like to see more work-arounds to open up exploration for those of us who are so anal that we have to explore every nook and cranny of a map and pick up every loose item that isn't nailed down.
f) Speaking only from personal preference I would have wanted a more detailed inventory system a la Deus Ex or System Shock.
Speaking of System Shock, i consider this one of the best contenders to be considered a "spiritual successor" to that game.  No Bioshock was not that for me.  Sci-Fi survival horror is a particular niche and difficult to pull off.
These guys did a great job with the atmosphere, tension, and game play.  The story is decent enough but predictable.  Not a lot of different directions you can take the story but a bad story can really hurt so this one was solid and got us where we needed to be in a believable manner.
There is a TON of source material that is canon for this series and I have high hopes for this game.  I picked up the season pass and DLCs after my playthrough to show my support and express my confidence in the team.
Thank you for a thorougly enjoyable game.

Alien Isolation redefines what it means for a game to be immersive.  It shies away from the usual FPS genre by putting you in the shoes of a vulnerable human being where every uncalculated action could be fatal.
There are very few weapons and ammo in the game and using them is usually a bad idea.  Any loud noises are a bad idea.  If not the Alien or the synthetics, it will be the humans who get you.
There's quite a bit of tension and sneaking isn't as simple as one might expect.  The Alien is extremely agile and can follow you anywhere you might think is safe.  It learns from your actions and adapts accordingly.  Hide in cabinets too often and it will use all sorts of tricks to get you to reveal your presence before busting open the cabinet.  It even fakes some of its actions, making you think it left the room running when in fact it's on its way back.  Some have complained about the repetitive tasks but they're never the same.  There is actually a reason behind every action and it's not always about the Alien as there are different parts of the game where the Alien isn't the center of interest.  This is exactly what makes Alien Isolation stand out.  A human cannot just take on a killing machine with bazookas and rocket launchers in a ship in the middle of space.  The need to be clever is an essential part of the game and trying to beat the adaptive AI is actually a lot of fun.
Technically, the visuals are stunning.  The dynamic lighting and volumetrics with astonishing attention to detail and grading with little to no slowdown on a 4 year old laptop give a very cinematic experience.  This is as close as it gets to the first Alien movie.  Such hard work to reproduce the original look and feel of the movie goes a long way.  The result is an experience so close to the movie that for once, it is possible to experience what the crew of the Nostromo experienced first hand.  Evey time I enter a new room, I stand baffled at how amazing the game looks.  The combination of high resolution textures, vectorised textures, dynamic soft shadows, shader effects and particle FX give it a very cinematic feel.  Lighting is by far the strongest aspect of the game as it is not only realistic, it's used in such ways that it helps tell the story.  This is film making in a game.
Alien Isolation is a pure gem in today's rogue FPS shooting genre.  A true masterpiece that should not be overlooked.

Seriously though this game is a 'better running' (though lag is still an issue and when you lag the screen smears and you are essentially blind for a second or longer) clone of other games that roll on the same formula:
- Spawn naked and die.
- Spawn naked and die.
- Spawn naked and gather enough for a base.
- Base attracts attention. Die. Respawn inside base. Die.
- Spear comes through the wall. Die.
The real attempt to break the formula is the infamy system. The problem is it doesn't fix anything. The infamy system is supposed to make people think twice about killing someone but it doesn't. The game itself isn't bad but if you aren't the type that enjoys killing and griefing people for no reason you should probably just keep your money.

Slime Rancher is an open world exploration game full of adorable blob creatures that can be collected throughout various areas of the game. Of course there is also a farming aspect to the game as well in which I can almost say is the secondary objective of this game, as exploration is rewarding enough, with enough work and dedication, with the right materials the farm can basically run itself, it's your job to expand it...
I find that the primary objective this game hits right on the nose is exploration. The first day I got this on the Steam Summer Sale (6/22/2017) I played about three hours before becoming truley adept to the strategy therefore becoming addicted to the game like Nicotine, I ended up pulling an all nighter like an idiot totalling to 10 hours the first day! But still there was something I could not grasp...the landscape. There could easily be 20+ hours of exploring the vast acres of wildlife, and by acres I mean literal miles upon miles or unique landscape. I have never gotten physically lost in a videogame before, I know the maps of Skyrim, Cyrodiill, Morrowind, and even Destiny like the back of my hand, even with hours upon hours of wondering the wilderness I can barely grasp the layout of the 2nd area.
Onto the orginisation of the game; the variety of slimes, food and landscape is astonishing. Right when it seems like every type of food and slime has been collected there always seems to be a few more you missed. Don't even get me started on the breeding system, I want to keep this review under a 10 hour read. Basically every Slime can be inbread with eachother casuing specific effects that may prove benifical to significant siduations.
Finally for the most important aspect of this game; personally this game hit hard. And I'm not talking performance wise, no, this game is a smooth 60 fps on highest settings, wonderfully optimised. This game got me in the feels. The tranquility of the sunsets, the quietness of the nights, the welcoming laughter of the playful pink slimes bouncing around in their open habitat. Each time I launched this game my common day-to-day stress withered.
I could go on and on about this game, honestly I left out about 90% of it but I just wanted to make a brief review so...
In conclusion, the design of this game is truly a masterpiece, even in Beta format. I'm excited to see what the devoloper has in store for the next update. Truly imagination is the essence of discovery, so get out there and see what the Ranch has to offer.

I tried a couple of times to get the PC port of Dark Souls 1 to work satisfactorily on my pc but in the end gave up because it was just super gnarly and full of issues.   This was exacerbated by not having a controller either, making working out what keys to hit a literal face roll.
I knew i wanted to get some of that sweet Dark Souls experience though so after waiting to see if the sequel's port was any better (it is) and armed with a smexy new 360 controller i coughed up my £40 and dived in.
So this is written as a standalone review of Dark Souls 2.  How it compares to the original i couldn't say, but after enjoying 2 immensely i'm now determined to get it working and find out.  Hey, third time's a charm and all that...
So Difficulty.  How to define Dark Souls difficulty?  Well it certainly is no respecter of your time.  There are quite a few pointless walk backs and what i think is unnecessary time wasting between attempts on bosses.  The hollowing mechanic can be punishing (although there are many ways to avoid it).  I wouldn't really call this difficulty though, frustrating yes, but only difficult in the sense that its annoying to lose your focus in the downtime, making it quite likely that after getting back to the attempt you'll immediately derp it up 5 seconds into the fight.
I would sum the difficulty up as this: 'You messed up?  Go back and do it again, but this time, try sucking less.'  Which honestly is fair enough.  I've played plenty of games that were equally harsh (especially in the 8 bit era).  The key is whether the game has you able to blame it or yourself for failure.  Fortunately, some issues not withstanding, 95% of the time you died because you messed up.    And so accepting that you then know what you've got to do, and when you finally nail that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tough enemy, that feeling of accomplishment is genuine, addictive and what makes this game great.
So yep, this game is rewarding, its also immediately satisfying to play.  Attacks have weight, momentum and risk.  Parrying takes skill, stamina needs to be conserved and utilised efficiently, knowing whether that enemy's combo is a 2 or 3 attack one is the difference between life and death.
The issues when you can blame the game though...Well there are some.  I'd recommend Matthewmatosis's 40 minute video critique for most of these issues, but for me the biggest annoyance for me was enemy lock.  The number of times it would randomly  pick the one furthest away to lock onto and spaz my camera out i lost count of.  When one enemy dies it automatically locks on the next, which you'd think would be useful, but more often than not leaves you with a spear lodged in your ribcage.   Worse still is lock on large bosses, and most bosses are large as you'd expect.  The worst offenders for me were the Royal Rat Authority and Giant Lord who both turned into a game of chase the left leg as the camera jerked about and the bosses rotated in circles trying to stomp on little ol' me.  Many deaths and much rage were had that way.
Graphically is pretty ropey in places, average at best.  Ascetically though it often is kinda beautiful; first seeing Majula's morning sun, the Dragon Aerie, approaching the castles... but it is somewhat spoilt by the obvious difference in resolution between the background and foregrounds, like some cheap film production where they couldn't afford to go on location.   It runs just fine though, even on my aging rig.
I enjoyed the discoverable lore, conversations were there to be listened to if you wanted to.  Story and background was hinted at just enough and some of the NPCs were memorable like Lucatiel and Pete Serafinowicz's Mild Mannered Pate.  The RPG elements, particular the meaningful choices in building a character, even though each soul level doesn't amount to much there are genuine reasons to take a point in each attribute and no 'right' way, or must have weapon really.  There will  always be popular weapons that are perceived as OP but everything is viable and skill is always key.
To be honest criticising a game is much easier than praising it, and again i'd just point you to that video above for more of that.  I don't want to spend so much time being negative which has already demanded 60hrs of my time and i'm not done with it (NG play throughs, trying different builds, not even mentioning the pvp which might actually be the most fun thing...)
There are so many cheap games, so many choices, Steam libraries become Steam backlogs and i'll sit there with 10 games installed and half played and no compulsion to play any of them, let alone finish them.  So when one comes along that demands my time to exclusion of all others, friends, food, fresh air, life generally, then that has to be a game to rank amongst the very best.  So yeah, would recommend.  Just ya know, don't get mad, get even ;)

All in all I would recommend this game. It surely had a bad start, but since then it is constantly improving.
The good things:
-No turn limits in the grand campaign. This finally allows defensive players like myself to enjoy their preferred playstyle. This is an improvement to previous TW titles.
-The province system. Gives you incentives to capture whole provinces to access edicts.
-Limited army numbers. This creates an additional tactical level. There are surely situation when you really need more armies, but a good planning in advance really helps.
-The faction require different playstyles based on the available units. This creates a high re-playability. Unlike e.g. Shogun 2.
Things that require improvement:
-The diplomacy options feel limited and sometimes seem to make no sense.
-A change from 1 year per turn to 4 or 12 turns per year would be really welcome.
-The availlabilty and strength of field artillery needs to be adressed. Right now it seems that every village chief has his own corps of mercenary engineers.
(-Some players claim that the siege AI needs to be improved. For me the AI never bugged and actually was really improved during the last patches. )
The DLCs:
-Blood&Gore: Pretty useful to help with the immersion.
-War beasts: The weakest DLC. Gives you flavour units for a few factions. Those units are rather useless in endgame.
-Greek states: A good DLC that lets you play as Epirus, Athens or Sparta. All three factions are rather defensive, escpecially Sparta.
-Nomadic tribes: Another fun DLC. You have to rely on cavalry only which forces you to play more offensive and tactical. There is no infantry available to hide behind. Gives you access to Royal Scythians, Messagetae and Roxolani.
-Pirates and Raiders: No opinion yet. You can test the playstyle with the free Getae faction.
- Cesar in Gaul: A mediocre DLC. You get the CiG short campaign that unfortunately has a turn limit. Additionally You get access to the Nervii faction. If You like to play a Gallic tribe then the Arverni are already available with the main game.
-Hannibal at the Gates: A good DLC. Again a short campaign with turn limit. Additionally two Iberian (Lusitani and Arevaci) and one Greek faction (Syracuse). Though sadly, Syracuse is basically just a copy&paste from Athens with slightly different faction boni.
Mods:
Quite a number of mods are available. Personally I would only consider one that gives me more turns per year. Best check the workshop for more informations.

I reached veteran rank 1 on my main and have beaten the main story line, so I believe I can list my impressions of the Elder Scrolls Online: Tamriel Unlimited, especially since it took me around 180 hours. Those hours include maybe 10-20 hours of PvP and me doing ABSOLUTELY EVERY SINGLE SIDE-QUEST AND DUNGEON in the Aldmeri Dominion faction zones. I have the achievement to show.
Lets get down to the important things. First of all, if you're one of those typical, ever-thirsty MMORPG fans who claim all MMO's of past (except your precious baby you love and hate, WoW) suck despite loving each new one for a month or two then abandoning it, ever searching for the next new big thing, then no. This game isn't for you. I recommend you try out FF14 instead, it's amazing how such a failure became an incredible revival.
ESO is a mega ultra casual MMO, and take this sincerely from someone who played Toontown for much longer than he should have. IF YOU RUSH THROUGH EVERYTHING, YOUR EXPERIENCE IS HARSHLY DAMPENED. If you're concerned about reaching max level above all else, you will hate this game. The grind that you have to try to find in this game is incredibly boring, because only quests give xp. Oh, but other MMO's give lots of quest xp too, what's the big deal? The big deal is that quests have some of the best voice-acting in MMO's to date.
The writing is generally good, and there's tons of optional text to go through. Again, this makes sense why some people claim they are boring because they spam through the text choices to continue to the next event. What IS a valid complaint is "quests are uninspired". In a different fashion, though. There are the few "kill x this, return x that" quests, but most get very wild and different in execution, including the theme or characters of the quest being presented differently than normal. However, they still boil down to three different scenarios: you wait for characters to finish a conversation, you do a Skyrim-tier puzzle (some involve reading, watch out people-who-despise-reading!), and Good/Bad karma choices. Believe it or not, the Good/Bad decisions you can make in quests do affect your gameworld, but in EXTREMELY minor ways. Like, we're talking about a character that won't be alive versus being alive later on. If the character lives, they just get to say more lines if you bother to talk to them, etc. Therefore, the karma choices aren't executed that well.
Combat is more or less the same as it was in beta. Two hotbars for skills, 5 each, can be swapped between. You cannot access more than that at once, ever.
Music is great and shares elements of tracks from Oblivion and Morrowind.
PvP is a GW2-like zergfest that isn't much fun, even in the noob PvP campaign, until you're an appropriate mid-range level like the 30's.
One surprising thing about this game is that the community is actually rather friendly most of the time. It still takes a while to find people to group with you at all and that leads me to a MAJOR flaw with the game...
the LFG system. I feel like it should work, but I also feel like absolutely no one uses it, so it doesn't work because it can't find anyone to group me with. You will be stuck eternally on searching for a specific dungeon, and if you do eventually get into a group for specifically the dungeon you're looking for, the members of the group will not respond, probably kick you out, or be in a completely different area. Aside from that glaring issue, most bugs and glitches have been eliminated since launch, making the game stabler than it initially was.
I don't know how much else I can describe the game, other than it being a super casual mmorpg that only a super casual mmorpg player can like, one that reads everything, listens to every npc fully, does all the quests... when played like that, ESO is very comfy. If you're expecting more than comfy, the game is mediocre.
Averaging it all together, game is a solid 7/10 now, and worth the money if you're someone who buys on amount of content in-game.
Goodbye.
EDIT: Very soon, the game will eradicate it's former system of level-gated, zone-gated content. They will go with the formula true Elder Scrolls games have used, where you can walk anywhere and do any quest at any level, with any friend.

Alien: Isolation is pretty much the perfect Aliens game. The polished graphics and sounds combine to create a terrifying environment to spend a few hours playing hide and seek with the formidable xenomorph. The alien and other adversaries behave exactly how you would expect and the tension hardly ever lets up.
Some of the criticism bestowed upon the game include the amount of backtracking required, but I found this helped the setting feel more authentic. The save points are pretty regular and there were no areas I couldn’t get through after one or two attempts. There is also some disapproval about the long length of the game, but I don't agree with this.
My only criticism of the game is the crafting system. There is an abundance of materials and most of the items I crafted were superfluous.
One tip for new players: the motion tracker points you to your next objective point. I didn’t realise this until the end of the game, after spending a lot of unnecessary time creeping around trying to find items – although this was fun!
Overall one of the best games this year.

An amazing experience. In my opinion this is the best game to be released this year, and probably since before 2010. Easily the best game set in the Alien universe and in the survival horror genre. Hopefully other developers will learn a lot from this. The tension, atmosphere and authenticity in this game are absolutely spot on. Play it on hard mode with headphones and it's just sublimely terrifying. Everything in the game just works together to increase the tension.
There's a lot of people online complaining about the randomness of the Aliens AI and how unfair it is.  I would recommend you don't listen to any bad reviews that go on about the aliens 'random' AI. I believe that these people all love playing Call of Battlefield Arena Tournament, running around with an automatic weapon, doing 360 flying noscopes, shouting about how good Chuck Norris' left testicle is. The A.I is only random to a point, the Alien reacts to the world around it. If you bump into a chair by accident and get eaten, that's unlucky. I've never died to it unfairly, it's always been my fault for not paying enough attention or doing something stupid. The Alien is supposed to terrorise you. That's it's job. If there was a way to exploit it, or an easy way to get past it, you might as well remove it from the game.
Definitely worth the money I spent on it, and I highly recommend it to everybody.

Dota 2 was no fun for me. It was overcomplicated, boring, and servers were awful (waiting for a game took 2 hours, and even after that, it was underwhelming).
SMITE isn't original. It doesn't bring something unbelievably new to the table, but, at least the control scheme is a lot easier to learn and understand, and it makes the game more action oriented than the other games in the genre.
The setting is also kind of original, pitting gods from different religions against each other, each with it's own unique skills and features. It's very entertaining to see an Egyptian god such as Osiris fighting against the Nord god Thor.
Every character is unique, every type of player is gaurenteed to find the one that fits him most. Can't decide who to pick from the starters? Rent a hero, then buy it.
My favorite type of player would be the Ranged Mage types, like Ra (Actually it's pronounced RRRRRRRRRRrrrrrrra), Zhong Kui, and Nox.
And now for the bad news - The community is bad. Most people will start blaming and get extremely overheated over losing or not having at least 10/1 K/D. This game is easy to learn, but hard to master, and you will stick out like a sausage covered Redneck in a vegitarian restaurant in Japan when you're a beginner. Reporting may help, but no behaviour is enforced and penalties to players who 'Troll' or misbehave or abandon ship are not doing their job.
Also the servers are horrible and it might take 10 minutes to just load the start screen. It might take 1-4 minutes to find a match after logging in which takes 5 minutes (when you're playing with your friends and hoping for them to actually manage to log in). Frustrating, to say the least.
With all of this said and done, I give SMITE a Ra Ultimate/10, because while sometimes it may be as if you fired it up for no satisfying result, at other times, you just feel "damn, it was worth it".

I think this game has just invented a whole new genre for itself: "Cat and Mouse" - with one hideously vile and intelligent cat!
Stealth games have a way to be played: watch the enemy, note the pattern of their movements, and time when they move - then you make YOUR move.  If the enemy detects you, you hide and wait for the detection cooldown until the enemy returns to their patrol.  Simple stuff, and actually enjoyable: the core ingredient of great games like the Thief franchise and Dishonored - games that really make good use of stealth.  This is the stuff I love.
But would a real adversary pace the same strip of ground with exact timing?  Would a real adversary detect your presence but forget you 30 seconds later?  Of course not.  A real adversary would become alert, would narrow their search area, would move faster and be more determined as they close in on you - and yes, if you keep hiding in the same types of location, you're kind of a dead giveaway - literally!  One thing a real adversary would never do is forget that you're there.  Once you're noticed, you WILL be hunted down.
Welcome to Alien: Isolation.
Movie license games are often quite terrible, and there's certainly been controversy over past alien games, but this one is different.  Imagine if you could step aboard the Nostromo back in the day when Ellen Ripley was the sole survivor along with an angry and determined alien species hunting her down.  Imagine if you could step into a 1979 realisation of a sci-fi environment that is somehow retro yet still feels properly sci-fi even now despite the chunky monochrome screens - like stepping right into the movie set and BEING Ellen Ripley.  Alien Isolation brings you that experience - raw, without new-age gloss, and without any sympathy as you realise that what you have at your disposal is pretty much nothing.
It's not the most horrific game (some might argue that it is not pure horror at all), and it's not a typical stealth game.  If you took the ingredients of horror, stealth and survival, you're close.  This game is about being hunted down.  Your adversary is faster than you, stronger than you, and quite possibly more intelligent than you might give it credit for.  Creative Assembly have crafted an AI that's totally unscripted, behaves randomly with unpredictability, yet like a digital 'Furby' it learns from everything its prey does, and learns by its environment.  There is no 'detection cooldown' or fixed patrol patterns.  If you make it fearful by a blast of flamer, it will soon become immune to the trick.  In fact, forget everything you ever learnt about playing a stealth game.  This is the closest thing to real-life stealth, and it's deadly.  You are definitely being hunted!
But it's not the alien that is wholly responsible for the gripping tension and fear of this game.  It's the game itself, and the way its story unfolds.  The game terrifies by what it doesn't reveal to you, like finding yourself in an eerily dark and silent area of the space station that previously had thundered with the noise of the alien pounding through the overhead vents, or coming face to face with one of the "Working Joe" androids - face expressionless (like a shop mannequin) but eyes that look right AT you, and follow you wherever you go.  These are genuinely unnerving and very much the fodder of childhood mightmares.  You KNOW something is not right.  There is something really not right, but you don't know what it is...  These moments genuinely cause discomfort and ensure you're ragged with nerves throughout.
Alien Isolation is a long game.  People talk of taking around 25 hours to complete it.  I took 42 hours - on EASY with no exploring!  You will not be given all the tools you'll need to open doors at the beginning of the game, but you will backtrack much later so don't worry about doors with impossible locking mechanisms.  Going back to these locked doors later in the game is not critical to your objectives, but they contain Nostromo recordings to fill out more of the story for fans - and recorded by cast from the movie.
I can't say any more because spoilers and more spoilers, but be warned that you're in for one heck of a ride!  If you ever wanted to put yourself through the same horror that Ellen Ripley faced in 1979's "Alien", then this game is it.

Alien: Isolation is the highly anticipated sequel to the original film from 1979, 'Alien'; it's made by Creative Assembly, the developers responsible for the Total War franchise. After a slew of disappointing games based on the Alien franchise, it was about time for a game to do the franchise justice; I can happily say that Alien: Isolation goes above and beyond my expectations and delivers a phenomenal game unlike any other.
The player steps into the shoes of Amanda Ripley, who is still searching for her mother 15 years after the disaster aboard the Nostromo. A representative from Weyland-Yutani informs you that the black box recorder from the Nostromo has been collected aboard the Sevastopol space station, and is ready for collection. You set off with your team to discover what happened to Ellen Ripley and the Nostromo, and get more than you bargained for with the presence of the Alien from the original film.
Right from the start, Alien: Isolation is an image of dedication and love for the source material. Locations in the game have been designed with a low-fi 70's aesthetic in mind, and the result is mind blowing; the Sevastopol and the Torrens are increasingly reminiscent of the Nostromo from the film, and the attention to detail is astounding. The game is graphically fantastic, and you'll find yourself amazed by the sights on numerous occasions (if you have the time to enjoy them, that is).
The gameplay is startlingly innovative, and is memorable for a number of reasons. You'll spend most of the game in stealth mode, avoiding humans and synthetics, and of course, the Alien. The Alien itself is terrifying to encounter; it's smart, and it will kill you many, many times. You can use flamethrowers and molotovs to avoid it in direct combat, otherwise it's an instantly gruesome death. You can also use flares and noisemakers (crafted via a simple but satisfying crafting system) to divert the Alien's attention and sneak by unnoticed. Combat with androids and humans is standard fare, however you are able to use your numerous gadgets to focus the Alien's attention on them, and thereby clearing the way to get through. The game puts heavy emphasis on flight over fight, and you'll feel a gratifying sense of accomplishment by completing sections quickly and quietly.
The Alien itself is one of the many highlights of this game. Just like the creature from the film, it can sense your movements if you move too quickly and clumsily, and will kill you in seconds if you become too careless. You can use your motion tracker to detect the Alien's whereabouts, but the beep emitted by the device can also give away your position and again result in death. All of these factors make you feel like you're fighting a genuine enemy, and is a refreshing change from the run and gun fare of recent years.
The developers have also put a great deal of care into the sound design of the game. Every creak, groan and beep emitted from the Sevastopol space station puts you on edge, and this in combination with the fantastic score makes the experience feel as authentic as it can get. Encounters with the Alien are filled with atmosphere, as you can hear the creature moving around in numerous vents and airducts.
There's also a large amount of content included in this game. The story mode took me roughly 20 hours to complete, and there is also a Survivor mode challenge map in addition to the two preorder DLC'S. Anyone who pays $50 for this game will certainly not be disappointed.
Aien: Isolation is the Alien game fans have been waiting for. As a huge fan of the film, I was extremely impressed by the game's ability to recreate what made the film so great, in addition to carving it's own niche in the survival horror genre. A solid game through and through, Alien: Isolation will remain memorable for years to come, and is a must-play for any survival horror afficionado. 9.5 / 10

Graphics: 6/10 - Good design, I like the cartoon type they have, but the overall quality could have been better, some textures are a bit messy.
Gameplay: 9/10 - An excellent heir to the mighty Dishonored. Faster, deeper, but also more complete and well rounded, with even more gameplay possibility since you have two characters. However, the story is a bit short. Even if the replay possibilities are enormous, I would have enjoyed a more sophisticated plot and longer story, like the first one offered.
Story: 6/10 - Almost too much linear and straightforward. At the beginning of the game, you know exactly what is gonna happen and how this is going to end. The bad guy lacks charism, even if the main protagonists gained some.
Level Design: 8/10 - All the levels are large areas with many available routes, secrets and bonuses all around. You can go straightforward or in depht, it will be very enjoyable all the like. The city of Karnaca is well represented, and you get to see various places. The only thing I miss from the original game is the steampunk/victorian vibe. It was not the goal of this game, but I miss it a bit nonetheless.
General feeling: 9/10 - I really enjoyed playing both Corvo and Emily, the gameplay is very rich and offers many possibilities that match the playground that Karnaca is. Every level can be done in a number of various ways, hence the replay possibilities the game offers.
Conclusion/Final note: 8/10 - A worthy successor of the first Dishonored. Extremely enjoyable, very fun to play, this game is a true playground to explore and own. Appreciable design even if not extremely beautiful. The music accompanies well the game but is rapidly forgettable. Arkane was playing with high stakes by creating a second Dishonored, but they did not mess anything up, and made an even better game than the first one. However, the story is a bit short and simple in my opinion, and even if it was not my case, Apparently the PC version suffers from many bugs, which sucks a bit.
If you enjoyed the first one, you should really play this game. Uf you are new to the series, I might recommend watching videos or trying the first one before, in case it's not your type of gameplay.

Ok fine I'll give an actual opinion.
This game is better than 90% of the games that came out at the time and are coming out now.
It's a good game, but it's not a good Dark Souls game. They seemed to want to honour and respect the original Dark Souls and Demon Souls, but they completly missed the point.
Souls game shouldn't be focused on difficulty, look up any interview with the original director, Hidetaka Miyazaki, and he always says that difficulty wasn't the point. Difficulty was used to set up a moment for the player. For example, when the second Gargoyle drops down into the first in Dark Souls 1, this sets up a moment of panic, as my chances of beating the boss have suddenly dropped. Or a better example is the first with Ornstein and Smough, what a feeling it was to finally beat this boss. Darks Souls just cranks up the difficulty for no reason. How can we make this boss harder? Add a bunch of minions to distract the player. The Worst examples are the Royal Rat Authority and the Belfry Gargoyles, the first being a complete copy of Siv , being nowhere near as memorable, and the other is just a copy and paste from DaS1, now there's 3 of them.
The combat of Dark Souls does not fit fighting multiple enemies, it's playing up it's weaknesses and not it's strengths, which is 1v1 combat.
The story is a carbon copy from DaS1, the music is not as good and there were like 2 bosses that were actually memorable, those being the Darklurker and the Royal Rat Vanguard. These are also both optional bosses.
Do I reccomend this game? Yeah it's still a good game. But it's a bad Souls game.

This game is incredible. It accomplishes its goal of modernizing the feel of Half-Life extremely well. It captures the sense of tedium in the intro, then in seconds pulls the rug from under your feet and completely reverses the atmosphere. Like the original game, it skillfully mixes the usual FPS enemies like shambling zombies and other guys with guns with more creative and unique enemies that catch you off guard and make you rethink and redesign your strategies.
The developers managed to combine the original feel of the gameplay, enemies, and weapons with updated visuals, sounds, and level layouts for an experience that is both new and nostalgic.
If you're a fan of Half-Life or first-person shooters in general, you owe it to yourself to play this game.

Your first few minutes in Hurtworld are promising. You walk about, picking up supplies, getting a feel for the game. You learn how to survive and craft. Then, you find other players,
who will kill you no matter what,
for no reason,
every time.
I would have enjoyed it if I didn't have to deal with the terrible community, or if at least SOME of them were friendly. I met no person on my travels who wasn't hostile to me. It doesn't matter what you do. Surrender. Give gifts. Salute. They don't care.
I get that it's supposed to be a "hardcore" survival game, but at this point in time, it's simply too difficult to last even 2 days with all of the online players hunting you down, especially if you're a new player. This game doesn't reward you for being smart or creative, because neither of those things will help you survive. Only luck (that predators don't find you) and grinding (for resources) will allow you to survive.
Gameplay is a grindfest combined with a diceroll chance that a player will find you (and they WILL find you), kill you, and take everything you have.
You will die. Often.

Dota 2 was no fun for me. It was overcomplicated, boring, and servers were awful (waiting for a game took 2 hours, and even after that, it was underwhelming).
SMITE isn't original. It doesn't bring something unbelievably new to the table, but, at least the control scheme is a lot easier to learn and understand, and it makes the game more action oriented than the other games in the genre.
The setting is also kind of original, pitting gods from different religions against each other, each with it's own unique skills and features. It's very entertaining to see an Egyptian god such as Osiris fighting against the Nord god Thor.
Every character is unique, every type of player is gaurenteed to find the one that fits him most. Can't decide who to pick from the starters? Rent a hero, then buy it.
My favorite type of player would be the Ranged Mage types, like Ra (Actually it's pronounced RRRRRRRRRRrrrrrrra), Zhong Kui, and Nox.
And now for the bad news - The community is bad. Most people will start blaming and get extremely overheated over losing or not having at least 10/1 K/D. This game is easy to learn, but hard to master, and you will stick out like a sausage covered Redneck in a vegitarian restaurant in Japan when you're a beginner. Reporting may help, but no behaviour is enforced and penalties to players who 'Troll' or misbehave or abandon ship are not doing their job.
Also the servers are horrible and it might take 10 minutes to just load the start screen. It might take 1-4 minutes to find a match after logging in which takes 5 minutes (when you're playing with your friends and hoping for them to actually manage to log in). Frustrating, to say the least.
With all of this said and done, I give SMITE a Ra Ultimate/10, because while sometimes it may be as if you fired it up for no satisfying result, at other times, you just feel "damn, it was worth it".

EDIT 1:
Since posting this originally (25th of November), the game has improved a fair bit, performance wise at least.
Of course my original complaints about the story are still present, and likely will forever, but in it's current state, as of the time of writing, is much much better. Arkane clearly is trying, but it would've been nice if they gave themselves a couple of months to make sure it ran well on everything that met the specifications.
Performance issues are still present, I still occasionally get stutters/freezes that last a second or two, but it is better than it used to. However, there are people with better builds than me (See: StealthGamerBR) that are still reporting issues.
Since the original review, I have played it a lot more, and noticed a lot more about the game, and I'm fairly impressed.
This is on a very good road to being a recommendation, and me finally feeling satisfied in the hype that I personally had, however I wont be changing until I believe this product is up to par to what it should be.
----------------------------------
Deleted my original review, it didn't say any of the problems that this game has.
One, the story and characters are okay. At best.
The only thing that makes the characters good is that they took most of them from the first game.
There's no new characters to care about, unlike the first game, where it was really easy to actually start caring about characters. But this game? No. All your friends are people from the first game. The only two new characters that they could've built upon disappear from the story very quickly.
The rest of the new characters are enemies, and not even that great ones like Daud.
There are some good ones, like Hypatia and Jindosh, but it doesn't make up for it.
The only characters I cared about, I cared about because of the first game.
This game fell into the exact same pit that The Force Awakens did, except the games' fall was much worse. Due to a lot of the characters being from the first game, it just feels like the devs yelling "HEY DO YOU REMEMBER THIS PERSON????" and felt like they put less time into creating new, better characters.
I know it sounds like I'm harping on the same issue, and I am, but this is a big issue to me, because the characters were such a large part of the first game, but this one feels like they didn't bother as much.
This game did a lot of things right, but a lot of things wrong. A lot.
The skill trees are great, the gameplay feels fantastic (when the performance isn't taking a dump on it), but Arkane dropped the ball on the story and characters.
This is really negative, I'll list the things I like about this game:
- Skill trees: All the abilities seem to have a progression that makes a lot of sense, and all of them seem very useful.
- Bonecharm crafting: This is a mechanic I really, honestly never expected, and it works, it is very useful. As a side note though, at the current time, it appears it may be bugged with stacking certain perks.
- Movement: They did this very well, to me, everything just feels right with it.
- Combat: It feels good. Not as good as D1, but on the same token it feels like it improved a lot on it, and is a lot more accomidating for combat, abilities-wise
- Delilah: She, although falling into my cameo gripe, is a good villain, even if she was a little better in the DLCs of D1
- Powers: All of the powers feel a lot better than they did in the first game, they did this very well.
I do like a lot of the game, I really do, but they did screw this up. A lot.
I cannot, right now, recommend this in good conscience.
Once these performance issues have been worked out, I would, although it requires a complete rework of the game to deal with my other issues.
This is unfortunate. I had faith in Harvey Smith, and Arkane.
But this is disappointing.

I think this game has just invented a whole new genre for itself: "Cat and Mouse" - with one hideously vile and intelligent cat!
Stealth games have a way to be played: watch the enemy, note the pattern of their movements, and time when they move - then you make YOUR move.  If the enemy detects you, you hide and wait for the detection cooldown until the enemy returns to their patrol.  Simple stuff, and actually enjoyable: the core ingredient of great games like the Thief franchise and Dishonored - games that really make good use of stealth.  This is the stuff I love.
But would a real adversary pace the same strip of ground with exact timing?  Would a real adversary detect your presence but forget you 30 seconds later?  Of course not.  A real adversary would become alert, would narrow their search area, would move faster and be more determined as they close in on you - and yes, if you keep hiding in the same types of location, you're kind of a dead giveaway - literally!  One thing a real adversary would never do is forget that you're there.  Once you're noticed, you WILL be hunted down.
Welcome to Alien: Isolation.
Movie license games are often quite terrible, and there's certainly been controversy over past alien games, but this one is different.  Imagine if you could step aboard the Nostromo back in the day when Ellen Ripley was the sole survivor along with an angry and determined alien species hunting her down.  Imagine if you could step into a 1979 realisation of a sci-fi environment that is somehow retro yet still feels properly sci-fi even now despite the chunky monochrome screens - like stepping right into the movie set and BEING Ellen Ripley.  Alien Isolation brings you that experience - raw, without new-age gloss, and without any sympathy as you realise that what you have at your disposal is pretty much nothing.
It's not the most horrific game (some might argue that it is not pure horror at all), and it's not a typical stealth game.  If you took the ingredients of horror, stealth and survival, you're close.  This game is about being hunted down.  Your adversary is faster than you, stronger than you, and quite possibly more intelligent than you might give it credit for.  Creative Assembly have crafted an AI that's totally unscripted, behaves randomly with unpredictability, yet like a digital 'Furby' it learns from everything its prey does, and learns by its environment.  There is no 'detection cooldown' or fixed patrol patterns.  If you make it fearful by a blast of flamer, it will soon become immune to the trick.  In fact, forget everything you ever learnt about playing a stealth game.  This is the closest thing to real-life stealth, and it's deadly.  You are definitely being hunted!
But it's not the alien that is wholly responsible for the gripping tension and fear of this game.  It's the game itself, and the way its story unfolds.  The game terrifies by what it doesn't reveal to you, like finding yourself in an eerily dark and silent area of the space station that previously had thundered with the noise of the alien pounding through the overhead vents, or coming face to face with one of the "Working Joe" androids - face expressionless (like a shop mannequin) but eyes that look right AT you, and follow you wherever you go.  These are genuinely unnerving and very much the fodder of childhood mightmares.  You KNOW something is not right.  There is something really not right, but you don't know what it is...  These moments genuinely cause discomfort and ensure you're ragged with nerves throughout.
Alien Isolation is a long game.  People talk of taking around 25 hours to complete it.  I took 42 hours - on EASY with no exploring!  You will not be given all the tools you'll need to open doors at the beginning of the game, but you will backtrack much later so don't worry about doors with impossible locking mechanisms.  Going back to these locked doors later in the game is not critical to your objectives, but they contain Nostromo recordings to fill out more of the story for fans - and recorded by cast from the movie.
I can't say any more because spoilers and more spoilers, but be warned that you're in for one heck of a ride!  If you ever wanted to put yourself through the same horror that Ellen Ripley faced in 1979's "Alien", then this game is it.

Alien: Isolation is the highly anticipated sequel to the original film from 1979, 'Alien'; it's made by Creative Assembly, the developers responsible for the Total War franchise. After a slew of disappointing games based on the Alien franchise, it was about time for a game to do the franchise justice; I can happily say that Alien: Isolation goes above and beyond my expectations and delivers a phenomenal game unlike any other.
The player steps into the shoes of Amanda Ripley, who is still searching for her mother 15 years after the disaster aboard the Nostromo. A representative from Weyland-Yutani informs you that the black box recorder from the Nostromo has been collected aboard the Sevastopol space station, and is ready for collection. You set off with your team to discover what happened to Ellen Ripley and the Nostromo, and get more than you bargained for with the presence of the Alien from the original film.
Right from the start, Alien: Isolation is an image of dedication and love for the source material. Locations in the game have been designed with a low-fi 70's aesthetic in mind, and the result is mind blowing; the Sevastopol and the Torrens are increasingly reminiscent of the Nostromo from the film, and the attention to detail is astounding. The game is graphically fantastic, and you'll find yourself amazed by the sights on numerous occasions (if you have the time to enjoy them, that is).
The gameplay is startlingly innovative, and is memorable for a number of reasons. You'll spend most of the game in stealth mode, avoiding humans and synthetics, and of course, the Alien. The Alien itself is terrifying to encounter; it's smart, and it will kill you many, many times. You can use flamethrowers and molotovs to avoid it in direct combat, otherwise it's an instantly gruesome death. You can also use flares and noisemakers (crafted via a simple but satisfying crafting system) to divert the Alien's attention and sneak by unnoticed. Combat with androids and humans is standard fare, however you are able to use your numerous gadgets to focus the Alien's attention on them, and thereby clearing the way to get through. The game puts heavy emphasis on flight over fight, and you'll feel a gratifying sense of accomplishment by completing sections quickly and quietly.
The Alien itself is one of the many highlights of this game. Just like the creature from the film, it can sense your movements if you move too quickly and clumsily, and will kill you in seconds if you become too careless. You can use your motion tracker to detect the Alien's whereabouts, but the beep emitted by the device can also give away your position and again result in death. All of these factors make you feel like you're fighting a genuine enemy, and is a refreshing change from the run and gun fare of recent years.
The developers have also put a great deal of care into the sound design of the game. Every creak, groan and beep emitted from the Sevastopol space station puts you on edge, and this in combination with the fantastic score makes the experience feel as authentic as it can get. Encounters with the Alien are filled with atmosphere, as you can hear the creature moving around in numerous vents and airducts.
There's also a large amount of content included in this game. The story mode took me roughly 20 hours to complete, and there is also a Survivor mode challenge map in addition to the two preorder DLC'S. Anyone who pays $50 for this game will certainly not be disappointed.
Aien: Isolation is the Alien game fans have been waiting for. As a huge fan of the film, I was extremely impressed by the game's ability to recreate what made the film so great, in addition to carving it's own niche in the survival horror genre. A solid game through and through, Alien: Isolation will remain memorable for years to come, and is a must-play for any survival horror afficionado. 9.5 / 10

You and your three mystery solving friends thought that it would be a good idea to go hunting for eight tape recorders across six different locales in Europe. When your friends heard that it would be dark out, no one showed up but you. They can still come along mind you, but for now you're all alone with your flashlight in the darkness. You're never truly alone though. The one that has caused the grizzly murders is here with you, stalking you, watching you with its eyeless face.
Its a nightmarish feeling to be stuck in a realm of darkness whether its a forest with a stream, a museum full of mummies and giant heads, an underground bunker with a submarine and so on. The only accessory on you is a flashlight with a narrow beam. Your feet feel covered in tar. It takes dozens of steps to move the slightest distance. You can run, but when you do, your flashlight sticks to the ground so its tough to gauge just how fast you're going or where you're going.
The one that watches you lights up the immediate area with its luminescent body so you can always see it. Every time it appears, its like metal scraping against metal to send a shiver up your weak and cowardly spine. Your only salvation is to look away and hope it leaves you in peace. If your friends were here, perhaps they could distract it, but no, you're here by yourself. Every moment you stare at its pale white figure you gain its attention more. Tension rise knowing that even if its far away in the distance, any second it can be right in your face. Look away! It wants your eyes.
Searching in the darkness, you hear static to gain your interest. You must be close to a tape recorder. How these things are still playing, you'll never know. The sound grows in its intensity as you pace around a stone figure looking for it. Your flashlight shines to it no matter where you were pointing it originally. There it is, the first of many you'll need to find before you can call it a night.
More darkness, panting as you run and screams from being watched from closer distances. Can it see you or is it as blind as its eyeless face dictates? You turn around to see where it is, if its still following you, but its gone for now. If you had friends with you, perhaps it is after them. Your own skin saved for one of theirs.
Sound in the shadows kicks up in the darkness again, you approach a jade stone. There must be a tape recorder behind it or around it. The green glows in your flashlight's gaze. Static blurs your vision and makes you tremble as your sanity slips away. There must be something special about the jade stones. Have you seen them before in the distance? Seated on the ground, growing out of a museum wall? Are they mere stones or are they the hard shelled cocoons of a viscous blind monster with teeth and claws?
Each night you go out, you feel the same, but you're a different person. You look different, but you'll never know outside of how you feel. Sometimes you feel brave, other times you feel swift or you have more stamina or less. Your name was Sarah last night, but tonight its Kurt. These bodies you inhabit look bright compared to the night's gloom you find yourself in. Its good to be a different person every night, because that's how you tell your friends apart, assuming they had ever shown up. All of it feels so irrelevant the differences between this body and the last are minimal even if something says you're special and unique. Perhaps its best that you're alone. Your friend Frank would probably mess it up with his blue hair and skeleton costume. You're all just bodies to the creature.
Use wisdom and courage to make it through night after night, avoiding the pale white figure that illuminates the darkness. Tuck your fears away to make it through to the next area of your choosing. Perhaps some other night your friends will join you. No one ever comes with you. Its all up to you to endure the startling scares and the shrill shrieks.
When its all over, you and your friends that never showed up are either victorious and can leave or dead at the hands of a ruthless beast that snatches you up one by one. As you cross over into what lies beyond, your steps are recounted and traced with lines across an empty sheet of paper along with how much time you survived. Was it a few seconds? Ten minutes? Thirty? You can survive indefinitely with large dark locales and only one demon hunting you.
Well now that the ambiance is over, its time to kill it with a real review. White Noise is a first person experience that has you searching for tape recorders across six different maps. White Noise Online is indeed online and sold in four packs at a slight discount, because you'll never find anyone playing when you are. In fact some of us would rather play alone in general. It would still be interesting seeing other people and their quirky characters like Frank with his blue hair and skeleton outfit and the Invisible Man or woman running around. It would probably ruin feeling of terror.
The maps are all flat and pitch black with no light other than your flashlight  They each have their unique themes and while I feel there's a good amount of detail and the textures look fair to good, other games look better and have more detail. It feels like they put effort into adding details to make an area feel less bland, but it still feels lacking.
The characters each have flare and color to them that feels cheap yet still elaborate with a good amount of detail. Its the art style of the characters that works against the creepy vibe the game has. Some of the art choices outside the game are unfitting for a game like this.
The underground bunker feels hastily thrown together and bland even if it had jail cells, train cars and a submarine in it. There's no way to go in any of them but the cells. The rest of the map just feels so vacant and empty and that's the case for the majority of the maps. Perhaps that's because the movement speed is so slow that it can take an excessively long time just to walk to the nearest door.
There are a lot of frills White Noise Online has that other contemporaries are lacking. The post game recap is good. The game tells you how to play and what your objective is. It lets you select a map or have one chosen at random. There are even difficulty levels before you head into a game.
The music and sounds set a good creepy tone. The sounds add a lot of shock value when seeing the creature and having sound cues for the tape recorder ensure that you can find it when you're close enough. Again, it feels like a step above other games that make it feel like the developers care and have the ability to go the extra step.
I'm on the fence with White Noise Online whether I should recommend it. Its a good game and above a lot of similar ones with the same objective. Its also cheap so that's always a push in the right direction. If you have friends with it that are willing to play, that's the only way you'll be able to play online.

When you are reading this review you are most likely sure that Black Mesa is a good remake of the first Half-Life, but you are not so sure about spending money on it, right?
Well, I hope my review is going to help you with your decision.
I am a fan of the Half-Life series since the release of the very first game in 1998 and I have played both parts with their respective add-ons over and over. Especially the first Half-Life - I know it entirely by heart.
When Black Mesa was finally released as a free stand-alone modification in 2012 (after seven years of development), I was eagerly anticipating re-visiting the Black-Mesa-compound - without Xen, since it was not included in the first release (and it is still missing).
What an awesome experience it was! Black Mesa was and is definitely the best remake of any game I have seen to this day. It changed everything necessary, but stayed absolutely true to the original. This was what Half-Life would look like, if it would be released today. If somebody would have told me that it was not made by a group of modders, but by Valve itself - I would have believed it.
The gameplay mechanics basically stayed the same; the level design was slightly adjusted, yet overall modernized. The dialogs were made more vivid: Characters like Eli Vance or Isaac Kleiner were no longer exchangeable clones without any noticeable relation to Gordon - now they clearly acted, sounded and looked like they did in Half-Life 2, but only as their 20 years younger versions.
Apropos sound: The soundtrack, made by Joel Nielsen, was phenomenal and worked really well with the ambience of the different places and situations. By the way: You can get it for free at
I do not think that I need to write something about the graphical differences. Black Mesa is based on the Source-engine, just like Half-Life 2 and therefore it looks very similar.
When I finished this wonderful modification, I was sure that, if Black Mesa would be released as a full-priced remake someday, I would buy it right away.
And surprise: After passing the Greenlight-program on Steam in 2012, it was released as a half-priced and somehow further enhanced Early-access-game on May 5th 2015. I got it right on day one.
Now for the big question: Is Black Mesa worth buying it?
Well, the buyable version is slightly enhanced and offers multiplayer and Steam-workshop support. And achievements and trading cards, but those are irrelevant for the game itself, at least in my opinion.
The still missing Xen levels are going to be released for the buyable version only. So if you want to experience the full make-over, you will have to buy it sooner or later.
Those are the pluses for the buyable version, not to mention that the game itself is extremely good, as written above.
There are a few noticeable bugs, such as deformed models of corpses, which appear after reloading a saved game. It does not sound like a big deal, but I did not recall seeing those in the mod-version. You can visit my screenshot library to see what I mean.
Same goes for the effect that objects in your sight are going to be stretched when you move your mouse in a direction that makes those objects go to the edge of your monitor. I also added two screenshots to visualize this description.
There are also some issues with the combat feeling: Some guns just do not feel right; the MP5 for example feels highly imprecise and some enemies can take too much damage. Vortigaunts for example do take two revolver shots before they go down, while they took only one in the original Half-Life. The Alien Controllers on the other hand can be shot down with two to three small bursts from the MP5.
So, should you buy it?
If you are a huge fan of the Half-Life-series and if you want to support the team behind this ambitious project: Yes, buy it. You will not regret it.
If you are not that much of a die-hard fan of the original and you still are unsure about it: Do not buy it just yet. Wait until the campaign is completely included and the bugs are fixed. Then you will be able to enjoy the game as it is meant to be. And that is going to be the point where we are going to see if the full thing is turning out to be as good as the stuff which is available today.

I can recommend this game. SCS software continues to develop the game with map extensions, new  truck models, new cargo. First thing I have to say about this game, don't expect it to be like Skyrim.
It's not Skyrim, it's not Oblivion or Morrowind or any other Elder Scrolls game for that matter. It's a freakin' MMO, and feels like any other MMOs. So only buy this game if you really like MMOs or the such. If you'd rather not buy it to try it out, see if a friend has it and try it out. Then buy it if you like it.
Now, for the actual review. ESO is pretty fun if you can get into it, and even more fun if you have friends to play it with. There is a MASSIVE amount of content in it. Many areas to explore, multiple dungeons to clear, and several playthroughs to be done. Questlines are different depending on which faction you side with, and all have a good amount of things to do.
Characters feel like they have a lot of personality, and you will definitely find people you love and hate. Areas look pretty and are diverse from one another.
Basically, if you like running around and killing things, you've come to the right place.

It is fun and inspiring to see one of the lowest and weakest animals on the planet flying all over your screen using grappling hooks and all sorts of gadgets to traverse through the levels.
The game engine is a little slower than a classic Mario game or Shovel Knight but that is because you are playing as a worm. I assume you can speed it up if you get certain items later in the game. There is so much room for this game to improve on its environments from the classic grassy background to all different kinds of backgrounds. It could give it a more exciting feel. There could also be different kinds of worms later in the game with different kinds of abilities.

I'm 3 hours into this game, and its a pretty basic little survival game. To me it is well worth the 5 dollars. Basically abandoned but works just fine most of the time in its current state. Understand that this is a PvP game. Everyone (and I do mean EVERYONE) is trying to kill everyone else, that's the point, and that's the fun of it. Do not get attached to anything you find, you'll probably end up losing it to the next guy, before the someone else kills him, and the cycle continues. Kill, loot, repeat.
When you finally gear up enough to get your first kill its going to feel amazing, and you might even find yourself on a roll killing a couple of people before you're offed yourself and become a loot-pinata. Servers are pretty unpopulated, but even if you're on a map with one other person you're going to run into them and one of you is going to kill the other unless you're both completely unarmed. In which case you both lucked out, now run away, loot the nearest building and hope to find a weapon before they do.
You will struggle to find food, stay warm, and to have inventory space enough to fill your basic needs. Weapons are scarce, ammo is scarcer, and your best bet is a melee weapon and no flashlight (ie no noise, no spotligBut as you keep playing  you just might find yourself surviving longer and longer.
To figure out the controls you can use the 'Help' selection on the start page for a list of keybindings. Theres basically no other in game instruction, and  It doesnt tell you that you use 1 + 2 to switch weapons, but thats how you do it. You can only carry 2 of them. Anyone complaining about the game being too hard is a acting like a pansy and has no business playing survival games.

Slime Rancher is one of those games where I wasn't entirely sure if I was going to like it. Sure, the slimes were adorable, and the idea of a space ranch seemed cool, but how far would that really go? Would I really want to do nothing but feed bouncing, smiling balls of goo for hours on end?
Short answer: Yes.
Long answer: That's not all that Slime Rancher is. It's a game that allows you to explore, a game that encourages you to experiment, and a game that's more about learning how to handle the challenges that come with each different type of slime than merely tossing them some food every morning. There's plorts to collect, upgrades to buy, and, naturally, hundereds of tiny, grinning, mischievous slimes to capture and care for. This is one of the few games where I'm actively watching to see what comes in the next update, as opposed to just letting things come as they do. It isn't because there's a lack of content, but rather that each update brings something new and exciting, something that adds to the gameplay tremendously.
Would I recommend this game? Absolutely. Sure, it's in early access still, but don't let that scare you away. As it is, it's still a solid and enjoyable game, and I doubt that I'll grow tired of it any time soon.

Amazing! That's the best word to describe this quick-action multiplayer game. Again, just as the other call of duty series it has a perfect storyline where you get a real band with the main characters.
Not as bad as most people predicted. The double jump, exo suits, laser weapons and all these new killstreaks take a while to get used to but once you are used to it, the game is great!

In each map are ladders so you can climb up on the places where you can get with your exo. There are also some nice features inside the maps which make you interact with it and able to change your tactics based on that. Like for example a tsunami in Defender.
On the other hand, all these special new stuff isn't 100% finished yet. The map Defender has some big lagg issues in the beginning of the first round. Which is just one round in Search and Destroy, but which is also half a game in Domination or up to an entire game of Team Deathmatch. Also you got sometimes some issues to connect to the multiplayer online services. They are still working on this to get it sorted.
The singleplayer is great, great storyline, and great interaction with the characters. Also the fact there is a famous actor playing the main character adds a nice touch to it. New items, new missions but still with the old school type of sneaky missions and all the rest.

One hell of a bad day.
It's one of those days for Amanda Ripley where everything is stacked against her and nothing ♥♥♥♥ing works. You go to a space station where the flight recorder of your mother's doomed ship The Nostromo is located. Suddenly, Amanda finds herself stuck there with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ humans, malfunctioning androids, and one xenomorph doing typical xenomorph things. Did I mention that on this space station nothing ♥♥♥♥ing works. I mean,
But, being an engineer, Amanda is all like "♥♥♥♥ IT, WE'LL DO IT LIVE. ♥♥♥♥ING THING SUCKS." And so you go on an epic journey of repairing this dump bit by bit until you can just get off the damn thing.
I don't want it to sound too tedious. Having to go repair things is really just a way to force you to stop cowering in a corner and actually go do something. You've got to make your way around this gigantic station, which in my opinion is the star of the show. The atmophere and everything that makes it: the architecture, textures, lighting, sound and music, really put you in that Alien movie. The god-damn sounds,
You have very few friends you bump into time from time but mostly you're alone, having to deal. Scrounge together some junk and think your way through this thing.
Then the Alien shows up looking all slick. As for the alien AI, yes it's random so don't try to figure out a route or anything. But, you can figure out cues and, most interesting, you can manipulate the alien with sounds. You can even weaponize him; don't like that human over there? Throw a noisemaker his way and let the alien deal with him.
And speaking of weaponization... I don't want to give the plot away but if you know anything about anything from the movies, of course this was going to come up in an Alien IP. Corporate malfeasance, disregard for human life, profit over people, abandonment, all the themes you expect from an Alien movie are here. Overall the story is good. The missions might make you feel like a cog in a machine but that's sort of the point. The narrative is a slow reveal of the fact that you and everyone else
cogs in the big corporate machine that has it's own plans.
This game really puts you through the wringer though. It'll challenge you and it can get quite exhausting. Just when you think you're out of it, the game throws you right back in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's pretty relentless in that sense of just throwing the player to the wolves again and again. Out of the frying pan and into the fire once more Ripley. And it is loooong, or it at least feels that way. So prepare yourself for one really bad day.
Buy if:
* You like Stealth-Horror games. The gameplay is almost identical to games like Outlast.
* You like the Alien movies, especially the first one. This game is probably the truest to its source material than any game based on a movie. They really took the Alien universe to heart when making this. The details, the architechture, the atmoshpere and even the social/economic environment and themes fits perfectly with Alien.
* You are in the mood for a game that will challenge you.
Do not buy if:
* You've never played a stealth-horror game. Alien: Isolation is a big game to tackle, I would recommend making sure you like the gameplay first. For that I would suggest Outlast. It's (mercifully) shorter and cheaper. If you end up liking that game and want more, check out Alien: Isolation.
* You can't stand repeating gameplay/backtracking. There will be times you will be killed just short of reaching a save point and you'll have to repeat material.
* You can't stand "go and do this" quests. Essentially, this game is a long marathon of these types of missions. "Ripley, the doo-dad that makes the machines work is broken. Walk over to this other place and make it work. Watch out for things that want to kill you."

In the world of Alien: Isolation, the developers at Creative Assembly have cast off expectations of space marines and machine guns, instead dropping players into the role of Amanda Ripley. It is Amanda’s goal to seek out evidence of her mother Ellen’s disappearance, but she soon finds herself following in her mother’s footsteps, running for her life from a lone Xenomorph in a crippled and isolated space station.
it was 20 minutes in that the advice of the recently-released E3 trailer for Isolation bubbled to the surface: Run, Hide, Survive. Escaping an alien killing machine without the aid of a machine gun, it seems, will be a situation in which cowardice, not courage, will lead to success. And even if Amanda Ripley is granted access to some weapons, using them is not an ideal strategy.
Stealth is the only viable option, and reacting as if a Xenomorph had walked through any door in the real world. Crouch behind cover, hide in lockers, scramble through ventilation shafts, and above all, do so quietly. The truly random decision-making powering the AI creature is beyond question, as our half-hour with the game showed virtually no repeated pathing or behavior. And while that’s good news for some diehard fans of terrifying games, it’s a fact anyone interested in playing Isolation must realize.
When caught in the midst of an escape – with the music’s bass throbbing in tune with the ‘beeps’ of Ripley’s iconic motion tracker, or the sudden swells when the creature closes in – it’s hard to appreciate all the small touches. The game’s lo-fi approach to future technology perfectly captures that of the 1979 film, and set designs sell the idea that Isolation is squarely grounded in the movie universe.
