Wow. I mean whoa. This game totally slipped past my radar for the longest time, probably because the world hates it.
It's not quite (okay, it's not at *all*) a MMO. It's not quite GTA. It waters down everything that it borrows inspiration from, taking a few core elements and leaving the rest for the vultures to eat.
What you get is a very rough around the edges, very "Windows 95" feeling game, which has a bit of driving (badly implemented), a bit of shooting (better), and a teeny tiny amount of character progression to keep away monotony.
APB asks you to choose a side, customize your character, and then you're spitted into a room with what look like quest givers except they don't really give you much and make little sense. Then out of nowhere you're force-joined to a mission already in progress (often anyway), given a marker to drive to, and a very poorly elaborated plot summary which is supposed to help immersion.
The fun comes from the idea that the people you're grouped with can be any slice of the players on your side, and same for the enemy. It's a random combination of people who've been playing together all day, people who joined to play for 5 minutes, trolls, and so on. Then you take your surly crew to meet their band of crab-infested♥♥♥♥♥pirates and see which of you gets the job done better.
It can be magical and almost telepathic when you get along well, it can be utterly hilarious if both sides are idiots, and ... admittedly often the matchups can be hell because one side got lucky and is totally stacked.
APB is best played with a variety of interesting people, intentionally shuffling up who you play with and seeing different ways of conquering the same missions, getting to know fun folks along the way. APB is at its worst when you want constant enjoyment or a sense of progression. It's not that. It's taking a break in a nice place to see a bit of random chaos of humanity.
You'll know you're done for the day when you don't *care* how many ways you can skin a cat anymore, and you're ready to come back when you fondly remember that one round you didn't even mean to stay up to play, but it seemed to defy logic and showcased every rare and crazy thing you'd ever seen someone do in the game, except all at once.
APB is the kind of game that needs to be reviewed as a genre of its own instead of comparing it to others, or else you'll be disappointed. But if I had to compare it to anything it'd be Mario Party, with the minigames and random quirkiness. Seriously, instead of reaching for GTA people should have been thinking of party games, it's basically a shallow cops-and-robbers party game.
One last funny note: Did you know that as of this review, hundreds of people come each day to dress up as anime characters and hang out in the game's mall-world? ... Yeah. *Why* does it have such a thing? Hell, why does it have anything it does, and why did it leave out the rest!
These are all good questions, but I truly think they don't need to be asked. The game makes its own internal sort of sense if you let go of hopes and expectations and take it on its own terms. The insanely detailed clothing system, for example -- I think it's pretty obvious it's there because it's a game about the fun of clashing personalities with other people, and it's emphasized even more if you get to look exactly how you want and show it to the world.
Let this one make sense to you, and it just might.

WMD does not excel at being the grandchild of the majorly superior Armageddon, nor does it play like a real Worms game.
New gameplay elements such as vehicles, buildings and crafting were interesting yet very unfitting. Crafting is an absolute joke, with customisation that resembles a light switch: 2 settings. On and off. That's it. You can't choose what can and can't be crafted and you can't have a maximum limit of crafted items. Vehicles are also very cheesy: They offer an absurd amount of mobility and damage reduction, and attacks that can deal over 50 damage in a turn. Vehicles again have very basic customisation; they're either there or they aren't and the drops of them stop at very broad integers, instead of an actual % rate we can change. Mounted guns are unique and interesting, but the Mortar is fully broken (if you line it up properly you can easily get 100+ in one turn). Buildings are so far the only new addition I can enjoy, as they allow a tactical advantage for cover.
WMD's arsenal is full of garbage filler (3 prods, flaming donkey?) and super weapons that make up most of the weapon box. I've seen more poison grenades and super weapons used more than i have bazookas and grenades. It's awful, and because most people will turn off crafting, this locks out over
the weapons in the game. It is ridiculous. Not only that, but staple weapons like the Kamikaze and Sheep Launcher are crafted weapons, and actually important weapons like the Petrol Bomb, Marked for Death, and even the drill are fully missing from the game.
Matches (if you can even find one with the 3 people still playing this game) boil down to "who can get a lucky craft crate and make a super weapon first", and because of the lack of utilities and weapons, you are almost forced to play a lightside style, meaning you face the enemy head on and use heavily terrain damaging weapons, instead of having the option to darkside, and go on the defensive, letting the lightside fall into traps. The flat terrain discourages the use of the ninja rope a lot, which is really sad, because I would like to see more new players rely less on jet packs and teleports to take up the skillful rope. (The rope also got a serious range nerf, it's so small now).
There's no doubt about it; WMD's art style is pretty, modern, and pleasing to look at. It runs very well on toasters, and the simplified layout is more welcoming to newbies. I don't like how much the UI has been cut down however. Scheme menus are missing a lot of features, such as custom crate percentages (there's only static 25, 100, etc choices).
The developers are very slow at addressing bugs and discussing content and this is the biggest reason why I don't reccomend this game. We have often had times where team members were inactive on forums for weeks at a time and more, and they were very vague with how they explained new content. This game is also filled to the brim with bugs. So many bugs. Audio glitches, replays not showing the exact replay, etc. These are all very hurting to the game's otherwise polished design.
WMD is a visually impressive game that lacks a lot of what originally made the Worms series great. New players will enjoy the game but veterans and old timers will not be as inclined to play this game. Devs are slow to reply to threads and features, and update the game even slower.
You're best off waiting for an Armageddon remaster at this point.

How should I start? At the beginning of course... Half-Life. Got this game orignally on the Playstation 2. This was and still is the sweatest version, even over Black Mesa... The PC version actually didn't dissapoint either surprisingly! Yes it's graphics were far inferior compaired to the Playstation 2 but they kept the orignal game playing exactly the same! It didn't look as sweat but more importantly it played exactly the same! It's primarely saving grace, or should I say Playstation 2's saving grace? Given the PC version most likely came out first.
Black Mesa... Black Mesa... It's weak points are set backs. We, the hard-core gamers of the orignal Half-Life really only want improved graphics which Black Mesa grives in abundance... The second half of Half-Life... granted I say it's a different flavor, is not a bad set of levels! I like them just the way they are! I don't want to see them change just for the fact of making them more... ENJOYABLE. It was off-set from the orignal game and almost felt like an entirely new game drafted on but dispite that... I liked the new pace. First half... surive. Second half... careful as all heck while you snipe. It really did feel like two different games under one title and the first was better over story which the second half mostly dropped all together. The thing is it's Half-Life's good points and bad that made it the hit it is and dropping those 'bad' levels from this series to be replaced with 'more fun' ones is ulimately going to detrack from the orignal. Yes, some of us hard-cores didn't care for the second half but I believe most of us don't care to see those last levels change too much either. It's the experience we loved and dislike at times but ballanced out just right! Don't take away my distastful levels! I've enjoyed them just the same! Make them look sharper with maybe a new thing or two do but I still want to be forced to edge forward and snipe because this level lost the story and became harder for the sake of harder because this was the end and the curve matched me perfectly! A challenge that pushed me to my limits without frustrating me to say forget it.
Is Black Mesa the better game over the orignal Half-Life... yes. Over the Playstation 2 version?... No. The Playstation 2 caught this game in it's most perfect form. Black Mesa looking better? Yes, but I'd still rather be playing the PS2 version! Save for graphics, that game can't be improved. Playstation 2 dialed it in perfectly at the perfect time when the system had just enough power to pull off the perfect remake of a perfect classic that just needed a graphic overhaul. If one looks at the memory this game takes on a CD!?! Not DVD?!? They made magic with memory and code that a lot of games five times bigger still can't take a shine to.
Personal option... Black Mesa is awesome. Playstation 2 version more so...  Unbelievable that the PS2 version did it under a gig which Black Mesa seems to eat like candy. I love what Black Mesa did just the same and the PC version despite it's rough graphics held on to the core playing that made it an awesome game but Playstation 2 found the sweat spot. The exact PC game just looking sweater but playing exactly the same with the same story. No devations... perfect! Black Mesa has one up on it's very graphics but then again, this game is still incomplete. The graphic upgrade alone to the first half makes this a game complete onto itself though and most of us wouldn't mind not seeing the second half done because this first half was done just that well. On the same note, I don't want the second half to change so much that I don't reconize it as the second part of the orignal Half-Life. Us Hard-core gammers love our games in orignal condition, good parts and bad and don't care to see even the bad parts dissappear too.
Black Mesa worth a thumbs up? That's a stupid question. If I ranted this long it's a appearent YES!!! It may not have all the flavors I care for but it follows the orignal Half-Life enough that I enjoy it just the same. Just wish they would meet their deadlines though and hope they don't change the last levels too much. Yes they did have their negatives but I've enjoyed them just the same on that note.

Quick review: A re-make of the original Half Life game, made by obvious fans of the original 1998 release (well before the Half Life: Source port) with modern grahpics, game engine and physics.
This re-make includes many of the humorous touches that made the original game great, although I did notice that it lacks the kind of lighting used originally (i.e. beams of light, which were largely fake, but very effective.)
It also lacks some of the scripted, multi-stage interactions of the original game, relying on direct activation instead. Some rooms have changed a bit, have fewer or different enemies, and I think fewer Administrator sightings.
All in all though, it's a modern and very accessible re-make of an original and great game.

Picking up a few years after the events of the first Dishonored, Dishonored 2 wastes no time in thrusting the game’s controls onto the player. After a brief but informative expository cutscene, the player is granted the choice of either playing as the protagonist of the original game, one Corvo Attano, or his daughter and ruling empress, Emily Kaldwin. For my own first playthrough, I opted to let old man Corvo sit it out and instead took to the rooftops in Emily’s perfectly fitted Burberry coat. Whatever difference this choice may make with regard to the overall experience, I can’t say, but even if Corvo’s campaign should prove half as strong as Emily’s, it would still be a candidate for the best game of the year.
Yes. It is that good.
Dishonored 2 is very much its predecessor’s sequel, and I mean this in the best possible sense. Its fundamental premise is instantly recognisable, yet enough changes have been made to the first game’s intricate Rube Goldberg-like design, with its creative confluence of abilities and gadgets, to make it feel new; inviting the player to experiment with the breadth of options all over again.
Even ignoring the many supernatural powers the player has the option of wielding, the most basic means of navigating the game’s environments have been enhanced to great effect. The player can now make much better use of climbing, as the possibility of exploring vertical space has been expanded. From a sprint, the player can also vault low obstacles while maintaining momentum, or slide, allowing for unique ways of eliminating hostile characters.
The arsenal of weapons available to the player is an extension of many of the ideas introduced in Dishonored, but thankfully, more work has been put into making a non-lethal approach more interesting than the first game allowed. While the classic blade, pistol, and grenade return largely unchanged, there are many new types of mines and crossbow bolts to grant the player full control of any given situation. Where tranquilizer darts amounted to the only ranged option a non-lethal player had in the first Dishonored, the sequel introduces a number of non-lethal varieties of ammunition which can do anything from cause momentary confusion to send enemies fleeing in physical discomfort.
As for the aforementioned supernatural collection of tricks, Emily and Corvo have access to powers uniquely tailored for them each. Corvo’s will be familiar to anyone who played the original game, but where he will use Blink to deftly navigate roofs and ledges, Emily instead sports Far Reach; a physical tether which she uses to pull herself in place, rather than the instantaneous displacement granted by Blink.
These distinctions in play, not to mention the ability to deny yourself access to the supernatural entirely, may very well invite a great number of repeat playthroughs for dedicated players.

In short, there is great inspiration to be found in how Dishonored 2 plays, which is in no small way perfectly complemented by its sublime art and sound. As its predecessor, Dishonored 2 draws from a couple of strong visual influences such as Victorian architecture, Romantic painting, and the odd dash of modern haute couture and Brutalism. It adds up to a depiction of an alternative 19th century  that is both familiar and exotic in equal measure. The human characters are once again beautifully portrayed as turn-of-the-century caricatures, and it is heartening to see a game which doesn’t shy away from giving us both male and female characters whose faces are bordering on the grotesque.
The environmental art and design is, perhaps, the game’s altogether single greatest asset. Not only are the game’s milieus very carefully crafted to allow for a great number of different approaches to its problems, but the logic put into realising them is nothing short of astounding. While I shan’t go into detail which may spoil the surprise, two levels in particular stand out in how environments are used and changed at the drop of a hat. All of it perfectly logical, all of it carefully thought-out. The consistency, care, and creativity displayed in Dishonored’s aesthetics is, quite simply, second to none in this industry, and Arkane has every right to feel proud of their work.
If any complaint is to be raised with regard to the game’s otherwise stellar looks, it would have to be regarding some of its animation. Characters committed to idle animations such as leaning on railings or tables will twist their torsos towards the player when talked to, with their arms following suit to awkward and unnatural effect. The lack of variation in specific contextual animations such as an enemy sentry being startled or suspicious may become evident after a few hours of play as well, but does not seriously hurt the game.
Daniel Licht returns as the series’ composer, delivering an original score that more than matches that of the first game. The emphasis remains on strings, guitar, and percussion. Worthy of a special mention is the hammered dulcimer, which yet again endows the game’s music with its very distinct metallic twang. In addition to the score, the game also features a handful of original songs performed by street musicians within the game’s universe. While these songs are of varying quality (both in terms of writing and performance), there are nonetheless some real gems such as ”On the Sands of Sweet Serkonos”, and even the lesser songs do a good job of further embelleshing the world of Dishonored 2.
As for story, while parts of the game may feel truncated at times, and while it is a possibility that some of my own enjoyment can be traced to having played and perused all of the original game’s contents, it still stands as a very respectable and, perhaps most importantly, a very empathetic story of loss and betrayal. The writing itself is competent and, in tone, appropriately evocative of the fictional period in history it aims to emulate. The core cast of characters is smaller and more thoroughly explored this time around, and with the protagonist being fully voiced, the overall feeling is one more intimate than the mute Corvo could achieve in the original.
Last but not least, the reappearance of the Heart should not go without mention. Perhaps the most inspired idea found in the first game, it serves the same overall purpose in Dishonored 2, with some added quirks (which I shall not name for fear of ruining anything). Pointing the heart at specific characters will give you some small insight as to their secrets and thoughts, and breadcrumbs though they might be, in many cases they are enough to significantly humanise the game’s characters, down to the anonymous beggars hiding in the dingiest back alleys of Karnaca.
On the more technical front, I’d be remiss not to mention performance. I’m aware that some players, including myself, experienced some performance issues on the day of the game’s release, but Arkane has since rolled out two quick beta patches which completely eliminated this issue, at least for myself. I have nothing but praise for the studio and their efforts in this regard, and I encourage players who posted very emotional and, perhaps, somewhat hasty reviews to revisit the game and amend their criticism accordingly should they have experienced the same improvements. Frankly, Steam’s platform for user reviews leave a lot to be desired, and the way in which a game’s reputation can unfairly be compromised forever, in no time at all, by what are perhaps the most fickle media consumers on the planet concerns me greatly.
But I digress. The essential thing to understand is that in a year which has seen a great number of fantastic games such as DOOM, Overwatch, and Mirror’s Edge: Catalyst, Dishonored 2 still stands out due to its unparallelled art, substantive choice in play, and supremely competent writing.

The third part of the Souls-Series. A good game, better PC-port than Dark Souls1. Still, 60 FPS cause faster weapon breaking and shorter invulnerability during rolls. Maybe not initially as challenging as the other parts, but you can manually increase the difficulty through use of some special items or the traditional ng+ and further. Overalls this is an entertaining RPG with sometimes frustrating groups of enemies and players as well as impressive scenery and quite a lot of equipment to choose from. But the most boss fights are pretty easy or have cheesy tactics which make them a waste of time. Also the biggest difficulty seems to come from just throwing packs of enemies at you at once rather than the enemies being hard themselves or the level design increasing your struggle.
The biggest flaw in my opinion is the soul memory system, which limits your co-op and pvp pool based on how many souls you have received on that character. That means that a level 1 playthrough can end up facing someone like level 200 because you just didn't level but received the same amount of souls or you cannot co-op endlessly in an area because you will increase your soul memory too much.
As of the release of the Scholar of the first sin-edition it is probably advisable to go for that, since it promises improvements and is not included in this version.
Overall good game, but hast certainly lost much of the Dark Souls charme.

No More Room In Hell is a standalone Half-Life2 modification. There can only be max. 8 players per game.

you can play objective mode in which you got to do specific tasks to reach the extraction point.

Melee combat is something you'll do most in this game so here is a little tip (left click and as soon as you hit / or don't hit the zombie press V to shove him off) no need to thank me :D. If I may say, AVOID the screenshots in the Steam's Store Page, it contains spoilers. Spoilers aren't good, especially for a story driven game like this.
Now for the review....
A simple (A)RPG anime game.
Game's made in RPG Maker, and there's a real work for the story and the gameplay. Note that this game does NOT support Steam Cloud, Achievements and Trading Cards. Be careful with your save games.
As commonly found in RPG, there's a skill system where you allocate points to make the character stronger as you beating the game and level up. You can also craft the equipments with materials found from dead monsters/chests. The battle doesn't take away you from main screen, but instead you'll be fighting enemies in the same screen without transition. Consider this as Devil May Cry in 2D sprites.
There's literally zero effort in progressing, though, as the game even allows you to utilize easy mode during 'hard' boss battles. As it stands, the main appeal of the game is the story and I agree, the story is that good despite of it being a simple theme - the girl who's looking for sister.
There are multiple endings, not difficult to find as the game even hints you how to get them. Make sure you save often on a different save slots.
And I'm surprised this comes with free price tag. So, if you have the slightest interest in Japanese anime-based game, this game's worth trying for.
Looking forward to playing the sequel - developer said it is coming.
PS: The OSTs etc are located in: D:\games\Steam\SteamApps\common\Eternal Senia\Audio (depending on where you install the game). The audio is quite well composed.

As someone unfamiliar with Slender Man (Yes, I live under a rock), many of the reviews weren't very helpful. Despite that the description sounded interesting, so I figured I would give it a try.
I wasn't sure how long it would play, so I started up a single player game. That was probably my first mistake. Unless you are really patient, the size of the map demands multiple players. Having multiple players also adds an element of strategy and teamwork to map exploration.
The first thing you do is choose a character which grants certain benefits and flaws. I didn't notice much difference between them, but then again I didn't really play enough to see.
What I did see was a game consisting of walking VERY SLOWLY through the woods in the dark. Every so often my screen would start to get fuzzy and I would see a non-descript monster which I then proceeded to run away from. There were various landmarks to see such as buildings and statues and the part of the map I saw was bounded by water.
The goal of the game is to find tape recorders scattered across the map. Since your only clue to their location is the sound they make, you spend the game listening very carefully to your surroundings. That being said, the ambient noise and background is fairly well done.
An interesting touch was that after you finished you could see a map retracing your movements. You could see when you walked in circles over and over again. You could also see any places you panicked, died, or found recorders.
PROS:
+ Good Ambient Background Noise
+ Character variation (even if its slight)
+ Interesting Recap Map
+ Can play with friends
CONS:
- The monster is boring and the game isn't scary
- SLOW movement speed, even when running.
- Flashlight is unusable when running. I don't know about you, but I would point it ahead not at my feet.
- Not very fun to play solo
Overall I cannot recommend this game, the slow movement speed really killed it for me. If you don't mind a "walking simulator", and have friends to play with, you might enjoy it, but you are probably better off looking elsewhere.

I am guessing that the game is unplayable single player. The character walking speed is not quite as hair-slicking back as your grandmother with her walker, that is the "sprinting" speed. Don't know about anybody else but I am able to run pointing a flashlight ahead of me rather than at my feet.

Playstation 2 dialed it in perfectly at the perfect time when the system had just enough power to pull off the perfect remake of a perfect classic that just needed a graphic overhaul. If one looks at the memory this game takes on a CD!?! Not DVD?!? They made magic with memory and code that a lot of games five times bigger still can't take a shine to.
Personal option... Black Mesa is awesome. Playstation 2 version more so...  Unbelievable that the PS2 version did it under a gig which Black Mesa seems to eat like candy. Quick review: A re-make of the original Half Life game, made by obvious fans of the original 1998 release (well before the Half Life: Source port) with modern grahpics, game engine and physics.
This re-make includes many of the humorous touches that made the original game great, although I did notice that it lacks the kind of lighting used originally (i.e. beams of light, which were largely fake, but very effective.)
It also lacks some of the scripted, multi-stage interactions of the original game, relying on direct activation instead. Some rooms have changed a bit, have fewer or different enemies, and I think fewer Administrator sightings.
All in all though, it's a modern and very accessible re-make of an original and great game.

To start I want to say that I did enjoy this game, it had alot of good elements, and a very compelling storyline, however its pros, do not really outweight its cons, at least for the current price of the game. (first sale price)
The main thing this game had going for it is its fandom, the aliens genra has always had a huge following and easily draws them in with pretty much any game they make for it, be it a game as fantastic as Aliens vs predator, or as terrible as colonial marines. That being said the game has many other elements that do make it rather enjoyable to play.
For example the visuals in the game are wonderful, clearly taking current graphic technology and putting it to work to give us a fanominal show of what games today can really do. Despite there being a few copy paste feeling locations where they had the same drinking bird in every room you went into, you could clearly still feel uniquness in every area of the station you go, from being a crowded resedential section, to a industrialized engineering bay you really felt like you were there, at least visually.
Lets not forget the story alone for this game is compelling enough stuff, driving you on further and further through the game, just to see what happens next. you really get connected with riply and want to see what her mother left behind and try to keep her alive long enough to enjoy what she finds. the characters are compelling and you grow to love, and hate some of them, though admitidely some of the characters in the game only have extremely small cameos only to be forgoten completely a few seconds later.
Which leads us into the cons for this game, to start simply put, some of the story, though compelling, felt forced. The story as a whole was great to follow, however some of the characters, or even the situations you got into, simply made no sense at all, you would seem to get really attached to 1 character, but then never see or hear from them again but for only 1 brief small moment somewhere much further down the line, like your suppsed to care about this character and what happens to them, which just simply isnt the case since there was no connection to begin with.
Despite those few flaws in the story however it was still in my opinion, good. However the stories flaws were not my main driving decision to not recommend this to others. My primary concern with the game was with the gameplay itself. Though to start with there was that element of fear, not knowing when or if the alien would come from the walls, what awaited you around the corner, it was a rush. but almost litterally after the first encounter with the alien, the fear was gone, other then a few very small jumpy moments when the alien would randomly kill you, there was no real fear of the alien. In fact after the first real death to the alien you pretty much learned that once he came at you, it was over and there wasnt anything you could do to really stop it, so you kinda just sat back and let it happen cuse why fight it.
The alien itself was completely unpredicatble, and honestly far to buggy and way to easy for you to die to it. If the alien sees you at all, hears you, senses you, your basically dead, you might be able to scare it off with fire, or explosives, but honestly that was more often just delaying the inevitable. it would be back in about 5 seconds, and know exactly where you were no matter where you were. Not to mention half the time hiding didnt even work, and even holding your breath and leaning back, did you no good against the alien and it just kill you wile you hide in a locker. This isnt also to mention the alien seems to randomly see you at times from across the map and come rushing right at you, and your only warning is the loud stomps of its foot steps. what made the alien worse I felt was that it almost always ignored the other threats in the game, completely ignoring the android threats in the game, which confused the hell outa me because the alien and the androids practically would just stand at stare at each other at times.
Which brings me to the other issue I had with the game, the combat system. I realize this game is supposed to be more about survival fear etc etc. but they added this combat feature to the game for a reason, and honestly its almost compeltely worthless. For starters, it takes about 4 shots if that to kill you, and though that is understandable, it doesnt make sense that its the same for every weapon, a shotgun or a pistol all deal the same damage no matter what, and that makes no sense to me, though in your hands, it does more? Not to mention the fact that these other threats only serve pretty much to get you killed since the second you fire your gun, the alien is pretty much right on top of you, though if they fire, the alien never comes and even when it does, it almost always ignores them and goes right for you. Ammo is never an issue in the game since 1 shot kills almost everything except for the androids, which I might add are the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ threat in the game.

So now that I finally  finished the game I wanted to make a quick faq/review on my own comparing to some of major reviews out there.
1. IS THIS GAME LONG?
A. Yes.
2.IS THIS GAME TOO LONG?
A. No. But... The game is not "too" long, it indeed takes quite a time to finish it but that's not useless gameplay. The story keeps up building tension and making things more difficult. There are a lot of times you'd think it's probably ending  but it's keeps going. Which I like because I gave money for this. Also it depends on how much you die and replay from last save cause it's manual. (hipsters...)
3. IS THIS GAME HARD?
A. Yes.
4. IS THIS GAME TOO HARD?
A. No. There's gonna be times you'll get stuck. Alien is unpredictable. Sometimes you will wait for ages to get killed, sometimes you'll go perfectly unnoticed and then get killed. It's not hard to play, it's hard not to die. Challanges are easy, get there, hack this. It's the creature and other enemies that will force you to go low and slow, which is frustrating sometimes as it also builds up tension. (for example, the alien is close, you see the exit, you go slowly so he won't hear you, and it takes ages, if you run he/it will get you right away)
5. IS THE STORY GOOD?
A. The story makes justice to the film. It's diverse, it keeps up the tension and makes sense. The rest is spoilers.
6. IS THE GAME SCARY?
A. Yes.
7. IS THE GAME TOO SCARY?
A. Kinda... It's common for AAA horror games to be in this sensitive zone (which I just made up), which is right between it's scary enough but not too much so we get the most sales possible. This is not the case. This game made me jump and swear a lot. There's been times I didn't want to play it because I didn't want to sweat. I ended up playing anyway. But still it can be even scarier that this. The difference between this and other games like the next Silent Hill is that this kind of fear seems real, where the other one is just creepy and weird and also if you have to use jumpscares to keep up the fear you're not doing a great survival-horror.
8. IS IT REPLAYABLE?
A. Yeah. There's a lot of AWESOME games that are not replayable at all. I mean, maybe I'm just the only one but I LOVE SO MUCH Metro 2033 but I can't get to play it again. Thinking about all the stuff you went through but still somehow I just get bored. With Alien Isolation I don't I'll have this problem, because it's so random, you'll never get the same experience. Also you can try and get the DON'T KILL ANY HUMANS trophy. Good luck with that.

I posted an earlier review of this game when I had about 20 hours in it. Back then I think I was still enjoying the game and so my review wasn't completely accurate due to buyers bias.
The game is... "Meh." When I first played the game I DID enjoy it. But now, after revisiting the game, I feel that this was me not being honest with myself and wanting the game to be good. After spending $50 on a game you kind of WANT it to be good so you think it's better than it actually is.
The Elder Scrolls Online falls into the same quagmires that most MMOs do. Grindfests, poor content, bland characters and items, and the lack of unique content. You might enjoy the game for your first 10 hours or so and then after that you start to regret your purchase.
Pros:
~A few challenging areas and bosses.
~Easy to learn
~Grouping with friends is fairly easy.
~Fun co-op and PvP with large groups of players.
~Getting Vampire/Werewolf bite is a fun challenge.
~Online community is friendly and helps out new players.
Cons:
~Get's buggy every once in a while. (Character voice overs and reactions are sometimes delayed.)
~PvP is pretty unbalanced when you're not with a large group protecting/helping you.
~Playing and completing quest above your skill level will give you LESS expirence. (This was recently added I believe)
~Bosses are mostly the same in terms of being unique.
~Making alternate characters and leveling them is SUPER boring.
~Stops being interesting fairly early.
~Non-story quests are mostly boring.
~Grindfests for boring items.
Conclusion:
Elder Scrolls Online is a okay game for gamers wanting to get into the MMORPG/Online gaming world. The community is super friendly which is always helpful when learning a new game. I personally don't like open world games because they split up the story and distract the player with sidequests because they can't think up of a long enough story. (This is why I don't like Assassin's Creed.) TESO has some of these same faults. There just isn't enough of the main story to keep me interested for long periods of time.
The game is mired by boring quests, and uninteresting combat, but compared to other fantasy MMOs it is better than others. If you like MMOs then you will probably get some enjoyment out of this game, but if you don't like grinding for loot and XP then this game isn't for you.

The basic aim of the game is to chop the tiki faces and avoid the tiki arms, it may sound easy but it sure isn’t. The game challenges you to play at pace and keep that pace going as the sections become more difficult.
With four luscious tropical environments and sixteen Tiki Men to unlock there’s certainly a lot for you to earn but you’ll have to be a master of pace to get them all.
It feels very much like one of those Flash Games you’d play at school when you thought no one was watching or when you’ve got a space couple of minutes. It’s by no means the most beautiful game but the look fits perfectly with the style of play, it doesn’t need to be anything more complex because it’s reflective of the simple, quick style you play.
There’s no multiplayer game modes or challenge your friends modes but that doesn’t mean to say you can’t compete with them. This game has a super simple leaderboard similar to Flappy Birds in which it sounds you your Best Score and your last score. So it’s time to get chopping and beating your friends high scores.

Warning: This review contains spoilers. Read at your own risk.
I can safely say, that this is one of the best video game remakes that i have ever gotten to experience in my life. It's the treatment Half-Life, one of the best FPS games ever developed, deserved.
Black Mesa, while having a special touch to itself, still reminds you of Half-Life when you play it.
Story: The story is the same as the original Half-Life. You play as the scientist Gordon Freeman, and have to escape from the Black Mesa Research facility after an experiment goes horribly wrong. On your way out, you will encounter hostile aliens such as Vortigaunts, who are invading the facility and killing everyone they see. Later in the game you will also have to fight against human soldiers who have been sent in to "clean up" the situation. The game's story is just as refreshing as the original game.
Gameplay: Gameplay wise, Black Mesa plays nearly the same as the original game. You use weapons, ranging from the iconic crowbar, pistols, SMGs, shotguns to rocket propelled grenade launchers and even alien weapons. However, there's been some noticeable changes to certain chapters, such as We've got hostiles and Surface Tension. People used to today's FPS games will find Black Mesa somewhat difficult to play, with it's old school mechanics such as crouch-jumping. But overall, the gameplay is great, and sometimes even better than the original.
Graphics: Despite the Source Engine's dated techonology, Black Mesa definatively manages to look beautiful, and is certainly how Half-Life should look with today's graphics. The scenery, NPC's, props... everything looks great.
Sound: Soundwise, Black Mesa does good most of the time. The music is fantastic, Joel Nielsen did a great job at composing the tracks for the game. However, it can occasionally feel out of place in the respective situations. The voice acting was pretty good too. The Scientists and Security Guards voices capture the feel of Harry S Robins respective Michael Shapiro. The Soldier's voice acting feels... better than they were in the mod version where they sounded like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
In conclusion, Black Mesa does a good job of bringing Half-Life to newer generations, even with some few flaws that it has. Even if you played the original game before, it's still worth paying to play this amazing remake.

The biggest difference between Half-Life 1 and Black Mesa: Emotion.
Half-Life 1 is a good game, don't get me wrong. But this...makes the game it's based off of feel sterile.
The updated graphics, the redesigned sections of level design, the music...all of it brings the legend of Gordan Freeman to life. The man who was nothing more than a glorified intern becomes a force of hope in an otherwise hopeless scenario, but he must find his own courage first.
It drips with atmosphere in ways Half-Life 1 never did...and without the cost of its timeless gunplay. In fact, it adds A LITTLE MORE. Truly, if I were to pick one moment from the game that spoke to me most, it is the headcrab utility elevator.
In Half-life 1, Headcrabs are waiting for you BEFORE you get on the elevator. But in this remake, there's no headcrabs...UNTIL you turn it on. When the elevator passes the point of being able to jump back to the floor above, headcrabs pour out of the vents and begin sliding down the angled shaft after Freeman. The music reinforces the feeling of panic and helplessness the player themselves feel as Freeman is overwhelmed by sheer numbers (Perhaps dying unexpectedly the first time). It is during this moment in the game that you feel like Gordan has undergone some sort of baptism by fire...and starts to become the Dues ex Machinima for the whole Resonance Cascade event.
Though not made by Valve, it might as well been. Perhaps even better than that.
The only negative I have is the lack of the Zen campaign section of the game...but it is still in early access, and in my opinion, if you're willing to spend $60 on something weak sauce as a COD or Battlefield campaign, you have bad taste if you can't justify the purchase for $20. It has multiplayer, it is an upgrade in all areas vs Half-Life 1, INCLUDING level design and storytelling. Seriously, even IF this game never updates again, IT'S WORTH IT. ESPECIALLY IF YOU ARE A HALF-LIFE FAN.
With other franchises betraying their roots in order to 'cater to a broader audience', this is not only a return to glory, but a game that simply DESTROYS anything else on the market in terms of campaign and core gameplay mechanics. I only have one other 'negative' to say about this game, but it is COMPLETELY subjective: It does not hold your hand. You will likely have your butt handed to you in multiplayer and campaign alike. It's fair, but not easy.

This game will make you cry
You're the daughter of the main character in the original series, off on an adventure to find out what happened to your mother in the events that took place in the movie Alien 15 years prior to this game.
You're going to sneak around.
You're also going to die
You will be killed by human and alien alike.  It will make you frustrated.  Dying triggers the single most annoying mechanic in the game, which also happens to be one of the reasons I love this game: the saves are few and you have to manually trigger them.  By this I don't mean you have a limited number.  But you are required to do it at save stations and they aren't exactly abundant.  This means if you die you are going to be repeating stuff you already did, and this can happen quite a bit if you aren't careful.  "Why do you love that?  It sounds horrid."  You're absolutely right, random internet guy.  But it does something else.  It adds to the intensity of the moment.  When you've worked really hard to complete the 6 side quests it takes to advance to the next portion of the game (no, I'm not exaggerating), and you hear that Alien crawling around in the hallways next to you or in the air ducts above you, you will sweat bullets walking 30 feet to the objective and nearest save spot, because if you're spotted, it's a one hit kill.  There is no getting away when you're discovered.
This fear will follow you for the entire game.  Ambient noises, lighting, set design and music are artistically crafted to foster an environment that is meant to make you hesitate.  The Alien doesn't really get easier to deal with, either.
Supplies are limited and distractions available are few.  Luckily for you, the Alien hates everybody on the ship, not just you, so well placed flares and noisemakers can help distract him with a meal while you jaunt around him.
The controls work well, at least how I've been playing.  I opted for the controller rather than a mouse and keyboard since stealth is more important in this game overall rather than quickness or accuracy.
Play with the lights off if you dare.
No performance issues whatsoever, the game exceeds expectations.

Alien: Isolation is a good game. I'm normally not a big fan of stealth mechanics, as they tend to be very tedious and frustrating. The gameplay is not pure stealth, thankfully, and in many situations it allows you to use distractions or combat to get past your enemies. The game is very immersive, and scares you more with the atmosphere rather than startling you with jumpscares (although there are a few of those in the game). The game was also hard enough to keep me engaged without it being too aggravating. The combat in the game wasn't the best, but it also wasn't meant to be the best. It serves mostly to let you escape from certain situations, not to solve all of your problems.
The game ran fine for me without any performance issues, and the game looked pretty good without being too demanding on my system. You shouldn't really need to worry about whether or not it will run on your PC.
The story was solid. It wasn't groundbreaking or phenomenal, but it kept me playing.
Overall, I would recomend that you buy this game. It's a good experience worth playing.

Definitely one of the best games I've played this year. A game that's all about choice - the choice to play as one of two protagonists, the choice to go lethal or non-lethal, the choice to go stealthy or guns blazing and finally the choice to use superpowers or challenge yourself by not. The level design is fantastic and every mission is better than the last (except for the final mission). There's a lot of different ways you can approach every mission and I was genuinely surprised by some of the alternate solutions to the objectives. I had a blast exploring every nook and cranny of the levels.
Both Emily and Corvo are a lot of fun to play and come with different sets of powers. All gameplay options are viable and both lethal and non-lethal approaches feel extremely satisfying. I actually enjoyed my first playthrough as Emily so much that I just had to play it all over again as Corvo. Playing through a game again right after you finish it is a rare occurrence these days as I struggle to finish games even once but I am already looking forward to a third "no powers" playthrough. Arkane Studios have outdone themselves with this worthy sequel, it's probably the closest thing to the older Thief games.
The only thing that's a bit lacking is the story which is pretty generic but that's balanced out by the brilliant alternate world setting, great characters and lore. The performance on the PC version is problematic as well (my rig was able to brute force through it though). Overall Dishonored 2 is a potential GOTY candidate, a game I liked a lot more than I expected.

Her new set of powers are refreshing enough to be interesting but still provide you with enough of the same to make your strategies from the first game valid. They've also definitely made it easier to differentiate between playing low or high chaos, which I quite enjoy since it feels more like a 'choice' rather than accidentally messing up an encounter and being screwed. Furthermore it feels like you have quite a bit more freedom in how to tackle every single mission, since there are many paths that lead towards the same goal, and it really challenged me to go explore.
All in all, what I loved about the original I love about Dishonored 2; the settings still feel almost magical and strange and make me want to explore, the characters all have their virtues and vices, the story is engaging and the stealth is actually fun instead of an impossibly frustrating task.

This negative review is AFTER Tamriel Unlimited was released. I wish I could recommend this game... But as far as the bottom line goes, it's your generic MMORPG with an Elder Scrolls skin. Extremely disappointing.
If the game wasn't completely predictable, meaning if every area and event weren't exactly the same, ESO might be fun. Instead all you do is follow one pattern: get a main quest which leads you to a new area that has a series of side quests. You complete these side quests until you're high enough level to do the main quest, and then the process repeats in each and every area. After 33 hours I've hit maybe level 34 while playing with my friend and have yet to run into a compelling, fun, challenging boss during any questline. Every boss was either the exact same piles of bones as the last one, some skeletons, or a 'strong' magister that terrorizes the land and!... dies in 5 hits.
There's next to no challenge in this game. I've only died when I screwed up, whacked a guard, then got pummled to death in 5 hits with no chance to react. Sneaking around guards to sell stolen goods is fun. At first. After the 50th time there's a clear and obvious pattern that you follow for 100% success which, in turn, makes stealing boring with no worry of consequences. How is this true to the Elder Scrolls style? The health and stamina bars may be Skyrim, but the skill system is totally watered-down MMORPG with small trees and limited choices. The lore might be Elder Scrolls, but the method of storytelling where you just can't give a crap is MMORPG. Anytime there are books or scrolls you're bombarded with 2000 words of text that you just can't be bothered reading, even though I loved reading books in Oblivion and Skyrim and Morrowind. The combat is... sadly, MMORPG, and feels like you're slicing through cardboard because there's next to no feedback on the attacks. Monsters spawn in dedicated locations, removing all randomness you get in Oblivion of running into a minotaur or in Skyrim of fighting off a spriggan or Morrowind of dying to some random mage in a cave.
In the first few areas the buildings have the exact same layout. Why? No one can explain why to me. Laziness on the developer's part? There wasn't a sense of grandness in the lore being told and I really had no reason to pay attention anyway because of the horrendous voice acting. Seriously, this bothered me the most. A few characters are good (and for some reason the same 3 guys do all the major voices, did Zenimax not have the budget for more GOOD voice actors?) but the generic Kajiit and Argonians sound like they were forced to speak with a stupid accent for a low pay while being passed off as 'good enough'. It's not immersing at all and you just wind up turning off voices altogether to save your ears of their terrible attempt at the Elder Scrolls races. I don't think I've heard voice acting this shoddy since Assassins Creed 3.
Besides that all that, it's a decent run of the mill MMO with Elder Scrolls thrown in. There's a lot to do, repetitive though it is, and the graphics are cool. Now that there's no subscription it's definitely worth $60 and a playthrough since you get more out of it than you do on say Call of Duty single player but I couldn't stick around till level 50. Even having said it's worth $60, I can't recommend actually spending full price on it. Wait for a sale.

ok so this is one of the few games i will actually make a review for, it's going to be completely honest and it's going to shine more light than other reviews i've seen will. The positive things will have a + in the beginning negatives will have a -
-So to start off it's a pretty fun game, all tho it can be very triggering. It's indeed pay to win even tho some people say it's not. There are a ton of guns you can buy that are better than guns you're able to get in game early on i'm not sure if you still can but there was(might still be) an option to try a gun for i think it's like an hour or a couple(a gun you buy) which is very unique. Upon trying one i did see it was more accurate and seemed to do a shot or two more damage(meaning one or two shots less to kill someone)
On the other hand if you can get well versed in certain guns you can still put up a fight. If you put a small amount of effort in you can actually almost hang with the p2w crowd. You unlock guns with slots for "mods" certain mods have certain buffs and debuffs ie hunter sight makes you less accurate while moving but makes you more accurate in marksman mode(rmb) and zooms a little further. These are completely f2p and the further you advance the more mods(up to 3) you can put on a gun. So p2w? Yes but is it severe p2w? No i have only a 1 mod and get plenty of kills playing smart so don't let it detur you.
+The customization in the game is amazing, it's what makes APB well APB(besides the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ stuff) You can customize cars, your outfit, your clothes, your character look, music etc.. You can even make themes(songs) and symbols(designs) and sell them along with cars and clothes. So you can even relax for a bit make some cool designs and sell them or even make cars and sell them which is pretty awesome(i love buying customized cars). There's a ton of different cars that people who buy the kits can customize(including rims, sounds, body kits etc...) which is awesome it makes the game that much more fun driving in a awesome car.
+There's some pretty cool faction based content, ie if you're a criminal(i am) you can mug pedestrians(lolol) for money or take a car and smash into certain places and steal stuff which you sell to certain people and then you launder the money. The higher wanted level you are(at 5 anyone can attack you) the more money you get when laundering. However after i believe about 5k an enforcer can witness you at any time and fight you for your money. As said before enforcers can witness you do certain things and arrest or engaged in a pvp mission with you.
+++++ You can upload music into the apb music player and play it while you're well playing. It's pretty awesome to run around and cause havoc while blasting your favorite music, it also will play out of your car if you're in it which is awesome.
----- The rank and MM system has been severely abused and has been allowed to be, hopefully they fix the♥♥♥♥♥♥show. In APB you can que for missions in which you get matched with people of your faction randomly and are sent to do open world activities for a crim such as burning a car or breaking into somewhere etc.. If a enforcers is qued up they will usually be dispatched against you in which the two factions fight while doing missions. The reason this is broken is because ranks(i think trainee, bronze, silver then gold) can play in the servers of one rank below. So silvers can go into bronze etc... which is not the end of the world i guess but it has been abused because there's plenty of golds who derank to say silver go into bronze then just sit in bronze rank back up to gold then sit in bronze as a p2w gold all day that's when it really gets to be a nightmare.

The biggest difference between Half-Life 1 and Black Mesa: Emotion.
Half-Life 1 is a good game, don't get me wrong. But this...makes the game it's based off of feel sterile.
The updated graphics, the redesigned sections of level design, the music...all of it brings the legend of Gordan Freeman to life. The man who was nothing more than a glorified intern becomes a force of hope in an otherwise hopeless scenario, but he must find his own courage first.
It drips with atmosphere in ways Half-Life 1 never did...and without the cost of its timeless gunplay. In fact, it adds A LITTLE MORE. Truly, if I were to pick one moment from the game that spoke to me most, it is the headcrab utility elevator.
In Half-life 1, Headcrabs are waiting for you BEFORE you get on the elevator. But in this remake, there's no headcrabs...UNTIL you turn it on. When the elevator passes the point of being able to jump back to the floor above, headcrabs pour out of the vents and begin sliding down the angled shaft after Freeman. The music reinforces the feeling of panic and helplessness the player themselves feel as Freeman is overwhelmed by sheer numbers (Perhaps dying unexpectedly the first time). It is during this moment in the game that you feel like Gordan has undergone some sort of baptism by fire...and starts to become the Dues ex Machinima for the whole Resonance Cascade event.
Though not made by Valve, it might as well been. Perhaps even better than that.
The only negative I have is the lack of the Zen campaign section of the game...but it is still in early access, and in my opinion, if you're willing to spend $60 on something weak sauce as a COD or Battlefield campaign, you have bad taste if you can't justify the purchase for $20. It has multiplayer, it is an upgrade in all areas vs Half-Life 1, INCLUDING level design and storytelling. Seriously, even IF this game never updates again, IT'S WORTH IT. ESPECIALLY IF YOU ARE A HALF-LIFE FAN.
With other franchises betraying their roots in order to 'cater to a broader audience', this is not only a return to glory, but a game that simply DESTROYS anything else on the market in terms of campaign and core gameplay mechanics. I only have one other 'negative' to say about this game, but it is COMPLETELY subjective: It does not hold your hand. You will likely have your butt handed to you in multiplayer and campaign alike. It's fair, but not easy.

This negative review is AFTER Tamriel Unlimited was released. I wish I could recommend this game... But as far as the bottom line goes, it's your generic MMORPG with an Elder Scrolls skin. Extremely disappointing.
If the game wasn't completely predictable, meaning if every area and event weren't exactly the same, ESO might be fun. Instead all you do is follow one pattern: get a main quest which leads you to a new area that has a series of side quests. You complete these side quests until you're high enough level to do the main quest, and then the process repeats in each and every area. After 33 hours I've hit maybe level 34 while playing with my friend and have yet to run into a compelling, fun, challenging boss during any questline. Every boss was either the exact same piles of bones as the last one, some skeletons, or a 'strong' magister that terrorizes the land and!... dies in 5 hits.
There's next to no challenge in this game. I've only died when I screwed up, whacked a guard, then got pummled to death in 5 hits with no chance to react. Sneaking around guards to sell stolen goods is fun. At first. After the 50th time there's a clear and obvious pattern that you follow for 100% success which, in turn, makes stealing boring with no worry of consequences. How is this true to the Elder Scrolls style? The health and stamina bars may be Skyrim, but the skill system is totally watered-down MMORPG with small trees and limited choices. The lore might be Elder Scrolls, but the method of storytelling where you just can't give a crap is MMORPG. Anytime there are books or scrolls you're bombarded with 2000 words of text that you just can't be bothered reading, even though I loved reading books in Oblivion and Skyrim and Morrowind. The combat is... sadly, MMORPG, and feels like you're slicing through cardboard because there's next to no feedback on the attacks. Monsters spawn in dedicated locations, removing all randomness you get in Oblivion of running into a minotaur or in Skyrim of fighting off a spriggan or Morrowind of dying to some random mage in a cave.
In the first few areas the buildings have the exact same layout. Why? No one can explain why to me. Laziness on the developer's part? There wasn't a sense of grandness in the lore being told and I really had no reason to pay attention anyway because of the horrendous voice acting. Seriously, this bothered me the most. A few characters are good (and for some reason the same 3 guys do all the major voices, did Zenimax not have the budget for more GOOD voice actors?) but the generic Kajiit and Argonians sound like they were forced to speak with a stupid accent for a low pay while being passed off as 'good enough'. It's not immersing at all and you just wind up turning off voices altogether to save your ears of their terrible attempt at the Elder Scrolls races. I don't think I've heard voice acting this shoddy since Assassins Creed 3.
Besides that all that, it's a decent run of the mill MMO with Elder Scrolls thrown in. There's a lot to do, repetitive though it is, and the graphics are cool. Now that there's no subscription it's definitely worth $60 and a playthrough since you get more out of it than you do on say Call of Duty single player but I couldn't stick around till level 50. Even having said it's worth $60, I can't recommend actually spending full price on it. Wait for a sale.

I will review all 3 aspects of the game in 1 review, the TL;DR version is simple... Worst COD I've ever played.
The first 5 missions featured nothing massively interesting or unique, it was relatively boring and didn't make a good first impression. Thankfully it sped up and more unique and engaging missions were available but still, not on the same level as previous COD's. I found the storyline to be above average, the concept of biological weapons and a central power house is a lot closer to reality than people believe... Sledgehammer's take on this was nice to see. UNFORTUNATELY, the characters audio and lips were so out of sync and on my second play through the audio had vanished completely (many people have experienced this). Beyond this the way cut scenes worked was nothing short of a joke, they were long and you had no way of skipping them (even if you had already seen them previously). Finally, a problem with every recent COD, it was FAR too easy... I played through on Veteran and died 3-4 times.
I disliked everything from the aesthetics, to the functionality and length. Why does it do round count in X^2? O.o Anyways, aesthetics are a minor flaw, the real problem is how painfully easy it is. On my first map, bio-lab, I reached round 144 (where my friend had to leave) and I thought we were great... I quickly realised we're not and the reason we reached that round number was because it is insanely easy. There are 12-15 maps to complete and you have to clear a certain amount of waves per map to unlock the following maps (around 25). It claims that each set of maps become more difficult but this is a clear lie, the only thing that was more difficult about them was maintaining concentration after the hours of boredom. The last wave had zombies and a cute twist but it's not worth all the time spent, it was used soley to boost DLC purchases... disgusting.
I don't know where to start so I've broken it down into what my main issues are with this game:
- General issues
- Movement > Accuracy
- Classes
- Ranked play
- Developer support, you buffed the laser?
My general issues are somewhat trivial and personal, but here they are. There's no public combat record, the combat record to me was a mark of who you were as a player and how good you were. In previous COD's you could see someone's stats in the pre-game lobby and if he had 100+ nuclears with 400 unstoppables and a 2KD you'd recognise that he is good... you also knew if his Win/loss ratio was only 0.5 that he was a camper. This is absent in AW and for no good reason, there is a private combat record so why hide it? And why hide the number of players ingame? With a lack of players on PC it's imperative for me to know how many people are in each playlist so that I know I'm not wasting my time searching for a SND game at 1am. I also believe this feature, or lack thereof, has resulted in less people playing gametypes that are not called TDM or Domination. Thankfully, FOV slider was implemented from day 1 :D but it resets every time you go into 3rd person... which SND forces -.-
Movement in this game sounded like a great idea but it has been pushed too far; you can jump too high and boost-dash too fast. It has increased the pace of an already fast FPS to a disgusting speed where no control can be maintained playing solo, any player can be anywhere on the map at any given time and you have no way to stop them... map control is now a myth. When a player dashes they move too quickly to be tracked, you have to alter your thought process to shoot at the area their dash will finish (unless you have a controller, controller players are a joke on AW). Due to this fundamental change the game is no longer about who can aim more, it is about who can button bash the most... we might as well rename it to Tekken warfare. In SND you will most likely enoucnter an enemy within the first 4-5 seconds, in the following 4-5 seconds it is entirely possible that the other team is already in your full flank. In CTF / Uplink you can run the ball / flag across map in little over 5 seconds... yet the respawn delay is set to 5 seconds? This would be fine if it was balanced, but it isn't... there is no negative aspect to the speed (except appearing on the mini-map, which can be easily countered and is not an issue in respawn gametypes due to the speed). In previous COD titles in order to be on the 3rd story of a building you had to sacrafice time and positioning for it, you could see limited areas of the map and in order to get down you had to fall or use a ladder / stairs which all come with disadvantages. In AW you can free flow between ground / 2nd / 3rd floors in seconds without any consequence.
Perks / equipment and streaks are perhaps the area they destroyed the most, since we already had a system that worked just fine. For someone who enjoys streaking, the perks are a mess, 4 of the neccessary streaking perks are in the 3rd slot with almost nothing useful in the 1st and 2nd slot. They've also removed deadsilence which means in SND the soundwhoring is a joke, it's not a big deal in respawn however. My primary problem with this is they removed it on the basis that they don't want perks that are 'essential'... YET THEY KEPT IN TOUGHNESS!?!?! I remember painkiller being annoying, it was disgusting, then we moved on and I was happy to leave deathstreaks in the past :) But AW went 'maybe we should bring back painkiller?, yeah maybe we should bring it back and make it readily available whenever you want with no sacrafice required'. Exo-Stim is a joke... INVISIBILITY is a joke. Yes if they're moving it's easy to see them but if they corner camp inside hills where nades and players are flying everywhere it's impossible to find them. The exo-abilities are reason enough to rage, nevermind anything else... but there's much more. Due to double jumping all forms of explosives are now completely overpowered, you can double jump and fire down a rocket launcher destroying everything (flak jacket doesn't save you), previously campers had to go to standard elevated camp spots to fire their noob toobs, now they have free reign to do whatever the ♥♥♥♥ they want and it's simply out of control. Stun grenades... stun grenades... please give me strength. Stun grenades are EBOLA. They stun you (this is fine), FLASH YOU, AND BUST YOUR AIM. They have 3 effects which no 1 perk can counter, meaning if you want to truly counter them you are forced to run 2 perks (which means sacraficing blast surpressor because toughness is essential) - this has hindered competitive drastically in my opinion. Finally, the streaks are completely useless unless they have 3 modifications which makes them slightly better, a fully upgraded Paladin requires 1800 score approximately and will get you 5ish kills... useless.
Ranked play is what I expected to be the only saving grace, however pre-patch it included momentum, non-competitive maps, 0 restrictions on class set ups and the availablity of on-going sessions to searching players. The amount of times I joined games into a losing situation because previously people had rage quitted... AND LOST POINTS because of it. I will not get into too much detail because they patched it and fixed many things, LASER STILL ISN'T BANNED THOUGH IS IT.
I am next to the character count so I have to be quick, THE DEVELOPERS ARE ♥♥♥♥♥. No dedicated servers, patch release took over 1 month, no anti-cheat... waste of time and money. On console (due to no aim assist when hipfiring) the laser was not OP so they buffed it, however PC aim is the same ADS or not, this shows how little COD developers care about PC players.

So, let me help you decide whether this game is worth your money or not.
I divided this review in pros and cons, so let's begin with the positive things. Don't be mislead by the displayed hours, I have played this game on console, since it was unplayable on the PC until yesterday.
Positive things:
The gameplay is pretty nice and smooth, just as it was in the previous title. There are some improvements, the movement doesn't feel as clunky as it did some times in the prior Dishonored.
The story is pretty ok, I guess. It definitely is not the very best storyline I have ever witnessed, but it is pretty ok and entertaining at times. I really enjoy the fact that you can choose whether you play Emily or Corvo.
The graphics are very nice, especially for people that really like the art-style of this genre. Overall textures are a lot smoother than in Dishonored which is quite nice.
They finally adressed the performance problems on PC and the game is now playable, at least on my rig. Perfect.
Negatives:
To be honest, the AI in this game is pretty stupid. It was not very hard to not get detected by the AI, which made the stealth aspect a little bit unsatisfying. I also played the campaign on normal and it was not very challenging which is unfortunate.
Overall I would not recommend paying 60 bucks for this game. I also bought it somewhere else and saved a little bit of money and it was definitely worth it.

Singleplayer: Not too bad overall- similar to previous titles in terms of gameplay.
If you only play the campaign in a Total War game then you should buy this, however expect an AI that feels hugely inferior to previous titles. Increasing the difficulty seems to just give your enemies full stacks of the best units instead of making them play better as well. I've had some graphical issues but nothing too serious and no huge game crashes etc. so not too many problems there.
Multiplayer: This is the main downside for me in this game.
Co-op campaign is dreadful.As soon as you get into medium/large battles you will get desync between you and whoever you are playing with. This problem has got better since launch but still makes it unplayable. Nowhere near as good as Shogun 2.
Multiplayer battles have similar issues. Often it is difficult to set up a battle with friends as the system routinely breaks and you have to set up the game again.
The battles online don't seem to have any sort of depth to them as everyone's army contains the same types of units. Ranged units are hugely underpowered against anything but other ranged units which ruins a whole side of the Infantry-Cavalry-Ranged triangle and makes battles extremely repetitive.
Overall: If you want a Total War game and haven't already played Shogun 2 and the FOTS expansion for it, buy that. The only place that game isn't as good is it has slightly worse graphics. If you desperately want to play as romans then buy Rome 1 people still even play that online.
Hopefully the next Total War CA release is better but I won't be preordering again from them.

Despite all of the wonderfully elaborate reviews proclaiming "I died, 100/10," there's a bit more to this game that urks me.
Dark Souls 2 comes off, to me, as a terrible fix to any and all issues in Dark Souls 1. I am going to indulge into Dark Souls 1's problems so you understand exactly what From has done to "fix" them.
From Software made Dark Souls 1, and even patched and balanced a few things in it that were a major issue, though this took a long, long time. The fixes made me happy. The PvP imbalances at the time were put to rest, but there were still issues. "Twinks" (Players upgrading their weapons and gear without levelling up, resulting in them invading lower-leveled, unskilled players and destroying them) were an issue, though they were few and far between. The invasion covenant, though difficult (in my opinion) to get to, allowed players an easy way to absolutely wreck other players, whilst the lawful covenant saw little action. There were also things such as grinding that people dealt with. All in all, Dark Souls had its problems, but it was such a beautiful and great game with great combat (ignoring infamous "backstab fishers" and "lagstabs"), a good PvP scene with an even more amazing PvE environment that truly felt connected as you walked through the land.
Dark Souls 2 does not contain this.
From has tried to correct many issues by making them the exact opposite of what they were. In essence, they've made previous problems worse in completely new and exciting ways.
1. Poise, the system of how-many-hits-you-take-until-you-flinch, was nerfed into the ground. It is no longer viable as you can get stunlocked by daggers wearing heavy armor. Daggers.
2. Twinking has been "fixed" by the horrid hellspawn, Soul Memory. Soul Memory is the new way you connect to others, not Soul Level like the previous game. Basically, when you kill an enemy or a boss, whether you spend those souls or simply possess them, you have increased your Soul Memory. The higher your Soul Memory, the higher the tier of players you will be matched with.    You cannot help someone on a boss forever like Dark Souls 1. Neither can you invade the same area. You are leveling up whether you choose to or not.
3. The invasion covenant requires you to rank up points in an arena where your losses make you lose points if you want to get the item to invade other players. However, you are going up against min/max genius SmelterHavels or Havelyns because the arena doesn't care about whether you're NG or NG+ like normal. You can be stuck in a permanent limbo unless you upgrade the difficulty of the bonfire area and buy the orbs for obscene prices, and even then, if you get too many souls, you are forced to level up and move on instead of stay in an area and act as an obstacle for a player. Because making the game difficult is From's job, not yours, kids. Except it's not difficult.
4. Grinding and Difficulty has been dampened. If you kill an enemy X amount of times, they will stop spawning unless you upgrade the difficulty of the bonfire. This would make grinding a terrible inconvenience, but sometimes it doesn't even make the enemies too much harder, removing any actual NEED of putting a kill-limit on enemies! It also allows any old fool capable of killing at least a single enemy a certain amount of times the ability to pass and join the ranks of actually decent players.
5. Fast Travel right off the bat. I had an issue with Dark Souls, I admit it. The land was damn huge. You had to walk to every here and there, miles upon miles, until you got the item required to Fast-Travel. I have enjoyed Dark Souls 2's Fast-Travel, but I now realize how terrible it is to implement it so early. You do not appreciate your environment. In Dark Souls 1, you walked through the entire land, looking at surroundings, understanding the key points, where enemies were, how to surpass them, all the way up until you got the Fast-Travel item. Even then, it didn't warp you EVERYWHERE. But in Dark Souls 2, the world becomes a series of Bus Stops. You're no longer looking around you and enjoying the sights, but travelling from A to B as if hurrying to work. It becomes mundane, and any flair in the world surrounding you becomes futile as you can simply pass it by through the simple act of lighting one of the millions of Bonfires scattered around everywhere.
There are many more problems involving bugs and glitches that are yet unfixed that allow people to pass certain blockades without the requirements, as well as cheaters that either cheat to troll or simply cheat so they can surpass the utter nonsense of Soul Memory's constant oppression.
Buying this game was a terrible choice, for I feel it may never be fixed, yet I wish I could play it. Please reconsider your decision of buying this game unless you can live with a dampened PvP scene, a dampened PvE scene, and a disappointing sequel. Hurtworld is a cool new game where your objective is to survive in unforgiving environments. Seriously unforgiving.
At the moment the game is in alpha, and yet I haven't encountered any bugs, which is very uncommon for an alpha game. Also, the interface for this game is great. It's easy to navigate making crafting and all of those things enjoyable.
So far my only problem has been the lag, and no, it's not my internet's fault. It's quite common to see in the chat something like "this lag though" or "anyone else lagging?" which is quite frustrating, but I guess it's acceptable for an alpha game.
Also, if you're a casual gamer going into this game expecting a nice, lovely, calm, and relaxing game then you are probably not going to have a great time. As the game description states itself, "Hurtworld is a hardcore multiplayer survival FPS with a focus on deep survival progression that doesn't become trivial once you establish some basic needs. Built for hardcore gamers, Hurtworld aims to punish."
So far I believe there are 4 biomes to explore, and every server is set on the same small map. Servers have a player limit of 50, and when 50 players are all running around in the same small map you will come across a few lone individuals or groups of people fairly often.
From my experience so far, hunger has been the main problem. And when you're starting out, it can be a real pain killing animals for food. Alongside this, temperature is also a very big problem when starting out. Although, I got slightly bothered when I did from hypothermia in the middle of the day. In a desert.
That's really all I have to say about the game so far, I'm sure there are many better reviews than my own out there so go check those out, as they probably do a hell of a lot better at explaining things than I did. But overall, in the game's current stage, I'm probably going to give it an 8/10, which is pretty darn good for a game that was released 11 days ago as an alpha.
