One problem the Call of Duty titles have had over the years is the fact that everything is just so... Well, horizontal. The maps have two floors, you can jump three feet and the closest to skill kills you see is when someone spins three times in mid jump throws a throwing knife and just proves to you that they have yet to even hear the world "clitoris," let alone see one. The high pitched whines of people who don't understand the concept of audio feedback matched only by the high pitched whines of the people who seem to speak feedback fluently.
In this iteration, the tables seem to have turned. Barely anyone uses voice chat and for the first time in the series; verticality is a thing. Now you can react when someone fires a round into your back by jumping into the air and dashing behind them to turn the tables and deliver an oh-so-sweet revenge kill. You don't feel like just a bag of flesh anymore, you feel like a soldier and more often than not, a damn fine one. Gone are the days when you had to be a god to achieve the highest scorestreaks and getting a killstreak to kill ten people was the only way to get the next streak. You can (and I have) work your way up to an orbital gunship by simply marking out enemies with your recon drones and UAVs. No longer are you restricted to using the old fashioned Harrier, AC-130, Nuclear Strike if you want to achieve MVP status. In fact, killstreaks pale in comparison to objective play for score.
The weapons admittedly require a little bit of balancing. If you go head to head with some of the most used weapons, odds are you'll feel as if you were playing conkers and your opponent was using a crane and a Volkswagen Golf while you were stuck with the seed of a Horse Chestnut tree. But that's where the beauty of the games' multiplayer comes in. You aren't limited to only three doorways and a window to get where you need to go. If you take one round to the toe, you aren't dead for sure anymore. Your exosuit offers you the ability to counteract the failings of all your previous incarnations in the series. You can dodge, duck, dip, dive and dodge to counter your foes; all while the world around you follows suit. There is new joy to be found in jumping into the air, plummeting two stories into the rear of an enemy team and unleashing a furious storm of explosion-propelled brass. You are both an object of death and a subject of it now; with your awareness, skill and reflex being the main thing to decide which you become.
The maps vary magnificently from an abandoned prison, broken for the most part but still with a functioning inmate tracking system (which you can use for your team if you are lucky enough to acquire it in a care package) to a multi-tiered holiday resort complete with swimming pool and the ability to fall off the edge to your death. But the glorious thing about each map is that you can always attack from the bottom, middle or top. If you go to the bottom level, you can almost always find a way to boost jump up to the middle and the top from there. This opens the game up to a new angle of attack. You have to be aware of what is below you, not just above you if you want to dominate the maps. Some maps are currently subject to some intense lag on some systems (particularly the maps Defender and Instinct); but the remainder work flawlessly.
Scorestreaks are fewer in this game but are easier to acquire and more variable as well. The addition of Scorestreak "Modules" has changed the way they are built, as you can decide just how your scorestreak will behave. If you want to have an orbiting gunship with a rocket turret which a second player on your team can control, it is doable. Your remote sentry guns can become self-targeting rocket or laser turrets which can engage targets in a 360 degree circle and your UAVs can paint your enemies on your HUD as a red silhouette visible through walls. You can even decide if you want certain killstreaks to retain the score you've earned towards them after death; all while you keep others as they were. The ability to persisently earn score towards a high value care package, while you still have your airstrikes, gunships and missile strikes earned per life is quite handy. You may notice I said four different kinds of streaks, which you can now have. There is a wildcard to have four scorestreaks on your class at once; which can make your progress towards the highest significantly easier if you can effectively combine your efforts.
You have thirteen points to allocate to your class and everything costs a point, so knowing what you do and don't use is very important now. If you never use your exo abilities such as a temporary riot shield, cloaking or faster movement; that point can be better invested in a second (or third) attachment for your primary weapon; or perhaps a missile launcher to counter those pesky UAVS and gunships. Your class is not far less limited with the thirteen points but without knowing what you work best with, it is useless to just spend them on anything. Your weapons can even have different variants; which change the stats or add a free weapon attachment at the cost of it being permanently attached. You can find these weapons in supply drops or awarded at 300 kills with the weapon the variant is for. If you found that a gun needs a boost in the rate of fire and doesn't need so much range; there is probably a variant you can acquire which will suit you.
Supply drops are special awards given for completing daily challenges or play time; which can give you a remarkably powerful weapon, bonus experience for a set time or even a nice little outfit for your character. Every kind of unlock is divided into permanent loot (self explanatory) or one of three rarity values, which can be traded in for a a set amount of experience. The rarity is not dependent on your level or what you have unlocked; as you can unlock a rare weapon variant for a weapon unlocked at rank 50, even if your kill/death ratio is negative and your rank is nowhere near what you need to use the weapon.
When you take all of these features and add them together; you get one of the most interesting and enjoyable Call of Duty titles in the series. It is exciting, different enough to be incredibly fun but still familiar enough to make it instantly playable and it's the best time I've had with a Call of Duty title since I used to play it with good friends. Even now, as a cripplingly lonely cynic, this game awakens the happy little mass-murdering psychopath that resides within us all.

This game is a step in the right direction for the CoD series of games,
- The new verticality of the game gives the player a whole new way of taking out enemies.
- The fasted paced nature of the game give the dexterity of the player a run for its money, yes a good computer is needed but it really is a good challenge for the player.
- The introduction of energy based weapons in interesting but is OP due to its INSANE hip fire accuracy and damage, resulting in someone getting called a 'Lazer Noob' by every player on the opposing team.
- My favoritve gamemode is Hardpoint based on it being the fastest paced gameode and easiest way to pick up kills.
- Uplink is a real pain but it is all part of the challenge.
- The map Defender generally seems to have a laggy start to the map which is a shame for a great map.
- I find that Ascend is a struggle to play games on with close range weapons becuase of its open nature, it also looks a little dull for my taste, also players dont tend to use the lower decks.
- Bio Lab is a very balanced map for all combat styles: but you must be a 'pro' to be exeptional on this map.
- Comeback is very vertical with lots of high ground to pick off enemies with maybe a little bit too much ease.
- Defender is a very balanced map for all combat style and their are lots of spot to fire from, but it is a fast paced map so plays move lots.
- I LOVE Detroit for Hardpoint, it has such a nice feel for close quaters combat and serveral ambush and sniping spots.
- Greenband is a very disapointing map, it is very asthetically pleasing but is just too open, no knooks and crannies.
- Horizon is a very good map to play S&D on because of its open areas the quickly turns to small intense areas.
- Instinct is a great map for gamemode that have lots of moving, but slower gamemodes cause players to camp chokepoints which makes this map lose a little respect.
- Recovery is great due to its mid game map change and and multiple level combat.
- Retreat is my favorite map to play Domination or Hardpoint becuase of its open areas and close combat points, it is hard for players in camp it which to me is exremely important.
- Riot is great map to get long shot kills and close quarter ambushing points, unfortunatally the sides back parts of the map are in less use.
- Flanking tactics are most useful in Solar because you can be held down by a sniper but flanking is easyly done to erase this problem.
- Terrace is a holiday destination turend warzone, constant chaos in Domination on this perfect vertical masterpiece.

Very fun take on the MOBA genre.  Rather than a top-down RTS game, this one is more like a behind-the-back shooter (though there are melee characters too!).  This means you can't scroll over the map to see what everyone is doing, but it makes ganks and moves with startup times more fun since you can sneak up on someone and set stuff up behind them.  There are no auto-target attacks, even your basic projectile has to be aimed, but characters can move while attacking so your "right-click" characters still have ways to pour DPS all over the enemy team.  Last-hits are also given a bit less emphasis, as you still get a little gold just by being near a minion as it dies.  It's still better for carries to score direct kills on minions, but at least this way you aren't just useless if you're new to the game and having some trouble with it, and it lets supports get a little more gold to buy actual high-tier items!  There's a lot less emphasis on active items as well.  In fact, you're given exactly 2 "active" slots (like LoL summoner spells you buy mid-match) and 2 "consumable" slots to work with, and your main item slots are all stats and passive effects.
If you liked the idea of MOBAs but wanted something a little simpler to get into them, or simply want a more action-oriented take on the genre, then give this game a try!
Also, you can do a one-time purchase to unlock ALL the characters if you're not into free-to-play stuff ;)

Oh, boy, this game!! It's just so darn CUTE! I don't really like fluffy games but the second I saw this I was hooked. And I'm really happy I took a chance early on, because the developers are not only dedicated to this game, but they take their consumers very seriously & fix bugs as quick as they can. For v.0.6.0 it feels like a complete game for hours.
So, let's talk about the game:
-Developers: They really care & listen to their audience. Feedback is put into the game and it feels genuine. Every update, which are frequent and plentiful, adds tons of content and more hours of gameplay. They boost replayability, as well, since it's exciting to start over when there's an entirely new function & area to explore
-Graphics & Sounds: The slimes are so adorable and the combinations are just as entertaining. The atmosphere and environment are polished & feel finished, even though they're still being upgraded. There isn't a ton of music to the game, but the few tracks they do have are wonderful and don't often sound repetitive. The warning music is daunting, but doesn't make you panic, which is refreshing. It's a feel-good game even with just the title screen on!
-Combat/Gear: There's tons of upgrades available when you figure out the economy system and they all help tremendously. The pacing in regards to how quickly you get the gear also doesn't feel too fast or slow; you generally get to the areas & largos you need the gear for around the time you can afford it. The upgrades don't make the game too easy, but they add more explorability & defense strategy when confonted by aggros. The AI isn't complex, but it doesn't feel dumb either. I can see them making changes to it as they finish the game.
-Story?!?!: I was surprised recently when I hopped on the game after a break, only to find that there was a new story integrated into it! That's very exciting, especially since there's also a new, mysterious area to explore. Additions to the player's lot include extra tidbits of the ranch's past, and it's very endearing and adds an element of connection between the player and the ranch. I look at every corner now just to find something new to read.
-Economy: It's well-rounded, polished, and works well. It's easy to get money after a while, but updates often include more things to spend money on, so I don't see it breaking the game. It'll change before the game is finished, I'm sure.
It's just a really good game and the developers deserve a lot of exposure for this. This is how you do an early access game: with dedication, determination, and heart. Many EA game devs lack these qualities, and we've seen how those turn out. Please get this game, it'll make you smile! :)

The Alien franchise has long been a fan favorite but not very often has it translated to games all that well. There are a few outliers however most of the Alien games have been atrocious and just didn’t bring the feel of the movies to the games, looking at you Colonial Marines. This is pretty strange because in the instance of the first two movies, Alien and Aliens, you have two vastly different movies; one horror and one action. You would think that developers could pull off one of the two. However besides AVP (1, 2 and 2009) this really hasn’t been done. Alien Isolation however attempts to bring the feel of the first movie in which Amanda Ripley is trying to survive on the ship without truly being able to kill the Alien.
Alien Isolation takes what made the first movie great and made it into a game. It is a Survival Horror game with a few shooter elements. Now this isn’t to say you can shoot and kill the Alien, oh no, this only angers said Alien (unless you are using fire). The shooter elements are mainly meant for the synthetics and the other scavenging humans on the station. Being as it is, this game being a survival horror, the objective is to get to where you need to go and not be caught by the Xenomorph (woo Alien terminology), synthetics and humans. You have various tools at your disposal that allow you to accomplish this including flares and noisemakers but for the most part the best way to avoid detection is to be careful and time your movements well while crouch walking. I think my biggest problem with this gameplay is that all this ends up being is just slow careful timing to avoid detection. Now Monolith threw a little wrench in this plan because they made the Xenomorph’s AI a little random. It never takes the same path and can return a second later after it left the room you are in. It can decide to stay in the vents and wait for you to pass one where it can grab you, wait to hear something or it could stay on the ground and search room to room and each locker inside. Church, our other reviewer, found that the Alien found him far too often despite him being completely quiet. However every instance of it finding me was thanks to my own fault; making noise or being too close to the front of the locker (you can move around in a locker and hold your breath too). The beautiful thing with the Alien’s random behavior is your path has to always change to your goal. I’ve had instances where I had to take several vents instead of the hallways just to avoid him but I’ve also had instances where he would get me inside the vents as well which means the motion tracker you get is your best friend.

Now I mentioned earlier that you have different devices (including your fireball magic) that you have access to in order to help you out. Most of these items including the Molotov, Noisemaker, Medkits, EMP bomb and others can be crafted by materials you find throughout the game however you can only hold so many. On top of that you gain five weapons that can help kill the humans and synthetics or ward off/anger the Alien. You eventually get the revolver, shotgun, stun baton, bolt gun (this is REALLY effective versus synthetics) and the flamethrower which is extremely effective scaring the Xenomorph off. With these weapons however there comes problems with using them. If you use one of the projectile weapons within ear range of the Alien, it will come to attack whatever made that sound. If you end up using the Molotov or Flamethrower too much then the Alien will be less frightened of it and will tackle you as it flees causing half damage.

In Alien Isolation you play as Amanda Ripley, Ellen Ripley’s daughter. It is set about 15 years after the events of Alien where Amanda is working with Weyland-Yutani in the hopes of finding out more about what happened to her mom. During all this a station called Sevastopol got in hold of the Nostromo’s (Ellen Ripley’s ship) flight recorder and Weyland-Yutani send Nina Taylor and Amanda Ripley to go get it from them. When they get there they noticed something is very wrong with the station. While doing a cable walk in space to get to the station there ends up being an explosion which separates Ripley from the two others that were with her. As she makes her way through the ship she ends up discovering that there is some sort of creature on board that is killing people and on top of that the Synthetics are killing humans and the humans are killing everyone else in order to survive. As it turns out a ship called the Anesidora was the ship that found the Nostromo’s flight recorder but while following the ship’s flight path they come to LV-426 which had the Alien eggs on the crashed ship. While investigating the ship one of the crew of the Anesidora gets attacked by a facehugger and it hatches on Sevastopol while getting medical aid. All during the game Ripley is trying to get into contact with the ship she was brought on in order to escape the station while trying to discover what happened to the Nostromo and Sevastopol. One of the best things about this story is the pacing and how fluid the game is. Not once do you feel like you are repeating things and the slow flow of the story is very much like how it was in the original movie. In Alien (film) you don’t even seen the Xenomorph until an hour or so into the film and the same could be said about the game as I didn’t encounter it until about an hour or two into it.

Now the graphics in this game are incredible but what really makes the graphics is the aesthetics or how close this game replicates the feel of the original movie. The hallways, the motion tracker, the rooms, doors, the station, even the Xenomorph itself are to the letter of the original movies and for fans of the series you’ll be in nostalgia overload. The game despite releasing in 2014 has the exact sense of being an old 80’s Sci-Fi. On top of that the set pieces are all beautiful and so well done. Alien isolation also has some of the best fire I’ve ever seen in a game which is quite impressive; that flamethrower is so satisfying. The particle effects are also incredible in that the lights will blink through the smoke and look incredible.
On top of the graphics this is probably the best sound effects I’ve ever heard in a game. Now any game that claims to be a survival horror needs to have great sound effects but every little sound in this game are so well done. Monolith matched the sound effects from the original movies so well that I felt like at times I was just watching the movies instead of playing (this doesn’t mean that the framerate was a “cinematic” 30 fps). The siren sounds, motion tracker, the Alien’s sounds and even the synthetics dying all sound amazing and Monolith should really be given a lot of credit for how well they did in this respect. Even the music does well to replicate the movies. It has that edgy feel where the music will suddenly get louder or it will play those quick reverberating notes that you hear all too often in Alien and Aliens.
Now screenshots can’t really illustrate how well they did so here is a video of me playing a bit; WARNING the first 10 seconds have spoilers:

Overall this game is an incredible homage to the Alien franchise and is up there for best game so far this year. The gameplay is quite solid albeit sometimes random and frustrating. The flow of the story and events is great and doesn’t feel like you have to do any minute tasks. The graphics and aesthetics are so well done and the sound and music is some of the best I’ve ever heard in a game. My only real complaint is that despite the game being fun I can’t really play it over again without knowing exactly what is going to happen. There are small DLC that expand the game further and the survival mode is a fun test of skills but the main campaign can really only be played once.
Final Score: 8.8

Picked this up from the Coop sale and immedately fell in love while blasting through hordes of terrorists and aliens with my actual brother!!!   My real Bro and I live really far apart and coop games gives us a great way to stay in touch.  If you have friends you can play with or even a Bro of your own I highly recommend picking this gem up.  The controls are easy to pick up and they feel smooth most of the time.  From start to finish there is non-stop action!  Explosions, screams, mayhem, and madness accompany nearly every moment and the shear amount of stuff going on at any given time make this a fanatasic twitch action platformer.  The levels develop nicely and the dificulty ramps up quite dramatically at times.  The new character unlocks are always amazing and give you another reason to keep pushing on.
Throughout my time in the campaign I only ever encountered one glitch which caused a boss to become unbeatable until we died and restarted the level.  My experiences only cover the coop campaign including the newest alien content (also totally amazing!), so I can't speak to how stable the deathmatch content is.  But the wifi connection was fine and my Bro and I had a smooth experince even with skype voice chat taking up some bandwidth too.  Ultimately my biggest complaint is with Indiana Jones's character who is somewhat useless as he can only kill with his knife or bombs!
If you've looked at this and thought "maybe it'll be worth but I just don't know..." I can honestly tell you that it is worth it!  Even for an early access game there is a good amount of content and it runs smoothly.  The developers have put together a good product and gotten many of the basics down solidly.  There is a ton of potential for growth and I can't wait for more content.

Dark Souls 2 is probably one of the best sequels I've seen for a series in the past 10 years, comparable to Mass Effect 2 as far as memorable sequels go.
From Software seems to have learned quite a bit from their port of DS1 to PC and happy to report that the major flaws of DS1's port have been addressed and resolved; resolution, 60FPS, GFWL (gone), keyboard functionality and netcode.
As far as the game goes, simply put, it's gorgeous. Plenty of awe-inspiring views and vistas, improved lighting, textures and character models.
Mechanically feels exactly the same as DS1 but with the immediately noticeable 60FPS makes the frame timing for parries and dodges that much harder/precise. Lots more PvP options and weapons help plenty in keeping things fresh. Each character type requires a totally different approach to certain areas whereas in DS1 strategies are slightly more universal.
My only let down to the game are the bosses. I feel the humanoid or armored knight style of boss was a bit overused; Old Dragonslayer, Dragonrider, Velstadt, Ruin Sentinels, Smelter Demon, Looking Glass to name a few. You could also make an arguement that many of the bosses are reskinned versions of DS1 bosses, I wouldn't disagree. You can clearly see the inspiration for each of the bosses. However, there are new and interesting boss mechanics that stand on their own. Looking Glass Knight, Executioner's Chariot, Prowling Magus...while not terribly difficult they do each add their own flavor.
Progression of the game is where it shines. The areas are much more difficult to go through than DS1 and to compensate they added a LOT more bonfires which helps for a first playthrough. So the formula has changed DS1=relatively tough areas with a possibly rage inducing boss at the end of that while DS2=rage inducing areas followed by a tense but managable boss fight. The only truly tough bosses for me were Smelter Demon, Royal Rat Authority (the start of it at least) and Lost Sinner on NG+.
I could spend more time writing detailed comments but just look at my hours played, the price of the game and the fact that I'm taking time to review it. Any game that gives you at least a dollar per hour of FUN play is a success. A must have for any fans of the series and a more balanced experience for newcomers to the unforgiving gameplay. If you have rage problems, have a go at the Dark Souls series and it will humble you if you can stomach it!

Amazing game, albeit rather difficult even for the experienced player. It's challenging nature really provides a sense of achievement for both the casual and serious player.
It combines both tactical, and smooth combat  for both PvE and PvP combat, and is perfectly suitable for those with either preference.
The game is visually stunning, and any that plays this game is bound to either love it immediately or grow to love it. It is an amazing addition to the souls series, and certainly reaches the high expectations set by its predecessor.
PS - Perfect dodging, and don't bother with a shield - they will only let you down.
EDIT :: This was a review drafted after my first playthrough of the game. Since, my outlook has drastically altered. I will not deny that it was enjoyable my first time, but the more I have played DS2 the more of its shortcomings I have noticed, and the more downfalls I realise it has. It is still a good game, but not as good as the above review would indicate.
If playing with a Mouse and Keyboard, the controls are clunky, and you have to deal with mouse delays of an entire second. You'll have to remap most of the bindings to suit playstyle, and be able to somewhat bypass the clunkiness.
Many of the areas, despite looking 'aesthetically pleasing', are wholly lacking innovation and the same applies to the world design. Much of it doesn't even make geographical sense, many of the areas overlap (and not in the intertwining sense of DS1 - but instead should actually be on each other.) I would give examples, but I don't want to 'spoil' the game.
A number of the bosses are unimaginative, and are even redesigns of bosses from DS2's predecessor. Yes, it's difficult to come up with new and exciting bosses, but when the vast majority are just your typical humanoid with a big sword; it would be nice that when you finally encounter a non-humanoid boss, it didn't happen to be a boss you fought in DS1 just with a different skin. Expanding on that -- lack of variety in enemies.
Most of the enemies in DS2 are humanoid soldiers. Swordsmen, archers, mages, the occasional big thing with a heavy weapon. Other types of enemies are few and far between. Also, enemy placement. Gosh this is a pain. Many of the combat scenarios in this game are a chore - using crowds of enemies to overwhelm the player instead of using strategically placed enemies to provide a challenge. The DLC solves this to an extent, but has a massive downfall in that it gave most of its enemies HUGE or almost infinite poise -- which means they cannot be staggered. Even when you're 2-handing a UGS and use the strong attack, and they just walk through it and smack you for half your health. It encourages you to wait for an opening, yes; but when this game favours scenarios where the player is attacked by multiple enemies that can't be staggered and can kill you in two to three hits, it becomes a little artificial.
Sloppy Combat

Terrible porting job, just a tad bit better than the original Dark Souls port: where the original was entirely broken in that the game ran like crap, Dark Souls II runs perfectly fine but you can tell that they didn't give the PC port much thought at all:
The default controls are incredibly awkward, but at least they are rebindable by default this time around (rather than having to mod them). One of the greatest sins though is the fact that you get EFFING XBOX 360 CONTROLLER PROMPTS!!! There's just no excuse for this and it makes the game a million times more confusing than it should be. For example, I have no idea how to unequip/equip armour and weapons. The game just doesn't tell you, and all the prompts are for a feckin' controller. This makes the ability to rebind your keys a whole lot less useful because you have no idea what function you are rebinding!
They also went around and mucked up some true-and-tested Dark Souls mechanics that we've grown to love; block is a toggle now (you can't just hold down block and release it when you feel like it) and to do a heavy attack you DOUBLE-CLICK rather than just HOLD DOWN the button/key as in the original. WHY?! WHY CHANGE WHAT WE'VE ALL GROWN ACCUSTOMED TO?!
And what's worse: as the game has VAC, trying to salvage this mess through modding (like you can with the original) will end up with you getting banned from the online portions of the game - and that is what Dark Souls is all about!
STAY AWAY FROM THIS MESS!!! DO NOT BUY!!! DON'T SUPPORT HORRIBLE PC PORTS!!!

What can I say? It is like the good ol' classic 2D worms games! With some new features, including vehicles and crafting! I've personally only golded all tutorials and am finishing the two of the campaign missions off completely, so I can only review the single player aspect, which is like most other worm games. You get different levels with different worms and voices. Some of the worms and voices will reoccur on other stages, however.
Most of the campaign is fun and a good challenge. Each time feels like a different match as the outcome keeps changing. Which is neat. Though it does suck when your perfectly executed mission ends up failing or ruining an extra objective due to a mistake and then you can never repeat it perfectly, but hey, that's life and keeps the missions fresh! There are a few missions and objectives which are very annoying though, mainly ones that rely on the NPC/AI to not kill themselves which ruins the extra objective. Another thing that can be annoying is when going for the extra objectives, it can be A LOT of restarting to get the perfect beginning which can be all the difference in completing some of these objectives, so it can get a bit tiring, espeically if you have a low tolerance for patience. But that's totally dependant on your skill level too, I'm sure a pro player probably executes everything perfectly or mostly perfectly, but I'm not too sure there haha. But as a casual worms player who plays to just enjoy himself and have some fun, it can get a bit tiring after a bunch of resetting with no action, however, once it gets to that point where you are sick of it, I just stop for the day and play it on another day!
My biggest letdown is how you cannot customize each worm. When I saw the trailers and every worm with a different helmet, I got really excited. I pre-ordered for the Yooka-Laylee heads but when I found out my team could only share the same head, I thought this really sucked. Especially when the videos looked as if each worm was customizable. So the lack of different hats on each worm is probably my only big letdown and I hope one day they make an update to change this. As I want each worm to look different. Plus, it's not hard to tell who your worms are, even if the opponent had the exact same, since you have coloured team names plus usually the worms are named uniquely as well. But even if you had the same exact different worms and names, you could still tell your worms from the colour. So I think they should add in the ability to have each worm on a team have a different hat. I really want my Yooka-Laylee team!
But overall, if you love worms, especially the 2D games, then I think this will fit your pallete! Even if you are just a casual dude, I'm sure you can get some good fun out of it. Probably more if you play with friends or even just online!

Ultimately, this game proved to be a dissappointing.  For context I usually am a Single Player gamer so like campaigns and do not normally go for Sci-fi shooters.  Like a lot of Sci-Fi shooters, from a story perspective this one just didn't really have me engaged and ultimately was a big let down compared to the previous iterations in this series.  Similarly, the set pieces were toned down and didn't seem to have the same adrenaline rush.
+ Fun for the most part, no brain shooter.
+ For a scifi setting, the weapons were solid, not many silly lasers or other guns.
+ Some nice scifi parts, such as the prison sequence.
- Long load times
- Terrible boat, airplane, etc. sequences.  They play like a poor arcade game and had no place in this game.
- Buggy.  Particularly the sound.  If you put this ins 5.1 expect problems, particularly during cinematics.  Graphics lag for no reason on a power house PC with a Geforce 780 TI water cooled.  No excuses.
- Poor man's crysis.  The suits just don't add much in such a linear game, "use special ability now", which made it ineffective.
- SciFi shooter syndrome.  Bad tech, bad story, unengaging storyline.  If you are going to do scifi, look at BioShock, Dishonoured, etc.
- Graphics were weak/average.  The same tricks were used as previous iterations of boxing down the levels, but despite some decent character animation, the over all set pieces were a let down.
Worse than other installments, I can not recommend it until it drops to 10-15$ (which i guess means 15 euros and 15 pounds in steam maths).

When I bought the game at release, I was kind of reluctant. The setting didn't appeal to me, the graphics were bizarre, and I wasn't a shooter player. But I got it anyway. You know how it goes: Relationship went down the drain, you need some distraction, and killing stuff that screams makes for great distraction.
I can't say the game grabbed me right away. It didn't. The first few levels were tedious, I got killed (just what my damaged ego needed), I got lost, and I had no clue what I was doing. I kept playing, though, and after a couple of hours the game really opened up. Another two or three hours and I was hooked. Borderlands 2 was the only game I played for several months, and when I discovered co-op with a friend, it advanced into the top-3 of the greatest games I've played to date.
So what makes it great? The gameplay, the loot, replayability, and the characters.
The gameplay: Like I said, I'm really not a FPS player (old, slow, awareness of a potato at times), but it's all fluid and it's not particularly punishing when you start out sucking like the ex that dumped you. The various classes all have a distinct playstyle, so you're bound to find at least one that you get a good handle on and that you'll have a great time with. The game does ramp up in difficulty,  but so will your skill (and failing that, your gear will get better and you'll feel as if you got more skilled).
The loot: While shooters typically don't work out for me for long-term fun, Diablo-like ARPGs always suck me in, in absolutely no time. The main reason is the loot. They are all giant slot machine, and every mob you slay might drop something fantastic. Borderlands 2 uses the same random loot (and loot tables) system like the best ARPGs, and it's like candy for those of us who never get tired of the thrill of the treasure hunt. You can play this for years without finding every item you desire, rolled just the way you want it, but you might get your most sought after drop after your next boss run. You never know, and it never gets old.
The replayability: The game has a ton of content even in the base game, and so much more is added by the DLC. Over the years, the level cap was raised twice, and we got a gauntlet to get from OP1 to OP8 levels to really test our skill (and it's hard). There are raid bosses (that can eventually be done solo), there's co-op, there's dueling, and there are three difficulty modes, which you can even reset and re-do the quests (to farm for quest rewards). You can play this for hundreds of hours without running out of stuff to do. This also includes increasing your Badass Rank (grants passive buffs to all your characters) by completing challenges and collecting all unlockable skins (many of which are drops).
The characters: If I had to nominate the game with the best NPCs, Borderlands 2 would be my undisputed choice. No other game I played comes close. NPCs like Tiny Tina or Mr. Torque, or even Handsome Jack, are memorable -- with lines that will pop up on your mind even after years, making you wonder where you had heard them before (like Jack's "I don't even know what to call you!"), and you probably won't be able to watch the news without exclaiming "Exploooooosions!" at one point or another. Really, the characters are hilarious, inappropriate, and downright fun. Great stuff.
So if you like loot, if you want to experience some crazy stories with messed up NPCs to tell your kids about, or if you just want to kill some sh!t for fun, this is a wonderful game. It stood the test of time well, and is unquestionable one of the best games I've played. I can only highly recommend it. You won't be disappointed. Promise!

First Playthrough with Emily on Hard difficulty. Low Chaos. Stealth
Her Powers and Abilities are similar, but also quite different to her counterpart in the prequel.
Including a movement spell (Far Reach) to either pull yourself towards a foe or a foe towards yourself.
(Shadow Walk) is surprisingly effective for taking out single enemies, but the mana consumption per transformationmay seem to much for "just a target". Me on the other hand, i used this to avoid enemy detection in close proximity, as it makes you look like a shadow and thus hiding your presence. Unless you literally stand and touch an enemy.
The last power, that I unlocked (and that Corvo doesn't have) is called "Domino", which grants you the ability to link targets with each other (up to 4). The linked targets will share the same fate. Like if you knock one linked target out, so will be the remaining ones. This also applies to a more lethal approach. Highly recommended for situations with a high amount of enemy presence.
The game in general has improved a lot over the 4 years between the prequel and the release of the sequel. The PC Masterrace had some major issues with framerate drops for low-ende/budget and high-end machines alike. The precision weapon of choice, the mouse, also had input lags, which made the gameplay a lot more choppy. After around 2 weeks, Arkane Studios released a hotfix for the mentioned problems and it seems a lot more playable, even though I finished my first run before the patch.
Gameplay 9/10 (includes the almost infinite ways of overcoming an obstacle, many many upgrades. Apparently not a traditional Open-world game)
Sound 9/10 (eerie winds, whispers, waves crashing against the ship,...)
Graphics 10/10 (improved shadow and lighting, HD textures, juicy animations:both lethal and nonlethal takedowns)
Story 8/10 (Not gonna spoiler it)
Replay value 9/10 (You should at least play this game 4 times with different approaches: High chaos/ low chaos Emily + High chaos/ low chaos Corvo)
If you loved the prequel Dishonored 1. You'll love this sequel even more!
Looking forward to the DLCs.

This is by far the best Worms game they've ever made. I've been a huge fan since Worms 1 and there's been quite a few missteps in the series' lifetime. But this one, oh boy, this one is a return to form!
I love the design of the Worms themselves. Gone is the over-cutesy look that took over in Worms 2. I never really liked that look. Worms are supposed to be cute, sure, but the cuteness comes from the worms believing they are tough but then you realize that they are just cute because, you know, they are friggin' worms!
Weapons and crafting are top-notch. Ninja rope is exactly as it should be. So many insane weapons to choose from.
Vehicles and mounted guns adds to the strategic possibilites which makes it unique among Worm games. So this is not just another remake of the Worms formula. This is taking it to the next level.
Grahpics and animations are simply superb. And with a level editor tool accompanying the game, that makes for some nice customization possibilites.
I can only come up with a single complaint. I want more editors! Speech bank editors, hat editors, tomb stone editors. This would really add to the personality. And then implement auto-download when playing in multiplayer. You should of course be able to turn that off so it just uses a standard speech bank if they can't be downloaded.
But yeah, I remember fondly making speech banks for Worms 1, and it hasn't really been possible since... Big letdown for me since I love modding my games.
That aside, this is almost a perfect Worms game. If you are looking for that, go buy it now! And let the mayhem BEGIN!!!

A nice attempt to try something new with call of duty. The story is rather interesting but does have a lot of moments of why this and why that....there is even a point in the game where I wish it branched off and allowed you to make this simple choice of following a special someone or not to allow more story info and even points of view on why the story is built on these paths.
There is some audio issues during loading which seem to be fixed now, but there is a slight issue with the loading screen as it does provide a video giving some background story but it finishes rather fast before the loading is done meaning your stuck looking at a black screen.....why they couldn't of made the video longer (like Modern Warfare 2 allowing you to watch a long video and skip once loading was completed) to cover the long loading is rather strange as there is a lot of background information they could of filled in to keep the player in check with the story.
The guns are pretty awesome as well as the ability to upgrade and improve your exo suit which comes pretty handy allowing you to slide and double jump...however each mission does restrict some abilities for example one mission may allow you to double jump then the next mission takes that away and gives you a climbing ability.
There are a few memorable missions, one being a bike ride, another a tank mission and of course the all out war stuff.
However the biggest issues are:
1. Call of duty still feels linear, instead of trying to attempt a more wider approach and more non scripted events. For example there is one mission where it's all out war and you see choppers flying low dropping off troops. This mission and only this mission you are able to climb up there at your own chosing and gun the crew down, you can even avoid that approach and take a rocket to it or steal a enemy tank to shoot it down. This whole approach felt awesome and more in the player control.
2. Feels short. I tried the story on medium and then veteran and felt the game rather short and not really challenging, namely Black ops series I found myself getting a beating in veteran as mass waves of enemies charge my location and throw the unlimited amount of grenades behind my cover but Advanced Warfare never gave me that challenge and most times I felt extremely overpowered which isn't a bad thing since I'm wearing this exo suit but I ended flying through the game rather fast.
To me it's a good start and finally something a bit different then the rest but still doesn't feel right....like it's missing something. However Kevin Spacey does help the story abit....I think they put all the graphics on his face though because he looks really detailed compared to my other teammates.....
I would recommend you wait for a sale if your aiming for the singleplayer elements. For the online I can't really say much only that the customization is nicely done and the whole usage of Exosuits for online battles are awesome...but there isn't much change, there is still TD, capture , Control and still the same amount of player limit as before.. They did have a survival mode but it gets boring pretty fast.

The actual Alien is a masterpiece of fear. It's solid sounding footsteps echo throughout the area you're in, you hear every movement as it crawls through the vents waiting to pounce.....but you can't see it until it's too late. CON:
- Can be repetative at times
- Hard is the optimal difficulty setting that uses every aspect of the game
- Only one Survivor Mode map
"CREW EXPENDABLE" and "LAST SURVIVOR" DLCs:

My review comes from a man who previously purchased this game for a dollar on Xbox 360. At the time, it was the best dollar I had ever spent on a digital game because this game is fun . . . if you have friends . . . and if you need to kill small amounts of time. The gameplay is very simple as you walk around searching for 8 tapes while avoiding eye contact with a monster and strange green statues., which is something I actuallly appreciate about WNO.
The visuals and music are also simple. That's fine. It makes it easier to see/hear the tapes you need to collect and the monster you need to avoid.
It's compared to Slender, and rightfully so. That's also fine. I liked Slender well enough.
I'd definitely recommend playing with friends and not taking this game too seriously.
However, the asking price is much higher than on Xbox. If, over time, new content is added beyond new maps and characters, then the price may be fair.
But, I still bought it and installed it on my Steambox. I had good memories playing it on my Xbox 360 with friends, and want it available on Steam. I will encourage my friends to buy it so I can play with them.
If you play alone, either wait for a steep discount or go all-in and buy the 4-pack to take advantage of what makes this game enjoyable - simple, stupid fun with friends.
I'll recommend buying it as a small co-op game.

This is a worthy successor to the best Worms title, Worms: Armageddon.
The problem with saying something like that is that Armageddon has a thousand little features and it's impossible for all of them to make it over to a new game, short of Team 17 literally just re-releasing Armageddon under a new name. So there will always be complaints and negative reviews from certain Armageddon fans because it was their favourite feature that was cut. There will be opposing voices who will say 'This is like Armageddon' and 'This is not like Armageddon'. Instead of listening to and trusting either of them, you have to scrutinise exactly what it was from Armageddon that you loved and found wanting from the series ever since. For me it was the following:
1. Fluid 60 FPS animation, with no jankiness, slowdown, or pauses before explosions. In short, performance.
2. Crisp, clean 2D artwork, without noisy and distracting backgrounds, but full of personality.
3. The clean, easily navigated weapons menu from Worms2/WA instead of the confusing unorganised mess introduced with Worms 2: Armageddon.
4. Tight movement and jumping physics, with various keys for different types of jumps
5. Fun 'rigid' rope physics
6. Support for lots of worms per map
All of this returns to the series with Worms: WMD. If this is what you have found lacking in recent Worms titles, you might find WMD something of a homecoming. I did.
But of course, this is not just about how like or unlike Armageddon this is. WMD also has its own identity, and introduces new mechanics:
1. Buildings are a fantastic tactical addition which add a minimum amount of cover from the start, kind of like a ready-made miniture base.
2. Crafting, in my eyes, replaces the old Armageddon system of each team choosing their personal superweapon. Instead, crafting lets you dismantle and create weapons on the fly according to the situation, so everyone will end up with a unique arsenal based on their creativity and playstyle. This is not overpowered: you can't, for example, dismantle lots of lesser weapons and create a more powerful one than what you started with.
3. Vehicles are probably the biggest change to the Worms formula. They work well, are fun and require skill to use, though on launch they played too prominent a role in the outcome of matches, and after listening to the community Team 17 has reduced their spawn rate.
And this segues into perhaps one of the most important positives to WMD, which cannot be overstated: this game is getting ongoing support from Team 17, who have committed to work with and listen to the community to make this the definitive Worms multiplayer experience. And this is already evidenced after the complaints of vehicles being too prominent, and the rapid changes introduced subsequently. What you're buying is a fully supported online multiplayer game, with ranked and unranked modes, which will be guided by the community and supported by the developers. Who knows, if there's a much-loved feature from Armageddon which is sorely missed - weapons, or customisation options - enough demand might see it happen later. To get such a deal for a game which in its present form is already so faithful to Worms: Armageddon, and yet with a modern touch, personality and innovations of its own, makes it a no-brainer of a purchase.

TL;DR: Advanced Warfare is fantastic and is the best multiplayer FPS of 2014 - at least, it would be if it was optimized.
Unmarked spoilers for Advanced Warfare's campaign below.
Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare is the BEST game in the franchise's history. THAT SAID, at time of writing I am unable to recommend it. The campaign is boilerplate, bland, very summer-action-blockbuster. It ambitiously promises something more than America vs. Terrorists/Russia/Current Antagonistic Eurasian Nation, but falls flat. The character writing is bland, as player character Mitchell and Will Irons are "best friends" whose little conversation is telling each other about their dads fir the first time. The faceless Marine that accompanies Mitchell, Will, and Cormack seems to know more about Will than his "best friend" does. The fantastic voice talent that is brought on board feels wasted, as Paul Telfer (Will Irons) is killed off in the first mission to establish DRAMA!!! and provide the inciting action for the main story, Troy Baker (Mitchell) seems to be just as bored of the plot as the player, narrating cutscenes with nowhere near the investment he had in Bioshock Infinite or sheer commitment as in Far Cry 4. The incredible talent of Kevin Spacey (Jonathan Irons) is wasted, as he plays a titan of a man plagued by his own demons who transforms into a G.I. Joe villain halfway through the campaign. Gideon Emery (Gideon) is the star of the show here, which would be great if he was the player character and not the invincible god of war we're told to follow for half the campaign. Writing is definitely the weak link in this campaign, as incredible art design and innovative movement are shoehorned into a "use all this cool stuff where we tell you to, when we tell you to" rail shooter that leans heavily on its scripted moments to impress, with Modern Warfare 2's Brazilian favelas replaced by Nigerian slums and the final level causing many players to say "Wait, didn't we do this same thing at the end of Modern Warfare 3?"
Now for the big one: the Multiplayer. (120 hours MP played, which won't be counted in my "hours played" on this review) Competitive MP is the best in the franchise, with the exoskeleton providing freedom of movement that harkens back favorably to Quake 3 or Unreal Tournament. CoD die-hards who shun faster-paced FPS titles like Halo, Titanfall, or the aforementioned arena-shooters decry that their modern military shooter is being ruined by dashes and double-jumps, but I disagree; Ghosts and Black Ops were more faithful modern military shooters, and even they had sliding, knife-wielding psychos, and the infamous Black Ops "dolphin dive". Combat is still lightning-quick, but the ability to make a quick dash to the side to evade fire, jump over your opponent to turn the tables, or even deploy a bulletproof shield from your exo changes the game significantly. Indeed, exo abilities provide new depth that is a breath of fresh air in otherwise stale shooty-shooty-whiz-bang, although they could stand to take a review pass (Exo Ping has a criminally short range, where Mute Device is next to useless; Trophy System is similarly pointless outside of objective gametypes). Supply drops, despite their drop rate that is maybe a little too slow (once every 45 minutes, where a TDM match can be over in 5), keep things interesting with unlockable variants for your weapons that let you find the variant that suits your playstyle, and cosmetic customization rivals Halo: Reach in level of quality. For anyone who wants to make a character that is very "them" in a FPS, Advanced Warfare is the one for you.
With all the good things I have to say about the multiplayer, I feel like this comes across as a positive review. The truth is, it would be, but while the game is quite fun, it's in a rough place technically. Despite Sledgehammer head Michael Condrey's assurance that dedicated servers are in place for Advanced Warfare, lag is a serious issue, and hackers when they are encountered are blatant and seemingly able to ruin the game with impunity. I've been killed around corners to find that on the killcam, I wasn't
around that corner, and Advanced Warfare has shown me more blatant snap-to-head aimbots than Counter-Strike, UT, and Titanfall combined. Additionally, the game's maps are fairly small. This is not necessarily a bad thing, as the normal game size is 6v6. However, it
a bad thing for those small maps to cause low FPS and framerate stalls on high-end hardware. I have frequent stutters on Recovery and Defender; with a i5-4690k 3.5 GHz processor, 8 GB RAM, and a NVIDIA GTX 970 @ 4 GB (meets or exceeds recommended specs), this is unacceptable.
A "fun" bit of trivia is that Advanced Warfare is written in Klingon. That is, from TVtropes: "...the documentation and variables in the game files are written in ... tlhIngan Hol, the language that was constructed for the Klingons in the Star Trek Universe." I can't shake the feeling that if Sledgehammer Games had spent less time teaching their staff a fictional language and more time refining their product, they'd have
FPS of 2014. As is, I'm waiting and hoping against hope that fixes are in the pipe that will let me edit this review into a "Recommended".

Picked this up from the Coop sale and immedately fell in love while blasting through hordes of terrorists and aliens with my actual brother!!!   My real Bro and I live really far apart and coop games gives us a great way to stay in touch.  If you have friends you can play with or even a Bro of your own I highly recommend picking this gem up.  The controls are easy to pick up and they feel smooth most of the time.  From start to finish there is non-stop action!  Explosions, screams, mayhem, and madness accompany nearly every moment and the shear amount of stuff going on at any given time make this a fanatasic twitch action platformer.  The levels develop nicely and the dificulty ramps up quite dramatically at times.  The new character unlocks are always amazing and give you another reason to keep pushing on.
Throughout my time in the campaign I only ever encountered one glitch which caused a boss to become unbeatable until we died and restarted the level.  My experiences only cover the coop campaign including the newest alien content (also totally amazing!), so I can't speak to how stable the deathmatch content is.  But the wifi connection was fine and my Bro and I had a smooth experince even with skype voice chat taking up some bandwidth too.  Ultimately my biggest complaint is with Indiana Jones's character who is somewhat useless as he can only kill with his knife or bombs!
If you've looked at this and thought "maybe it'll be worth but I just don't know..." I can honestly tell you that it is worth it!  Even for an early access game there is a good amount of content and it runs smoothly.  The developers have put together a good product and gotten many of the basics down solidly.  There is a ton of potential for growth and I can't wait for more content.

Well I just "finished" Black Mesa, the graphically improved version of the original Half-Life, and I have to say I was very impressed! Not only is the game Graphically enhanced but the voice lines are all redone and it really is a new game consisting mostly of new textures with a few pulled from HL2, there's also a variety of new npc models made exclusively for Black Mesa. They even included unique models specifically for Dr. Kliener and Eli Vance as their models for HL2 were originally based off the 2 or 3 models for scientists in the original.
Although, you might be wondering why I put "finished" in air quotes and that's because the game isn't actually 100% completed yet, they have everything done up until you go into the portal to get to the Borderworld of Xen. Once you go into the portal you get a message saying the assignment has been postponed as they're gathering more research. Essentially what they're saying is that it's not done yet but once it's finished it will be added to the game free of charge!
However even without Xen the game is a fantastic deal! It really helps bring the original Half-Life into the modern age of gaming whilst staying true to the story and game play of the original! As a result I can whole heartedly recommend Black Mesa to anyone who would like to revisit the original Half-Life or to anyone who has never played Half-Life but would like to try it out and find out the origin of the series!

Alien Isolation is a “true love story” the Alien loves to kill you. The team at Creative Assembly were given an impossible task to try and raise the “Alien Franchise” from the dead and I feel they did a fantastic job. I saw the reviews saying "too long" and "too may endings", I said it is the game that keeps giving. Creative Assembly made a great game and I can’t wait for the sequel.

First off, the good elements of the game: It captures the feel of the original alien movie very well. It is genuinely tense in many parts due to the atmospheric audio and sound track. The graphics side of things are also quite impressive, the game is fairly nice to look at. However my expereince so far of the game is overall disapointing.  It is by no means a bad game, but it does not quite live up to the expectations. My biggest complaints are as follows:
Firstly, you learn very quickly that the game is a console port. As a result the control of your charcter in the game does not feel as sharp as a pc game should. However this is a fairly minor complaint and the game does allow you to turn off aim assist to limit the horrible feel of a console game.
Secondly, and probably one of the biggest problems I had with this game are the enemy characters and the AI. The game features not just a big scary alien, but also hostile human and synthetic enemies. I first encountered the armed human enemies who I decided to try and avoid as this stealthy style of game play seemed to be what the game was all about. This method worked fairly well most of the time, but when I found myself in one situation where I needed to get passed a room full of eneimes I failed every time. I kept getting discovered and gunned down wether I used distrations or tried different routes when trying to sneak passed. I lured all my enemies and hid in a vent, but rather than continuing on with thier search they all gathered arouned the door near the vent I was in as if they knew they couldn't attack me because they hadn't techinically found me yet, but they also didn't look any further past where I was hiding making it impossible to slip by. At this point I was so sick and tired of trying the stealth approach that I leapt out of the vent and charged my hunters with the crow bar like weapon. They all noticed me and raised their guns but since they were all standing so closed to eachother only the enemy directly in front would attempt to attack me. The others just stood there waiting thier turn while I slowly clubbed each one to death. In the end I mananged to fairly easily take out 4 guys with guns by myself with a crow bar.
On that point, the guns. After killing all my armed enemies I naturally thought, woo I can hoard all thier shiny new guns. However I was wrong, the game only allows you to kick the guns around on the floor that have been dropped by your conquered enemies. You have to wait untill you get to the room with the special gun just for you because apparaently that is the only weapon you know how to pick up.
So from this I learned that the AI in this game was not necessarily as intelligent as the sales pitch made out. Next I encounted the android or synthetic enemies. There was a moment where you are hiding in a vent and the game shows you a random person being attacked and killed by a synthetic. This I figured was the game telling me, "ok so the synthetics will attack you now ok?" However since by this point I had a gun I decided to have a crack at one I found by himself. I shot the robot in the back of his head which understandably provoked him. However no matter how many more bullets I unloaded into his face he didn't go down. When he finally cornered me I discovered they the synthetics are also capable of catching almost every hit with the crow bar making it useless to attack them as well. I know these characters are supposed to be robots not people, but why give me weapons at all? This encapsulates my main problem with this game over all. The game is difficult in a really lazy way. You get weapons and guns and the like only to find out that in order to stop you being rambo, the game simply turns off the effect of these weapons on most of the enemies. Robots come at you even if you fired enough bullets that they should no longer have a head. However this lazy neutering of the weapons is worst of all with the feature character of the game, the alien.
Obviously you can't just kill the alien because there is only 1. However, during my first few encounters with the creature which were actually quite tense I always managed to sneak past him. Finally howver there was a moment when he saw me from the other end of a long hall way and immediately charged towards me. I pulled out my selectively useful revolver and fired off round after round thinking I could distract or stun the monster for a moment to make my escape. However the alien wasn't too bothered and charaged straight on at me. In fact my bullets didn't even seem to exist when fired at the alien. Literally, there was no impact animation or anyhting on the alien it was as though I was firing blanks. The game essentially says, 'no you can't kill the alien so we are just going to turn your guns off when you use them against our baby" It really feels as though the guns, or at least the ones that fire bullets, are in the game specifically for use against the other human enemies only. Again this game is by no means bad, just not as good as it could have been or as it was marketed to be. You quickly become aware of the limitations and controls the game places over you so that you play the way it wants rather than how you want.

So, I just beat this game. Lets see...
This game offers the next logical step from Amnesia. In Amnesia, it was too easy to adapt to the monsters, and eventually, it got a bit tiresome. However, when it became tiresome, you were able to relax a bit more, and advance through the store which ended quite fast.
Alien Isolation offers something similar, but the NPCs are not so easy to adapt to. They do follow certain patterns of logic, but not set paths. So instead of knowing "This guy goes to A, and then to B, and then to C." you instead learn "When I do A, this thing does B, so I need to do A and then act on C." You learn to out think the programming, rather than just predicting it.
It mixes in a number of RPG elements that Amnesia never did, allowing you to craft medical kits, noise makers, and a variety of other tools which help in survival. Saving these up, using them only when needed is key, in classic survival horror tradition.
As you learn the game, you will start to be able to relax a bit more, and you wont always be on the edge of your seat. As you start to be able to out smart the enemy, the game becomes something more of a stealth game than a horror game.
Ultimately, the story is very Alien. If you enjoyed the story of Alien, you will enjoy the story of Alien: Isolation.

Great voice acting and writing and although it is not exactly a "normal" Elder Scrolls game, it doesnt feel like a regular MMO at all. People dont have their nametags hanging over their heads, you have to focus on them to see if they are even real players, which is a nice touch, it is more immersive this way IMO. So if you are looking for an MMO that is different (in a good way IMO) check this out. I appreciate artists not going down the "tried and trusted" methods nearly all  MMO games seem to follow these days and take risks with new ideas.
Note that this is not as "in depth" as Skyrim but it makes up for that with its online elements. I think a lot of the hate is from the previous release (that I never played to be fair), because seriously, this game is really great.  It still has crafting and enchanting and all that, its just a bit of a different game. As long as you are not expecting a focused single player RPG, I dont think you will be disappointed. But don't expect a standard MMO either! They really have done something different (and good) here.  Seeing as this no longer has a monthly subscription, that easily makes it one of the best non-subscription MMOs out there, certainly the best one I have played so far.

The Just Cause series is, fundamentally, a large interactive series of epic explosions. All three games have relied on the principle that you have to "Liberate" or defeat military bases by killing the people inside and destroying the structures (Fuel tanks, satellite dishes, etc.). This can be achieved in any way you see fit, either by using Rico's grappling hook to grapple them to other objects and tear them down, going in with a helicopter and just blasting the living hell out of it, being strategic and using the environment to your advantage, or a combination thereof. The amount of military vehicles available for you to utilize in your destructive fantasies is unprecedented, and honestly I think liberating bases to unlock them is one of the more rewarding parts of the game.
Now while I enjoy liberating the military bases, the towns are another story. You have to liberate them too, and ocne you've liberated one you've liberated them all. You always have to destroy a couple speakers, tear down a statue or two, liberate a police station by raising the gate and "Calling in the rebels" and sometimes releasing prisoners by hacking the jail cell doors. It's really, really uninteresting.
Getting around the environment is additionally quite fun, and you have a number of methods to choose from. You can simply grapple around, you can use your parachute to pull you around the environment and keep you in the air, you can jump off a cliff with a wingsuit and literally fly around, you can steal a poor civillian's car and drive, you can call in a rebel drop and have a tank and some weapons dropped out of an airplane for you, or you can use a helicopter or plane. I mean, if you have trouble getting around the island, it's your own fault.
Overall the gameplay is pretty much what makes the Just Cause series.
9/10
The Just Cause series is renowned for its absolutely MASSIVE open world. I'm told by the game it's over 1000 square kilometers, it doesn't exactly feel quite THAT big but I'll take their word for it.
To be perfectly honest, I prefer Just Cause 2's map simply because of the diversity in environments and biomes, however Just Cause 3 has an absolutely stunning map as well - with certainly more cliffs to go wingsuiting off of.
This game's map is completely destructible and interactive. You can tear down trees (But why would you, really?), you can blow up bridges, and you can send enemies flying off cliffs with your grappling hook. It's amazingly fun to just explore the world and try to liberate provinces.
The game is set on the mediterranean island of Medici, to which I must give praise as the island feels very genuinely like a little European region. It's kind of a combination of Italy, France, Spain and Greece. Very cool and interesting.

Square Enix's Just Cause 3 puts you in control of rebel badass named Rico Rodriguez. The massive open world's design is incredible. The graphics and world design are stunning and beautiful. This review will cover several parts of the game.
Story:
The story of Just Cause 3 is really the only part of the game that is lacking. The characters are all designed very well of you can really feel emotion for them but the story just lacks the compelling need to countinue. Maybe this is because it's simply shadowed by the incredible feeling of destroying a base, or grappling helicopters to the back of jets, of even trying to collect the incredibly rare Sqaulo X7.
Gameplay:
Just Cause 3's gameplay is by far the strongest part of the game. It has some of the best explosive animations I've ever seen. The diffuculty is perfect for the game, it's only hard if you make it. You could easily take out a Military Base if you took the time to prepare and used proper strategy. Or you could go with the hard (but more fun in my opinion) way, you just fly in there and blow up everything.
Graphics:
Just Cause 3's graphics are right on par for next gen games. There certainly not the next massive breakthrough for graphical technology but there not lacking at all.
Animations:
The animations that are used in this game are incredible. The attention to detail is uncanny. Anything from Rico's pant leg blowing in the wind to an incredible nuclear explosion are drawn with the attention to detail for a game of the year.
Overall Verdict:
Just Cause 3 is an amazing game with a infinite amount of fun. I've had the pleasure of playing it on PC as well as PS4 and found everything. The animations are awesome, the world design incredible, gameplay is beautiful. Overall for sure one of the best games of 2015.

Dishonored 2 continues to carry the torch for modern stealth games where the original left off, and while doing so, integrates many welcome refinements to the formula of the original game.
My overall opinion of Dishonored 2 and the content of this review are mainly determined by the categories as listed below.
The game is beautiful. The painterly palettes and somewhat cartoonish character proportions are maintained in Dishonored 2 and the atmosphere is intensely immersive. There are countless details to be noticed, and most often these details lead to rewards. The levels are more interactive than ever with grandfather clocks, typewriters, and other objects being able to distract guards. Guards are also more intelligent and may become alert upon noticing open doors and comment in such ways as, “Who opened this door?”
The designs of the environments are just as well done as in Dishonored. The cityscapes are breath-taking and pleasantly vertical, most often able to explore from the ocean floor to rooftops. There are now many more NPC’s that can be seen and interacted with. Some may lead to unexpected side quests, but generally serve to populate the world.
All of the details as well as the way the world’s inhabitants behave within it add up to an entirely more immersive experience. The game’s atmosphere both demands and holds my attention and I think that is wonderful.
Dishonored 2, above all else, emphasizes options and customization. Newly introduced are deeper skill trees for existing and new powers as well as the very interesting ability to craft Bonecharms. Dishonored 2 also improves upon the original game's excellent gameplay.
The gameplay received numerous refinements, ones that are very natural and would likely be sorely missed if playing through the original Dishonored again. The player can now peek over cover rather than sidle around while looking for guards. In the first game, I would frequently be caught while trying to look around the side of cover, so this is a very welcome change. Also, barriers can now be vaulted over. It feels great to be able to keep my momentum going while running, without awkwardly or even failing to jump over the barrier as was previously possible.
Non-lethal playthroughs are now far more viable. There are (finally) non-lethal drop takedowns as well as non-lethal combat takedowns. As an exclusively non-lethal player, it was great to hear that more options would be available to me.
I have not played as Corvo, but I’ve heard that his powers retain most of their original functions as in the original Dishonored. Emily’s powers are quite different. Shadow Walk makes me feel like a demon and is very cool to look at. Far Reach, while appearing to work like Corvo’s Blink behaves very differently. You can both travel to and grab things with Far Reach and I have had a great deal of fun with the ability. Dark Vision seems to function exactly the same as in the original Dishonored besides a different visual post-processing effect.
I have (not yet) used Mesmerize, Domino, or Doppelganger, but am familiar with their use and am excited to update this section in the future.
I realize that the majority of players do not have a pc quite matching my specs, but nonetheless, my experience been great. I play on a 1440p Monitor, at Ultra Settings, and usually keep V-sync on @60fps.

The story is also kinda dull and I just don't care at all about these characters. I'm just not interested enough to try and find the other endings.

1) Explosions.
2) Violence.

4) More explosions.
5) Even more explosions.

However as far as actually having fun - i had only mediocre amount of it because of how raw and bugged this game seems to be.
The worst issue for me was the camera - it doesn't follow your character and instead tries to follow everyone at once. This results in players constantly getting out of screen bounds, falling and dying. Too often i can't distinguish my character due to insane amount of explosions, fire, bullets and other particles being on screen. The camera also constantly shakes which makes it even worse and sometimes just pans to random parts of the screen for not reason. Basically playing this game involves a lot of random tries and death's, and barely any skill, safe for fighting some bosses.
It also doesn't really support controller - there is no rumble, controls are over sensitive and switching in menus is just awful. Quite often my character kept jumping, rolling or walking forward by himself with me barely touching the controller.
There are also connection issues.
To summarize - right now this game is just too chaotic for me to have any fun. I get that this is exactly the point why everyone seems to be enjoying it but its just not my cup of tea. I like destructible environments, i like explosions, i respect Contra and movie heroes references but i hate that camera too much to recommend it anyway.

The Souls series returns in a more "modern" fashion. Character drawn story along with less confusing and more linear style map design lend to a more Souls newb friendly stlye of introduction into the series. Death is still a constant and small mistakes cost you dearly as you venture through Drangelic, a land filled with undead, monsters and even more viscious kinda of foes ready to make you lose your souls.
This game features bonfire teleportation right from the start, so getting back and forth to the town and where you are adventuring takes no time at all. A rather dissapointing downside to this is the seemingly overabundance of bonfires. Some are quite literaly less than a minutes jog through trash mobs. The game does allow different viable builds than previous incarnations (double greatshields is a thing) and the areas are gorgeous, if not a bit out of place (i.e. from a large windmill a lift takes you up to a volcano). The astetics seem a bit off and the challange does not quite measure up to what Dark Souls was, and therefore no where close to the near insanity of Demon Souls. Of course the game gives you many options to make the game harder if the initial challange is not up to your speed.
The qualms I have with this game are easily overlooked with how well the world works and the fluid combat. Of course there are still some builds that seem much stronger than others, but learning how to play the build you choose well can more than make up for the perceived lack of damage output. As always, PvP is a large part of the series, but in this one it seems even more part of the game and in many instances it is rather forced, which might make some new players a bit uneasy. This only really becomes an issue after the first playthrough when you are opened up to having not just NG people invade you and as you are able to accrue sin.
Overall, Dark Souls II is a soild game and worth playing through multiple times. Even if the layout of the areas is mostly linear, there are still plenty of secrets and interesting builds to toy around with until you find your sweet spot. Grab your sword and start hoarding those souls. You will need every last one you can find to regain what humanity you will have left after playing this monsterous game.
