Dishonored 2 continues to carry the torch for modern stealth games where the original left off, and while doing so, integrates many welcome refinements to the formula of the original game.
My overall opinion of Dishonored 2 and the content of this review are mainly determined by the categories as listed below.
The game is beautiful. The painterly palettes and somewhat cartoonish character proportions are maintained in Dishonored 2 and the atmosphere is intensely immersive. There are countless details to be noticed, and most often these details lead to rewards. The levels are more interactive than ever with grandfather clocks, typewriters, and other objects being able to distract guards. Guards are also more intelligent and may become alert upon noticing open doors and comment in such ways as, “Who opened this door?”
The designs of the environments are just as well done as in Dishonored. The cityscapes are breath-taking and pleasantly vertical, most often able to explore from the ocean floor to rooftops. There are now many more NPC’s that can be seen and interacted with. Some may lead to unexpected side quests, but generally serve to populate the world.
All of the details as well as the way the world’s inhabitants behave within it add up to an entirely more immersive experience. The game’s atmosphere both demands and holds my attention and I think that is wonderful.
Dishonored 2, above all else, emphasizes options and customization. Newly introduced are deeper skill trees for existing and new powers as well as the very interesting ability to craft Bonecharms. Dishonored 2 also improves upon the original game's excellent gameplay.
The gameplay received numerous refinements, ones that are very natural and would likely be sorely missed if playing through the original Dishonored again. The player can now peek over cover rather than sidle around while looking for guards. In the first game, I would frequently be caught while trying to look around the side of cover, so this is a very welcome change. Also, barriers can now be vaulted over. It feels great to be able to keep my momentum going while running, without awkwardly or even failing to jump over the barrier as was previously possible.
Non-lethal playthroughs are now far more viable. There are (finally) non-lethal drop takedowns as well as non-lethal combat takedowns. As an exclusively non-lethal player, it was great to hear that more options would be available to me.
I have not played as Corvo, but I’ve heard that his powers retain most of their original functions as in the original Dishonored. Emily’s powers are quite different. Shadow Walk makes me feel like a demon and is very cool to look at. Far Reach, while appearing to work like Corvo’s Blink behaves very differently. You can both travel to and grab things with Far Reach and I have had a great deal of fun with the ability. I'll try to keep this short and sweet, but it's a pretty in-depth game so I don't know how easy that will be. To start, you're not going to enjoy this game if you go into it expecting:

Alright, so. This isn't a massive improvement on Just Cause 2 in the same way that Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers wasn't a massive improvement on The Fellowship of the Ring. The Just Cause series is, fundamentally, a large interactive series of epic explosions. All three games have relied on the principle that you have to "Liberate" or defeat military bases by killing the people inside and destroying the structures (Fuel tanks, satellite dishes, etc.). This can be achieved in any way you see fit, either by using Rico's grappling hook to grapple them to other objects and tear them down, going in with a helicopter and just blasting the living hell out of it, being strategic and using the environment to your advantage, or a combination thereof. The amount of military vehicles available for you to utilize in your destructive fantasies is unprecedented, and honestly I think liberating bases to unlock them is one of the more rewarding parts of the game.
Now while I enjoy liberating the military bases, the towns are another story. You have to liberate them too, and ocne you've liberated one you've liberated them all. You always have to destroy a couple speakers, tear down a statue or two, liberate a police station by raising the gate and "Calling in the rebels" and sometimes releasing prisoners by hacking the jail cell doors. It's really, really uninteresting.
Getting around the environment is additionally quite fun, and you have a number of methods to choose from. You can simply grapple around, you can use your parachute to pull you around the environment and keep you in the air, you can jump off a cliff with a wingsuit and literally fly around, you can steal a poor civillian's car and drive, you can call in a rebel drop and have a tank and some weapons dropped out of an airplane for you, or you can use a helicopter or plane. I mean, if you have trouble getting around the island, it's your own fault.
Overall the gameplay is pretty much what makes the Just Cause series.
9/10
The Just Cause series is renowned for its absolutely MASSIVE open world. I'm told by the game it's over 1000 square kilometers, it doesn't exactly feel quite THAT big but I'll take their word for it.
To be perfectly honest, I prefer Just Cause 2's map simply because of the diversity in environments and biomes, however Just Cause 3 has an absolutely stunning map as well - with certainly more cliffs to go wingsuiting off of.
This game's map is completely destructible and interactive. You can tear down trees (But why would you, really?), you can blow up bridges, and you can send enemies flying off cliffs with your grappling hook. It's amazingly fun to just explore the world and try to liberate provinces.
The game is set on the mediterranean island of Medici, to which I must give praise as the island feels very genuinely like a little European region. It's kind of a combination of Italy, France, Spain and Greece. Very cool and interesting.
7/10

Summary:
When I first saw the trailers to the brand new Call Of Duty, I thought to myself “Wow, the future! Lasers and super-human abilities!” But then I remembered the reputation COD has: a repetitive, money-milking Shoot- ‘Em-up franchise that is dominated by 12 year olds. This may be true for the past three, or dare I say four, COD’s that have been released, the boring and recycled ‘Ghosts’ that actually re-used scenes and missions from past COD’s to use in their pathetic attempt of a survival-based shooter and the way-to long and broken game that is ‘Black Ops II’ that had more bugs and glitches than R2-D2 with hot soup poured over his tin head.
The reputation of COD was not a good thing, people expected total crap, as they’d been force-fed it for almost four years, but this year’s release has broken free of that low-standard expectancy, and it feels great. This year’s Advanced Warfare seems to break out of the shell of linear gunfights, shooty-shooty kill all non-Americans and while you’re at it slip in some DLC that gives me another map to get camped on, Advanced Warfare has waddled out of the♥♥♥♥♥♥storm reputation COD once had, and has taken a few stabs at being new, innovative and exciting. And let me tell you, they landed those stabs well. No Hitmarker.
Review:
Advanced Warfare takes place in 2054 through to 2061, and has us take on the role of Mitchell, a young American solider who feels he should join the army because you know, that’s what all the cool kids do. The moment you jump into CODAW’s singleplayer, it gives us a nice long cut scene, showing Mitchell and his friend Will waiting to be dropped into a ravaging war between North-Korea and the Americans, the war that we, in reality are potentially close to, so a pat on the head to CODAW for realism. Unlike other COD’s, AW takes actual character building and realistic emotions into it, the first mission where Mitchell and Will are talking about why they joined, and it’s because they felt like every other soldier, “To serve my country”, “To get away from it all”, or “Because my friend did”. These are realistic themes and reasons, ones that AW use to make the characters feel small, insignificant, and then when the game speeds up, they grow, and become more powerful. It’s a nice use of pacing and also credibility. The story then follows Mitchell getting wounded, taken in by a private military company and then being exploited by turning him into a weapon for the militaries own use. AW does not try anything too drastic; all events in AW feel real and very possible, the growth of private military organizations, a corrupt government and the over-development of technology, which we rely too much on, and one day will turn on us.
The game itself uses features like no other COD has. It completely takes a dive and get’s 9’s and 10’s all round. For start, every mission puts you in a map where the environment can be influenced by your actions. Ah, there’s a cheeky sniper in that tower, how about instead of spending ten minutes trying to shoot the menace, I blow the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s’ tower up, not only removing him from this world, but also squashing the enemy squad below it, and the dust from the explosion has caused the helicopter above it to panic, buying me time to move and strategize. It’s features like this that allow me to think and play using things other than my gun, it’s a realistic thinking game, so much more strategy has been planted in.
Another example: Exo-Suits, not only an awesome combat feature, but also a realistic possibility. These suits are given to you in every mission and allow you to perform special moves and maneuvers, like jumping high, or running faster, how about invisibility or a grapple hook? Not only are these powers awesome to use and just watch, but make me play the game in a totally different way. I can now scale buildings, punch through walls and grapple onto a tank, but the best part? They aren’t overpowered, your enemies have these powers too, so they’re just as powerful, but it’s how you use these powers that give you the upper hand, also you have a battery meter to make sure you don’t go too crazy, a nice little boundary.
AW really has gone to town on it, and it works, it takes elements from the old games and uses them to make COD feel like COD again, with all the awesome elements put in on top. It has QuickTime cinematics, so you can interact with the cut scenes it’s something to do at the least. AW brings back vehicles too, ones that feel useful and needed, you can speed through a valley in a high-tech jet, or stomp around in the desert in a eight-foot tall Mech suit, all of these ‘upgrades’ to your person feel real and make you more powerful than ever before. AW just has that charm about it that doesn’t get old; it’s a daring game with the old-school style underneath it all. This allows die-hard fans to like it, and newcomers.
I suppose the only complaint is the weapons, they look cool, sound awesome and feel more punchy, but there’s nothing that really separates them that much, there’s the rifle that goes bang, bang, then there’s the one that goes bangity, bangity, bangity, oh, and of the course the ba-ba-ba-ba. They are new and never seen before, but maybe it’s just me. They all felt a little like the same thing, but hey there’s a laser cannon in this game that makes people explode in this game, so forget what I just said.
Verdict:
CODAW is new, fresh and charming. What do I mean by charming, it just has that loyal honest vibe to it; it’s realistic, old school but brings new cards to the table that you can’t dislike. Awesome maps, check, Likeable and tangible characters and situations, check. It really does have it all. A round of applause to Sledgehammer games for this roller coaster, and as for the next COD in 2015, good luck, you’re gonna need a lot of lasers and robots to outdo this one!

Eternal Senia is a relatively short action RPG with simple, intuitive controls and a charming story. The game is challenging enough without being either frustrating or boring, and due to its length it does not outstay its welcome. While a fun game, I am at present not confident enough to reccommend it.
The core gameplay loop of the farming game is do X to get Y so that you can do X better/more efficently. It is at the heart of Stardew Valley, Harvest Moon, Story of Seasons, and even Slime Rancher. The trick however is to mix up and vary the gameplay enough that it takes a long time for the player to come to a realization of how pointless the loop is. As well as making it about the journey more than the destination to encourage new playthroughs.
Stardew, and to a much lesser extent, Harvest Moon, have many activities to distract the player with. But Slime Rancher is closer to Story of Seasons at present. It's fun, but it lacks the variety and depth needed in this genre. The reason why I do not reccommend it at the moment is because I am unsure if they intend on adding such varience to the gameplay.
One could argue it comes down to preference. I however feel there is a right and wrong way to do the 'farming' genre. Story of Seasons and Slime Rancher are both fun games, but ultimately feel lacking and hollow over time.

People dont have their nametags hanging over their heads, you have to focus on them to see if they are even real players, which is a nice touch, it is more immersive this way IMO. I appreciate artists not going down the "tried and trusted" methods nearly all  MMO games seem to follow these days and take risks with new ideas.

Great successor to Dark Souls. The Good: The game is ♥♥♥♥ing fun. I enjoyed the hell out of it. The best part was the ability to warp immediately and between any of the bonfires, similar to how Demon's Souls did it. The story in the game, still as obscure and not in-your-face as the first game, is wonderful. There are a few references to the first game, both obscure ones and plain, the most obvious probably being the Old Dragonslayer at the beginning of the game. The combat in the game is well done, with plenty of spells to choose from and even adding a new type: hexes. The combat is fluid and fun, strength being much stronger than it was in the first game with dexterity underpowered and almost not viable. The PvP is very satisfying, and winning a 1v2 gives the same satisfaction beating Orenstein and Smough solo in the first game brought. The art style I thought was terrible at first, but after spending some time with it, grew on me and I now think it's a very nice looking game. The music is decent, but I wouldn't say it's one of the game's strong points. The Bad: Most of the bosses are pretty much the same- big dudes in armor with similar movesets, making the bossfights boring and repetitive after a while. Despite the *much* larger world, it feels like there's way less to explore due to the lack of shortcuts and secrets the first game had, removing that amazing awe I always feel about how connected everything was in Dark Souls 1. In addition to that, the game was much less punishing than its predecessor, as the game feels much easier in comparison to the first Souls game, not giving me the same satisfaction I got before after beating a boss I've been struggling with (that is, I only struggled on one boss out of the 31 bosses in the game). In addition to all that, the most frustrating and annoying thing for me was the areas in the game. The Gutter was, let's be real, Blighttown all over again. And Blighttown was great- but I played through it already. I don't want an easier version of it thrown at me, I want new and exciting areas. And while the purpose of it may have been TO feel like Blighttown for story purposes I'll leave you to decipher, it still felt like I was being cheated out of a new experience (this being one example of a few different areas that are basically copes). The Ugly: The game is, hands down, great. I beat it in one 36 hour session, staying up two nights in a row to beat it. In that time I beat every boss except one- whether that's just a testament to how good I am at video games or that the game is simply not challenging, I'll let you decide on your own. Despite the repetitive nature of the bosses and the similarities between the areas in the first game and second the combat is phenomenal and the game is worth your time. And while some people would say it's unfair to compare the game to it's predecessor and I should think of it as it's own game, with this franchise in particular I don't want to do that. The franchise is known for how punishing it is, and if the game doesn't live up to the standard I have for that, I am going to be slightly disappointed. For all that, the game is great, I love it very much, and I recommend it.

White Noise Online is multiplayer-based Slender-type game, by which I mean it's a horror game where you go around collecting eight randomly placed objects while avoiding a monster that's hunting you. Slenderman isn't actually involved here, and there's some twists to the formula here to keep it interesting, but the baseline is that this is an online co-op Slender-type game, and that fact will either sell you or turn you away from the game.
You play as one of over 20 characters in some very dark environment collecting cassettes. Strange statues line the environments, and a strange glowing monster chases you through the depths of darkness, with an intent to kill. However, the story here is rather non-existent, with the only narrative coming from an opening scene before the title screen, and the audio content that plays on the cassettes themselves when you pick them up.
The cassettes emit a static sound to alert you that they're nearby, which is helpful to the formula as the stages in this game are bigger than most Slender-type games and the monster is notably more aggressive. One feature kind of cool and creepy about the monster is that he makes appropriately unnerving sounds to both sort of alert you where he is, and unnerve you. It can be creepy to be in a tight-corridor area and not see him, but it sounds like he's right next to you. Staring at the monster will slowly deplete your 'health', and he'll kill you if you let him get too close to you. There are also green-glowing statues placed around the environment randomly, and staring at them or getting too close will have the same effects the monster has (though of course the statues can't move). The statues emit a static-sound similar to the cassettes (though different enough to tell) to lead players to a tricky end.
There are four difficulty levels, which mostly determine the difficulty of the monster, how many statues there are, and cassette placement possibility.
The game also has a panic-system that's kind of similar to what you'll find in Clock Tower 3 or Haunting Ground. When you are isolated and alone, your character will start panicking (which can be noted when the character starts making panicked sounds and the screen starts acting up), and eventually starts tripping all over the place and making a lot of noise, which attracts the monster. This can be settled by either collecting cassettes, or finding other people.
How prone they are to this depends on what character you play as. There are over 20 different characters, and they all have different stats. These are represented by an image for each 'category' (the images can be confusing at first, can read up on what each one means in the How to Play section on the options menu), with a notice of if they're stronger or weaker in this area than other characters (represented by a +1 to +3, or a -1 to -3, if not shown then they are neutral, or default, in that area). Areas effected include sanity (take less damage from the monsters attacks), flashlight battery life (the longer you keep your flashlight on, the more it will flicker and start becoming dimmer and dimmer), movement speed, stamina (for running), scout (the further distance you can get from characters before panicking), evasion (how high you are on the monsters priority list), and more. You only start with four characters, while the other ones are unlocked by playing the game and accomplishing tasks.
There's also some fun multiplayer mechanics that are rather well thought-out. Firstly, death. When a player dies, they then become a ghost, which is visible to the living players as a blue silhouette of the character that died. The ghosts can stick around the living players to help prevent them from panicking, or they can go out and scout for cassettes. The ghosts see the level much more brightly than the living do, and they also move a lot faster around the level. However, they cannot see the monster, but can spot cassettes. This can be helpful in downtime and to be helpful even after death. The second feature cool for multiplayer is the results screen, which displays fun information like the total distance each person walked, number of cassettes each individual collected, how many times they were hit by a scare attack and 'screamed', how long they survived, etc., along with a map that shows the routes that each player took during the course of the game.
The game currently has six maps, though the devs have noted if it does well they plan to add more. The maps are fairly varied, with themes like tropical island, government base, museum, snowy forest, and the like. There are three different map 'styles', with two maps under each style. The first is big-open levels that have monuments, like the original Slender. The second are closed-spaces interior maps with twisting corridors, rooms, and labyrinth-like structures. The final are 'island' stages, which has parts of levels connected with tunnels, bridges, and the like, with the level segments being separated like islands.
This game was an Xbox Live release originally, the main difference in the Steam version right now is that all characters are now unlockable (as opposed to some characters only obtainable by owning other games), achievements, and they've updated the graphics some. This said, more updates may arise in the future to further differentiate it.
In short, it's a very confident Slender game, actually one of my favorites. The online multiplayer is fun and well-thought out, and the game still manages to be tense and scary at times. If you like Slender-based games and have wanted or are interested in trying a multiplayer-based version of that type of game, this is it. There really isn't any better, and the game does very well at what it sets out to do. However, if you don't enjoy Slender-type games, or the multiplayer focus doesn't interest you, this probably won't interest you. The game maybe works better in short bursts than long marathons, but it's still a fun little multiplayer horror game.

TL;DR: For the price, why not? It's fun if you're playing with friends and actually scary depending on the level.
Played two games with 2 other friends. The first map we played was, I believe, the Chateau? The second was the Area51 type zone.
At first I was a little disappointed, we all were. It didn't seem _that_scary to us. Once we quit griping and actually ventured out to find the tapes it started to become a LOT more fun. By far, the most fun came from the closed up, almost labyrinthine, design of the second map. Panicking and losing each other, watching your friends die, having to continue on with their ghosts in tow, it was all so much fun.
The ambient sound is really creepy and lends itself perfectly to the atmosphere.
The graphics were decent and definitely worked in favor of the game's target atmosphere. Dark, creepy, and lots of fog so your rendering times are fast and everything runs smooth.
The built-in voice chat worked fine and helped out a lot. Usually we use Skype but we decided to let the game do it's thing.
The price. I mean come on, 6$? You can't beat that!
Being able to continue playing as a ghost after you die was fun. Helped the search.
All very
complaints.
There are NO subtitles. Nobody in my group could hear almost anything the people on the tape recorders said. It sounded like it might have been interesting too. :(
Not being able to see the actual lit up areas from other people's flashlights. It would be nice to let your friends flashlights light up the hallway you're walking down too.
Collision was sometimes irritating, getting stuck on some boxes while you're running away. Not much to be done about that, just try to steer while you panic?
Tension was slow to build depending the maps. I mean, yeah, a creepy forest is creepy and all, but being trapped down in a bunch of confined hallways is infinitely worse.
For first time players, picking a character is irritating because you don't know what the modifier symbols for them do exactly. (Increase speed, decrease sanity) Once you play a game or two, you get it, but at first glance as a beginner it's a tad much.

If you played, or even heard of the game "Slender," then you know what to expect. If you haven't heard of Slender, then White Noise Online will be a new experience.
It's an arcade-esque experience where players run around in the dark in search of 8 tapes while being pursued by an eldritch abomination.
The graphics are simple, and slightly cartoony, which helps to make the game more bareable for the easily frightened.
The price is good for what you get, although you only need an hour to see all the game has to offer.

There's not much of a story to this game, put simply you and three others investigate different locations in order to discover the truth by collecting tape recorders which contain information. The recording itself is not important, it does add some back story but not needed for gameplay, you must collect 8 recorders while avoiding the evil manifestation that slowly pursues you.
Sound familiar? I bet you have. Its very similar to how a slender game plays with the addition to having coop, that said it doesn't mean the game isn't fun, the opposite if for a short while. I would suggest not binging, as you will exhaust all the fun in one play-through. Decent quality graphics and atmosphere, its recommended playing in the dark with headphones and no voice enabled, especially if you are playing with others, you don't want to ruin the experience the first time.
I was disappointed that it was another clone of a slender game, I honestly expected something like a polished version of Damned with clue searching and puzzle elements. I do like that tape recorders are randomly placed, so the game stays fresh. The developer missed out with only one monster model, that should have changed it to have a different monster (with different abilities) tailored to a scenario. There's few scenarios but that balances with options to allow you to change how the map is played like difficulty. You have a choice to choose characters each with strengths and weaknesses, that can change the play style, which once again I was hoping the monster would use your weakness against you.
Overall, it's a cool coop game but I would preferred a little more content, it gets a pass from me because its five dollars, less with a fourpack.
3/5 Add more puzzles like keys to find for locked areas, hidden chambers, etc. More coop elements like requiring people to work together to progress and more locations to play through (No manor/mansion scenario!? Really?) but the core gameplay and the rest of the game is fine.

I've always been a fan of the original worms games, seeing a new "Very Positive" worms game available I thought this game might actually be decent.
The game itself is good and is fun to play, the vehicles, turrets, buildings, crafting, and turrets are a nice interesting addition to the game.
My main problem is the fact vehicles are overpowered, using a helicopter you can fly all the way across the map, shoot the enemy team and fly back again.
The mechs are similar and provide the user the ability to hover and jump across most/all of the map.
This is very evident when you play ranked matches and the first person to spawn their worms chooses the helicopter instantly.
The game in its current state takes out a lot of the skill, you can just craft mega bunker busters, for instance, doing 60 damage a pop or even save up for a concrete donkey, armageddon or OMG Strike.
The ranked play as it currently stands takes out all the skill that should be in the game, every ranked game I have played consisted of spawning on/near the helicopter and attempting to control the helicopter the remainder of the game.
When you play online with friends the game itself is much better -providing you both are on the same operating system or you can't play together- as you can turn off a lot of the settings that break the game in its current status.
However, you cannot spawn AI while making your own public/private games, there is no way to set a player limit, E.G. 2-6 players max and when people do join you can't change the game to a private game resulting in you kicking people repeatedly if you don't want a 6 player game.
There are no game modes like Forts anymore and you are stuck just doing the standard team death match each game online.
I can't knock the story mode or training missions aside from the AI being a bit too easy.
To summarise, if you like single player games or you want to play online with a friend you can do this in the game, the game is missing a lot of customisation that was implemented in original worms games e.g. Armageddon, and you cannot play with AI and a friend at the same time.
So, I wouldn't recommend the game in its current state, Team17, you have some work to do.

Alien: Isolation - (You're No Colonial Marine)
The game is gorgeous. Just like basically every review has stated the design is right out of the 70's futurism aesthetic. It looks so much like it was designed in the same world as the Nostromo it's not even funny. The lighting is probably the best part of it. Whether it's a dark area that's only punctuated by the light from some monitors or an area with a swinging bulb (or even better, the Alien coming out of a ceiling vent and knocking a lighting fixture with its tail). Creative Assembly's use of lighting is simply remarkable.
Gameplay wise I'm reminded of a cross between Thief (the original) and System Shock 2. Like SS2 the Sevastopol is the primary character you interact with. Most of the time you're simply there; nothing but you, the station and the various terminals, speakers and stuff around you. When you do come across other people (or androids) most of the time it's time to hide and avoid them. There are some characters that you come across that aren't going to simply kill you but they're the exception.
Stealth is old-school. There's no light crystal, no indicator where enemies are on the map, no sound-level indicator. It's all eyes-up and ears-open. And it works. Being aware of where your enemies are, listening for their conversations, footsteps and other telltale signs of their presence is how you stay out of sight. Human and android enemies appear to have a fixed patrol route (at least the ones that move) so by observing them from a place of safety you can plot out an avoidance scheme. You also have some tools that you can build to help you. Noisemakers will draw enemies that hear them over, flares might (haven't really tried) draw attention and there are a few weapons as well if you really need to get into a fight. Ripley can only take a few hits (and healing takes time) so it's far better to avoid fighting whenever you can.
Interacting with the various systems on the station also take time. It's about two seconds from when you first trigger the interaction to when you can actually use the system. It also takes a couple of seconds from when you stop interacting with the system until you're back in control and able to move. I've seen complaints about that but that's what really makes being aware of your enemies important. If you can't simply hop onto a rewire terminal to trigger an alarm in an area of the map that you're not in so it will draw the enemies away it makes you consider if that's the best strategy.
Saving is another area that I've seen complaints. The game autosaves at each level start but there are no other autosaves. To save you have to find a terminal, insert your ID card, wait three seconds for the card to be read and then you can save. These terminals are frequent but not everywhere. You can save at any time you come across a terminal but you're not going to be given terminals for every room or corridor. This forces you to keep aware and ready to react. Usually I'm not keen on limiting saving (saving usually should be controlled by the player with autosaves occurring when the developer feels like it) but in this case the save system is so integrated with the game that it feels like it would cheapen the difficulty of the stealth by allowing the player to save anywhere. Instead I find myself always asking "Is it worth it to head into a risky situation that I don't have to in the hope of finding something useful?" as well as planning my way through the maps with the locations of save terminals influencing that path.
As for the Alien... it's a mixed bag. It appears that the Alien can be in one of three modes regarding the map area you're in: not present, stalking or active. When the Alien's not present you basically have free roam (presuming no human or other enemies are present) and noise isn't an issue. I cannot state for certain that there's no risk of the Alien showing up if you make a lot of noise but I've been in one firefight (well, I was shooting and the android was dying.) and never heard the telltale signs that the Alien was approaching.
When the Alien is stalking it's in the walls/vents/ceiling. You hear it moving around and it will take up sentry at certain places (like ceiling vents) and attack anything that moves near it. They provide enough indications that the Alien is present that it doesn't seem unfair if you walk into it's trap. Again, I can't state unequivocally that it won't come out if you make a lot of noise, but I haven't had it do so.
When the Alien is active it's in the map with you, moving around and hunting. Unlike the humans it doesn't have a set patrol route, though it does appear to have preferred locations. In one area there's a large central room with doors on two ends and windows on the sides. The Alien liked to stay around that room, presumably, because it could see pretty much every part of the area. Hiding isn't win-mode either. If the Alien sees you hide: you're dead. If it sees you go into a room and then doesn't see you in the room it will begin searching potential hiding spots. There's no guarantee that it will find you (and there's a breath-hold mechanic that helps you avoid detection) but I still had a couple of times where it found me with no real indication as to what gave me away.
Sneaking past the Alien is an exercise in patience, timing, distraction strategy and pathing. Finding the shortest path between your goals will often help you avoid the Alien by simply not being exposed very much. Sometimes this means not exploring very much, using vents or avoiding redundant paths (like corridor loops). A well timed (and aimed) noisemaker has so far been the most useful in getting past the Alien when it's hunting around a choke point but you can only carry three (and only enough resources to make three more at any given time) so care must be taken when choosing to use one.
Ultimately the biggest problem with the Alien (so far) is that it's only ever in one of those three modes. It simply doesn't make much sense for the Alien to come running (entering active mode) for some sounds and not others or to respond to a triggered noise, search the area and not find anything and then not head off looking for elsewhere. It takes a lot of the tension out of the game once you realize that if you see the Alien you know that you're simply going to have to avoid it. If the Alien had the potential to show up at any noise and leave at any time (i.e. model it's behavior as always stalking the entire station) then the tension would easily stay high. As it is, it doesn't feel much more tense (most of the time) than any given level in the original Thief. You're tense because you know that if you make a mistake you'll be squished but not because you don't know when the Alien might appear.
Ultimately the Alien's AI does make the game flawed. I don't think it's as bad as some of the reviews stated though. I paid $40 for it and am not regretting it. I don't think I'd regret it at $50 either. I do hope it sells enough that Creative Assembly can take a stab at a sequel. I think they've got all of the components right except for the Alien. Repeating everything that's good and focusing on improving the Alien could make a sequel as much a refinement as Thief 2 was over Thief.

The Alien game you hoped for!!
Difficulty - Hard
Completion Time - 21 Hours
The first Alien film was probably one of the most iconic Sci FI Horrors the world has ever seen. Ridley Scott created a world that was full of mystery and horror. All the other Alien games were based on James Camerons action oriented experience with Pulse Rifles and Smartguns.  Creative Assembly are the first developer to go back to the roots of Alien, and what made the film such a terrifying experience.
What this game gives you is pure magnificients in what the original film was all about, tight claustrophobic environments and the 1970s look on the future. With big CRT monitors and huge oversized buttons on every panel and door. This game will make you feel Isolated with tense atmosphere and a menacing Alien that stalks you throughout.
With regards to the Alien, it is probably the best A.I I've seen in a game. The Alien truly creates a terror which haunts you throughout the game. You don't have Pulse Rifles or Smartguns, the weapons you do have are completely useless against the Alien. All you have is you're own wits and craftable items which can be used to distract or lure the creature away from you.
Some of you may say that 20 hours may seem excessive for a Survival Horror game but I enjoyed it immensely. The game does pace out quite well while giving you breaks from the Alien on certain missions.
So for those of you who love Survival Horror you will enjoy this game. If you have patience and are a fan of the Alien Universe, this is the game you have been waiting for!

Alien: Isolation was the best survival "horror" game I've played since Dead Space, why the horror in quotes you may ask? While the xenomorph certainly is scary and menacing at the start, you will slowly start to learn each and every piece of it's arsenal and how to manipulate it to your advantage. This knowledge will diminish the scare factor to a certain degree but that is not to say that you won't be on the edge of your seat, you certainly will, though I do feel the survival aspects are far stronger here. That being said the game does a good job at mixing things up throughout, keeping you busy even when the alien isn't around and always keeping you in the dark as to what will happen next.
The plot is possibly not it's strongest point but still plays out in a way which feels parallel to the original Alien movie, but always making sure that you feel like a part of the action. One scene in particular was so nostalgic that I just had to explore every inch of it, and exploring a 3D replica with such high detail was a sheer delight. That attention to detail carries through to almost every aspect of the game as well, each set piece is oozing with atmosphere and feels so masterfully crafted that you could be forgiven for thinking Ridley Scott constructed it himself, and I guess in a way he did since so much respect was clearly given to the source material.
Dealing with the complaints of the games "length" I would have to say that, while it may have benefited from a slight trim, I didn't feel it ruined the experience at all. Often a lull is necessary to help the sense of dread reestablish itself, in this case I think we will know more once we see the sequel. Overall the time I had with Alien: Isolation was out of this world, and I certainly recommend it to any fan of the Alien universe.

First of all, I haven't played Dark Souls 1 or Demon Souls. And I know this renders my review useless to many people ^^
I'm now 6hours into the game and here is what I have to say so far:
The graphics are quite good. Don't get me wrong, it could also be much much better but the design is pretty nice and my old PC had much more problems with games that looked a lot worse so the programming department did a good job.
Learning to fight even small enemies is lots of fun. After the Intro Video I got killed by some rat-like creatures about 20 seconds in the game and I even got an achievement for dying which was nice :)
Then after a couple of hours or so I killed my first boss and literally did a celebratory fist pump. I died a lot to even get to the boss and killing him was a huge success.
Of course dying plenty of times by the hand of the same enemy can be frustrating and I had do turn of the game a couple of times because I was sick of it ^^ but I always wanted to try it again after a short break. I'm sure some will not start this game again after they get frustrated. Pretending this game is mainstream would be a huge lie. There is no quest log (at least I haven't found one) not map to show you a route and no quicksave. If you think you are up for a challenging game than you should really think about DS2.
No for the part I absolutely didn't like about the game.  Being punishing in fights and not taking you by the hand to guide you  from quest to quest is one thing. I like it when a game is difficult. But the difficulty should never be the basic mechanics of a game. There is almost no information about the classes you can choose from at the start, I haven't found any information (in the game itself) on the attributes and I just googled how to use a torch. Stuff like that shouldn't force me to tab out of the game. I know the veterans know this stuff but this information should still be available in the game itself (and if it already is it should be more accessable).
All in all I think it's a fantastic game. The lack of a proper tutorial etc is inconvenient but shouldn't stop you from playing it.

I do recommend this game but only if you are a person who likes the ancient Romans or similar. The game lacks depth, for example, I have played 300 hundred hours of this game and that has been over half a year. Rome total war 1 was better because of the engine it used. The engine used for this game was meant for RANGED combat, not melee. This is why there is just a complete moshpit and no orginisation what so ever. The ancient Romans didn't break formation like they so easily do for this game. Now I have over the reccomended specs and I still have a frame rate drops. This is unacceptable. Napoleon, Medieval and Empire don't have framerate drops for me, so why does this? Total war Rome 2 was cleary rushed by Sega in order for them to get some more money. This can be seen from the amount of DLCs which have had to been added to the game. The old AI designer was fired? Why? This new one which has creatred the AI for Rome 2 is not the best to say the least and that's putting it mildly. If you have below the reccomended specs, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME! This is because when I played with just under it, it barely ran on the main campaign screen, never mind the battles! Even with above average specs, the game still looks terrible! In today's day and age I would expect to see these graphics on the PS4 or Xbox 1.
In conclusion if you want a MILDLY historicly accurate Roman game then go straight ahead... but only if it's on sale. But be warned, if you want to play as Sparta etc, you will have to buy the MoneyMakingDowanloadableContent (MMDLC). Out of 5 stars? 3. An average game... hopefully Creative assembly and Sega can top Napoleon and Rome 1 otherwise, the Total war series looks like it will die.

Over all a good game for me.  I'm sure you know that you are encouraged to take a more a stealth and sneak approach.  But you can destroy as much as you want.  Which approach you take gives you a different summary at the end.
Game environment was not what I'm used to after playing Fallout 4 for a while.  It is has a Portal aspect in that you try to figure out a different way to move through the world.  The puzzle aspect doesn't feel like a puzzle.  Most of the time it was more like "I have to get over there or get around those people." and not a puzzle box.
Of the two characters you can play I picked the newer one, Emily.  There are some different powers depending which character you chose.  Each power you get can be improved upon and since you can't max out everything you'll have to decide to which ones you want to focus on.
If you hate insects this game will un-nerve you. There are 'Blood Flies' that you have to navigate through/around and their buzzing while you crawl past them could make you a little tense.
One specific thing I really enjoyed was the Outsider's Timepiece.  That was really well implemented. A game that was built around just that idea would be fantastic.
I also appreciated not having a gigantic boss.  Sure some characters are more difficult to deal with than others as well as different situations but in never felt ridiculous.

The game itself is amazing. The gameplay and the story are fluid. The stotyline is an epic continuation of the first story complete with references to all the original DLCs. I persoanlly have no major gripes about the game and I run ona  mid-range PC. My son, who also plays, stated his only complains were the weird mouse sensitivity (which I agree with) and the changinf of the the Outsider's voice talent (as the Outsider is his favorite supporting character (I myself have no qualms with the new actor)). I've only experieience 3 glitches to date (and one I'm not sure was a glitch). The first was a crash I experieinced when crafting a 3-prong bone charm which caused a crash every time, once I progressed a little farther the crash went away. The second was  when I crafted my first 2 4-prong bonecharms and they instantly duplicated (not sure if this is intended or not). The last one came in the form of a corrupted save file that wouldn't load, which I deleted and haven't had again. The first major patch fixed any issues that I had with mouse sensitivity and it seems to have smoothed the graphics as well.
Overall, even with a nasty PC launch I think the game is great and any glitches I've experienced have NOT taken fromt he game for me. I highly recommend it to my friends that enjoyed the first game.

The first Alien film was probably one of the most iconic Sci FI Horrors the world has ever seen. Ridley Scott created a world that was full of mystery and horror. All the other Alien games were based on James Camerons action oriented experience with Pulse Rifles and Smartguns.  Creative Assembly are the first developer to go back to the roots of Alien, and what made the film such a terrifying experience.
What this game gives you is pure magnificients in what the original film was all about, tight claustrophobic environments and the 1970s look on the future. With big CRT monitors and huge oversized buttons on every panel and door. This game will make you feel Isolated with tense atmosphere and a menacing Alien that stalks you throughout.
With regards to the Alien, it is probably the best A.I I've seen in a game. The Alien truly creates a terror which haunts you throughout the game. You don't have Pulse Rifles or Smartguns, the weapons you do have are completely useless against the Alien. All you have is you're own wits and craftable items which can be used to distract or lure the creature away from you.
Some of you may say that 20 hours may seem excessive for a Survival Horror game but I enjoyed it immensely. The game does pace out quite well while giving you breaks from the Alien on certain missions.
So for those of you who love Survival Horror you will enjoy this game. If you have patience and are a fan of the Alien Universe, this is the game you have been waiting for!

Alien: Isolation was the best survival "horror" game I've played since Dead Space, why the horror in quotes you may ask? While the xenomorph certainly is scary and menacing at the start, you will slowly start to learn each and every piece of it's arsenal and how to manipulate it to your advantage. This knowledge will diminish the scare factor to a certain degree but that is not to say that you won't be on the edge of your seat, you certainly will, though I do feel the survival aspects are far stronger here. That being said the game does a good job at mixing things up throughout, keeping you busy even when the alien isn't around and always keeping you in the dark as to what will happen next.
The plot is possibly not it's strongest point but still plays out in a way which feels parallel to the original Alien movie, but always making sure that you feel like a part of the action. One scene in particular was so nostalgic that I just had to explore every inch of it, and exploring a 3D replica with such high detail was a sheer delight. That attention to detail carries through to almost every aspect of the game as well, each set piece is oozing with atmosphere and feels so masterfully crafted that you could be forgiven for thinking Ridley Scott constructed it himself, and I guess in a way he did since so much respect was clearly given to the source material.
Dealing with the complaints of the games "length" I would have to say that, while it may have benefited from a slight trim, I didn't feel it ruined the experience at all. Often a lull is necessary to help the sense of dread reestablish itself, in this case I think we will know more once we see the sequel. Overall the time I had with Alien: Isolation was out of this world, and I certainly recommend it to any fan of the Alien universe.

This is an interesting and colorful game, and somewhat refreshing for a MOBA.  The game uses an interface similar to a third-person combat game and requires considerably more aiming and movement coordination than what is normally called for in a MOBA.  Moreover, the gods (heroes) that one can pick from are generally well made aesthetically and are often amusing - the flavor, so to speak, is quite good.  Many gods are also interesting to play, and the game is decently balanced as a whole, such that better teamplay is usually the difference between winning and losing.
With that said, however, there are also some fairly serious flaws at present.
First and foremost amongst these is that the game betrays its own premise, a MOBA requiring aiming, manuevering, etc. rather than merely pointing and clicking, by including a number of ludicrously easy to play gods that are very nearly automatic in their function.  Quite a few gods require that one be precise and careful all of the time, miss rarely, etc., such as Serqet, Artemis, and others, while a good number of other gods simply aim in the general direction of an opponent and cheese you with a simple combination of abilities that you have to try to miss with, e.g. Ah Puch, Anubis, Zeus, Bacchus, Ares (ultimate), etc..  Then there are other gods who have essentially automatic and uncounterable abilities, e.g. Ne Zha's ultimate, which allows the player to simply beat away on an opponent with no fear of recourse save for being mobbed as soon as he returns to the ground, or Thanatos' ultimate, which allows the player to fly around the map and instagib anyone who happens to have 40% or less life left at will, provided that one nails a rather easy landing near them (if the victims are running away, anyways).  Such abilities and the relative ease of use for some gods, which require barely any aiming and manuevering skill, contradicts the game's basic premise of being a MOBA that relies more on the aforementioned combat skills and rewards mediocre play far more than it should be rewarded, and renders a number of more difficult (and more fitting Gods, considering the game's basic premise) to often be inefficient choices.
Second, while the game is ultimately designed for team play and especially for Joust and Conquest modes, the god balance in itself, to say nothing of the previous issue of somewhat contradictory design, leaves some things to be desired.  While not uncounterable, Hel is a strong example of the game's balance problems insofar as individual gods are concerned.  Hel is designed to be a versatile mage who can support her team with both direct support abilities like AoE healing in her light form and with damaging attacks in her dark form, switching as appropriate.  This is all well and good, until one notices that she can simply stack spell power, and effectively spam both damage and healing by switching forms rapidly with little to no penalty, as her form bonuses do not provide much incentive to make a deliberate choice about what one is doing in a given combat situation - this allows a player to essentially ignore her general role and simply force things to happen, as she can often simply outheal and outnuke any would-be assailants once she is sufficiently powerful.  The other major gameplay issue regarding balance, as I see it, is that the warrior class of gods does not scale particularly well into the late game, owing to generally lacking itemization choices for them and the weakness of defensive statistics in this game.  One is caught between trying to be tough enough to actually brawl a bit, which is supposed to be a strength of warriors, and doing enough damage to actually be a threat that has to be managed, as warriors' CC abilities are generally weak, especially in comparison to guardians.  However, warriors tend to have rather mediocre base health for their role, unlike guardians, and as protection scaling is weak (100 = 50% DR, 200 = 33% DR) and penetration plentiful (e.g. -33% for one item, up to -20% and - 20 on another, etc.), one ends up being fairly squishy and doing only a bit of damage late in the game even if one has a balanced gear set.
The third point of criticism I have would be that the quality of life functions in the game could use some work.  While the UI is fine, the game's disconnect and deserting system are fairly clumsy, and at times inconsistent.  If one happens to get disconnected while in the hero selection screen, the game treats this as if one had left in the middle of an actual, ongoing round, with a normal stacking ban from queuing.  There is also no distinction built into the game's deserting system regarding the nature of one's abandonment of a round: a crash, disconnect, etc. are all treated as if one simply quit, and as I understand it, this would be fairly simple to fix by having some check of system events. The automated crash report system also takes forever to load, and the game does not actually try to rejoin the game one was in before it loads.  This waiting on the crash report system usually results in being out of the game for about five minutes or so, which obviously is a very bad thing, and also, again, can result in being banned temporarily from queuing through no fault of one's own.  Moreover, there is no compensation for having to play with an incomplete team.  One does not even get the missing player's experience and gold allotment if the player had left the starting area before leaving or disconnecting, and you are not allowed to simply give up on the round without consequence, so one is typically stuck in a rather unenjoyable fight, waiting to lose or surrender.  A last point is that the game's player reporting system, while not exactly transparent, does not seem to be particularly precise either - one can lose goodwill (an incentive to not abandon rounds) if someone reports you, which is fine in normal circumstances, except that it seems possible for others to maliciously report you, with no real justification, and cause you to lose goodwill (this seems to have happened to one of my friends at one point).  An appeal system or some other defense against such abuse, separate from contacting the support team, would seem wise.
Overall, SMITE is an entertaining and fairly interesting game, and is often quite fun.  Be prepared, however, for some very frustrating situations as well, if you play it long enough.

10/10 - A game of trial and error. Of pattern recognition. Of hopelessness. Of frustration and of jubilation. Dark Souls 2 is a deeply rewarding and satisfying experience. Packing a plethora of weapons and armour, it encourages deep character customization from its individual weapons' scaling, speed, weight, durability and down to their raw damage outputs; there are always new weapons to try. Added to this, is the fact that characters can be respec'd with ease, so long as the player as a soul vessel; around 4 or 5 of these can be found per playthough. Tired of playing with this mage? Perhaps I'll make a tank character, covered in heavy armour carrying an enourmous club. Or perhaps a nimble character with dual whips? Encouraging plenty of replayability.
The Dark Souls series has always been known for its difficulty. You died? It's because you didn't look where you were going and fell. Or you allowed yourself to get swarmed by some aggresive axe-wielders. Or you rushed around a corner too quickly and took a mace to the face. The game can be punishing - but fairly so. When it comes to fighting the game's memorable bosses, it can be as tough or easy as you want it to be - taking them on with two summoned helpers while you spam magic attacks at a safe distance or go it completely alone, fighting up close and personal.
While I absolutely loved this game, there are some criticisms. The people you meet along the way, while the voice acting in this game is top notch; the characters themselves aren't as intriguing as previous iterations. Nor is the music as memorable as some of the scores found in both Demon Souls and Dark Souls 1. The PvP is also terribly flawed; as it's now based on soul level and its not unusual to be up against people of severly higher levels.
Either way this game was amazing. A must buy. Must play.

First, this game is very complex. No matter what you run it on issues may occur, thats just a given and it should be accepted as such. Creative Assembly is very good at getting on fixes that are listed on the website thankfully, which means that if you played the game a month ago its now time to jump back on and see how they have changed the experiance for yourself. Secound, i am showing favoritism for a reason. This series is something i have played for years, i am both happy and dissapointed with changes made over time, but. Total War is something you will not find in any other game. The scale and structure cannot be called unique because of its historical context. But as a tactical stratagy game it is unrivaled. Rome 2 also is starting to introduce a more social, and cultural aspect, which is still new and lacking. Though it may add much if improved for later games/expansions (not dlc). Lastly, to talk about the game itself Rome 2 is amazingly detailed (although the high tier requirements are considerable) The amount of diversity through factions, enviroment, playstlye, and technology is quite impressive. Its quite easy for the player to become immersed in his faction and surround and miss the actual scale of the campaign map, untill its too late. Unfortunatly the naval gameplay was incoporated poorly with little control over ships and preventing naval tactics. I also recomend using a mod to change the game to 6-12 turns per year. The current system is unrealistic and prevents generals from leveling, leading to swapping out generals every few turns and never becoming attached so that your heart truly aches when your most prominate commander was assasinated. If you have doubts about this game, do not think poorly of the entire series, please try shogun 2.

15 hours was the magic number where Just Cause 3 stopped being enjoyable. In that time I zipped around Not-Italy on a wingsuit, blew up two dozen military bases, freed countless towns, and completed another dozen or so story misions.
The story is complete dreck; held back by poor writing and even worse voice performance. It can hold a certain camp appeal, but only as it sails through on its way "so bad it's actually bad" territory. Even worse, the game locks away a few toys behind these missions (and the even worse challenges).
Thankfully, going from base to base, blowing everything up on the way, is a great deal of fun at first. This eventually becomes routine, especially once the story requires certain handfuls of provinces to be freed before it continues.
Just Cause 3 nails the movement mechanics. Switching between running, gliding and parachuting is fiddly at first, but eventually clicks into place. The only downside I found was the lack of a sprint button, slowing ground combat to a crawl, compared to the whizz-bang moments in the air.
A grappling hook that you can attach to anything has novelty appeal. Attaching soldier A to exploding plane B is a laugh the first time, but is a much slower process the second. Hooking two things together is the agonisingly slower alternative to just shooting it.
For the price I paid, I got a level of satisfaction I'm happy with. Just Cause 3 lacks a hook to make it great, so it had the good sense to be stupid and loud instead.

Chances are, you know what you're getting into when you play a Worms game. It's a fun tactical turn based combat and some of the new additions really are quite hilarious.
The new MECH is probably one of the best additions as it has such an overwhelming amount of power and increases the movement of the worms. More often than not, worms games are often quite slow, with some of the pacing beingbroken up by teleporters or the ninja rope. But the Mech makes the game play more like a traditional 2D platformer as you can walk at decent speeds, jump and hover. I would be very interested in seeing this type of fast paced strategy in a new type of game actually... Sometimes these new vehicles can intefere with the classic pacing and gameplay that many fans are used to. But personally, I enjoyed it.
The only major con I have right now is that I have been struggling to get matchmaking working effectively, there were not many lobbies up and I would recieve errors when joining ot hosting my own game. I suspect these will be addressed in the future. Additionally, I'm not that much of a fan of the crafting mechanic. It detracts from the core action and means that to craft eficiently, you need to craft during the enemies turn. I really would love to spend more time watching the action instead of my attention being turned to making sure I craft soemthing new.
In summaray, I really enjoyed what I played and I think that if you had fun playing any previous Worms games, you'll enjoy this one!

My review is strictly from the perspective of a Skyrim player, and a casual gamer with no understanding of an MMORPG, and 0 RPG experience in general (except for Skyrim).
I enjoyed Skyrim for it's beautiful landscapes and variety of customization. I felt connected to the AI units in the game. I don't know much about the fighting sequences or controls, but I found them enjoyable and easy to get used to.
With this game; however, as a Dark Elf, I spawned in some barren wasteland with dull landscapes, and 4 hours into the game, I was still stuck at the same regions. I purchased this game knowing this would include all of Tamriel, but to be kept away from Skyrim for so long? Geez! Also, whose bright idea was it to make the in-game text painfully smaller? The fighting, while similar to Skyrim, was a bit lacking. In this game, talking to AI was just a waste of time. I did not know what's going on, who's who, and what the story was. It felt like the game just kept throwing an infinite number of mindless quests my way with a cat's head and a kangaroo's tail forcefully attached to a chihuahua. The levels of customizations weren't too appealing to me either. I had a huge load of gold in the 4 hours I'd played, but it was all in vain as merchants weren't clear enough, neither were raw materials.
As far as the game's stability goes, I hadn't noticed any glitches to be honest, but I did keep getting tossed out of the game. In another game, Team Fortress 2, when my connection drops out or gets laggy, I get stuck. With this game, laggy connection just throws me out entirely.
If you're expecting Skyrim here, don't bother and move on. I don't know if you have a background in MMORPG or whether having that background would make this game more enjoyable, but if you've got an open mind and would be willing to expect anything, please, do try it out.
I just ended up getting a refund. I don't know if I acted too hastily in forming an opinion, but it just wasn't enjoyable enough for me. Who knows, I might end up giving it another shot in the future, but it's a no from me for now.

This is not a good game. I don't want to be overly dismissive - there's a lot of good content here: it's beutiful, the characters (not the quests, the characters) are well written, and the combat is engaging (even if, in the end, it doesn't affect much to go from "tab-targeting" to "location-based" in PvE). It becomes a bit insulting after 30 minutes or so.
And then the MMO part? Not well managed becuase nothing is instanced. Turning off world-threatening devices is less awe-inspiring when 5 strangers are doing it with you. It just makes no sense and turns the game into a "lets press E here and get to the next point even more". Then add in 20-30 people doing the same thing at the same time for a super-low enemy saturation: so you rarely have to/get to fight becuase everything is killed by others.  Nothing seems epic or even notable. Quests should not feel like grinding, but ESO somehow pulled that off (though the characters are, as I said good).
Also, everyone seems super-exited about theft. Every time you go to a town you see 3-4 people stealing. Can you report them? No. Can you do anything? No. It's a fine SP mechanic transplanted to an MMO.
In short, this feels like a Diablo 2 (for really simple quests) mixed with Elder Scrolls view/combat - and the servers are overcrowded.  It would be an okay Single Player game, but the game crams too many players into zones without making anyone feel like its a joint effort.

Lets me state this so it is simple for everyone, one of the best games easily
For any devs who may end up working on a System Shock 3 or a reboot, a playthrough of Alien: Isolation should be a pre-requisite to getting the job.

You know those moments in every alien movie and trailer when ripley is cornered, hidding, holding her breath while the alien hangs over her, breathing... drooling... This game is that moment, from beginning to end.
Alien Isolation is not just a video game, its a horrifying experience that will change you. Unlike other games of the genre, AI is not about blood, gore, ghosts, or other cheap scares, the threat here feels real. You are being hunted, and you have hone your instincts and use everything you find to survive. The moments that scare the most; the times when you want to quit and run; are the hardest to look away from, and the most rewarding to survive.
This game isnt scary as much as it is stressful. Much like the movies, AI is more of a thriller than a horror game. That being said, it isnt for everyone, certainly not the faint of heart. Like any good scary experience, AI will test your limits, and you will discover wether your own instincts are to fight or flee.

Finally we have a game worthy of the Alien franchise.
The creators of Alien: Isolation obviously 'get it'.
Every aspect of this game is perfectly in-universe. the maps are sets built for Alien. The creature comes as close as possible to representing what was only shown in breif, dark moments in the film.
The music and sound create a thick, oily ozone-smelling atmosphere that immerses you deeply into the grim, dark, uncaring world of the Alien franchise.
Controls are spot on. The way your body moves is perfect. Level geometry is built in such a way that, even in a panic, you know where to hide the moment danger strikes.
This is NOT a survival horror game.
This is a true Alien game. It is, I dare say, the sequel to the Alien film.
The fact that it is horrifying is incidental. The fact that you feel like you are barely holding onto the next moment of survival is incidental: this is what this universe feels like. This is what a true Alien game should be.
This is a game, set after Alien, that is built from the same creative essense, and truly exists in canon. The fact that it is a 'survival horror' game is simply by nature of these ingredients it was made from.
Totally engrossing, gripping, visceral, natural.
All there is are your tools, the game world, and the incredible characters that populate it. You never thing "this is a great game I'm playing" because you are too busy playing it, feeling it, and desperately holding onto survival.
Cutscenes are prerendered, and they are at an inconsistent, sometimes choppy 30fps.
Anti aliasing forced by your control panel is unsupported. The built in antialiasing is a bit less strong than I'd like.
T2X is the best the game has, and is fine.
These little technical issues are easy to overlook. Everything else is so superb and well crafted, it doesn't matter.
Visuals are perfect. AI is perfect. Music and Sound design are more than perfect. Gameplay/body feel/minigames to operate doors and computers is wonderful.
Full marks. Buy it now.

After the debacle that was Aliens: Colonial Marines Alien: Isolation, developed by The Creative Assembly, is a lovingly crafted and brave new take on the Alien franchise in videogame form. The most important thing to understand about this new entry into the series is it's radical shift in game-play design from those of which were, by an large, iterations on the same game-play first experienced in Doom. And it was with no surprise that the franchise was going to take this well trodden path as the sequel to the original film in the series was John Carmack's main inspiration in developing Doom.
By diagnosing the main problem with one of videogame's most popular genres The Creative Assembly have opted to make the player feel as vulnerable as possible in order to instil a genuine sense of dread and tension throughout the game. The game doesn't allow players to horde backpacks full of guns and ammo but instead forces you to use any meager gadget you can concoct in order to distract your enemies as opposed to mowing them down with little cost to your resources or safety. There are guns introduced later in the game and surprise surprise here in lies one of the games strange inconsistencies with the Alien cannon and potential flaws in it's game-play.
After a slow burn introduction to the Sevastopol Station, a crumbling space port in it's last stages of being decommissioned, the game starts out incredibly reminiscent of Bioshock allowing the player to venture in at their own pace discovering computers containing personal logs by Sevastopol inhabitants and audio recordings that help to organically deliver the narrative element of the game. Once further into the Sevastopol, and the main elements have been introduced, the game-play really takes off with the Alien and other enemies all working together to create a wonderfully organic emergent gameplay style that is never scripted and always seems unique throughout repeat playthroughs. And repeat playthroughs of individual missions will become commonplace to even the most seasoned and skilled players as The Creative Assembly have done something truly amazing with the AI of it's titular enemy by designing it to work with heightened sensors that enable it to respond dynamically to sound and situations as opposed to being moved on predetermined paths with basic AI programming. In short this game is ♥♥♥♥ING HARD!
The look and feel of the game is stunning, albeit it with a minimal amount of dodgy cut-scenes, poor human facial animations and shader aliasing problems, as the lighting and graphical fidelity convinces you that you are in the world of Alien, one of cinemas most stunning and meticulously designed films. The Alien's design and animations are far beyond anything I've seen in any game and it's clear where Sega have really channeled their money opting, with minor cost to less vital parts of the game, to really bring the Alien to life.
However there are some problems with the game, although minimal, and these are down in large part to the second half of this massive game. When I say massive I can tell you it must have taken me over 25 hours to complete the game on Normal difficulty on a very exploratory play-through and once the game reached the 15 hour mark for me, which would have been an ample length for a game of this kind the Alien "goes on vacation", for the third quarter of the game, leaving you pining for it's return. Once the game finds itself without an Alien you are left to contend with the station's second most deadly entity, the Androids, who prove to be somewhat less fulfilling. The game also chooses to ignore some vital elements of the Alien's life cycle introduced by James Cameron in the second movie which I feel are to it's detriment.
On the whole Alien: Isolation is one of the most tense and claustrophobic horror stealth games I've ever experienced and I heartily recommend to it to any and all that have even the slightest interest in horror and sci-fi. Well done CA the Alien is finally back in town!

Eternal Senia takes you on an epic journey through the eyes of a young girl named Senia. Although simple in presentation, this game exemplifies how the ARPG genre should be through innovative changes to classic mechanics and a strong focus on story and ambiance.
The graphical style and user input are sure to inspire feelings of nostalgia for gamers over 30. A throw back to a time when fundamental game play mattered more than death counters or clicks per second, Eternal Senia is a fresh new experience that anyone looking for a little bit of relaxing fun at any age should be able to pick up and enjoy.
This game has:
Game developer and publisher Holy Priest has delivered a gift in the form of Eternal Senia, completely free of charge, back to the game-playing community that embraced him many years ago within Ragnarok Online. I have no doubt that others who take the time to experience this labor of love will be similarly motivated by his inspirational work.
In the end, the game is shorter than I would like. I also would have preferred more graphics options including native support for 16:9 displays and the ability to play in a windowed fullscreen mode, however these are minor technical points compared to the positive aspects of the game. For what is essentially a hobbyist project, Eternal Senia is an unqualified success worth taking note of.

WIthout a tutorial to speak of, teamwork is even harder than it would be normally, and the scarcity of ammo compared to the overabundance/respawning of zombies makes for a frustrating experience sometimes, in that you don't really feel like it was your fault that you lost but rather that you just got screwed over.
That said, definitely worth checking out, especially if you have some friends willing to coordinate.  That slow, tense action is hard to find elsewhere!

I haven't finished the game yet, I have been taking it slow and having a lot of fun. The story started off great, with new and more lively areas to explore. The lore is further revealed and dives deeper into the this mostly mysterious world that that the story takes place in. I will definitely be doing a few play throughs.
I much enjoy the brighter areas to explore, it adds a nice mix up and contrast from the dark storyline. The first Dishonored was mostly a dark game set in a dark time in dark places. This is still a dark story but there is a bit more going on in the environments. They are more open offering more ways to get through. Bodies don't disappear after a while any more, so depending on how you want to play, you really need to hide them well. There are new abilities to master and offer fun in creating new ways to take out your enemies.
I also like the new bonecharm crafting system. It is a nice way to add extra customization to abilities and in a way further develop your character.

I think this is a great game and I hope the devs will continue this franchise as I want to explore more of the world they created.

OVERVIEW: This review comes from a huge fan of Worms Armageddon and for over a decade I keep buying these damn games thinking they are going to nail it. This game was a step in the right direction but a few key changes just leave me bored very quickly and wonder what the Devs were thinking on the new systems that were added.
GRIPE : The options to create interesting game modes is the most lacking from any Worms entry. It is very basic with just a few toggles of what weapons to have on and such. I really enjoyed the SHOPPER game type in Armageddon and it is not possible to accurately create.
GRIPE : They have added buildings interiors and it breaks the game for me. You cannot see any worms in these building interiors unless you have a worm in them yourself. So you never really know what’s going on during a online match. You might think it’s down to 1v1 and your playing your heart out to beat this guy, you beat him down with you only a inch away from death…. And then you realize he had another worm that never moved the whole game that was just hiding in a building interior….and you lose. Dumb, just a very very very dumb addition to the series.
PRO : The art style, gameplay, and performance of this Worms game is the best it has been in about a decade.
GRIPE : The crafting system added is another failed implementation. You can deconstruct and build things once every turn… no not just YOUR turn, EVERY TURN OF THE GAME. This leads to a online match of 6 people who are more focused on doing their crafting panel in hopes to build a Armageddon, then actually focusing on the epic grenade toss you just did. I finished entire matches online where I was zero invested because I was just trying to figure out what crap I could craft and deconstruct instead of focusing on the game.
GRIPE : Vehicles… I don’t even feel like going into it but no, no they are not fun and yes, they will get you killed faster than if you just avoid them all together.
PRO : Roping finally feels right again and you can pull off some sweet moves with it. Also the sheep on a rope is an awesome new weapon.
FINAL:  Just save your money, this is not the Worms from your nostalgic memory. You will realize around hour 3 that you have no desire to play anymore and then will be bummed that you just crossed the steam refund threshold and are now stuck with this game.

I spawn and the first guy i run into claims friendly so i let him know this is my very first server. He shows me around and teaches me the core basics of the game. I spawn in the desert again and one of them approaches me saying hey sorry buddy as he tries to sweet talk me i give him a taste of his own medicine and kill him with my hatchet as his friend comes running up.
