In space, no one can hear you scream; but in my house, my wife heard me scream several times. Man screams, obviously.
Alien: Isolation is the very definition of Survival Horror drawing it's influences from one of the best survival horror movies in the history of cinema - Alien. Creative Assembly (a studio best known for Total War games) has managed to create one of the most atmospheric immersive game world's I've ever experienced.
Even if you've never seen the Alien movie, this game will draw you right into the it's world with some of the best lighting and soundtracks I've ever experienced in a game. It's even more of a bonus if you have seen the movies, as you'll be drawn into a world that seems familiar... perhaps too familiar, as I found myself totally drawn into the game yelling out 'NOOOO!' whenever I was attacked by Alan, the French sexpest Xenomorph.
In fact the entire mythos of the Alien haunts you throughout the game, with the level of expectation and suspense building up almost constantly.
The OST ques and motiffs drawn from the original Jerry Goldsmith OST, only the music is static it's dynamic and swells and ebbs with the action. There were times when the music was pounding causing fear and panic, and the Alien wasn't even on the screen. If this game doesn't win an award for it's OST and Sound Design than I'll be lost for words.
There are some issues with the game, such as the pacing. I felt as though a few chapters stretched the game out longer than it needed, even if they were designed to allow you to rest and regain composure after some hectic momenets. Yet, I don't feel it ruined the game.
I'm trying to avoid going into too much detail as I don't want to ruin the game, as ultimately this is a game best experienced; played in the dark with headphones on with the screen a foot away from your vision. Go in blind and enjoy.
In short - an amazing experience for Alien fans and perhaps one of the true great Alien games available today. It really captures the essence to the Alien movie in both spirit and gentle nods. Might be a frustrating experience for some, who don't understand the aura around the creature stalking you.

This game is for the most part, a masterpiece. The first 10 to 12 hours are pure perfection, in my opinion. It has the best graphics/atmosphere/sound design that I've ever seen, EVER, in a videogame. It even menages to top two of my favorite games, Bioshock and Dead Space, in all of those aspects. If you've ever wondered what'd be like to live the horrors of the 1979 film Alien, then look no further, Alien Isolation is the game for you. That being said, it has one of the most frustrating last couple of hours that I can recall in any modern videogame. There are, at least, 6 fake endings. Those last few hours are filled with lazy level design, jump scares, loud noises and lots of repetitive filler that could've been cut out from the game entirely. The same goes for the ending... Although not terrible, it certainly didn't live up to my own, personal hype. All in all, Isolation is a brilliant game. The Alien is like nothing I've ever seen. Masterful A.I all across the board, perfect graphics and sound design. Can't describe how happy I am that we finally got the Alien game that we deserve. Absolutely worth picking up.

What is better than a challenging game that makes each failure painful and each success sublime? One with a deep story (an optional story for those who like to listen), great atmosphere, tons of different playstyles, and the ability to cosplay. It is hard not to enjoy Dark Souls II despite the pain it can cause you.

Dark Souls is game in a series based around misconceptions. Yes, this game is harder than most big name titles out there but why it is hard isn't because the game is made to punish the player. Yes, "Prepare to Die" is a correct saying when talking about Dark Souls. This is a game about trial and error and what makes this game "hard" is simply getting used to the learning curve. Once you learn that wildly swinging your weapons will get you no where and you should memorize your enemies attack patterns then you're already on your way to completing the game. For those that played the previous games, this wont deliever the same shock you had when you first entered the souls series. You'll still die but you'll be able to comfortably get through the game with a few dozen deathes before completion. Possibly even less due to the ammount of summoning signs currently available so two friends or two random strangers can help you tackle any boss making some boss battles cake.
The game has also improved a lot since the previous games, players can no longer block attacks forever with their sheilds and can now be punished by a sheild break that will lead to a powerful counter attack, every play style is now acceptable from spell casting to duel wielding to even sheild walkthroughs, and all the weapons have their uses even the whips and brass knuckles. Death is more penalizing in this game with each time you die you slowly lose more and more of your general health as you hollow and being hollow no longer makes you safe. Even as a Hollow you can still be invaded and killed further by players. The plus to this though is that a player no longer has to horde around 10+ humanity to make their weapon due the most damage but human effigies are tougher to come by and can be gained by helping other players. A con for the game has to be it's level design. While the previous Dark souls, levels flowed one into another seemlessly, this game you see the breaks clearly so it looks more like patch work. The addition of torches is a dissappointment to the series since there are only 2 levels where you actually need to use one and only One of those levels is a level where you need to use it for sight.

The worst thing about this game is the keyboard and mouse controlls. Just leaving it as it comes makes it so you need three hands to play the game. Another thing to mention about this is that you can not bind functions to mouse buttons!
My only other "bad" point about this is that, in my opinion (and this couls also just me getting better at the game from the previous game) that the game has gotten "easier". Conclusion:
All in all, I think that the game was great, so great that I actually bought it twice (one on Xbox on release day and one on PC two days after it's release) and I would recomend people looking for a challege and something new to play.

Muffin Knight is a puzzle platformer based on the now infamous unity engine. There has been many assetflips based around this poor engine, however from time to time you get something that might be worth playing. This was my main objective as I embarked on a quest to see weather this would be a gem or another black mark upon the engines already unfavorable reputation.
The short description of this game would be its like Suer Crate Box however instead of being free it cost you 7 of your hard earned euros.
The fundamental game play is very basic and easy to get into. You are put in a very vertical 2d map and your objective is to collect as many muffins as you can while stopping the creatures from exiting the map at the bottom just like in Super Creat Box a free game.
Unlike Super Crate Box Muffin Knight offers you a variety of differently themed levels that you progress trough be earing stars in each level.
While you progress you earn points that you can spend in a skill tree kind of deal where you can also upgrade your health. By default you can only collide with one enemy unless you invest in health upgrades. The skills tree is not at all very interesting and could very easily been left out of the game completely as it doesn’t make the games any more enjoyable.
Just like in Super Create Box a free game you unlock new and interesting characters as you progress all with different and sometimes interesting weapons. Such as deadly rainbow pop a black mark on Muffin Knight if you ask me. The dead memes are plentiful. All characters can be upgraded in the skill tree. Sadly the upgrades are not that interesting as it is the standard shoot faster deal more damage upgrades we see in most games.
Now you might have noticed that I have been comparing this game to another game called Super Creat Box. To me it is obvious that this game was only made to grab a bit of money off of the success of the last mentioned game. The game is competent in what it tries to do however there is not enough innovation in Muffin Knight for me to recommend this game to you more than I would recommend you to take a look at Super Crate Box as it is a better game with less fluff and no
dead memes. Oh yeah btw Super Creat Box Is also free.
In conclusion. Go get Super Crate Box.
If you want a score for Muffin Knight here it is. 0.5/Super Crate Box

Background: I didn't play the first Just Cause. The second one I purchased from sale and played through a few times with a good amount of time spent collecting things and doing random sandbox stuff. This third one I bought on launch day and just recently reached 100% completion with around 45 hours of playtime.
The game really shines in its audiovisual department with explosions having a decent amount of low frequency sounds and flaming visuals to make them feel impactful and blowing stuff up is just as fun as it was in the previous game. The wingsuit is a nice addition to the movement techniques once you get used to it and how it is different from the familiar parachute gliding.
You now have more tools at your disposal to wreak havoc with, most of which you have to unlock doing challenge missions and a few that come with progressing in the story. To me, the most notable addition to the core gameplay is that the standard grapple hook tether wires can now be retracted between objects to make them crash together. You start with being able to shoot 2 wires, but with full upgrades you can have 6 with pulling force strong enough to lift cars. There are also rocket booster explosives that, along with tether wires, are the main tools for doing sandbox-y things.
However, there's not a lot of variety in the general gameplay at moment. The enemy AI doesn't really pose any threat so you kinda have to enjoy the core mechanics and be good at figuring out creative ways of causing destruction. The challenge missions could've used at least a few more different categories. Though technically optional, the challenges are scored based on completion time, amount of destruction, accuracy etc. depending on the type and you can get 0-5 gears from each one. The gears unlock equipment of the specific challenge type, but once you have seen all the different types they start to feel a bit of a chore to complete especially when going for 5 gears.
The random collectibles seem a bit tacked on as well, though I'm glad that compared to the 2nd game there is a reasonable amount of them and, unlike in some sandbox games, they actually unlock stuff like access to unlimited fast travel or additional weapons and vehicles. Unfortunately the guns don't have a lot of differences in feel between them and some of the vehicles (especially the motorbikes) are really wonky to control.
Like most of the other reviews have pointed out, there is a forced online leaderboard system that tracks your efforts in various different feats such as longest headshot distance, highest elevation gained with a parachute or longest distance drifted in a land vehicle. It's a cool idea on paper, but it should work more seamlessly in the background and include an option of opting-out of it or at least hiding the displayed messages that pop-up when someone manages to best you at some feat.
In conclusion, the game is pretty much what I expected from the 3rd installment; It has the same campy feel to the story missions, base "liberation", stunt driving, vehicles that explode like a pile of gasoline and matches from smallest of bumps and so on. Although the list of negative things I listed is long, there really are only a few major annoyances that could and most likely will be patched out in the near future. I'm hoping there'll be some worthy DLC packs to expand the list of available activities currently in the game.
Would I recommend it? Yes, but with an asterisk that in its current form you might find it repetitive and thus not lasting long enough to justify full-priced purchase.

Alien: Isolation is the very definition of Survival Horror drawing it's influences from one of the best survival horror movies in the history of cinema - Alien. Creative Assembly (a studio best known for Total War games) has managed to create one of the most atmospheric immersive game world's I've ever experienced.
Even if you've never seen the Alien movie, this game will draw you right into the it's world with some of the best lighting and soundtracks I've ever experienced in a game. It's even more of a bonus if you have seen the movies, as you'll be drawn into a world that seems familiar... perhaps too familiar, as I found myself totally drawn into the game yelling out 'NOOOO!' whenever I was attacked by Alan, the French sexpest Xenomorph.
In fact the entire mythos of the Alien haunts you throughout the game, with the level of expectation and suspense building up almost constantly.
The OST ques and motiffs drawn from the original Jerry Goldsmith OST, only the music is static it's dynamic and swells and ebbs with the action. There were times when the music was pounding causing fear and panic, and the Alien wasn't even on the screen. If this game doesn't win an award for it's OST and Sound Design than I'll be lost for words.
There are some issues with the game, such as the pacing. I felt as though a few chapters stretched the game out longer than it needed, even if they were designed to allow you to rest and regain composure after some hectic momenets. Yet, I don't feel it ruined the game.
I'm trying to avoid going into too much detail as I don't want to ruin the game, as ultimately this is a game best experienced; played in the dark with headphones on with the screen a foot away from your vision. Go in blind and enjoy.
In short - an amazing experience for Alien fans and perhaps one of the true great Alien games available today. It really captures the essence to the Alien movie in both spirit and gentle nods. Might be a frustrating experience for some, who don't understand the aura around the creature stalking you.

Initial performance aside (their latest patch did a lot to improve it) and focusing on the gameplay, I'm very satisfied with Dishonored 2.
-The story is captivating from beginning to end, no matter what path you choose. I chose to go the harder route of not killing anyone, even main targets, and it provides the same satisfying challenge as it did in the first game. There's also a rich side-story, told through books and some by talking to people.
-The world is beautiful and detailed. It's visually apparent that designing the world was really a labor of love. I couldn't find any bits of it that seemed unpolished.
-The controls felt fluid and easy to use and master. Didn't change much from the first game, but there wasn't anything to improve on.
-As far as game length is concerned, it took me just about 21 hours from beginning to end. That was with a generous amount of checkpoint reloading due to my obsession with not killing anyone along the way and trying my best to never be seen. I'm guessing if you were to choose a more...expiditious way of dealing with your enemies, the game would probably take a good 4 or 5 hours less.
-Keep in mind that part of Dishonored's charm is that I get to go back and play it again with a completely different approach. I can also choose to play as Corvo, which adds more dimension to my available choices. Could result in a lot of replay value, which helps justify the price tag.
Overall I'm inclined to give it a solid 9/10. The only thing it lost 10/10 on was:
-Occasionally I would be killed by closing or opening a door on myself. Anytime I was meant to be pushed out of the way, but collided with an object, I would instantly die.
-Emily's grappling ability would sometimes short itself repeatedly, causing a bit of frustration. The marker would clearly have me landing on top of my target, but I'd pretty much end up smashing face into it, and either falling to my death, or at the very least making a racket when I landed on something.
Runs a bit low res on my 290X but with 1.2 runs ok. The game can get annoying when trying to do a stealth and merciful run but its growing on me. Still think Dishonored 1 >> 2.

The PC release for Dishonored 2 was garbage. We all know this. It's unfortunate, and thankfully Arkane is aware and actively trying to fix this. This review will not be talking about the garbage PC release, this review will be discussing the game itself. I refuse to doc points for an issue that has nothing to do with the product as intended. I played Dragon Age: Inquisition at a literal 5 frames per second, with dialouge constantly freezeing, stuttering, and repeating itself. All on a laptop that cost me $200 and was 4 years old at the time. It was not what Bioware intended at all, and I loved the game regardless.
So - needless to say, I'm not very picky, and I enjoy suffering. (I do - however - recognize that while DA:I wasn't truly broken, Dishonored 2 is. I have a computer that is within the reccommended specs and yet it crashes, without fail, before the Bethesda spash screen, and therefore I had to commendeer a computer belonging to a family member that would Actually Run The ♥♥♥♥ing Game, Thank You Very Much.)
SO, for those of us lucky souls that can actually run the game, here is my review:
Dishonored 2 took everything that I loved about the first game, and everything I didn't love (like, at all. I'm looking at you, Delilah's Coven) and made it better. My playstyle for Dishonored is non-lethal, adaptave stealth (meaning that when♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan, as it often does for me- because I am bad at video games, I run and get up to the nearest point where the enimes won't care about me anymore). Throught my run of Dishonored 1, this meant a lot of sitting and watching, learning guard movements, abusing Dark Vision, and hoarding sleep darts. It was a painful process, seeing as how I have little paitence, and the atmosphere of the game always sucked me in, putting me on edge, making me one jumpy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
It doesn't help that I spook easily.
Dishonored 1 showed us a world with rich, lush lore, an intriguing story, and poor Corvo, who literally didn't deserve any of this. Dishonored 1 gave us a strange, slightly evil, but mostly neutral deity. Dishonored 1 gave us a lot of things, and I'm going to assume you know the rest of the super cool♥♥♥♥♥♥Dishonored 1 gave us, and get on with it.
Dishonored 2 keeps with its theme of "Play your way" - to the point of giving us the ultimate option of choosing our protagonist, and even choosing if we want to go with supernatural powers or not. (My utmost respect to those who have already done Clean Hands and Ghost runs without powers - you're all heros.)
Speaking of powers, DH2 gives us even more powers, in the for both Corvo and Emily. I have yet to do a run with Emily, (a shame, I know, mostly because I'm still exploring with Corvo) but let me just say, I am extrememly excited to see what shenanigains I'll be getting into with her powers.
Bonecharms and runes are craftable items now, after purchasing the "crafting" abilitiy from the Ehnancements section of the Powers tab, and while I didn't much experiment with crafting runes, I did make the most of the bonecharm crafting, and found myself enjoying it quite a lot, espically the new, rare black and corruped bonecharms that you can find scattered about the world.
More new things in DH2 include: non-lethal weapons and combat mechanics, enemies, bloodflies, and the Outsider's voice.
I found myself so, so happy to find that there's now the ability to non-lethally dispatch guards during a swordfight, once you block them and get them off balance, you punch them in the throat and choke them out, which, Ow, but hey, it's better than death. In DH1 you were allowed 10 sleep darts, and I found myself disappointed that in DH2 we're only given a maximum of 5, but then I quickly got over it after finding the new Howling and Stinging bolts, which blind and cause enemies to flee and forget, respectively.
Drop assassination now also has a non-lethal counterpart as well. Actually, everything I can think of has a non-lethal counterpart now, which is fantastic.
New enemies include Clockwork Soldiers and Elite Guards, both make you rethink your strategies that might've worked on your regualar enemies. Both are satisfying to take down. Bloodflies are gross, and really annoying, and as Corvo I find the best way to deal with them is to just blink past them. However, setting them on fire is good too. Also, much more satisfying. (Burn, you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ bugs!)
The Outsider has a new voice actor, and I found myself to be very... saddened by it. I loved the voice actor in the first game. But as I played on in DH2 I grew to really, really enjoy this new side of the Outsider. This new voice, these new mannerisims. He gets up in your space, chastises you, and genuinely feels like the 15-year-old turned Void-God he's supposed to be. Human emotions, inhuman perception. A lot of people hate it, I respect that, but I also feel that maybe, just maybe, it's because they turned their noses up too quick. (Or, they genuinely dislike it and that's a totally valid opinion! I can respect that. I thought Lush was really good as the outsider too, I just happen to feel that Taylor rocks it as well.)
I love, love, loved this game. I love a lot of things about this game. I love the characters, I love that this game made me cry, made me feel for these characters. I love that we got more context on the Outsider, saw a deeper part of him. I love that this game is fun as all hell, the controls feel good, everything about this game just Feels Good.
There is, however, one thing that I hate.
I hate that it's so short.
That, however, is proabably a good thing. That this game makes me want more, makes me crave more.
Replay value for Dishonored 2 is very high, even for someone like me who has a hard time rereading books, or rewatching movies because I already know the ending, and I get bored with it.
Dishonored 2 is my personal GOTY, and I give it a 9.5/10. The half-point is docked because, while I love it, I felt some aspects of the story were a bit rushed. (I'm looking at you, introduction sequence. I'm looking at you.)

This game is just amazing. They may have dumbed a few things down and changed the system so that battles end quicker, but it's far better than not understanding what to do.
Yeah it was buggy at first, but get this, ALL GAMES ARE! They patch big and small things frequently as some games and their creators should look into instead of just doing patches every few years after a little spurt right after release.
They did dumbed down the family trees and in truth they really have no use in the game, but really there isn't any real point to them unless your playing for Rome or Carthage but otherwise it isn't a big deal. I'll admit it is just a waste of time for them to exist as well as half the time all you do is blackmail or something of the sort which does nothing but drain money from your nation's economy so don't waste your time with it.
And the big one...super fast battle times. I love the battles being as fast as they are. I mean yeah if you put your men in a big blob and charge them at the enemy odds are that you could win. Of course that is only when playing on easier difficulties and your men aren't upgraded such as later on in the campaign. The battles are fast because, get this, not everybody has time to sit at home all day cause you can't move out of mommy and daddies house and they don't care. This may be a huge surprise but some people work 10 or more hours a day and have families to care for or simply have other business to do, also the sun doesn't hurt so you don't need to spend all day inside playing games. Yeah, I like to game for a few hours and whatnot but I don't want to spend an hour playing a siege battle or almost an hour playing a field battle. So as many people complain about the battle times know that I don't and I am all in when it comes to the speedy victory.
When playing on easier difficulties and sometimes on harder ones you don't neeed to be very strategic. So go ahead and make a big man-blob and charge your enemy. But get this...you will lose way more men that way. Going back to the battle time we don't all have time for a hour long field battle so it might only take ten minutes to fight it out. Here's the thing though, if you don't leave reserves for flanking or filling gaps, have cavalry flank around, or any other sorts of things you will lose most if not all of your army and then have to retreat from your objective and retrain or restart with a whole new army and general. The strategic aspect is still there you just have to be faster about it.
The DLC's...awesome. They are really really fun and I enjoy playing them. The additional units and factions are really cool and sure they could be free but it's not that expensive especially when you have a job and can pay for them yourself instead of reaching into mom and dad's pockets for money. The Greek, Nomadic, and Pirates and Raiders culture packs are amazing. They add 11 new factions that you can play and trust me when I say that they are worth every dollar, quid, euro, whatever. They add whole new cultures to contend with, units to play with, and whole new systems for world domination. Not to mention Hannibal at the Gates as well as Ceasar in Gaul adds units into the game which also makes them more worth it in my opinion.

Alright. So, I really liked the first Dark Souls game after heavy recommendations from a friend. That means, like a lot of reviews, this write-ups got that bias going.
Dark Souls II feels a lot more influenced by Demon's Souls this time around. You have Majula acting as your main hub. You level up there, upgrade your flask, and most shop NPCs will migrate there when you find them. This is okay, but I really preferred Dark Souls, where the "hub" didn't have much to offer, encouraging you to constantly explore.
Combat improved in a lot of areas, and got weaker in others. While there's less "bad" weapons in the game, most of the ones you would want don't show themselves until much later on in the game.
Shields aren't as good, save for Tower Shields. Defensive-minded equipment in general does not seem as attractive this go around in general.
In this regard, a lot of it felt like it came from rolling or trying to block. It seems these actions are now tied to a stat, not so much an assured constant like in the last game. This makes it more difficult early on to avoid attacks, more-so when attempting to wear heavier armor that hampers your rolling. Also with better two-handed options, and dual-wielding/power stances, you find yourself seriously stuck between having meager defense, or salvageable defense with meager attack power.
Magic's a lot better. When dealing with other players, you'll be quick to notice the lack of Pyromancers in comparison to the other schools, something that was not the case in the last game. Magic has gotten so good, actually, that it's actually become almost mandatory to use. Many bosses have high physical defense, particularly against slashing attacks, while suffering very noticeable elemental weakness. In addition, there's many "support" spells that greatly boost your survivability in fights, or provide other welcome utilities.
The overall level design was kind of meh. Not as many grand areas, or creative ways of traversing. Not bad design, mind, just not as good as Dark Souls 1. Going back to the structure of the world map, it's interesting to see it immediately start off with having a choice of multiple directions to go. It felt a bit detrimental to me, actually, as the linearity near the later part of the game was aggravating. There's a lot of that in this one, and it'll be different depending on how you build your character. But the anguish will be the same.
Bosses were a huge disappointment, unfortunately. They felt bland, they didn't seem as challenging at all. Most of my hardships were due to funky rolling. Weapons made from boss souls also don't seem to be nearly as good as most other weapons in the game. Overall, a lot of them felt the same, and I didn't get the same feeling of accomplishment as I did in the earlier titles. Just felt like they made the trip to the bosses harder, and the bosses themselves easier. I really, really would've liked this the other way around.
The Covenants in this one seem better, but still a bit lacking. There's still some go-nowhere covenants that are either the starting covenant, or just have nothing more to offer once hitting max rank. The invasion oriented covenants this time around seem to be more reluctant about it. There's no re-usable invasion orbs, and the means of acquiring the cracked-versions can be tedious. This results in far less invasions, at least on the character's first playthrough.
Overall, still a great game, and been playing the crap out of it. Happy they brought it to PC.

BROFORCE (you have to say it as a growling shout, or you don't do the game justice) is a game about action heroes. Actual action heroes, as it turns out. Oh, sure, the names change. But with a list of playable characters that includes "Rambro", "MacBrover", and "B.A. Broracus" I think we all know the score.
Don't worry, I'm going to try to steer clear of mentioning any but the earlier-unlocked characters in this review. For the best effect, I recommend not spoiling the list for yourself. One of the most fun parts of Broforce is the anticipation of the next unlock, and witnessing the reveal to the sound of the character's name being shouted by the thoroughly-manly announcer.
BROFORCE is a run-and-gun platformer. The game moves briskly, but not so much so that you can't keep up. It's a nice speed that feels appropriately actiony without feeling unfair. Controls are slick and responsive. Deaths will usually be your own fault, and are accompanied by a noticeable lack of frustration. We all know that feel, right? You die in a game, have to start the level over, and curse either very loudly or under your breath, depending on who's nearby. In Broforce, I don't have that. The game plays so well, the action so entertaining, that having to try again only serves to prolong the enjoyable experience.
The environments are almost entirely destructable. The effect reminds me of Worms, but with a little more detail to it. When you destroy some dirt, a block or two above it may also crumble. Destroying the ground underneath of a support will cause the support to fall apart piece-by-piece. Blocks in ruins will fall and crush anyone underneath. You can blow up explosive barrels, of course, but you can also send propane canisters rocketing satisfyingly into anything in their path, pushing enemies through walls and then detonating after a short distance. Think the conclusion to the final battle in the film version of
The main draw of the game is the still-growing number of Bros to play as. You don't get to pick your Bro, they're randomly chosen from the ones you've unlocked so far. Unlock more Bros by rescuing more P.O.W. Bros from cages through the game. Each Bro rescued gives you an extra life and turns you into a new Bro. The new Bros are unlocked after you do this certain numbers of times. At the moment, I believe it takes some 300 rescues to catch 'em all.
The other way to change Bros is to die (and have at least one life remaining). I've seen people complain about not being able to choose who to play as, but I stand by the current model. It's the same sort of thing I really enjoyed about the way Bastion forced you to use each new weapon for a short time. You can't just pick one thing that works and run through the entire game using only that thing. It would get boring before you were even halfway through, and there's not a chance you wouldn't blame the game for that. Having to use each one, whether you like it or not, allows you come to appreciate the pros and cons of each instead of ignoring the new thing to stick with your favorite.
The Bro lottery simply means that you have to develop your tactics on the fly. Let me tell you, I hated MacBrover at first. Instead of firing bullets at everything, you now have to throw timed explosives at them. And his special is just a remote-detonated version of that. What a rip-off, right? WRONG. SHUT UP. YOU SIT BACK DOWN AND YOU LISTEN, GODDAMN YOU. Turns out, MacBrover is pretty much the bane of
bosses. Most Bros can only shoot straight ahead. They may have a special that lets them lob a grenade or whatever. But those specials are limited, and the grenade will honestly probably just bounce a safe distance away from your target, anyways. MacBrover's explosives will detonate more-or-less exactly where you drop them. And since it's his main attack, he can do this
. Find a nice perch and unload, man. Plus, I mean, once you get the hang of it, dropping explosives so that they stick to the general rabble is pretty fun, too.
Now imagine an entire game, FILLED with Bros, all of whom have their pros and cons just like MacBrover. Now imagine that you never know who you'll be playing as next. Getting somebody who meshes well with the situation at hand means plowing through that situation while your heart drips with physical glee. Getting somebody who isn't perfect for the situation means being confronted with a fun challenge where you have to work your way through it like a man.
There's a good variety to your enemies, as well. You'll kill loads and loads of the basic mooks, but you have big guys, dogs, bomb-tossers, and more. Each of the bosses manages to be pretty unique. I mean, you know, they're mostly just giant death machines that fire big guns at you. But they move differently, fire different types of big guns in different trajectories... look, point is, you won't get bored of the enemy variety, alright?
BROFOOOORCE is still in Early Access, meaning you can expect loads more content in the future. At the moment, one playthrough will probably run you maybe 3-5 hours. The game's enough fun, though, that you shouldn't be surprised if you play it all over again once you're done. Maybe in co-op, this time. The Steam Workshop will extend the length of the game
a bit. Plus the new Alien campaign (inspired by the Alien series of films) is only just around the corner, and that'll help. New Bros come out now and then, and the devs still have more ideas up their sleeves. You shouldn't be afraid of the "Early Access" label on this one. You'll get your money's worth.
I mentioned co-op. There are actually several multiplayer modes. Co-op is the main one. At the moment, online co-op can be a little laggy at times. It's not perfect. It's not terrible either, though. I've played through the full campaign with a friend, and while there were times where the effects of my friend's actions would play out before they actually performed those actions (often resulting in everything turning into sudden explosions and chaos so that I quickly lost track of what was going on, and usually died as a result), as I said, we did
the campaign, and the majority of that time consisted of both ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles.
There is an issue with the way the online game treats things like the local game, however. Even online, the screens tries to keep everyone in it at once. If it fails, then it will focus on one person, meaning that the other player can't really see what they're doing. 98% of the time, this isn't a problem. But there was one boss that moves vertically that really tripped us up. My strategy is to climb the boss as quickly as possible. My friend's strategy is to not do that. He immediately finds himself offscreen, dead, and waiting for me to ride the boss to death or success.
I'll probably update this review every now and then until the game is out, and then I may or may not rewrite it to reflect the final product. If you don't see anything after this paragraph, then the former hasn't happened, yet. If you're even reading this paragraph, then the latter hasn't happened, yet. Anyways, get some BROFORCE, bro!

I love the art style and music. Has no voices but it is a free game so I'm not complaining, especially for spot on Sound FX such as sword hits, magic, ect... For a simple game, it is really put together flawlessly. I enjoyed every moment of this game, from the story line to knowing the characters to the crafting mechanics and so on. I also love the fact that you do not have to put more then at least 15 minutes of farming enemies to get items for crafting better weapons and armors, such a plus. There are 3 Chapters to the game. There are also only 3 endings to the game and little side quests to do if you want to beef up the main heroine. I thank you so much for putting it on Steam for free. ALSO, the boss fights are pretty fun, not super easy but also not that hard, it feels just right.
For the people who are curious about the story and gameplay:
You are playing Senia, our main Heroine. She is searching for her sister, Magalete. who has gone missing for 3 days. The only clue she has is a rumor, that Magalete went to explore The Tower of Eternity. You then start the game climbing inside the tower. The game does an excellent job explaining to you how to play.  You will learn 4 skills during the story line with the game showing you how to use it and what benefits it provides. Each skill has unique uses such as a Dash Attack and AoE (don't want to spoil the others) . The game's crafting system is simple and gathering the materials to craft them is a breeze. The game has monsters that can drop materials to craft, a dungeon room that gives you crafting materials and a excellent place to level,  a torn page of attack/defense/critical that may drop (you need 4 torn pages to craft it into a book which then permanently gives you a +1/+2 ect.. which you can do up to 4 times for every chapter), and may even drop health or mana droplets to heal you. Before I played multiplayer, I told every gamer I met about how groundbreaking and fun Black Mesa was, now it looks like I'll need to warn people to stay away from it.
The final straw is that a half finished but very good campaign and an awful mulitplayer combat experience does NOT warrant the equivalent of more than twice as much as minimum wage.

Alien: Isolation captures the 80's retro magic of the traditional Alien movies with the futuristic notion of space travel to bring you a stealth-based action/horror experience that you won't forget.
__________
Synopsis:
You play as the Amanda Ripley, the daughter of Ellen Ripley from the movie Alien, as she attempts to find any trace of her mother that disappeared 15 years ago. Using a plethora of hand-crafted gadgets and weapons, you must make your way around the Sevastopol, fixing critical ship mechanics and finding more information about your mother's disappearance. Be warned; there are many more dangers than you think.
_____
Story: The story is a pleasant mix of predictable, yet surprising elements, coupled with an almost overwhelming sense of dread at what comes around the next corner. It borrows many elements from Dead Space, but not all of them positive. As Issac did, you board a derelict spaceship and start finding mechanisms to repair in order to progress throughout the story. After a while, however, you feel like the game has adopted a "Murphy's Law" type of philosophy, and the game seems to drag out towards the end after fixing almost everything on the ship by yourself. The actual story is good, but suffers towards the end of the game.
Graphics: Marvelous graphics and environments really capture the essence of the traditional Alien movie. Light years from Earth, yet staring at an old Macintosh using an IBM keyboard shows a level of attention to detail that is not regularly seen. The environment really helps impose a sense of helplessness and dread as you realize the ship has gone to hell.
Functionality and Gameplay: A:I gives a sense of empowerment, yet helplessness to the player. While you may acquire new weapons and gadgets to kill your enemies, the goal at the end of the day is not to get yourself killed. Coupled with the lack of resources to blast everything with your shotgun, combat is often the last resort. Therein lies a small problem: As you acquire new equipment, you might have a desire to use it to make your life simpler. Often enough, it actually is only usable in a very particular circumstance, and sometimes makes your life harder. The name of the game is being a shadow; staying out of anyone and anything's way. At times this can be incredibly frustrating, but there lies the magic. It really gives you that sense of helplessness. There are enemies around that WILL kill you if you make yourself known, but killing them may not be feasible.
_________________________

**This review contains no spoilers**
I don’t normally review games on these portals but this is an exception and dammit it’s worth it.
It’s been a while since I last completely immersed myself into a single player game having looked forward to it  for many months after announcement. The last game was Metro Last light which was an unexpected surprise considering I played several hours of Metro 2033 and had to uninstall it as I got really bored (and continue to get bored after repeated attempts at getting back into it).
My gut told me that Alien: Isolation was something different. From the get go CA’s steady updates about the game, showing gamer reactions during play testing and easy to digest information being released felt transparent.
Among forum members fears ran wild as to whether the game would live up to the mostly user generated hype and as early reviews started to crop up close to release many people thought it was done for. IGN/Polygon and a couple others rated Isolation with average scores saying it was either too lengthy or too difficult....
Thankfully we actual gamers know what’s what and at the time of writing Isolation has hit the 2nd spot in the UK game sales ranking. Position 1 being the latest FIFA (meh).
Just goes to show professional reviewers aren’t all what they’re cracked out to be.
Let’s get the engine out of the way first. It’s outstanding. CA made a custom engine for this game and the visuals will blow you away especially once you unlock additional reflections and effects. Unlocking has zero hit on performance and even on low to mid end hardware the game runs and looks fantastic.
At an ultra wide resolution of 3440x1440 the game works really nicely and gives full immersion. If you’ve got one of these monitors then you’re in for a treat. The FOV at 55 is the equivalent  of 85 in other games, just be sure to select that.
The gameplay is sound too and the ambience reminiscent of Ridley Scott’s original film. They had access to all of the data archives from the original film so everything is authentic to the movie and it feels like you’re playing a continuation of the film.
There are a few quirks with AI but nothing major. Play on hard and you will be killed many time, the Alien is brutal as are the Working Joe androids. If their eyes glow white you’re safe but if they are red then stay well away unless you have plenty of shotgun shells
It’s nice to see a game not restricted to an aspect ratio or framerate. A game that isn’t a shoddy console port but a PC game giving our platform its all.
I’m still some 12 hours in but felt I had played and seen enough to be able to write an accurate review so far. I would easily give it a 8.5 or 9/10. No game is ever a perfect 10.

I do not recommend this game in it's current state. First, a little background:
I've been playing Worms since 1998. I briefly played W2 before W:A came out, and I've been a huge W:A fan ever since and still play it online. I also own all of the other Worms games a well, and played the heck out of them. (Thousands of hours...)
[EDIT - 5/17/2017 - Since I posted this initial review, certain things have changed, so what you read here may or may not still be accurate. Post questions below!]
_____________________________
1. The game was marketed as having 'over 80 weapons and utilities,' yet 2/3 of those items are currently locked down by a crafting system, and due to a current lack of customization options, we cannot even create custom schemes with those items included by default - they MUST be crated. (The best ninja rope is one of those items that has to be crafted, which makes most rope-based schemes a joke currently.)
2. Crafting sucks. We can craft during EVERY SINGLE TURN, not just once per 'round.' Depending on game settings, crafting materials can be very common, which means that people craft the same OP items over and over again. Since this game launched I have seen more donkeys used in matches than I have in months, possibly years of playing other Worms games. SERIOUSLY. Even in schemes in which crafting materials are a little harder to come by, it's totally possible for your opponent to be able to craft the perfect weapon to win the game, even if you have the HP / position advantage.
3. Vehicles are cheesy and OP. They provide 'free mobility,' meaning that you can use them to get to places that you would normally have to use teleports, ninja ropes and parachute to get to. They also deal some pretty good damage and can 1-hit-KO Worms in the right spots. Whenever vehicles are enabled in a scheme, it no longer feels like Worms.
4. Of the total weapons in the game, many of them are redundant. We have three baseball bats, three versions of the prod (for god's sake), a FLAMING DONKEY... need I go on? There's MANY classic weapons and utilities missing from the game that should be included in a future update, because the balance of the game now is completely off. WMD is all about big explosions, big damage, and cheap, cheesy gameplay. If you just want casual fun with friends, you might like it, but if you are a Worms veteran, you'll find it extremely disappointing.
5. The ranked system in place right now only covers 1 ranked scheme. The scheme itself is poorly designed, and the ranking system is not Elo-based, like any competitive, ranked game should be. For now, the ranking system rewards people who 'grind' ranked games over and over and over for points. Ranked stats are not an indicator of actual player skill in this current state.
6. Explosions have a larger area of effect than before. What I mean is that it is harder than ever to judge whether or not you will take damage or get pushed from an explosion going off near your worm. Distances that were safe in the past are no longer safe.
7. Worms can fall from much higher heights than before and not take any damage, and when a worm does take fall damage, it's very little.
8. Many weapons need nerfed / balanced, such as the firepunch, which sends enemies flying much further than before. It's deadly now.
9. There is no global chat lobby. There is in-host text chat, but you have to click on a phone icon in the corner of the screen to access it, and many people don't even know that. Many people don't even know how to voice chat. The chat needs to be visible and persistent in hosted lobbies, not something you open or close with a button. This is PC, not console. We really need a global chat lobby so players can talk, get to know each other, share tactics, rules, schemes, ideas... etc.
10. The game community is horribly divided. We have people playing on PS4, XB1, Steam, Mac, Linux, and GOG. I know that cross-play is supposedly going to be implemented for Steam/Mac/Linux, but no word on GOG cross play, which is a true shame. Odds are we will never have cross play with console-based players either, which sucks because many people I know ONLY own it on console, and they're good players.
11. The unlockables from playing through the single-player content are nothing special. They should be more interesting / desirable. The same applies for ranked play. Weapon skins are an okay touch, but can we not bring back something truly awesome, like flaming power bars?
12. The price. While I know that I will get $30 worth of enjoyment out of this game, eventually, I think that the price tag is too steep for people in many countries. I feel that the game should be discounted by at least $5 USD. Most people want it reduced by $10.
13. The pre-order content fiasco. Team17 included an "All-Stars pack" for pre-order purchases. This pack contains vanity items, as well as some exclusive weapons that you can use in-game. If the person hosting a game owns the All-Stars DLC, everyone has access to these (craftable) weapons. Well, there's a couple of problems: First of all, putting any weapons behind a paywall is deplorable. Secondly, basic staples of Worms such as the kamikaze and sheep launcher are a part of this pre-order bonus. So what this means is that not only do you not get to use kamikaze in matches if you don't have access to the DLC, even if you do have access to it, you have to CRAFT a kamikaze just to use it. Isn't that delightfully absurd?
14. The gameplay simply isn't very fun. At the moment we do not have nearly enough customization / scheme options, and as stated before, many of the weapons that are in the game are locked down by the crafting system. Vehicles have far too much importance, we lack defensive / darksider capabilities in the form of utilities, etc. The game feels really boring to play due to lack of content.
15. We are missing numerous awesome features from past Worms titles. No WormNET, no 'hostingbuddy,' no Wormpot, a landscape generator that leaves much to be desired (although I must say the procedurally generated landscapes look amazing!) in terms of variety of landscapes, as well as an editor for drawing on the map, allowing girders to be placed on the map, etc. There's no worm classes, dynamic water, or physics objects from Revolution / Clan Wars, which were all positive additions to the series because they made the gameplay deeper and more strategic. There's no built-in clan system like in Clan Wars.
16. The way the fkeys are mapped to weapons makes no sense to me as a W:A veteran. F7 now has the ninja rope, and I think parachute is somewhere under F2. Of course we cannot customize any of this in any way.
17. The overall balance of the game caters to casuals / noobs. Vehicles, crafting, lots of high-powered weapons, lack of defensive utilities, weird hitboxes, explosions that can damage you even though you LOOK to be safely far away, and so on and so forth... these all come together to present a game that feels very luck-based and chaotic, rather than having that solid, strategic feel that was present in the previous titles, especially W:A and Clan Wars.
18. There's an overall lack of content. We currently only have 6 terrain themes. We don't have nearly enough personalization items, like hats, voice banks, victory fanfare, etc. There's dozens of weapons missing that should be in the game. It feels very empty.
WMD has potential to be an awesome Worms game if Team17 would listen to the suggestions in the forum and implement them. It's not a bad game per se, it just needs more work.
TL;DR - if you are a newcomer to Worms, or have a little experience but you're just a casual "for fun" player, you will likely enjoy WMD. If you are a hardcore, competitive Worms player (especially a veteran W:A player), WMD will likely disappoint you.
